questions.follow_up_answer: AC 61-27 (Instrument Flying Handbook guidance) or more practically, AC 90-105 which addresses approval guidance for RNP operations including RNAV (GPS) approaches — directly applicable to flying GPS approaches in a helicopter under IFR. It covers equipment requirements, crew training, and operational considerations for RNAV procedures, which are the most common approach type available at smaller airports where helicopter IFR operations frequently terminate. Understanding this AC helps a pilot ensure their aircraft is properly equipped and that they meet the training and currency requirements before flying RNAV approaches in IMC.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA AC Numbering System; AC 90-105; AC 90-87; AC 61-series; FAA-H-8083-15B

questions.question: What is the Airman Certification Standards document, and how does it differ from the older Practical Test Standards?
questions.answer: The Airman Certification Standards (ACS) is the FAA's current standard for airman certification testing that replaced the Practical Test Standards (PTS) for most certificates and ratings. The ACS expands on the PTS by integrating aeronautical knowledge, risk management, and flight proficiency elements into a single, unified document. While the PTS primarily described skills tasks, the ACS adds explicit knowledge and risk management standards that must be met during both the knowledge test and the practical test. The ACS is considered the definitive guide for both applicants and examiners.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA Instrument Rating ACS (FAA-S-ACS-8); FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 5

questions.question: For a helicopter instrument rating checkride, which publication does the examiner use to determine the tasks you must demonstrate, and where can you obtain a current copy?
questions.answer: The examiner uses the Instrument Rating – Helicopter Airman Certification Standards (ACS) to determine which tasks must be demonstrated. A current, official copy is available free of charge from the FAA's website (faa.gov) under the 'Airman Testing' section. Applicants are expected to be familiar with the applicable ACS before their checkride because the examiner is required to conduct the test in accordance with that document.

questions.question: The ACS organizes each task into three columns or elements. What are those three elements, and what does each one require of you as an applicant?
questions.answer: Each ACS task is organized into three elements: (1) Knowledge — the applicant must demonstrate understanding of specific facts, concepts, and principles related to the task during the oral portion of the exam; (2) Risk Management — the applicant must demonstrate the ability to identify, assess, and mitigate risks associated with the task; and (3) Skills — the applicant must physically demonstrate the task to the tolerances and standards specified. An applicant must meet all three elements for each task to receive a satisfactory grade.

questions.question: During your oral exam I ask you about a task that is listed in the ACS but the specific helicopter you're flying doesn't have the equipment required for that task — for example, it lacks an autopilot. How does the ACS address equipment-dependent tasks, and what is the examiner's responsibility?
questions.answer: The ACS acknowledges that not all aircraft are equipped to demonstrate every task. If the aircraft used for the practical test is not equipped to perform a specific task, the examiner must note the limitation on the applicant's temporary airman certificate and on the 8710 application. The certificate will be issued with a limitation reflecting the missing task. The applicant is not failed for the inability to demonstrate a task solely due to equipment limitations, but the examiner must document the deficiency. The applicant may later return to demonstrate the task in appropriately equipped aircraft to remove the limitation.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA Instrument Rating ACS (FAA-S-ACS-8) Introduction; 14 CFR 61.43(f)

questions.question: You are preparing for your instrument helicopter checkride and you notice that the ACS lists specific acceptable altitude and heading tolerances for tasks like holding and approaches. Explain why understanding those tolerances before the checkride matters, and give an example of a consequence of consistently exceeding the tolerance during a task.
questions.answer: The ACS tolerances define the minimum acceptable standard of performance — they are not targets but outer limits. Understanding them before the checkride allows the applicant to practice to a higher standard and recognize when they are approaching an unsatisfactory performance boundary in real time. For example, during an ILS approach the ACS typically requires the applicant to maintain localizer and glideslope within ±¾ scale deflection during the final approach segment. If the applicant consistently exceeds this tolerance — such as flying a full-scale deflection below the glideslope — the examiner must evaluate that as an unsatisfactory performance for that task, potentially resulting in a disapproval for that area of operation. Knowing the tolerances helps a pilot self-monitor and make corrections before the examiner is required to take action.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA Instrument Rating ACS (FAA-S-ACS-8); FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 5

questions.question: As a helicopter instrument candidate, you study the fixed-wing Instrument Rating ACS because it's more widely available online. Should you be relying on that document for your helicopter checkride preparation? Explain why or why not.
questions.answer: No. You should use the helicopter-specific Instrument Rating ACS. The FAA publishes separate ACS documents for different aircraft categories. The helicopter instrument ACS contains tasks, standards, and tolerances that are specific to rotorcraft operations — such as hovering tasks, autorotation considerations, and helicopter-specific approach tolerances — that differ from fixed-wing standards. Using the wrong ACS could leave you unprepared for helicopter-specific tasks the examiner is required to test, and could cause you to prepare for tasks that are irrelevant to the helicopter checkride. Always verify that the ACS you are studying matches both the certificate/rating you are seeking and the aircraft category.

questions.question: During a checkride debrief I tell an applicant they received an unsatisfactory on a specific task but I don't specify which ACS knowledge, risk management, or skill element was unsatisfactory. As an applicant, why does knowing the ACS structure matter in this situation, and what recourse do you have?
questions.answer: Knowing the ACS structure matters because the examiner is required to conduct the test in accordance with the ACS and must identify which element — knowledge, risk management, or skill — was not met when issuing a Notice of Disapproval (Form 8710-2). If the examiner cannot or will not specify the failing element, the applicant can reference the ACS to understand what was tested and whether the disapproval was issued correctly. The applicant's recourse includes: (1) asking the examiner to clarify which element was unsatisfactory and which task area; (2) reviewing the Notice of Disapproval for accuracy, as it must correctly reflect the failed areas; and (3) if the applicant believes the test was not conducted in accordance with the ACS, they may file a complaint with the local FSDO. On retest, only the unsatisfactory task areas need to be repeated, not the entire practical test.
questions.follow_up: If you receive a disapproval on the knowledge element of a task but demonstrated the skill perfectly, do you have to re-fly that maneuver on your retest?
questions.follow_up_answer: Not necessarily. On a retest, only the tasks for which a Notice of Disapproval was issued must be repeated. However, the examiner conducting the retest has discretion to evaluate any task to ensure overall competency, per the ACS guidance. If the disapproval was issued only for the knowledge element of a task, the examiner may focus the retest on oral questioning for that knowledge element rather than requiring a re-flight of the maneuver — but the retest examiner retains the authority to test any task they deem necessary to ensure the applicant meets the full ACS standard.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA Instrument Rating ACS (FAA-S-ACS-8) Introduction; 14 CFR 61.43(f); FAA Order 8900.2

questions.question: The FAA periodically revises the ACS. As an instrument helicopter pilot, what is your responsibility regarding ACS revisions, and how would an outdated ACS study guide affect your checkride if the standards changed between your study period and your test date?
questions.answer: It is the applicant's responsibility to ensure they are using the most current version of the applicable ACS when preparing for a checkride. The FAA publishes the effective date on the cover of each ACS, and current versions are always available on faa.gov. If the ACS was revised between your study period and your checkride date, the examiner is required to test you to the current, revised standards — not the version you studied. This could mean new tasks were added, tolerances were tightened, or risk management elements were updated. Presenting an older version of the ACS to an examiner does not excuse an applicant from meeting the current standard. CFIs and applicants should subscribe to FAA updates or check the FAA website periodically to ensure currency of their study materials.
questions.follow_up: If you arrive for a checkride and discover the ACS was revised two weeks ago adding a task you have not prepared for, can you legally postpone the checkride, and who bears the cost?
questions.follow_up_answer: Yes, you can request to postpone. You are not required to attempt a checkride if you believe you are not prepared for the current standard, and proceeding when you know you are unprepared for a required task would likely result in a disapproval. There is no FAA regulation that forces you to continue with a scheduled checkride. However, the practical matter of cost — examiner fees, aircraft rental, rescheduling — is a contractual matter between the applicant and the examiner/school, not governed by the FARs. The FAA does not reimburse or regulate those costs. The responsibility for knowing the current ACS rests with the applicant, so the preventive measure is to verify the ACS version close to your checkride date, not to rely on postponement as a safety net.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA Instrument Rating ACS (FAA-S-ACS-8); 14 CFR 61.43; faa.gov Airman Testing page

questions.question: What is the official name for the FAA-approved flight manual specific to rotorcraft, and what two pieces of identifying information must appear on its title page?
questions.answer: The official name is the Rotorcraft Flight Manual (RFM). The title page must display the specific helicopter's serial number and registration number (N-number). This ensures the manual is tied to that exact airframe, not just the aircraft model or type.

questions.question: Under 14 CFR Part 91, are you legally required to comply with the limitations in your helicopter's Rotorcraft Flight Manual? What section of the RFM contains those limitations?
questions.answer: Yes. 14 CFR 91.9 requires a pilot to comply with the operating limitations specified in the approved Rotorcraft Flight Manual. Those limitations are found in Section 1 (Limitations) of the RFM. This section is FAA-approved and carries the force of regulation — it is not advisory.

questions.question: Your helicopter's fuel quantity gauge reads one-quarter full. According to the RFM and federal regulation, how accurate is that reading required to be?
questions.answer: Fuel quantity gauges in helicopters certificated under 14 CFR Part 27 are only required to be accurate when reading empty. A quarter-tank reading carries no regulatory accuracy requirement. This means you must not rely solely on the fuel gauge — always cross-check with known fuel quantities, flight time, and a pre-flight fuel check to verify actual usable fuel onboard.

questions.question: You're planning a flight to a mountain destination at high density altitude. You notice a VNE placard in the cockpit showing a lower speed than what you saw in the RFM performance charts at sea level. Why might those values differ, and which one governs your flight today?
questions.answer: VNE (never exceed speed) varies with altitude and gross weight. At higher altitudes, the rotor blades operate at higher true airspeeds for a given indicated airspeed, and blade tip Mach effects become limiting factors at lower indicated airspeeds. The cockpit placard is specific to the current conditions and is the governing limitation — it reflects the adjusted VNE for your operating environment. You must comply with whichever value is more restrictive, and the placard is the real-time reference required to be in view during flight.

questions.question: During your preflight, you discover the RFM is missing from the cockpit. The owner says 'there's an identical one in the hangar from a sister ship — same model, same year.' Can you legally use that manual for this flight?
questions.answer: No. The RFM must be specific to the individual helicopter — it must bear that aircraft's serial number and registration on the title page. A manual from a sister ship, even an identical model and year, is not the approved flight manual for your aircraft. Operating without the proper RFM aboard is a violation of 14 CFR 91.9 and potentially 91.203, which requires the aircraft to have its airworthiness certificate and applicable operating limitations available in the aircraft during flight.

questions.question: An emergency develops suddenly in cruise flight. You reach for the RFM emergency procedures section. According to best practices outlined in the Helicopter Flying Handbook, what should you already know before you even open that section?
questions.answer: According to the FAA Helicopter Flying Handbook, at a minimum the pilot should have memorized the first steps — sometimes called 'immediate action items' — of each emergency checklist before flight. In a real emergency, there is often no time to look up and read Step 1. Pilots who have pre-memorized those initial actions can execute them immediately, then use the checklist to confirm subsequent steps. This is why the emergency procedures section should be studied and internalized, not just carried in the aircraft.

questions.question: A Supplemental Type Certificate (STC) has been installed on your helicopter — an upgraded avionics suite. The STC paperwork includes a new Rotorcraft Flight Manual Supplement (RFMS). What is the legal standing of that supplement relative to the original RFM, and where must it be kept?
questions.answer: An FAA-approved RFMS issued with an STC carries the same regulatory force as the original RFM for the systems and limitations it covers. It is an FAA-approved addition to the flight manual and is required to be kept with the aircraft. In most cases the RFMS must be inserted into or stored with the original RFM so it is available during flight. Limitations in the RFMS — such as operational restrictions on the new avionics — are legally binding on the pilot under 14 CFR 91.9. If the RFMS restricts or amends a limitation in the base RFM, the RFMS takes precedence for the affected system.
questions.follow_up: What happens if the RFMS for the STC is lost or unavailable — can you still legally fly the aircraft with that STC equipment installed?
questions.follow_up_answer: No. If the RFMS is required by the STC and is unavailable, the aircraft is not in an airworthy condition for operation with that installed equipment. You would need to either retrieve the RFMS, ground the aircraft, or — if possible under the STC terms — deactivate the affected system and operate under the base RFM. Flying without required approved documentation violates 14 CFR 91.9 and 91.203.

questions.question: Your RFM performance charts show a hover ceiling of 9,500 feet density altitude in ground effect at maximum gross weight. Your actual conditions today put you at exactly that density altitude and gross weight. An experienced pilot on the ramp tells you 'those charts are conservative — manufacturers pad the numbers, you'll be fine.' How do you evaluate that advice, and what does the RFM's legal status mean for your decision?
questions.answer: The RFM performance charts are based on a standardized test aircraft in new condition, flown by a test pilot under controlled conditions. They represent a baseline, not a guarantee — real-world performance can be worse due to engine wear, blade erosion, humidity effects not fully captured in density altitude calculations, and technique. Operating at the charted limit means you have zero margin. The legal status of the RFM is clear: the limitations section is FAA-approved and compliance is required under 14 CFR 91.9. The performance section, while not a hard regulatory limit in the same way, defines the envelope the manufacturer certifies the aircraft to operate within. Accepting that advice and operating at the limit with no margin represents poor risk management — the Helicopter Flying Handbook explicitly cautions against the word 'probably' and advises choosing options known to work rather than those that will 'probably' work out.
questions.follow_up: If you're 200 pounds under max gross weight but your density altitude is still 9,500 feet, how does that change your analysis, and what specific RFM section would you use to determine your actual hover ceiling?
questions.follow_up_answer: Being under max gross weight meaningfully improves your hover ceiling. You would use the hover in ground effect (HIGE) or hover out of ground effect (HOGE) performance charts in the RFM Performance section, entering with your actual gross weight and current density altitude to determine your actual ceiling. A 200-pound reduction could add several hundred to over a thousand feet of margin depending on the aircraft. You'd also confirm conditions like rotor RPM, engine bleed air usage, and any applicable chart notes — then apply a personal operational margin of at least 10–15% to account for real-world variables not captured in standardized test conditions.

questions.question: What is the Aeronautical Information Manual (AIM), and who publishes it?
questions.answer: The AIM is the FAA's official guide to the U.S. National Airspace System. It is published by the FAA and provides pilots with basic flight information, ATC procedures, aviation safety information, and guidance on how to operate in the NAS. It is not regulatory, but it reflects current FAA policy and best practices. The AIM is updated periodically through change notices.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA Aeronautical Information Manual (AIM), General Information

questions.question: The AIM is not a regulatory document — so why must a helicopter pilot be familiar with it?
questions.answer: Although the AIM does not carry the force of law, it reflects official FAA policy, standard operating procedures, and ATC expectations. Deviating from AIM guidance can lead to miscommunications with ATC, increased risk of incidents, and potential enforcement action if the deviation also involves a regulatory violation. Many FARs direct pilots to follow AIM procedures (e.g., radio communication procedures, lost communication procedures), making AIM knowledge operationally essential for safe IFR and VFR operations.
questions.regulatory_ref: AIM Preface; 14 CFR 91.123 (ATC instructions); FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13

questions.question: Name at least four major subject areas covered in the AIM that are directly applicable to helicopter IFR operations.
questions.answer: The AIM covers: (1) Navigation aids (VOR, NDB, GPS, ILS, etc.) and their operational characteristics; (2) Airspace classifications, dimensions, and operating requirements; (3) ATC procedures including clearances, communications, and lost comms procedures; (4) IFR flight procedures including departure, en route, and approach procedures; (5) Meteorology and weather services available to pilots; (6) Emergency procedures and distress/urgency communications; (7) Safety of flight topics including wake turbulence, TCAS/ACAS, and LAHSO; (8) Aeronautical charts and related publications. All of these directly apply to helicopter IFR operations.

questions.question: You are planning an IFR helicopter flight and want to verify whether RNAV (GPS) approaches at your destination require GPS equipment to be certified under TSO-C129 or TSO-C145/146. Where in the AIM would you find this information, and what does it say?
questions.answer: AIM Chapter 1, Section 1-1-18 covers GPS/GNSS and RNAV equipment requirements. For RNAV (GPS) approaches, the AIM specifies that IFR-approved GPS equipment must meet TSO-C129a (standalone GPS) or TSO-C145/C146 (WAAS GPS) standards and must be installed per an approved STC or aircraft certification. WAAS equipment (TSO-C145/C146) is required for LPV and LNAV/VNAV approach minimums; TSO-C129a suffices for LNAV-only minimums. The avionics must also have a current database and the approach must be retrievable from that database.

questions.question: Your helicopter loses two-way radio communication while operating IFR in VMC. According to the AIM and applicable FARs, what actions should you take?
questions.answer: Per 14 CFR 91.185 and expanded in AIM Chapter 6, Section 6-4-1: In VMC, you should continue in VMC, land as soon as practicable, and notify ATC by the most practical means. You must squawk 7600 on the transponder. If IMC is encountered or VMC cannot be maintained, follow the lost comms IFR procedures: fly the route assigned, then expected, then filed; maintain the highest of the MEA, assigned altitude, or expected altitude; and begin descent for approach at the EFC time or ETA, whichever is earlier. After landing, notify ATC immediately.

questions.question: The AIM dedicates a section to helicopter-specific IFR procedures, including special approach considerations. What does the AIM say about flying helicopter point-in-space (PinS) approaches, and when would you use one?
questions.answer: AIM Chapter 5, Section 5-4-18 covers helicopter instrument approaches including PinS approaches. A PinS approach is designed for helicopters and terminates at a point in space (waypoint), not directly over an airport or helipad. The missed approach point is a point in space, after which the pilot proceeds visually to the landing area using 'proceed visually' or 'proceed VFR' instructions printed on the approach plate. 'Proceed visually' requires the pilot to maintain visual contact with the landing area throughout the visual segment and does not allow cloud clearance descent below MDA. 'Proceed VFR' allows the pilot to continue under VFR rules after the MDA is reached. PinS approaches are used when a helipad or hospital rooftop cannot be served by a traditional instrument approach due to terrain, obstructions, or layout.

questions.question: The AIM is updated periodically through change notices, but the underlying FARs governing IFR flight may not change at the same time. If you find a conflict between what the AIM recommends and what a specific FAR requires, which takes precedence and how should you handle the discrepancy?
questions.answer: The FAR always takes precedence because it is regulatory and has the force of law, while the AIM is advisory and informational. When a conflict exists, the pilot must comply with the regulation. However, apparent conflicts often arise from the AIM providing more detailed operational guidance on how to comply with a broadly written FAR, rather than a true contradiction. If a genuine conflict is identified, the pilot should note the specific regulatory citation, operate in compliance with the FAR, and consider filing a report with the FAA (ASRS or directly) to flag the discrepancy. Examiners expect pilots to understand the regulatory hierarchy: Constitution > Statutes (49 U.S.C.) > CFR (FARs) > AIM/ACs (advisory).
questions.follow_up: Give me a specific example where following AIM guidance alone — without reading the underlying FAR — could lead a helicopter IFR pilot into a regulatory violation.
questions.follow_up_answer: One example is VOR currency for IFR flight. The AIM discusses VOR operational checks and general navigation concepts, but 14 CFR 91.171 specifically requires a VOR operational check within the preceding 30 days for IFR flight using VOR navigation. A pilot who relies solely on the AIM's general navigation guidance without reading 91.171 might not realize the specific 30-day currency requirement and fly IFR with an out-of-currency VOR, constituting a regulatory violation. Another example involves alternate airport weather minimums — AIM Chapter 5 explains the concept, but the specific 1-2-3 rule and exceptions (including the helicopter alternate minimums on approach charts) are governed by 14 CFR 91.169, and the chart-specific alternate minimums can be more restrictive than what the pilot infers from the AIM.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.171; 14 CFR 91.169; AIM Preface (advisory nature); 49 U.S.C. regulatory hierarchy

questions.question: Where in the Rotorcraft Flight Manual (RFM) can you confirm that the manual you are holding applies to the specific helicopter you intend to fly?
questions.answer: The title page of the RFM must contain the helicopter's specific serial number and registration number. If those do not match the aircraft you are about to fly, that manual does not apply to your aircraft. Per 14 CFR Part 91, pilots must comply with operating limitations in the approved RFM for that specific aircraft.

questions.question: Fuel quantity gauges in a helicopter are only required by regulation to be accurate at one specific indication. What is it, and why does this matter when using an outdated or unapproved flight manual?
questions.answer: Fuel quantity gauges are only required to be accurate when reading empty, per 14 CFR 27.1337(b)(1). This matters because performance charts and fuel planning data in an outdated RFM may have been revised due to STC changes, updated power settings, or corrected range figures. Flying with stale performance data combined with an unreliable fuel gauge compounds the risk of fuel exhaustion.

questions.question: What is the regulatory requirement that makes it mandatory for a pilot to use current, approved operating limitations rather than a convenient but outdated copy of an RFM?
questions.answer: 14 CFR 91.9(b) requires the pilot in command to operate the aircraft within the operating limitations contained in the approved Rotorcraft Flight Manual, markings, and placards. The approved RFM is specific to each aircraft and must reflect current revisions. Using an outdated version that does not incorporate current revisions or Airworthiness Directives could result in operating outside approved limits without the pilot's knowledge.

questions.question: You are preparing for an IFR flight in a turbine helicopter and pull out a Jeppesen approach plate that is three cycles old. The procedure appears identical to what you remember. What specific risks does flying that approach with an expired chart introduce, and how could it affect your flight?
questions.answer: An expired approach chart may not reflect changes such as revised minimums, new obstacles requiring higher MDA/DA, frequency changes, updated missed approach procedures, NAVAID decommissioning, or temporary flight restrictions that have become permanent. In a turbine helicopter capable of high-altitude IFR flight, encountering a revised obstacle clearance requirement mid-approach with outdated minimums could result in CFIT. Even if the plate looks the same, you cannot assume it is identical — the FAA or Jeppesen may have issued a revision with no visible change to the main diagram but an updated NOTAM-driven note. Always use charts current for the date of flight.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.167; FAA-H-8083-15B IFR Flight Planning; AIM 5-4-5

questions.question: A student hands you their copy of the Helicopter Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-21) — not the 'B' revision — for ground instruction. They say 'it's basically the same thing.' As the instructor, what specific risk does this introduce, and how do you address it?
questions.answer: Using a superseded edition of a handbook introduces the risk that the student is learning from procedures, diagrams, or aerodynamic explanations that have since been corrected or updated by the FAA. For example, the 'B' revision of the Helicopter Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-21B) contains updated content on autorotation, emergency procedures concepts, and SRM. Accepting 'basically the same' is the kind of normalizing language that contributes to error chains — the FAA notes that approximately 80% of accidents involve human factors, and complacency about currency of training materials is a human factors risk. Direct the student to download the current revision free from FAA.gov before continuing ground instruction.

questions.question: You are planning a night IFR cross-country in a helicopter using a VNE placard as your primary reference for never-exceed speed. The RFM you have onboard has not been updated to incorporate a recent manufacturer revision that lowered the VNE at certain altitude/gross weight combinations. Walk me through the risk chain that could develop from this single oversight.
questions.answer: The risk chain begins with a documentation gap — the RFM does not reflect the current manufacturer-approved VNE. At altitude and high gross weight, the pilot references the outdated placard or RFM chart, which shows a higher VNE than is actually approved. The pilot accelerates to that speed, unknowingly entering an over-speed condition that exceeds structural or rotor system limits. At night in IMC, the pilot may not observe or feel early indicators of rotor system distress. The outcome risk is structural failure, loss of tail rotor effectiveness, or rotor system overspeed — all potentially catastrophic. This is a textbook error chain: each link (outdated RFM, no revision check, night IMC, high gross weight) alone might be survivable, but combined they are not. Breaking any single link — verifying the RFM is current before flight — prevents the entire chain.

questions.question: An operator running a small Part 91 flight department tells you they save costs by not subscribing to a chart update service — instead, they check NOTAMs before every flight to catch any changes. Is this an acceptable substitute for current charts, and what are the limitations of that strategy specifically for helicopter IFR operations?
questions.answer: NOTAMs are a required preflight action under 14 CFR 91.103, but they are not a complete substitute for current charts. NOTAMs capture temporary changes, but permanent charting updates — such as revised obstacle data, new procedures, changed frequencies, or updated minimums resulting from a construction survey — appear on updated charts, not necessarily in NOTAM format. Additionally, NOTAMs have an expiration date and are not guaranteed to capture every interim charting change. For helicopter IFR operations, where crews may conduct steep approaches, offshore operations, or use helicopter-specific procedures (e.g., Copter ILS, Point-in-Space approaches), the risk of missing a chart revision is amplified because helicopter approach categories and minima differ from fixed-wing. Relying solely on NOTAMs introduces the complacency risk that the FAA associates with human factors accidents. Current, subscription-based chart services are the operationally accepted standard.
questions.follow_up: What is the specific regulatory citation that defines the pilot's preflight obligation regarding current aeronautical charts, and does it mandate a specific chart currency standard?
questions.follow_up_answer: 14 CFR 91.103 requires the PIC to become familiar with all available information concerning the flight, which includes current aeronautical charts. However, 91.103 does not specify a chart cycle currency requirement by name — it uses the word 'available.' The practical standard applied by the FAA is that charts must be current for the date of flight. For IFR operations, 14 CFR 91.167 and the instrument currency rules in 61.57 reinforce that procedures and airspace data must reflect current conditions. An examiner or investigator would use 91.103's 'all available information' standard to hold a pilot accountable for not using a current chart that was available to them.

questions.question: During a checkride debrief, a candidate argues that because the helicopter's emergency procedures section of the RFM hasn't changed in 10 years, there's no real risk to memorizing those procedures from an old copy rather than the current approved document. How do you, as the examiner, evaluate and respond to that argument?
questions.answer: The argument reflects a normalization of deviation — a known human factors risk factor. The candidate is assuming stability in the document rather than verifying it. The risk is that Airworthiness Directives (ADs), manufacturer service bulletins incorporated into the RFM, or FAA-approved RFM revisions may have altered emergency procedure steps, changed power settings during emergency operations, or modified the sequence of actions for engine failures or tail rotor malfunctions. The FAA's own guidance in the Helicopter Flying Handbook (Chapter 5) states that emergency procedures should be learned, at minimum in their first steps, before flight — using the approved, current document. Because the emergency procedures section is among the most safety-critical portions of the RFM, the consequences of a single outdated step during an actual emergency are potentially fatal. The argument also demonstrates a broader ADM deficiency: dismissing risk because of absence of known harm is not the same as the absence of risk.
questions.follow_up: If an AD mandates a change to an emergency procedure in the RFM, and the operator has not yet incorporated that AD revision into the physical RFM onboard the aircraft, what are the airworthiness and legal implications for the PIC who flies that aircraft?
questions.follow_up_answer: An Airworthiness Directive issued under 14 CFR Part 39 is legally mandatory for the registered owner/operator and must be complied with by the compliance date specified. If the AD requires an RFM revision (an operational limitation change), the aircraft is not airworthy until that revision is incorporated, per 14 CFR 39.7. A PIC who operates the aircraft in that condition is operating an unairworthy aircraft in violation of 14 CFR 91.7(a), which prohibits PIC operation of a civil aircraft that is not in airworthy condition. If the AD also changes an emergency procedure the PIC is using from memory based on an old copy, they are simultaneously operating contrary to approved operating limitations under 91.9(b). This is a compound violation with potential certificate action and — if an accident results — significant legal exposure.

questions.question: I'd like you to teach me why a helicopter pilot is required to comply with the Rotorcraft Flight Manual. Walk me through the regulatory basis for that requirement.
questions.answer: The instructor should explain that 14 CFR 91.9 requires the pilot-in-command to comply with the operating limitations specified in the approved Rotorcraft Flight Manual (RFM), markings, and placards. The RFM is an FAA-approved document specific to each individual helicopter — it is tied to a specific serial number and registration. Because it is FAA-approved, deviating from its limitations without authorization is a regulatory violation, not just a procedural one. A good teaching point is the difference between the required sections (Limitations, Emergency Procedures, Normal Procedures, Performance) versus optional sections that manufacturers may include.

questions.question: Teach me the significance of the fuel quantity gauge accuracy requirement in the helicopter RFM. What does the regulation actually require, and why does that matter to a student pilot?
questions.answer: The instructor should explain that per 14 CFR 27.1337(b)(1), fuel quantity gauges are only required to be accurate when they read empty — not at any other quantity. This is a critical teaching point because students often trust fuel gauges the way they trust a car's gas gauge. The practical lesson is: always verify fuel quantity by visual inspection before flight, not by relying solely on cockpit gauges. The instructor should connect this regulation to preflight habits and risk management — an inaccurate gauge reading half-full could mean any quantity above zero. This is a direct safety implication of understanding the applicable regulation.

questions.question: Teach me what VNE is, where to find it in the helicopter, and how it differs from a fixed-wing aircraft's VNE in terms of how the value is determined.
questions.answer: The instructor should explain that VNE (never-exceed speed) is the maximum airspeed the aircraft is certificated to fly — exceeding it risks structural damage or loss of control. In a helicopter, VNE is found both in the RFM limitations section and on a placard in the cockpit. A key helicopter-specific teaching point is that VNE is not a fixed number — it varies with altitude and gross weight. As altitude increases, the air is thinner and rotor blade tips approach transonic speeds at lower airspeeds, so VNE decreases with altitude. The cockpit placard or RFM chart provides the current applicable VNE for the aircraft's conditions. This contrasts with many fixed-wing aircraft where VNE is a single posted airspeed.

questions.question: You're teaching a student who just received an IFR clearance with a departure procedure they've never flown. They ask you, 'Do I have to fly this DP?' Teach them how to answer that question and what the regulations say.
questions.answer: The instructor should teach the student that a DP is not automatically mandatory — but once you accept it in a clearance, you are required to comply with it. Before departure, a pilot may decline a DP by including 'NO DP' in the remarks section of the flight plan or by verbally advising ATC prior to receiving the clearance. However, if the clearance is read back and accepted without objection, the pilot is legally bound to comply with the procedure. The instructor should also explain the distinction between obstacle departure procedures (ODPs) and standard instrument departures (SIDs), noting that ODPs with '(OBSTACLE)' in the title are designed for terrain/obstacle clearance and may be especially important in mountainous helicopter operating areas.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.123; FAA-H-8083-15B IFR Flight Planning and Clearances chapter; AIM 5-2-8

questions.question: A student asks you to teach them about BasicMed — specifically whether they can use BasicMed to fly a turbine helicopter on a cross-country tour. Walk them through the key regulatory requirements and limitations.
questions.answer: The instructor should teach that BasicMed is governed by 14 CFR Part 68 and 14 CFR 61.113(i). Key points to cover: (1) The aircraft may be up to 12,500 lbs maximum certificated takeoff weight — turbine helicopters are not excluded; (2) No more than 6 total occupants (pilot plus 5 passengers); (3) Maximum altitude of 18,000 ft MSL; (4) Maximum airspeed of 250 KIAS; (5) Operations must remain within the United States; (6) No compensation or hire operations; (7) The pilot must have held a valid medical at some point after July 14, 2006; (8) A medical education course is required every 24 months and a physical exam by a state-licensed physician every 48 months. For the cross-country tour in a turbine helicopter, BasicMed is permissible as long as all conditions are met — there is no prohibition on turbine aircraft under current rules.

questions.question: You are teaching a student the relationship between human factors and aviation accidents. Using FAA source material, teach them why understanding this relationship should change how they make decisions in the cockpit.
questions.answer: The instructor should teach that approximately 80% of aviation accidents are attributable to pilot error and human factors — this statistic comes directly from FAA-H-8083-21B. The key teaching points are: (1) Most accidents are not caused by a single catastrophic mistake but by an 'error chain' — a series of smaller poor decisions that compound; (2) Breaking even one link in that chain can change the outcome, so pilots must stay alert to accumulating problems; (3) Experience in a specific aircraft type matters more than total flight hours — accident rates decrease significantly after 100 hours in type; (4) Single-Pilot Resource Management (SRM) is the framework for managing these risks, integrating situational awareness, workload management, and risk assessment. The instructor should connect this to the practical discipline of avoiding 'probably' thinking — if a course of action will only probably work out, choose the option known to work.

questions.question: While teaching a student about the RFM, they ask a great question: 'If the RFM is specific to each serial number, what happens to the legal standing of that manual if the helicopter undergoes a major modification — say, an STC installation?' Teach through that question and demonstrate how you would help a student find the answer.
questions.answer: The instructor should teach that when an STC (Supplemental Type Certificate) is incorporated, the aircraft's approved data is amended. The STC holder's approval documentation — which becomes part of the aircraft records — may include a Flight Manual Supplement (FMS) or revised limitations that must be carried in the aircraft and treated with the same authority as the base RFM. Under 14 CFR 21.50, the STC holder must provide instructions for continued airworthiness. If the STC changes operating limitations (e.g., a new engine, new avionics affecting VNE), those new limitations are legally binding under 14 CFR 91.9. The instructor should teach students to always verify whether an STC is installed and whether a corresponding Flight Manual Supplement is present and current — it is part of the required airworthiness documentation. The teaching method modeled here is Socratic: guide the student to the right regulation rather than just providing the answer.
questions.follow_up: If a student found that an STC Flight Manual Supplement was missing from the aircraft but the STC modification was physically installed, could they legally fly the aircraft? What regulation applies?
questions.follow_up_answer: No — the aircraft would not be in an airworthy condition. Under 14 CFR 91.7, the PIC is responsible for ensuring the aircraft is in airworthy condition before flight. An installed STC without its required documentation (including the FMS) means the aircraft does not conform to its type design with all required approved data, rendering it unairworthy. The pilot should ground the aircraft and work with maintenance to obtain the correct documentation before flight.

questions.question: You are demonstrating how to teach the concept of the region of reversed command to an instrument helicopter student. I am going to evaluate your teaching technique. Teach me this concept and explain why it is uniquely critical in IMC helicopter operations.
questions.answer: The instructor should teach that the region of reversed command — also called the 'back side of the power curve' — exists at airspeeds below L/DMAX (the speed of minimum drag). In this region, slowing down requires MORE power to maintain altitude, not less; if power is not added, the aircraft will continue to decelerate and descend in a compounding spiral. In IMC, this is acutely dangerous for helicopters for two reasons: (1) Helicopters routinely operate at low airspeeds during approaches and transitions where they are already in or near this region; (2) Without visual references in IMC, a pilot may not recognize the deceleration until it has progressed significantly. The instructor should tie this to proper instrument scan discipline — monitoring airspeed, vertical speed, and power simultaneously — and to the importance of stabilized approaches at a published reference speed. A good teaching technique includes drawing the drag curve, identifying L/DMAX, and showing the student exactly where common helicopter approach speeds fall on that curve.
questions.follow_up: If your student is flying a stabilized ILS approach at the published approach speed and then slows below that speed in IMC — perhaps due to a gust — what is the immediate correct control response, and why is adding back-pressure on the cyclic the wrong instinct?
questions.follow_up_answer: The correct response is to simultaneously add power (collective) and stabilize or increase airspeed with cyclic forward input — not to pull back on the cyclic. Pulling back increases AOA and drag further, which on the back side of the power curve causes the aircraft to decelerate and sink more rapidly. Without additional power, the increased collective will also cause rotor RPM to decay. The pilot must resist the instinct to 'pull up' and instead fly the aircraft to a stable airspeed with coordinated power and cyclic inputs. In IMC this requires complete trust in the instruments and a disciplined, trained response — which is exactly why this concept must be thoroughly taught before a student ever flies an approach in IMC.

tasks.title: Task L. Endorsements and Logbook Entries

questions.question: When you give instrument flight instruction to a student, what specific entries are you required to make in that student's logbook?
questions.answer: Per 14 CFR 61.51(h), an authorized instructor must enter the following in the student's logbook for each lesson: (1) the date of the flight, (2) total flight time or ground training time, (3) location where the lesson took place (departure and arrival airports or training area), (4) type of instruction given, (5) the instructor's signature, and (6) the instructor's certificate number and certificate expiration date. For instrument instruction specifically, the logbook must also indicate whether the time was actual instrument, simulated instrument, or flight simulator/FTD time.

questions.question: What is the difference between how 'actual instrument' time and 'simulated instrument' time must be logged, and why does that distinction matter?
questions.answer: Actual instrument time is flight time during which the pilot operates the aircraft solely by reference to instruments because the weather conditions require it — meaning the pilot is in IMC. Simulated instrument time is flown in VMC conditions while wearing a view-limiting device such as a hood or foggles. Both types must be logged separately and identified as such per 14 CFR 61.51(g). The distinction matters because instrument currency requirements under 14 CFR 61.57(c) allow both types to count toward recent experience, and certain ratings or endorsements may require specific amounts of actual versus simulated time. Instructors must ensure their entries correctly reflect which type was flown.

questions.question: As a flight instructor, are you required to keep your own personal logbook record of instruction you have given? What must it contain?
questions.answer: Yes. Per 14 CFR 61.189(a), a flight instructor must maintain a record in their logbook, or a separate record, of each person they have provided flight training or ground training to. This record must include: (1) the name of each person trained, (2) the date of the training, (3) the type of training provided, and (4) a description of the endorsement given, if any, including the regulatory basis for the endorsement. This record must be retained for 3 years.

questions.question: You just completed a two-hour helicopter instrument training flight with a student. During the flight, the first 45 minutes were in actual IMC conditions and the remaining 75 minutes were under the hood in VMC. How should the logbook entries be structured to correctly reflect this flight?
questions.answer: The instructor must ensure the student's logbook entry reflects: (1) total flight time of 2.0 hours, (2) 0.75 hours of actual instrument time (the 45 minutes in IMC), (3) 1.25 hours of simulated instrument time (the 75 minutes under the hood in VMC), (4) the date, departure and arrival points, (5) the type of instruction given — in this case instrument flight instruction, (6) the instructor's signature, certificate number, and expiration date. The instructor should also make a corresponding entry in their own training records per 14 CFR 61.189(a), noting the student's name, date, and type of training provided. Mixing actual and simulated into a single 'instrument time' category without distinguishing them would be an inaccurate logbook entry.

questions.question: A helicopter student asks you to sign off their logbook for instrument approaches flown in a full-motion Level D simulator during your training session. What specific logbook entries must be made, and does this time count toward their instrument rating requirements?
questions.answer: When logging simulator time, the logbook entry must reflect: (1) the date, (2) the type of simulator or FTD used (including the make and model or the FAA approval level — e.g., Level D FFS), (3) the training location or operator, (4) the type of training conducted, (5) the instructor's signature, certificate number, and expiration date. Per 14 CFR 61.51(b)(1), simulator time is logged separately from actual flight time. For instrument rating purposes under 14 CFR 61.65, a student may use time in an approved FFS or FTD toward instrument experience requirements, with the amount creditable depending on the device level and rating type. Up to 20 hours of instrument time may be credited in an approved device when used with an authorized instructor. The instructor should also log the session in their own records per 14 CFR 61.189(a).

questions.question: You provide ground training to a student on instrument approach procedures — no flight is involved. Are you required to make a logbook entry for this, and if so, what must it include?
questions.answer: Yes. Per 14 CFR 61.51(h), an authorized instructor must make an entry in the student's logbook for ground training given, just as for flight training. The entry must include: (1) the date, (2) the amount of ground training time, (3) the topics covered, (4) the instructor's signature, certificate number, and expiration date. Additionally, the instructor must log this in their own records per 14 CFR 61.189(a), including the student's name, the date, and a description of the training provided. Ground training logged this way can support endorsements (such as an instrument knowledge test endorsement) and may count toward ground training hour requirements for an instrument rating.

questions.question: A student presents you with a logbook that has instrument flight time entries signed by a previous instructor, but those entries do not specify whether the time was actual or simulated instrument — it just says 'instrument time.' As the new instructor of record preparing this student for their instrument checkride, what is your responsibility regarding those entries, and what risk does this create?
questions.answer: Those entries are technically non-compliant with 14 CFR 61.51(g), which requires that instrument flight time be logged and identified specifically as either actual instrument or simulated instrument time. As the new instructor, you cannot retroactively correct another instructor's logbook entries — doing so could constitute falsification under 14 CFR 61.59. Your responsibility is to document this discrepancy and advise the student. For practical purposes, ambiguous entries may not be acceptable to an examiner or the FAA as proof of the required instrument experience under 14 CFR 61.65. The student should, if possible, contact the previous instructor to correct the entries in the student's own logbook with an addendum. Going forward, you must ensure all entries you make clearly distinguish actual from simulated time. The examiner may question the validity of those entries during the oral exam, and the student may need to re-accomplish some of that flight time with proper documentation.
questions.follow_up: If the student says the previous instructor is no longer reachable and cannot correct the entries, what options does the student have to address this for the checkride?
questions.follow_up_answer: The student has a few options: (1) Re-fly the questionable instrument time with you as the instructor, ensuring all new entries are properly documented as actual or simulated. (2) Obtain a written statement from any witness to the original flights if possible, though this has limited regulatory weight. (3) Contact the FAA Flight Standards District Office (FSDO) for guidance, as the FSDO may accept a signed affidavit from the student explaining the circumstances. (4) Ultimately, the examiner has the authority to accept or reject the logbook entries during the checkride. If the examiner determines the entries are insufficient, the checkride cannot proceed until the deficiency is corrected. The safest path is to re-fly the time in question with proper documentation before scheduling the checkride.

questions.question: You are a CFII who also holds an instrument rating for helicopters. During a training flight, you and your student both flew portions of the flight under the hood. Can you log instrument time for the portion the student flew while you were acting as the safety pilot? What are the exact conditions that determine what each of you may log?
questions.answer: This is a nuanced logging situation. You, as the CFII providing instruction, may log flight instructor time for the entire training flight. For instrument time specifically: during the portion the student flew under the hood, you were serving as the required safety pilot per 14 CFR 91.109(c). A safety pilot serving as required crew may log that time as second-in-command (SIC) time per 14 CFR 61.51(f)(2). However, you may not log it as instrument time because you were the visual safety pilot while the student manipulated the controls on instruments — only the student (who was manipulating the controls) may log that period as simulated instrument flight time. You cannot simultaneously log the same flight time as both safety pilot and instrument pilot. For the portion you flew under the hood while the student acted as safety pilot, you may log that as simulated instrument time for your own currency. The key principle is that only the pilot actually manipulating the controls on instruments during any given period may log instrument time for that period.
questions.follow_up: Can a CFII log both flight instructor time and pilot-in-command time simultaneously during a training flight with a student?
questions.follow_up_answer: Yes. Per 14 CFR 61.51(e)(3), a flight instructor may log PIC time for all flight time while serving as the authorized instructor in an operation requiring more than one pilot, or when the flight instructor is the sole manipulator of the controls of an aircraft for which they are rated. Per 14 CFR 61.51(e)(1), a pilot may log PIC time when they are the sole manipulator of the controls of an aircraft for which they hold the appropriate category and class rating. When the student is flying, the CFII remains the responsible PIC per 14 CFR 61.51(e)(3) because they are the acting authorized instructor, and may log PIC time for the entire flight. The student logs the time they are sole manipulator of the controls as PIC time only if they hold the appropriate rating for that aircraft — if not, they log it as flight time but not as PIC. So yes, the CFII can log instructor time and PIC time concurrently, but instrument time logging depends on who is actually manipulating the controls while on instruments.

questions.question: Before a student pilot can solo a helicopter, what pre-solo knowledge test must be completed, and who administers it?
questions.answer: Before solo flight, a student pilot must pass a written knowledge test on the regulations and the airspace where the solo flight will be conducted. The test must be administered and reviewed by the student's flight instructor, who must also review any incorrect answers with the student before signing off the endorsement. This is required by 14 CFR 61.87(b).

questions.question: What specific maneuvers and procedures must a flight instructor certify that a student pilot has demonstrated proficiency in before endorsing them for helicopter solo flight?
questions.answer: Per 14 CFR 61.87(d), for helicopter solo, the instructor must certify the student has demonstrated proficiency in: preflight, run-up, takeoff, straight-and-level flight, turns in both directions, traffic pattern procedures, area departure and arrival, collision avoidance, wind correction, hovering, hovering turns, hovering figure eights, normal and crosswind takeoff and landings, normal and crosswind autorotation, emergency procedures, and after-flight procedures.

questions.question: Where must the solo endorsement for a student helicopter pilot be recorded, and what are the validity rules for exercising solo privileges?
questions.answer: The solo endorsement must be recorded in the student pilot's logbook by a certificated flight instructor. Per 14 CFR 61.87(n), the solo endorsement for a specific make and model helicopter does not expire once entered in the logbook. However, to actually exercise solo privileges, 14 CFR 61.87(p) requires a separate endorsement from a flight instructor within the 90-calendar-day period immediately preceding the solo flight. Additionally, the student pilot certificate itself is valid for 60 calendar months from issuance (per 14 CFR 61.19).

questions.question: Your student passed their pre-solo written test two weeks ago, you reviewed all the wrong answers together, and they have demonstrated all required maneuvers. Today you plan to send them solo for the first time in the Robinson R22. Walk me through exactly what endorsements you must enter in their logbook and what those endorsements must state.
questions.answer: You must enter at least two endorsements in the student's logbook: (1) The pre-solo aeronautical knowledge endorsement (AC 61-65, Endorsement A-4) confirming the student passed the knowledge test on 14 CFR Parts 61 and 91 applicable to the flight, and that you reviewed all incorrect answers. (2) The pre-solo flight training endorsement (AC 61-65, Endorsement A-5) stating the student has received and logged flight training in the specific make and model—Robinson R22—and has demonstrated proficiency in the maneuvers and procedures of 14 CFR 61.87(d) and is competent to make solo flights. The endorsement must include the make and model of helicopter, your signature, certificate number, certificate type, and date. The 90-day currency endorsement (A-6) is also technically required before the student exercises the solo privilege and may be combined with the initial solo endorsement if done on the same day.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 61.87(b)(c)(n); AC 61-65H, Endorsements A-4, A-5, A-6

questions.question: A student pilot completed their pre-solo knowledge test and received all endorsements 95 days ago. They want to go out and solo today. Can they legally do so, and what must happen first?
questions.answer: No, they cannot legally solo today without additional action. Under 14 CFR 61.87(p), a student pilot may not exercise solo flight privileges unless they have received a flight instructor endorsement within the preceding 90 days certifying that the student has received training and is proficient to make solo flights in the make and model helicopter. Since 95 days have passed, the 90-day endorsement has expired. The student must fly with their instructor again, demonstrate continued proficiency, and receive a new 90-day endorsement before soloing. The original make-and-model endorsement (A-5) does not expire, but the recurring 90-day endorsement (A-6) is required every 90 days to exercise the privilege.

questions.question: A student has been training in a Robinson R22 and is ready for solo. Their parent says they just turned 14 years old last week. Is the student eligible to solo, and what minimum age requirement applies to helicopter students specifically?
questions.answer: Yes, the student is eligible to solo. Under 14 CFR 61.87(a), the minimum age to act as pilot in command of a helicopter on a solo flight is 14 years old. This is different from fixed-wing aircraft, which require a minimum age of 16 for solo privileges. Since the student has just turned 14, they meet the age requirement. The instructor must still verify all other prerequisites are met: student pilot certificate obtained, pre-solo knowledge test passed and reviewed, and all required maneuvers demonstrated to the instructor's satisfaction, along with proper logbook endorsements.

questions.question: An instructor endorses a student for solo in the Robinson R22 on January 15. In March, the student begins training in an R44 and demonstrates proficiency in that helicopter. Can the instructor simply add the R44 to the existing solo endorsement, or is a completely new endorsement required? What are the logbook entry implications?
questions.answer: A completely new, separate endorsement is required for the R44. Under 14 CFR 61.87(n), the solo endorsement must specify the make and model of the helicopter the student is authorized to fly solo. The R22 and R44 are different make and model aircraft. You cannot modify or amend an existing endorsement—doing so would be improper and potentially fraudulent alteration of a logbook. A new endorsement meeting all the requirements of 14 CFR 61.87(c) and (d) must be entered in the logbook for the R44 specifically, including confirmation that the student has demonstrated the required maneuvers in the R44 and passed a knowledge test applicable to that operating environment. A new 90-day endorsement for the R44 is also required before the student exercises solo privileges in it.
questions.follow_up: What if it's the same make—say, both are Robinson helicopters—but different models like the R22 versus the R44? Does the pre-solo knowledge test need to be re-administered?
questions.follow_up_answer: Yes, even though both are Robinson helicopters, the R22 and R44 are different models and a new make-and-model endorsement is required for the R44. Regarding the knowledge test, 14 CFR 61.87(b) requires the test to cover the regulations and airspace applicable to the solo flight. If the operating airspace is the same and the applicable regulations haven't changed, an instructor has some discretion, but best practice and most conservative interpretation is that a new knowledge test review should be conducted since the aircraft performance, limitations, and systems differ. The instructor must be satisfied the student understands the specific aircraft. The instructor's endorsement certifies competency in that specific make and model, so a fresh review and endorsement is the appropriate standard.

questions.question: A student pilot presents you their logbook and it shows a solo endorsement signed by a previous instructor dated 18 months ago. The student wants to resume training with you and solo next week. As the new instructor, what must you do before you can legally send this student solo, and can you rely on the previous instructor's endorsements at all?
questions.answer: You cannot simply rely on the previous instructor's endorsements to send the student solo next week. As the new instructor, you must personally evaluate the student before issuing any endorsements. Specifically: (1) You must fly with the student and verify they are still proficient in all the maneuvers listed in 14 CFR 61.87(d) for the specific helicopter make and model. If they are not, you must provide remedial training until proficiency is restored. (2) The 90-day endorsement from the previous instructor is certainly expired (18 months ago). You must issue a new 90-day endorsement per 14 CFR 61.87(p) in the student's logbook, signed by you with your certificate number and date. (3) You should review the pre-solo knowledge test documentation to confirm the test was properly administered and incorrect answers reviewed—if you have doubt, re-administer or review with the student. (4) The original make-and-model endorsement from the prior instructor does not expire and technically remains valid, but as the new signing instructor for the 90-day endorsement, you are personally certifying the student's competency, so you must be satisfied before signing anything.
questions.follow_up: What if the student tells you they have been flying with a family member who holds a commercial certificate but is not a CFI, and they logged that time as solo time in their logbook? Is that logged time valid, and does it affect anything?
questions.follow_up_answer: No, that logged time is not valid solo time and cannot be counted toward any solo requirements. Under 14 CFR 61.51(d), solo flight time is time when the pilot is the sole occupant of the aircraft. However, for a student pilot to log that time as solo, they must be acting under a valid solo endorsement from a flight instructor. Flying with a non-CFI commercial pilot does not constitute solo flight—it's dual instruction time only if the person providing instruction holds a flight instructor certificate, or it's simply logged as pilot flight time if the commercial pilot was acting as PIC. Time logged with a non-CFI cannot be credited as solo time toward student pilot requirements. Additionally, the family member with a commercial certificate but no CFI certificate may have violated 14 CFR 61.193 if they were attempting to provide flight instruction, which requires a flight instructor certificate.

questions.question: What is a logbook endorsement, and why may it be required for certain helicopter training events such as touchdown autorotations?
questions.answer: A logbook endorsement is a written, signed statement from a certificated flight instructor recorded in a pilot's logbook that certifies the pilot has received training in, and is proficient in, a specific maneuver or operation. Touchdown autorotations are an emergency procedure; 14 CFR 61.87(d) requires an instructor to train the student in emergency procedures, and 61.87(e) requires the instructor to endorse that the student is proficient before solo flight. While the regulation addresses emergency procedures generically, many flight schools and instructors impose additional specific endorsements for touchdown autorotations as a prudent risk-management practice, given the maneuver's potential for aircraft damage or injury.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 61.87, 14 CFR 61.93; FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook

questions.question: Which Special Federal Aviation Regulation (SFAR) directly affects helicopter pilot training and testing, and what does it require in terms of logbook endorsements?
questions.answer: SFAR 73 applies to Robinson R-22 and R-44 helicopters. It requires pilots to receive specific training and an instructor endorsement before acting as PIC of an R-22 or R-44. The endorsement must be entered in the pilot's logbook by an authorized flight instructor who has completed the Robinson-specific awareness training. The SFAR addresses the unique low-inertia rotor system and mast bumping risks associated with these aircraft.
questions.regulatory_ref: SFAR 73 (14 CFR Part 61, SFAR No. 73); 14 CFR 61.31(k)

questions.question: A student helicopter pilot wants to practice solo touchdown autorotations at the local airport. What training and endorsement are required, and who must provide them?
questions.answer: Before a student pilot may perform a solo touchdown autorotation, a certificated flight instructor must train the student in emergency procedures (which include autorotations) per 14 CFR 61.87(d), and then endorse in the logbook that the student is proficient in those maneuvers per 14 CFR 61.87(e). The endorsing instructor must hold at least a flight instructor certificate with a helicopter rating per 14 CFR 61.195. Note: the regulation addresses emergency procedures as a category; individual schools or instructors may require a separate endorsement specifically for touchdown autorotations as best practice, though this is not explicitly mandated by 61.87.

questions.question: You are a recently certificated private helicopter pilot who just purchased a Robinson R-22. You have your private certificate but have never flown an R-22. Can you legally fly it as PIC? What endorsements or training are required?
questions.answer: No, you cannot legally fly the R-22 as PIC without first complying with SFAR 73. SFAR 73 requires that before acting as PIC of an R-22, a pilot must receive ground and flight training from an authorized instructor and obtain a logbook endorsement from that instructor certifying the training was completed. The training must cover the specific aerodynamic characteristics of low-inertia rotor systems, low-g pushover hazards, mast bumping, and recovery techniques. Additionally, the endorsing instructor must themselves have completed a Robinson-approved awareness course. A private certificate alone, without the SFAR 73 endorsement, does not authorize PIC flight in the R-22.
questions.regulatory_ref: SFAR 73 (14 CFR Part 61, SFAR No. 73), specifically paragraphs 2 and 3

questions.question: A helicopter flight instructor has a student who is ready to solo but has only been trained in power recovery autorotations. The instructor is considering endorsing the student for solo flight including solo autorotation practice. What must the instructor consider regarding touchdown autorotations specifically?
questions.answer: The instructor must ensure the student has been trained in and demonstrated proficiency in all maneuvers required under 14 CFR 61.87(d) and (e) before endorsing for solo flight. For helicopter students, the endorsement must specifically address each maneuver the student is authorized to perform solo, and any limitations. If touchdown autorotations are to be included in solo operations, the instructor must have trained the student in that specific maneuver and found the student proficient before endorsing it. It would be inappropriate and potentially unsafe—and likely a regulatory violation—to endorse a student for solo autorotation practice if training was limited only to power recovery autorotations. The instructor's solo endorsement under 61.87(e) carries legal and safety accountability, and the instructor may appropriately restrict the endorsement to exclude touchdown autorotations if the student has not demonstrated proficiency in them.

questions.question: Besides SFAR 73 for Robinson helicopters and solo autorotation endorsements, describe two other examples of FAA-required logbook endorsements that a helicopter pilot may encounter during their training or certification pathway.
questions.answer: Two additional examples include: (1) The complex or high-performance aircraft endorsement under 14 CFR 61.31 — although more common in fixed-wing, this concept applies whenever an aircraft requires specific training per the regulations or manufacturer requirements, and for helicopters, turbine-powered aircraft training under 14 CFR 61.31(e) requires an endorsement before acting as PIC of a turbine-powered aircraft. (2) The instrument proficiency check (IPC) endorsement — under 14 CFR 61.57(d), a pilot who has failed to meet instrument currency requirements must receive and log an IPC from an authorized instructor, who must provide a logbook endorsement. Additionally, tailwheel endorsements and high-altitude pressurized aircraft endorsements are FAR 61.31 examples, though the turbine and IPC endorsements are the most relevant for helicopter instrument pilots.

questions.question: A flight instructor endorsed a student for solo touchdown autorotations three months ago. The student has since been flying dual with a different instructor and the original endorsing instructor believes the student's autorotation technique has degraded significantly. Does the original endorsement remain valid, and does the original instructor have any authority or obligation to act?
questions.answer: The original logbook endorsement does not automatically expire based on a time limit for the solo authorization itself (as long as the solo privileges remain within the 90-day endorsement window under 14 CFR 61.87(n) for student pilot certificates, or the specific endorsement terms). However, under 14 CFR 61.195(b), an instructor may not endorse a student for solo flight unless that student is proficient at the time of endorsement. Once endorsed, the regulation does not provide a formal revocation mechanism for a prior instructor. The original instructor has no direct authority to unilaterally revoke a logbook endorsement after it has been given. However, if the student is currently flying with a supervising instructor, that instructor holds the current responsibility for assessing the student's currency and competency before authorizing further solo operations. The prudent course of action is for the original instructor to communicate concerns to the student's current instructor, who may then determine whether a new evaluation is needed before further solo autorotation practice is authorized.
questions.follow_up: If a flight instructor discovers after the fact that they endorsed a student who was not actually proficient — perhaps because the instructor rushed the evaluation — what are the potential consequences for that instructor?
questions.follow_up_answer: An instructor who endorses a student who is not actually proficient may face serious FAA enforcement action. Under 14 CFR 61.195, an instructor must not endorse a student unless that student is proficient in the maneuver or area. Providing a false or unsupported endorsement could constitute falsification of records under 14 CFR 61.59, which carries potential certificate revocation. The instructor could also face civil liability if the student is subsequently involved in an accident during solo autorotation practice. The FAA may investigate the endorsement as part of any accident or incident investigation, and the instructor's logbooks and records may be subpoenaed. The instructor's CFI certificate could be suspended or revoked under 14 CFR 61.415.

questions.question: A helicopter pilot holds an instrument rating and has been flying an R-44 IFR for years. SFAR 73 requires an endorsement for the R-44, but the pilot completed this training before SFAR 73 was amended. The pilot's logbook shows old endorsement language that doesn't exactly match current SFAR 73 requirements. Is the pilot legal to act as PIC in the R-44 today?
questions.answer: This requires careful analysis of the specific SFAR 73 amendment dates and what training was completed. SFAR 73 has been revised, and the FAA has generally provided transition provisions for pilots who completed training under earlier versions. A pilot who received training and an endorsement under a prior version of SFAR 73 should review the current SFAR 73 text to determine if their prior training satisfies current requirements or if recurrent or additional training is now mandated. SFAR 73 includes recurrency training requirements — pilots must receive SFAR 73-compliant training every 24 calendar months to maintain PIC privileges in R-22 and R-44. If the endorsement is outdated beyond this 24-month recurrency window, the pilot is NOT current and may not legally act as PIC regardless of certificate held. The pilot should obtain current SFAR 73-compliant training and a fresh endorsement from an authorized instructor to restore legal PIC status.
questions.follow_up: Suppose this pilot is asked to conduct an IFR training flight in the R-44 as a flight instructor, not as a student or PIC under their own certificate, but as the instructor of record with a safety pilot aboard. Does SFAR 73 still apply?
questions.follow_up_answer: Yes, SFAR 73 still applies. SFAR 73 requirements apply to any person acting as PIC of an R-22 or R-44, and when a flight instructor is the sole manipulator of the controls or is acting as PIC, they must hold a current SFAR 73 endorsement. The presence of a safety pilot or the instructor role does not exempt the pilot from SFAR 73 compliance. Furthermore, 14 CFR 61.195 requires that a flight instructor must be current and qualified in the aircraft being used for instruction. An instructor without a current SFAR 73 endorsement who conducts flight instruction in an R-44 would be in violation of both SFAR 73 and 14 CFR 61.195, and any endorsements given during such instruction would be invalid.
questions.regulatory_ref: SFAR 73 (14 CFR Part 61, SFAR No. 73), paragraphs 2(b) recurrency requirements; 14 CFR 61.195; 14 CFR 61.51

questions.question: When you endorse a student pilot for an initial private pilot helicopter practical test, what specific information must appear in the logbook endorsement?
questions.answer: The endorsement must include: (1) a statement that the instructor has given the applicant the required ground and flight training, (2) that the applicant has met the aeronautical knowledge and experience requirements of 14 CFR Part 61 for the certificate sought, (3) that the applicant is prepared for the practical test, (4) the instructor's name, certificate number, certificate type, and expiration date, and (5) the date the endorsement was made. The endorsement language follows AC 61-65 sample endorsements.

questions.question: What FAA application form does a student use when applying for an initial private pilot certificate, and where is it submitted?
questions.answer: The applicant uses FAA Form 8710-1 (Airman Certificate and/or Rating Application), which is now commonly completed through the FAA's Integrated Airman Certification and Rating Application (IACRA) system online. The completed application is submitted to the designated pilot examiner (DPE) or FAA inspector administering the checkride. The examiner reviews and signs off the application as part of the checkride process.

questions.question: What is the difference between the endorsement required for an additional aircraft category/class rating versus an endorsement for an additional aircraft type qualification within a category the pilot already holds?
questions.answer: For an additional category or class rating (e.g., adding helicopter to an existing airplane certificate), the instructor must endorse that the applicant meets the training and experience requirements of 14 CFR 61.63 for that specific category/class, and a new practical test is required. For an additional aircraft qualification within the same category/class (e.g., adding a specific make/model requiring a logbook endorsement under 61.31), the instructor endorses the pilot as proficient in that make/model; in many cases no practical test is required, only the endorsement itself. High-performance, complex, or high-altitude aircraft endorsements under 61.31 are examples of the latter.
