The pilot must obtain explicit clearance regardless of method of surface transit and maintain situational awareness of active runways at all times.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA AC 91-73B; AIM 4-3-18; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 9; 14 CFR 91.129

questions.question: You are holding short of Runway 27 at a towered airport in your wheel-equipped helicopter. ATC instructs a fixed-wing aircraft to 'line up and wait Runway 27.' Two minutes later, ATC clears that aircraft for takeoff. While scanning, you momentarily lose visual contact with the departing traffic as it accelerates on the runway. ATC then transmits: 'Helicopter 3WF, Runway 27, cleared for immediate takeoff.' What factors should you evaluate before initiating any movement, and what is the safest course of action if you are not confident about the departing aircraft's position?
questions.answer: Before moving onto Runway 27, you must evaluate: (1) Confirmation that the previously cleared fixed-wing aircraft has indeed departed and cleared the runway — loss of visual contact during a takeoff roll means you cannot confirm separation; (2) Whether 'immediate' implies ATC believes the runway is clear and the departing aircraft is airborne — however, ATC's instruction does not eliminate your pilot-in-command responsibility to verify safety before entering; (3) Runway length and whether a delayed or aborted takeoff by the preceding aircraft could put them still on the runway. The safest course of action: if you are not certain the runway is clear, do not enter. Communicate to ATC immediately: 'Helicopter 3WF, request a short delay — I've lost visual on the preceding departure.' ATC will either confirm the aircraft has cleared, provide updated traffic information, or issue a revised clearance. A 'cleared for takeoff' instruction does not override your PIC authority under 14 CFR 91.3 to refuse or delay if you determine entry is unsafe. Accepting an immediate clearance when safety is uncertain trades compliance for risk — an unacceptable trade.
questions.follow_up: If ATC responds, 'Helicopter 3WF, preceding traffic is airborne and clear — runway clear, continue immediate takeoff,' and you still cannot visually confirm the other aircraft, are you required to comply?
questions.follow_up_answer: No. While ATC has radar and positional information you may not have, and their confirmation significantly raises your confidence level, you as pilot-in-command retain ultimate authority under 14 CFR 91.3(a) to deviate from any clearance if you determine it necessary for the safe operation of your aircraft. If you are still not satisfied — for example, in reduced visibility conditions at night where a rejected takeoff by the other aircraft would be invisible to you — you may request an additional delay or a visual confirmation. In practice, ATC's confirmation in clear conditions should generally be sufficient to proceed; however, the legal and safety authority remains with the PIC. You should also file a NASA ASRS report if the situation involved any ambiguity or near-miss elements to document the occurrence without punitive action.

questions.question: You are taxiing your wheel-equipped helicopter at an airport with an operating ATIS. While copying the ATIS, you become distracted and taxi past a poorly-lit runway hold short sign at night, entering Runway 9 without a clearance. You immediately recognize the error. Walk me through exactly what you should do in the next 30 seconds, and what reporting obligations follow.
questions.answer: Immediate actions in the first 30 seconds: (1) Stop the helicopter immediately—do not continue further onto the runway; (2) Transmit to ATC immediately: state your callsign, advise that you have inadvertently entered Runway 9 without clearance, and request instructions—for example, 'Tower, Helicopter 3WF, I've inadvertently entered Runway 9 without clearance, request instructions'; (3) While transmitting, simultaneously scan for approaching traffic—both in the landing direction and departing direction, using all available lighting and visual cues; (4) Follow ATC's instructions precisely—they will either instruct you to exit via a specific taxiway or hold position; (5) Activate landing/nav lights to increase conspicuity if not already on. Post-incident obligations: (1) File a NASA Aviation Safety Reporting System (ASRS) report within 10 calendar days—this provides a waiver from certificate suspension for unintentional violations under FAA Order 2150.3C, but only if no investigation was initiated before filing; (2) Cooperate with any ATC facility incident review; (3) Conduct a personal debrief identifying the root cause—in this case, task saturation from ATIS copying while taxiing, a common and preventable human factors failure. Note: ASRS immunity does not protect against revocation, criminal prosecution, or civil penalties, and the FAA may still pursue enforcement under 14 CFR 91.129.
questions.follow_up: You file the NASA ASRS report within 10 days. Three weeks later you receive a Letter of Investigation from the FAA regarding the runway incursion. Does your ASRS filing guarantee that no certificate action will be taken against you?
questions.follow_up_answer: No — the ASRS filing does not guarantee immunity from all FAA action. The ASRS program provides a waiver from certificate suspension for unintentional violations, but it does not protect against: (1) revocation of an airman certificate; (2) criminal prosecution; (3) civil penalty actions; or (4) violations that involve accidents or deliberate disregard for safety. In a runway incursion case involving an unintentional error, the most likely outcome is that the ASRS filing will protect you from a suspension, but the FAA may still issue a warning notice or Letter of Correction. The key requirement is that the violation must be unintentional, not deliberate, and the ASRS report must be filed within 10 calendar days of the occurrence. The pilot should consult an aviation attorney when responding to a Letter of Investigation.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.129; 14 CFR 91.25 (NASA ASRS immunity provision); FAA Order 2150.3C; AIM 7-7-2

questions.question: When taxiing a helicopter with wheel-type landing gear, what is the primary hazard associated with excessive taxi speed?
questions.answer: Excessive taxi speed reduces the pilot's ability to stop or turn safely within the available space. At higher speeds, the helicopter's center of gravity is more susceptible to lateral shifts during turns, increasing the risk of dynamic rollover or loss of directional control. Additionally, high taxi speeds reduce reaction time to unexpected obstacles, personnel, or surface hazards.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 9 (Basic Flight Maneuvers) and Chapter 11 (Emergencies and Hazards — Dynamic Rollover)

questions.question: What general speed reference is used as a guideline for helicopter ground taxi speed with wheel-type landing gear?
questions.answer: A safe taxi speed is generally described as a walking pace — approximately 3 to 5 miles per hour — or slow enough that the pilot can stop the helicopter within a safe distance. The exact speed will vary with surface conditions, ramp congestion, wind, and slope, but the principle is to taxi no faster than necessary to maintain controlled, predictable movement.

questions.question: How does rotor RPM and rotor disc position affect directional control and speed management when taxiing a helicopter on wheels?
questions.answer: During wheeled taxi, the rotor disc is the primary means of directional control — cyclic inputs tilt the disc to provide translating force for steering. Rotor RPM must be maintained within normal operating range so the rotor disc remains effective for control. If RPM is too low, disc effectiveness is reduced and the pilot loses the ability to steer precisely or stop lateral drift. Additionally, a tilted disc combined with high taxi speed can increase side load on the landing gear.

questions.question: You are taxiing a wheeled helicopter across a sloped ramp on a windy day. The wind is from your left at 15 knots. How should you adjust your taxi speed and cyclic inputs through a left turn, and what risk does this scenario present?
questions.answer: In a left turn with a left crosswind, the tail of the helicopter will tend to weathervane left, and the wind may assist the turn more than expected—increasing the risk of the tail swinging through too quickly and the helicopter entering a skid. You should reduce taxi speed before initiating the turn and apply left cyclic (into the wind) to counteract the left crosswind's lifting effect on the advancing blade side and prevent unloading of the upwind wheel. On a slope, the upslope wheel may bear less weight, increasing the lateral rollover risk. The combination of slope, crosswind, and turning creates a dynamic rollover scenario; slow, deliberate speed control is essential. Cyclic should be positioned into the wind and upslope throughout the turn.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 9 and Chapter 11 (Dynamic Rollover)

questions.question: During a wheeled taxi turn on a congested ramp, you notice you are approaching a parked aircraft faster than expected. What speed and control errors likely led to this situation, and how should you correct it?
questions.answer: The most likely errors are entering the turn at too high a taxi speed, failing to reduce collective sufficiently to limit forward momentum, or misjudging the turn radius required to clear the parked aircraft. To correct: smoothly reduce collective to decrease thrust and slow forward movement, apply aft cyclic to further reduce speed, and use pedals to assist directional alignment if needed — while avoiding abrupt inputs that could cause a skid or load shift. If stopping is necessary, lower collective fully and apply wheel brakes if available. This scenario illustrates why speed must be pre-managed before turns, not corrected during them.

questions.question: How does excess taxi speed during a turn specifically increase the risk of dynamic rollover in a helicopter with wheel-type landing gear, and what makes helicopters more vulnerable to this than fixed-wing aircraft?
questions.answer: Dynamic rollover occurs when a pivot point is established — such as a wheel — and the helicopter begins to roll around it faster than the pilot can correct with opposite cyclic. Excess taxi speed during a turn increases lateral momentum, which amplifies the rolling tendency once the pivot point is engaged. Unlike fixed-wing aircraft, helicopters have a high center of gravity relative to the landing gear footprint and lack inherent lateral stability from wings. The rotor disc also contributes to rolling forces rather than resisting them. If the roll rate exceeds the cyclic correction capability, recovery is not possible and rollover will occur. This is why speed must be kept low during all turns, particularly on uneven surfaces.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 11 (Dynamic Rollover)

questions.question: A student pilot taxiing a wheeled helicopter consistently enters turns at appropriate speed but then gradually accelerates mid-turn as they focus on steering. As an instructor, what specific risk does mid-turn acceleration create that does not exist at a constant slow speed, and how would you teach the student to manage it?
questions.answer: Mid-turn acceleration is particularly dangerous because it combines increasing lateral centrifugal force with an already-established turn radius and potential pivot on one wheel. As speed increases in the turn, the outward (centrifugal) force grows with the square of velocity, rapidly increasing the likelihood of the outer wheel becoming a pivot point for dynamic rollover. The student's fixation on steering is causing a classic task saturation error — they are managing direction but not energy state. Teaching strategy: have the student pre-configure a fixed collective setting before entering the turn so taxi speed is governed passively, not actively managed during the turn. Reinforce that the turn itself is the highest-risk moment and demands the most speed discipline, not the least. Practice slow taxi turns in a clear area with emphasis on collective discipline before adding directional complexity.
questions.follow_up: If the student corrects the mid-turn acceleration problem but now consistently slows too much before turns — almost stopping — what new risk does that introduce?
questions.follow_up_answer: Slowing nearly to a stop before every turn is not inherently unsafe, but it introduces the risk of the helicopter settling onto one wheel or a skid (if on rough surface), creating the very pivot point that dynamic rollover requires. Additionally, very slow taxi speed with wind present can cause the helicopter to weathervane unpredictably, and rotor efficiency may be reduced at near-zero groundspeed if RPM is not well managed. The ideal speed is slow and consistent — not stop-and-go — because smooth, predictable energy management avoids both dynamic rollover from excess speed and loss-of-control scenarios from near-zero speed in crosswind or sloped conditions.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 9 and Chapter 11 (Dynamic Rollover); FAA-H-8083-9B Aviation Instructor's Handbook (task saturation)

questions.question: You are evaluating a commercial helicopter applicant during a wheeled taxi on a wet concrete ramp. They maintain appropriate speed throughout but make one sharp, abrupt pedal input during a turn. Even though the speed was safe, why might this still be an unsatisfactory performance, and what specific hazard did the abrupt pedal input create?
questions.answer: Even at low taxi speed, abrupt pedal inputs during a turn can transfer yaw momentum to the rotor system and landing gear simultaneously. On a wet surface, the wheel with reduced vertical load during a turn may skid laterally, shifting the pivot point unpredictably. More critically, sharp anti-torque pedal inputs can cause the tail to swing faster than the pilot anticipates, especially if the rotor is producing significant thrust — this can turn a controlled maneuver into a skid or yaw oscillation. On wheel-type gear with limited directional damping, rapid yaw can cause asymmetric wheel loading. Per ACS standards, smoothness of control inputs is a distinct evaluation criterion. The applicant demonstrated speed awareness but failed to demonstrate control harmony — an unsatisfactory performance in the skills portion and a risk management failure because abrupt inputs are a leading cause of ground handling accidents even at low speed.
questions.follow_up: The applicant argues that the abrupt pedal input was necessary because a ground vehicle entered the taxiway unexpectedly, and they needed to stop the turn immediately. How does this change your evaluation, and what would the correct technique have been?
questions.follow_up_answer: The scenario introduces a legitimate threat response, which the examiner must consider. However, the correct technique for an unexpected obstacle is to reduce collective to decrease thrust and slow the helicopter, combined with smooth cyclic aft to arrest forward movement — not an abrupt pedal input, which primarily affects yaw, not stopping distance. Pedals do not stop the helicopter; collective does. If the applicant's instinctive response to a threat was an ineffective control (pedals instead of collective), this reveals a training deficiency in emergency ground response, which remains unsatisfactory. Credit is given for recognizing the threat and reacting, but the evaluation should note the incorrect primary control selection under pressure — a risk management deficiency worth additional training regardless of outcome.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 9 and Chapter 11; Commercial Pilot ACS HI.VIII.D

questions.question: When ground taxiing a wheel-equipped helicopter, what is the primary control used to direct the thrust vector, and how does it differ from a fixed-wing aircraft's nosewheel steering?
questions.answer: In a wheel-equipped helicopter, the cyclic controls the thrust vector by tilting the rotor disk in the desired direction of travel. This is fundamentally different from a fixed-wing aircraft, which uses a steerable nosewheel or differential braking for directional control. The pilot must apply cyclic in the direction of the intended turn to vector rotor thrust and steer the helicopter on the ground. Pedals control tail rotor pitch for torque compensation, not ground steering.

questions.question: What is the risk of applying excessive forward cyclic while ground taxiing a wheel-equipped helicopter at higher speeds?
questions.answer: Excessive forward cyclic tilts the rotor disk forward aggressively, reducing blade-to-ground clearance and risking blade strike with the ground or obstacles. Forward rotor tilt also reduces vertical load on the wheels, increasing rollover risk. Additionally, excessive forward thrust can cause unintended acceleration beyond the pilot's braking capability, increasing the risk of a ground collision or runway exceedance.

questions.question: When should brakes be used versus collective reduction to slow a wheel-equipped helicopter during ground taxi?
questions.answer: Collective should be reduced to minimize rotor lift and reduce ground speed during normal deceleration, while brakes are used for fine speed control and stopping. Brakes alone should not be relied upon as the primary deceleration method at higher taxi speeds because abrupt braking can cause dynamic rollover or nose-low attitude with rotor blade-to-tail clearance issues. The preferred technique is to reduce collective first to minimize lift, then use brakes smoothly to come to a complete stop.

questions.question: You are ground taxiing a wheel-equipped helicopter on a sloped taxiway that descends toward a congested ramp. The helicopter is picking up speed and you apply the brakes firmly. Describe the potential risks and what your correct control inputs should be.
questions.answer: Applying firm brakes on a downslope can cause the nose to pitch forward abruptly, driving the rotor disk toward the ground. This reduces blade-to-ground clearance and risks blade strike. Additionally, if one brake grabs harder than the other, the helicopter can veer off the taxiway centerline. The correct response is to simultaneously reduce collective to minimize rotor lift and reduce the tendency for the nose to pitch down, apply brakes evenly and progressively rather than abruptly, and use aft cyclic to keep the rotor disk from over-tilting forward. If slope and speed require it, consider hovering taxi instead of ground taxi for better control.

questions.question: During a left turn while ground taxiing a wheel-equipped helicopter, what cyclic input do you apply, and what happens if you instead try to use left pedal to initiate the turn?
questions.answer: To execute a left turn while ground taxiing, you apply left cyclic to vector the rotor thrust to the left. If a pilot incorrectly uses left pedal input to initiate the turn, left pedal increases tail rotor pitch, which yaws the nose left momentarily but also adds drag, potentially causing a skid or uncoordinated ground movement. Since the tail rotor is not designed as a steering mechanism on the ground, using pedals as the primary turning control can result in loss of directional control, asymmetric forces on the landing gear, and possible tip-over tendency depending on terrain and speed.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapters 9 and 11

questions.question: A student pilot ground taxiing a wheel-equipped helicopter is maintaining a consistently nose-high attitude by holding aft cyclic. What specific risks does this create, and how should you correct it?
questions.answer: Holding excessive aft cyclic during ground taxi tilts the rotor disk rearward, vectoring thrust aft. This can slow or stop forward movement but also increases the risk of the tail boom striking the ground if the helicopter settles or the tail is lower than expected. Additionally, excessive aft cyclic at higher collective settings can partially unload the main wheels, reducing brake effectiveness and directional control. The correction is to establish a neutral or slightly forward cyclic attitude appropriate for the taxi speed, keep collective at the minimum necessary to maintain the desired ground roll, and use brakes for speed control.

questions.question: During ground taxi in a wheel-equipped helicopter on a wet or icy surface, how does the interaction between thrust vector, brake use, and collective setting change compared to a dry surface, and what failure mode becomes most likely if the pilot does not adapt technique?
questions.answer: On a contaminated surface, braking effectiveness is significantly reduced, meaning the pilot cannot rely on brakes to arrest acceleration or complete a stop within the expected distance. The pilot must reduce taxi speed considerably before reaching any turn or stopping point. Collective should be kept at the minimum necessary to avoid unloading the wheels, because even slight rotor lift reduces tire friction further on a slippery surface. Thrust vector changes via cyclic must be made very slowly and smoothly because abrupt cyclic inputs on a low-friction surface can cause the helicopter to yaw or slide laterally before the pilot can correct. The most likely failure mode is dynamic rollover — as the helicopter slides sideways, one wheel can catch on a patch of higher friction while the other continues to slide, creating an unintended pivot point. Without immediate corrective collective reduction, the helicopter can roll over before the pilot can respond.
questions.follow_up: If you feel the helicopter beginning to slide laterally during ground taxi on ice and dynamic rollover begins, what is the one control input that must happen immediately, and why can't cyclic alone stop the rollover?
questions.follow_up_answer: The immediate required input is to reduce collective to zero, or as close to zero as possible, as quickly as possible. Collective reduction unloads the rotor system and removes the rolling moment that is driving the rollover. Cyclic alone cannot stop dynamic rollover because once the roll rate exceeds the cyclic's ability to produce a counteracting moment through rotor tilt — which happens very quickly — the geometry of the roll places the rotor thrust vector on the wrong side of the pivot point, actually accelerating the rollover. Only removing rotor lift by lowering collective can break the rollover sequence once it is established.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 11 (Dynamic Rollover)

questions.question: You are ground taxiing a wheel-equipped helicopter and the left brake fails completely. Describe how you would use thrust vector management to safely bring the helicopter to a stop without creating a new hazard.
questions.answer: With complete loss of one brake, the pilot should avoid using differential braking, which would induce an uncontrolled yaw. The correct technique is to gradually reduce collective to unload the rotor and allow aerodynamic drag and rolling friction to slow the helicopter. Maintain neutral cyclic or apply only minimal corrective cyclic input to maintain centerline. The pilot should select the widest available clear area and come to a stop primarily through collective reduction rather than relying on the one remaining brake, which could induce unwanted directional control problems. If necessary, transition to hover for full directional control before repositioning. The situation must be reported to maintenance immediately and entered in the aircraft maintenance log per 14 CFR 91.417, as operating with failed brakes is a known aircraft defect. Whether flight may continue depends on whether brakes are required equipment per the aircraft's Rotorcraft Flight Manual or Minimum Equipment List.
questions.follow_up: After stopping safely, can you continue the flight with the known brake failure, assuming no other maintenance discrepancy exists?
questions.follow_up_answer: This depends on the specific aircraft's Rotorcraft Flight Manual (RFM) and whether the aircraft is operating under 14 CFR Part 91. The pilot must determine whether brakes are required equipment per the aircraft's Minimum Equipment List (MEL), if one exists, or whether the RFM lists brakes as required for airworthiness. Under 14 CFR 91.7, the pilot in command is responsible for determining the aircraft is airworthy before flight. If the brakes are required for airworthiness per the RFM or equipment list, the flight may not continue. The discrepancy must be entered in the maintenance record per 14 CFR 91.417 regardless of the flight decision.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.7, 14 CFR 91.417; FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 9

questions.question: When taxiing a wheel-equipped helicopter, what is the primary concern regarding rotor clearance that doesn't exist when operating a skid-equipped helicopter on the ground?
questions.answer: A wheel-equipped helicopter can roll or taxi at higher speeds and cover more ground distance, increasing the risk of encountering obstacles, terrain changes, or other aircraft within the rotor disk's sweep. The rotor blades extend well beyond the fuselage — often 15 to 30+ feet depending on the aircraft — so the pilot must mentally account for that full rotor diameter when taxiing near hangars, other aircraft, fuel pumps, signage, and personnel. Because the helicopter moves more quickly on wheels than it would when hover-taxiing, there is less reaction time to stop before a blade strikes an object.

questions.question: What does the term 'airframe clearance' mean in the context of taxiing a wheel-type helicopter, and what parts of the airframe are most commonly at risk?
questions.answer: Airframe clearance refers to maintaining adequate separation between any structural component of the helicopter and ground obstacles, surfaces, or other objects during ground movement. For wheel-equipped helicopters, the most commonly at-risk components include the tail boom and tail rotor (which can strike runway lights, signage, or uneven pavement if the tail swings during a turn), the main rotor blades at low RPM (which can droop and contact berms, embankments, or elevated obstacles), and the skids or sponsons on some designs. The tail rotor is especially vulnerable during turns because its arc extends behind the pivot point.

questions.question: Why is rotor blade droop a clearance hazard specifically during ground taxi on a wheel-equipped helicopter, and when is blade droop most pronounced?
questions.answer: Rotor blade droop occurs when main rotor RPM is low — particularly during engine start/shutdown or during very slow ground operations — causing the blades to sag downward under gravity rather than remaining extended by centrifugal force. At low RPM, blade droop can reduce tip-to-ground clearance significantly, making it possible for a blade to strike an obstacle that would otherwise be well clear of a fully-spinning rotor. Droop is most pronounced at RPM below the normal operating range, such as during engine start before RPM reaches governed speed or during shutdown as RPM decays. Wind gusts can also cause flapping or flap-back that reduces clearance unpredictably.

questions.question: You are ground taxiing a wheel-type helicopter on a busy ramp in a crosswind of 15 knots from your 9 o'clock position. Describe the rotor clearance risks you'd actively manage and how the crosswind affects them.
questions.answer: A crosswind from the left (9 o'clock) will cause the advancing blade side to develop more lift, causing the rotor disk to tilt. If not corrected with right cyclic input into the wind, the upwind blade may rise while the downwind blade droops, reducing ground clearance on the downwind (right) side. You should apply cyclic into the wind (right cyclic in this case) to level the disk and maximize blade-to-ground clearance on all sides. Additionally, the crosswind can cause the fuselage to weathervane, meaning the nose may want to turn into the wind; on a wheeled helicopter this can cause an unintended turn that swings the tail rotor arc toward ramp equipment or other aircraft. You must use differential braking and anti-torque pedals to track the intended taxi path. Finally, wind gusts can cause unpredictable blade flapping, so you should increase situational awareness for obstacles within the full rotor disk radius.

questions.question: While ground taxiing your wheel-equipped helicopter, you need to make a 90-degree right turn in a tight area near a row of parked aircraft. Walk me through how you would assess and manage both airframe and rotor clearances before and during that turn.
questions.answer: Before initiating the turn, I would stop and perform a visual assessment: identify the full sweep of my rotor disk at current RPM (accounting for blade droop at idle if applicable), locate the tail rotor arc on the left side as the tail swings outward during a right turn, and confirm that no parked aircraft, ground equipment, or personnel are within those clearance zones. I would also check for pavement drop-offs, runway lights, or tie-down chains that could contact the airframe. During the turn, I would execute it slowly using differential braking and pedals, continuously scanning the tail rotor clearance as it arcs outward to the left. If the area is too tight to safely complete the turn in one motion, I would use forward and reverse taxi increments (if the helicopter is equipped with reversing capability or by using the natural tendency to back-taxi). I would not rush the turn and would be prepared to stop immediately if clearance becomes questionable. A spotter outside the aircraft is the safest solution in confined ramp areas.

questions.question: You are taxiing a wheel-type helicopter across uneven terrain — specifically crossing a drainage ditch that is marked with low reflective posts on each side. What clearance risks are present and how do you mitigate them?
questions.answer: Crossing a drainage ditch introduces several clearance risks. As the front wheels descend into the ditch, the nose pitches down and the rotor disk tilts forward. This causes the forward blade tips to move closer to the downslope terrain while the aft blade tips move higher. Conversely, as the nose climbs out the other side, the disk tilts aft and the forward blade tips move away from the opposite terrain. The reflective posts on either side of the ditch could enter the rotor disk arc if the helicopter drifts laterally. Mitigation includes: crossing at the widest point of the ditch, approaching straight-on (perpendicular), maintaining slow controlled taxi speed, using cyclic inputs to keep the rotor disk level (perpendicular to gravity) rather than allowing it to tilt with the aircraft's pitch attitude relative to the terrain—this keeps blade clearance more consistent as the helicopter negotiates the uneven surface. If uncertain about rotor-to-post clearance, use a ground spotter or hover-taxi across the ditch instead.

questions.question: A student pilot taxiing a wheel-type helicopter tends to focus their visual scan on the nose of the aircraft and the taxiway centerline, similar to how they'd scan while driving a car. As an instructor, how would you explain the fundamental difference in the visual scan required for managing rotor and airframe clearances during helicopter ground taxi, and what technique would you teach to develop that scan?
questions.answer: The car-driving mental model is one of the most dangerous habits a student can bring to helicopter taxi because a car's track width is fixed and narrow, while a helicopter's rotor disk is a large rotating hazard extending equally in all directions from the hub. I would explain that a helicopter taxi scan must be three-dimensional and 360-degree rather than a linear forward scan. The student must simultaneously track: (1) the ground path ahead for surface hazards, (2) the full rotor disk arc — especially the blade tips — relative to hangars, aircraft wingtips, and tall obstacles on both sides, (3) the tail rotor arc behind and to the side, especially during turns, and (4) the tail boom clearance over anything the helicopter might be rolling past. The technique I teach is the 'clock scan': systematically visually sweeping from 12 o'clock (forward) to 3, then 6 (tail), then 9, and back to 12 in a continuous cycle, pausing at each position to confirm clearance. I also teach students to choose a reference object at each clock position and estimate whether a rotor blade could reach it — if you can't confidently say no, you stop. This habit must be built before the student ever taxis in a congested area.
questions.follow_up: What if the student asks why they can't just rely on a ground spotter every time to manage clearances — isn't that safer than trying to develop a full-cockpit scan?
questions.follow_up_answer: A ground spotter is a valuable mitigation tool but never a replacement for pilot situational awareness — and relying entirely on a spotter creates its own risks. Spotters can be distracted, may not understand rotor arc geometry, may communicate ambiguously, or may not be available at all. If you taxi into a situation where the spotter gives a wrong signal or loses sight of a hazard, the pilot who has been passively following directions has no independent assessment of the situation and cannot react before a strike occurs. FAA guidance makes clear that the pilot in command is ultimately responsible for the safe operation of the aircraft at all times, including during ground operations. The correct model is: the pilot maintains an active independent clearance scan and uses a spotter as a supplemental resource in high-risk situations, not as the primary clearance method. Additionally, in remote operations or unfamiliar fields, spotters won't be available, so the scan must be a trained, automatic habit.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 9; 14 CFR 91.3 (PIC responsibility)

questions.question: During a night taxi operation in a wheel-type helicopter on an unfamiliar ramp, what factors make managing airframe and rotor clearances significantly more difficult than during a daytime taxi, and what risk mitigations are specific to night ground operations?
questions.answer: Night taxi introduces several compounding clearance risks that don't exist during the day. First, depth perception is severely degraded at night, making it difficult to judge the distance between rotor blade tips and obstacles that may be only partially illuminated. Second, many ground obstacles — tie-down rings, low signage, fuel hose reels, ground power units, and parked aircraft wingtips — are at or below eye level and may not be lit or reflective, making them nearly invisible in the area beyond ramp lighting. Third, shadows cast by the helicopter's own lighting can create visual illusions about the position of obstacles. Fourth, the rotor disk itself is invisible at night except for blade tip lights (if installed), meaning the pilot has no direct visual reference for the disk's sweep. Mitigations specific to night operations include: conducting a thorough walking survey of the taxi route before engine start to identify unlighted hazards, using a briefed and positioned ground spotter with a light source at all times, minimizing taxi speed to allow maximum reaction time, using the helicopter's landing light and any available ramp lighting to illuminate the path ahead, reviewing the ramp diagram and knowing approximate distances to structures before moving, and if any uncertainty exists about clearances, stopping and hover-taxiing instead to regain visual reference from a higher vantage point.
questions.follow_up: If your landing light fails during night taxi and you have no spotter available, what is the appropriate decision and why?
questions.follow_up_answer: The appropriate decision is to stop the aircraft immediately in place, set the parking brake if equipped, and do not continue taxi until the lighting situation is resolved or a spotter is obtained. Without a landing light and without a spotter, you are operating blind relative to rotor and airframe clearances in the darkness ahead and to the sides — this is an unacceptable risk level that cannot be mitigated by technique alone. Options include: requesting that ground control or ramp personnel illuminate your route, contacting maintenance for a light fix, or waiting until conditions change (e.g., dawn). Proceeding would be a willful acceptance of a known hazard with no mitigation, which could constitute careless or reckless operation under 14 CFR 91.13. The PIC must refuse to accept unnecessary risk even under schedule pressure or operational urgency.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 9; 14 CFR 91.3; 14 CFR 91.13

questions.question: Before beginning a ground taxi in a wheel-equipped helicopter, which checklist(s) should you complete, and at what point in the sequence do you complete them?
questions.answer: At minimum, the pilot should complete the Before Taxi checklist (sometimes combined with the Before Takeoff or Run-Up checklist depending on the specific aircraft's POH/RFM). These are completed after engine start and before any ground movement begins. The specific checklist items and order are dictated by the Pilot's Operating Handbook or Rotorcraft Flight Manual for that aircraft. Completing checklists before movement ensures all systems—hydraulics, rotor RPM, engine instruments, controls—are verified within normal ranges prior to taxi.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.9; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 9 (Basic Flight Maneuvers); POH/RFM (aircraft-specific)

questions.question: What is the purpose of completing a checklist before taxiing a wheel-equipped helicopter, rather than relying on memory alone?
questions.answer: Checklists exist to ensure that no critical item is missed due to distraction, complacency, or task saturation. Memory alone is unreliable, particularly under stress or during high-workload phases. For a wheel-equipped helicopter preparing to taxi, a checklist verifies that flight controls are free and correct, rotor RPM is in the normal range, engine and transmission instruments are in the green, hydraulics are operational, brakes are checked, and the aircraft is configured for safe ground movement. The FAA strongly advocates the use of written checklists rather than 'do-lists' performed from memory.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 9; AC 120-71B (Standard Operating Procedures and Checklists)

questions.question: What specific flight control check is typically included in a before-taxi checklist for a wheel-equipped helicopter, and why is it important?
questions.answer: The flight controls check confirms that cyclic, collective, and anti-torque pedals are free of obstructions, move through the full range of motion without binding, and respond in the correct direction. For a wheel-equipped helicopter, this check also includes verifying that wheel brakes are operational. This is critical because a control restriction or incorrect rigging discovered on the ground prevents a potentially fatal in-flight emergency. The check is done with rotor turning at idle or operating RPM so that any resistance in the system under load can be detected.

questions.question: You're taxiing a wheel-equipped helicopter and realize you skipped the hydraulics check on the before-taxi checklist. You're already 200 feet from the parking spot. What do you do, and what is the risk of continuing without completing the missed item?
questions.answer: The correct action is to stop the aircraft using the wheel brakes, hold position safely clear of traffic, and complete the missed checklist item before continuing. Continuing without verifying hydraulic system status risks discovering a hydraulic failure only after significant control forces develop during taxi or takeoff. Helicopters with hydraulic boost systems can become very difficult or impossible to control safely if hydraulics fail and the pilot is unprepared. Stopping and completing the checklist is not a sign of poor airmanship — it demonstrates disciplined adherence to procedures, which is exactly what the examiner is evaluating under this ACS task.

questions.question: During a practical test, you are taxiing a wheel-equipped helicopter and the examiner asks you to explain what you just verified on the checklist before beginning taxi. How do you demonstrate knowledge of what you completed?
questions.answer: A competent pilot should be able to verbalize each item as it was accomplished — not just recite the list from memory, but explain what was checked and what an abnormal indication would look like. For example: 'I verified rotor RPM was in the normal operating range per the green arc on the tachometer, engine and transmission oil temperatures and pressures were in the green, flight controls moved freely and correctly, hydraulic pressure was in the normal range, and wheel brakes responded when tested.' This demonstrates that the checklist was used as a verification tool, not just paperwork. The examiner is looking for understanding, not rote recitation.

questions.question: A wheel-equipped helicopter's POH provides a checklist covering ground operations before and during taxi. Explain the purpose of this checklist and why following it in sequence is critical to safe taxiing operations.
questions.answer: The ground operations (taxi) checklist in the POH/RFM is a sequential verification completed before and during taxi to confirm that all systems are operational, the aircraft is configured correctly, and the pilot has received and understands clearances. Typical items include engine instruments, rotor RPM, flight controls, hydraulics, radios, transponder, lights, and brake function check. The checklist must be followed in the exact sequence and items specified in the aircraft's approved POH/RFM; skipping items or completing them from memory introduces significant risk of system failure, loss of directional control, or failure to comply with ATC instructions. Always reference the specific aircraft POH rather than assuming a standardized checklist structure across different helicopter types.

questions.question: You are operating a wheel-equipped helicopter at an unfamiliar airport and the crew at the FBO hands you a locally produced 'simplified taxi checklist' that omits several items from the POH. Are you permitted to use this substitute checklist, and what is your responsibility as PIC regarding checklist authority?
questions.answer: No — as PIC, you are not permitted to substitute an operator-produced or FBO-produced checklist for the approved POH/RFM checklist if it omits required items. Under 14 CFR 91.9 and 91.13, the PIC is responsible for operating the aircraft in accordance with the limitations and procedures in the approved flight manual. The POH/RFM is FAA-approved for that specific aircraft; any checklist used must be consistent with it. A locally produced checklist that omits items such as hydraulic checks or flight control verification could cause a pilot to miss a critical airworthiness item. The PIC has the authority and responsibility to reject any non-approved procedure and use the aircraft's own checklist.
questions.follow_up: What if the aircraft's POH checklist was left in the hangar and you only have the FBO's simplified version — can you still legally taxi the aircraft?
questions.follow_up_answer: Technically, there is no FAR that requires a paper copy of the checklist to be on board (unlike the POH itself under 14 CFR 91.9, which must be in the aircraft for required-manual aircraft). However, flying or taxiing without access to the approved checklist introduces serious safety risk and may constitute careless or reckless operation under 14 CFR 91.13 if a critical item is missed. The correct action is to retrieve the POH or obtain an approved copy before proceeding. Some operators maintain digital copies (EFB) as an acceptable alternative. The pilot should not proceed using only a third-party simplified list.

questions.question: During the checkride, you complete the before-taxi checklist and begin taxiing the wheel-equipped helicopter. The examiner then says, 'What would you do if you discovered mid-taxi that a checklist item you completed gave you a false sense of security — for example, you checked the brakes but the parking brake handle was already off and the brakes are actually fading?' How do you respond?
questions.answer: This is a trap question about the limits of checklist use and the need for continuous situational awareness. A checklist verifies a snapshot in time — it does not guarantee continued system performance. If brake fade or degraded braking is noticed during taxi (e.g., increasing pedal pressure required, pulling to one side, extended stopping distance), the pilot should immediately reduce taxi speed using collective reduction and pedal braking to the extent effective, steer clear of obstacles, communicate with ground control, and stop the aircraft. Depending on severity, this may require shutdown and maintenance inspection before flight. The checklist confirmed brakes were functional at the time of check — the pilot is responsible for ongoing monitoring throughout taxi. The examiner is testing whether the applicant understands that checklist completion is a starting point, not a guarantee.
questions.follow_up: If brake failure occurs during taxi and you cannot stop the helicopter conventionally, what technique can a helicopter pilot use that a fixed-wing pilot cannot?
questions.follow_up_answer: A helicopter pilot can use the collective to reduce rotor thrust and effectively reduce the load on the wheels, and can also use the rotor system to arrest forward momentum by pulling aft cyclic to tilt the disk rearward, creating a braking aerodynamic force against forward movement — a technique unavailable to fixed-wing pilots. In an extreme case with adequate clear area, the pilot could transition to a hover to fully stop ground movement. These options make wheel-equipped helicopters more recoverable from brake failure than fixed-wing aircraft, but they require the pilot to recognize the situation early and react promptly.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.13; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 9 and Chapter 11; Aircraft POH/RFM

questions.question: When is a pilot expected to use an airport or heliport taxi diagram during ground operations, and what regulatory or ACS requirements apply?
questions.answer: ACS skill HI.VIII.D.S2 requires demonstrated knowledge and use of published airport diagrams during taxi operations as evidence of safe airmanship and situational awareness. While 14 CFR Part 91 does not explicitly mandate diagram use, it requires safe operation (91.13) and compliance with ATC clearances (91.3). Using a published airport or heliport diagram during taxi is standard operating practice and is essential for maintaining situational awareness, identifying taxiway and runway locations, preventing runway incursions, and verifying compliance with ATC taxi instructions. The use of diagrams is a specific ACS knowledge and skill requirement for the commercial helicopter pilot practical exam.

questions.question: Where would you find a published airport diagram before conducting ground taxi operations at an unfamiliar towered airport?
questions.answer: Published airport diagrams are available on FAA-issued airport/facility directory products (Chart Supplement), on the FAA's Aeronav website, in the terminal procedures publications, and through approved electronic flight bag (EFB) applications. Many airports also have taxi diagrams included in the printed or digital terminal procedures. Pilots should obtain and review the current airport diagram before arrival at any unfamiliar airport.

questions.question: What information on an airport taxi diagram is most critical for a helicopter pilot taxiing on the surface with wheel-type landing gear at a large commercial airport?
questions.answer: The most critical information includes: runway and taxiway designators and their layout, hot spots (areas with increased collision or confusion risk), hold short lines, runway crossing points, helicopter movement areas or designated taxi routes if depicted, compass rose or north orientation, and any NOTAM-flagged closures. For helicopter-specific operations, any designated helicopter taxiways or ground movement areas should be identified and cross-referenced with the current ATIS and ATC clearance.

questions.question: You are taxiing your wheel-equipped helicopter at a busy Class B airport and ATC clears you to 'taxi to Runway 28R via Alpha, Bravo, hold short of Runway 28L.' You have the airport diagram in front of you. Walk me through how you would use that diagram during the taxi.
questions.answer: I would first locate my current position on the diagram and identify the full route: follow Taxiway Alpha to Taxiway Bravo, then proceed toward Runway 28R while stopping prior to the hold short line at Runway 28L. Using the diagram, I would note the geometry of the intersection, verify that the taxiway designators match the signage I see on the ground, anticipate any turns or complex intersections ahead, identify any hot spots along the route, and confirm the hold short location before I reach it. I would keep the diagram accessible throughout the taxi—not just look at it once—to maintain continuous situational awareness and compare the chart to what I'm seeing on the ground.

questions.question: You arrive at an airport where no official published taxi diagram exists. How does the absence of a diagram change your ground taxi technique in a wheel-equipped helicopter?
questions.answer: When no published diagram is available, I would increase reliance on other resources: the current ATIS for active runways, taxiway signage and markings on the surface, progressive taxi instructions from ATC if needed, and any general airport information in the Chart Supplement (formerly A/FD). I would taxi at a slower pace, especially at intersections, to allow more time for visual verification of signs and markings. I would not hesitate to request progressive taxi instructions from ground control. The ACS standard acknowledges this situation with the phrase 'if published'—the skill is to use a diagram when one exists, and to exercise increased vigilance and ATC assistance when it does not.

questions.question: During a checkride, you receive a complex taxi clearance at an unfamiliar airport and you're not sure you correctly heard all the taxiway names. The airport diagram is on your kneeboard. What is your correct course of action?
questions.answer: I would read back only what I am certain of to ATC and immediately request clarification on any portion I did not clearly copy. I would use the airport diagram to visually confirm the route as I read it back, cross-checking the taxiway names I heard against the diagram's layout to see if it makes geographic sense. If anything is ambiguous, I would say 'Ground, I need to verify the routing—please confirm the full clearance.' It is never acceptable to proceed with a taxi clearance that you are uncertain about. Stopping and clarifying is always correct. ATC expects readbacks and will correct any errors.

questions.question: A published airport diagram shows a hot spot labeled HS 3 along your ATC-assigned taxi route. The diagram legend describes it as a complex intersection with limited visibility. You are taxiing a wheel-equipped helicopter. How do you specifically address that hot spot during the taxi, and what is the significance of hot spot designations from a regulatory or advisory standpoint?
questions.answer: Approaching HS 3, I would slow my taxi speed well in advance, verify my position on the diagram, and visually scan all directions at the intersection before proceeding—treating it similar to a runway crossing in terms of deliberate look-before-proceed technique. I would confirm I have any required clearances if a runway is involved. Hot spots are depicted on airport diagrams by the FAA and ICAO as numbered circular labels; they are advisory in nature and defined in the Chart Supplement and on the diagram legend. They highlight areas of increased risk for runway incursions or confusion based on accident and incident history. While not regulatory requirements themselves, ignoring a known hot spot when it's published and you have the diagram constitutes a deviation from good airmanship and the ACS skill standard of using the diagram appropriately.
questions.follow_up: If you reach that intersection and the taxiway signage doesn't match what the diagram shows, what do you do?
questions.follow_up_answer: I would stop the helicopter in a safe position, clear of any runways or active movement areas, and contact ground control immediately to clarify my position and request assistance. I would not proceed into an uncertain intersection. This is a potential hot spot for runway incursion. I would also cross-reference the ATIS and any NOTAMs I received—signage discrepancies may be due to a published or unpublished construction area. The correct action is always stop, think, and communicate before proceeding when positional uncertainty exists.
questions.regulatory_ref: AIM 2-1-19; AIM 4-3-18; FAA Safety Team FAAST runway incursion guidance

questions.question: You are operating a wheel-equipped helicopter at a joint-use military/civilian airport. The FAA-published civilian airport diagram only shows the civilian side. ATC clears you to taxi through a portion of the ramp that appears to be on the military side. How do you handle the diagram limitation and what should you do before moving into that area?
questions.answer: I would recognize that the civilian airport diagram does not give me full situational awareness for the military portion of the airport, and I would not assume the military ramp has the same taxiway designators or layout depicted. Before proceeding, I would contact ground control and request clarification or progressive taxi instructions for that specific area. I would ask if there is any additional taxi chart or ramp information available for the military area, and confirm that ground control has positive control over that surface. I should also check NOTAMs for any joint-use restrictions or special instructions. Operating beyond the limits of your published diagram without supplemental information is a situational awareness risk—the ACS skill standard is to use the diagram appropriately, which includes recognizing its boundaries and limitations.
questions.follow_up: What if the military authority has a separate published diagram for that ramp area—are you required to have it, and where would you get it?
questions.follow_up_answer: There is no specific FAR requiring you to possess the military diagram, but good airmanship and the ACS standard of using 'an appropriate airport/heliport diagram or taxi chart, if published' implies that if a relevant published diagram exists and covers the area you are operating in, you should have it and use it. Military ramp diagrams may be available through the Defense Internet NOTAM Service (DINS), DoD Flight Information Publications (FLIP), or by coordinating with the base operations office in advance. For planned operations, I would obtain it during preflight planning. For an unexpected clearance, I would request progressive taxi from ground control rather than proceeding blind.
questions.regulatory_ref: ACS HI.VIII.D.S2; AIM 4-3-18; DoD FLIP publications; AIM 2-1-19

questions.question: On a wheel-equipped helicopter, what is the general rule for whether the nosewheel should be locked or unlocked during ground taxi operations?
questions.answer: The nosewheel should typically be unlocked during ground taxi so the helicopter can turn and maneuver freely. Locking the nosewheel is used for specific operations such as run-up or when the helicopter is being repositioned in a straight line and directional stability is needed. Always refer to the specific helicopter's Rotorcraft Flight Manual (RFM) for the manufacturer's guidance on nosewheel lock procedures.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 9; applicable aircraft RFM

questions.question: Why does a wheel-equipped helicopter with a steerable nosewheel or tailwheel have a lock mechanism in the first place? What purpose does locking serve?
questions.answer: The lock mechanism prevents the nosewheel or tailwheel from castering freely, which keeps it fixed in the straight-ahead position. This is useful during engine run-up to prevent unwanted turning from torque effects, during high-power operations on slopes, or when the helicopter needs to track straight without pilot steering input. Without locking capability, uncontrolled castering could cause the aircraft to veer unexpectedly during certain ground operations.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 9; applicable aircraft RFM

questions.question: Before you hover-taxi a wheel-equipped helicopter, how do you verify the nosewheel or tailwheel position and lock status are correct for that operation?
questions.answer: You verify by consulting the specific RFM checklist for the helicopter model, which will specify the required nosewheel or tailwheel position and lock/unlock status for hover taxi. Depending on the aircraft, there may be a cockpit indicator light or tactile feedback through the controls to confirm lock status. A visual check by a ground crew member can also confirm wheel position. Never assume the status — always verify per the checklist before beginning taxi.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 9; applicable aircraft RFM

questions.question: You are ground taxiing a wheeled helicopter and attempt to turn left, but the helicopter tracks straight ahead and resists the turn. What is the most likely cause, and how do you correct it?
questions.answer: The most likely cause is that the nosewheel or tailwheel lock is engaged, preventing the wheel from castering and following the intended turn. The correction is to stop the aircraft safely, disengage the wheel lock per the RFM procedure, verify the lock is released (via indicator or checklist confirmation), then resume taxi. Attempting to force a turn with the wheel locked can stress the landing gear, create a dynamic rollover risk, or cause the helicopter to tip unexpectedly.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 9; applicable aircraft RFM

questions.question: You are about to conduct a high-power engine run-up on a wheeled helicopter parked on a flat, paved surface. Should the nosewheel be locked or unlocked, and why does it matter for safety during run-up?
questions.answer: The nosewheel should be locked for a high-power run-up. During run-up, increased torque and vibration can cause the helicopter to yaw or creep on the ground. With the nosewheel unlocked, the wheel may caster and allow the aircraft to rotate or drift unexpectedly. Locking the nosewheel keeps the aircraft tracking straight and provides a more stable platform. Additionally, wheel chocks and rotor brakes (if equipped) should be used as supplemental restraints per the RFM. Always confirm lock status via the cockpit indicator before applying power.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 9; applicable aircraft RFM

questions.question: During a checkride, a candidate taxies a wheeled helicopter to the runway with the nosewheel locked, makes the turn onto the centerline without incident, then departs. As an examiner, why is this still a critical error even though the aircraft moved without apparent difficulty, and what unseen risk did the candidate create?
questions.answer: Taxiing with the nosewheel locked while attempting to turn places extreme lateral stress on the nosewheel strut, fork, and associated gear components — stress the landing gear is not designed to absorb in a lateral direction. Even if the helicopter completes the turn without visible difficulty, the locked wheel is dragged sideways rather than rolling freely, which can cause hidden structural fatigue, tire damage, or strut damage that may not be immediately apparent but could fail on landing. Additionally, if the helicopter's weight shifts during the turn (e.g., on a cambered taxiway), the risk of dynamic rollover increases significantly because the locked wheel acts as a pivot point, not a freely rotating support. The candidate demonstrated a lack of understanding of system limitations and created a latent airworthiness issue. This is a task failure under skills element HI.VIII.D.S3.
questions.follow_up: If the candidate argues that the helicopter 'felt fine' and the gear 'appeared undamaged' after landing, what action is required before the helicopter can legally return to service, and who has authority to make that determination?
questions.follow_up_answer: The aircraft cannot be returned to service without an inspection by an FAA-certificated airframe mechanic (A&P) or an inspector authorized under 14 CFR Part 43 who can assess the nosewheel strut, fork, bearings, and associated structure for hidden damage. Under 14 CFR 91.7, the pilot in command is responsible for ensuring the aircraft is airworthy before flight, but the determination of airworthiness after a suspected overload event requires a qualified mechanic. If there is any doubt, a maintenance record entry must be made describing the event, and the aircraft must be grounded until released by an appropriately certificated individual. The pilot cannot unilaterally declare the aircraft airworthy after a known improper operation.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 9; 14 CFR 91.7; 14 CFR Part 43

questions.question: You are flying a wheeled helicopter on a wet, sloped ramp and must reposition the aircraft by hover-taxiing across the slope. The RFM is silent on nosewheel lock/unlock for sloped hover taxi. How do you make that decision, and what additional risk factors does the nosewheel position introduce on a slope?
questions.answer: When the RFM does not directly address a specific configuration scenario, you apply the manufacturer's general principles and consult available guidance such as the Helicopter Flying Handbook and your training. For a sloped hover taxi, the nosewheel should generally remain unlocked to allow free castering during directional changes. However, on a slope, a freely castering nosewheel introduces the risk of the wheel turning downslope under gravity if the helicopter settles during a low hover, which can initiate a dynamic rollover scenario. The pilot must maintain sufficient altitude to prevent wheel contact during turns, keep groundspeed very low, and be prepared to abort the taxi if the aircraft settles unexpectedly. On a wet surface, both locked and unlocked wheels increase skid risk, so the preferred technique may be a true hover (wheels clear of the surface) rather than a surface hover-taxi. PIC authority under 14 CFR 91.3 allows the pilot to deviate from any rule to the extent necessary to meet an emergency, and good aeronautical decision-making under the PAVE model requires evaluating the environment before committing to the maneuver.
questions.follow_up: If you discover mid-maneuver that the nosewheel has castered 90 degrees sideways and the aircraft is beginning to settle on the slope, what is the immediate correct response and why?
questions.follow_up_answer: The immediate response is to apply collective to arrest the descent and return to a clear hover, preventing the cocked nosewheel from contacting the ground. If the wheel contacts the ground while cocked sideways at any groundspeed, it creates a lateral force at the gear that — combined with the slope and helicopter weight — dramatically increases dynamic rollover risk. Once safely in a hover, the pilot should use pedals and cyclic to straighten the aircraft's heading so the nosewheel aligns with the direction of travel before any further descent. The collective is the primary tool to buy time; attempting to correct the heading by yawing while descending with a cocked wheel can make the rollover risk worse. The maneuver should be aborted if safe alignment cannot be achieved.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapters 9 and 11; 14 CFR 91.3; applicable aircraft RFM

questions.question: When taxiing a wheel-equipped helicopter on the ground with a direct headwind, where should you position the cyclic, and why?
questions.answer: With a direct headwind, the cyclic should be held slightly forward (into the wind). This keeps the rotor disk tilted forward, which prevents the wind from getting under the aft portion of the disk and causing the nose to pitch up or the tail to lift. It also keeps weight on the forward part of the landing gear for better directional control.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 9 (Basic Flight Maneuvers / Ground Taxiing)

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of proper flight control positioning during ground taxi in a wheel-equipped helicopter?
questions.answer: The primary purpose is to prevent the wind from imposing asymmetric aerodynamic forces on the rotor disk that could cause loss of directional control, tipping, or dynamic rollover. Proper control positioning counters wind effects and keeps the helicopter stable on its landing gear throughout the taxi.

questions.question: With a direct tailwind during ground taxi on wheel-type gear, how should you position the cyclic, and what condition are you specifically trying to avoid?
questions.answer: With a direct tailwind, hold the cyclic aft (toward the tail, into the wind). This prevents the wind from getting under the forward rotor disk, which could cause the nose to pitch down and the tail to rise — potentially causing a tail strike or loss of directional control. Aft cyclic keeps the disk tilted into the relative wind.

questions.question: You are taxiing a wheel-equipped helicopter with a 15-knot wind coming from your left at approximately 90 degrees. Describe exactly how you would position the cyclic and collective, and explain your reasoning for each.
questions.answer: Position the cyclic into the wind — in this case, to the left — to prevent the wind from lifting the upwind (left) side of the rotor disk and causing the helicopter to roll or tip to the right. The collective should remain low to keep full weight on the landing gear, reducing the risk of dynamic rollover. Tilting the disk into the crosswind counteracts the lateral aerodynamic force and helps maintain directional stability throughout the taxi.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 9; Chapter 11 (Dynamic Rollover)

questions.question: During ground taxi on a ramp, you notice the helicopter is starting to weathervane into the wind despite your pedal inputs. What does this tell you about the situation, and how do you correct it while maintaining safe directional control with the landing gear still on the surface?
questions.answer: Weathervaning means the wind is overpowering your antitorque authority. You should reduce taxi speed so pedal inputs become more effective, and adjust cyclic to keep the rotor disk tilted into the wind to reduce asymmetric lift forces. If the wind is gusty or very strong, it may be safer to stop, get assistance, or reposition using ground crew. Attempting to force directional control with excessive pedal at speed can induce yaw oscillations or allow a gust to cause a tip-over.

questions.question: You are taxiing a wheel-equipped helicopter and the wind is from the left quartering front (about 45 degrees off the nose from the left). How do you position the cyclic, and is there any concern about rotor blade clearance on the downwind side?
questions.answer: With a left quartering headwind, position the cyclic forward and to the left — into the wind — to keep the rotor disk tilted against the wind and prevent it from being lifted on the upwind side. On the downwind (right rear) side, the descending blade may have reduced clearance as the disk tilts. You must be aware of tail rotor, fences, parked aircraft, or other obstacles in that quadrant. Maintain a slow, controlled taxi speed and remain vigilant about ground clearances on the downwind side.

questions.question: A student taxiing a wheel-equipped helicopter in a strong right crosswind begins applying left cyclic as trained, but the left main gear starts to lift slightly. You take the controls. Walk me through exactly what happened aerodynamically and what control inputs you use to correct the situation without causing a dynamic rollover.
questions.answer: The left cyclic tilted the rotor disk into the wind, creating a horizontal component of rotor thrust to the left — but at some point, the combination of crosswind lift and lateral rotor thrust began to unload the left main gear. This is the onset of dynamic rollover around the right gear acting as a pivot point. To correct: smoothly reduce collective immediately — this removes excess lift and reloads the left gear with weight. Simultaneously, ease the cyclic to a more neutral position rather than adding more left cyclic, which could worsen the rolling moment. Never apply opposite (right) cyclic aggressively once rollover has started, as this can increase disk tilt and aggravate the condition. Once the gear is re-loaded, gradually re-establish the correct into-wind cyclic at a lower intensity. The critical error was likely excessive left cyclic combined with collective that was too high.
questions.follow_up: What is the critical rollover angle for most helicopters, and at what point is recovery no longer possible?
questions.follow_up_answer: Most helicopters reach an unrecoverable dynamic rollover condition between approximately 5 and 8 degrees of roll depending on the design. Beyond this angle, the rolling moment produced by the rotor exceeds what collective reduction can overcome and the helicopter will continue to roll over regardless of control input. This is why early recognition — at the first sign of gear unloading — and immediate collective reduction are critical. Waiting even a second too long can place the helicopter past the point of no return. Reference: FAA-H-8083-21B, Chapter 11 (Dynamic Rollover).
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 11 (Dynamic Rollover)

questions.question: You are taxiing downwind on a rain-slicked taxiway in a wheel-equipped helicopter. The wind is 20 knots from behind you. Explain how the combination of tailwind, wet surface, and wheel-type gear changes your control strategy compared to a dry, calm-day taxi, and what loss-of-directional-control scenario concerns you most.
questions.answer: With a tailwind, cyclic goes aft into the wind to prevent the disk from being forced forward and causing nose pitch-down. On a wet surface, wheel braking effectiveness is significantly reduced, so any yaw or directional deviation requires more anticipation because you cannot rely on differential braking to rescue a skidding turn. The scenario of greatest concern is a ground loop — where the tail swings downwind faster than you can correct with pedal and the nose swings into the wind, causing an uncontrolled rapid yaw on the wet surface with the gear potentially side-loading and tipping. To mitigate: keep groundspeed very slow (walking pace or less), use smooth coordinated pedal inputs well in advance of any needed turn, keep collective low to maximize gear friction, and avoid any sharp turns. If directional control feels marginal, stop and reassess rather than continue the taxi.
questions.follow_up: If you lose directional control on that wet taxiway and the helicopter begins rotating, what is your last-resort option before a rotor strike occurs?
questions.follow_up_answer: If the helicopter begins an uncontrolled rotation on the ground with rotor turning and a rotor or tail strike is imminent, the last-resort action is to reduce collective fully to load all gear weight and slow the rotation, while simultaneously rolling the throttle to flight idle or activating the engine shutoff — removing rotor thrust entirely to arrest the dynamic. This sacrifices the aircraft systems but may prevent a catastrophic rotor strike or rollover. This is an extreme emergency measure and should only be used when all other control options are exhausted and structural damage is otherwise certain.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 9 (Taxiing), Chapter 11 (Dynamic Rollover / Ground Handling Emergencies)

questions.question: When taxiing a helicopter on wheel-type landing gear, which control is primarily used to initiate forward movement from a stationary position?
questions.answer: The cyclic is used to initiate forward movement by tilting the rotor disk forward. A small forward cyclic input causes the helicopter to begin rolling forward. The collective may be adjusted slightly to unload the skids or wheels as needed, but cyclic is the primary control for establishing direction and initiating taxi movement.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 9 – Basic Flight Maneuvers

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of the collective during a ground taxi on wheel-type landing gear, and how should it generally be positioned?
questions.answer: During ground taxi on wheel-type landing gear, the collective is kept relatively low — enough to partially unload the landing gear and reduce friction, but not so high that the helicopter becomes airborne. The collective should not be used to control taxi speed directly; rather, brakes and cyclic are used for speed control. Raising collective too much risks inadvertent liftoff.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 9 – Basic Flight Maneuvers

questions.question: During ground taxi in a wheel-equipped helicopter, what is the proper technique for slowing down or stopping?
questions.answer: To slow down or stop during ground taxi, the pilot applies the wheel brakes while simultaneously moving the cyclic aft slightly to reduce the forward rotor disk tilt and prevent the nose from pitching over. Brakes are the primary stopping device on wheel-equipped helicopters. The collective should remain low but not be raised during braking, as excessive collective application could cause the helicopter to become light on its gear.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 9 – Basic Flight Maneuvers

questions.question: You are taxiing a wheel-equipped helicopter on a sloped taxiway that angles downhill toward the ramp. How do you coordinate cyclic, collective, and brakes to safely control speed on the downslope?
questions.answer: On a downhill slope, the helicopter will naturally accelerate due to gravity. The pilot should apply aft cyclic to reduce forward disk tilt and counteract the downhill tendency, use the wheel brakes intermittently or continuously as needed to maintain a slow, controlled taxi speed, and keep collective low to avoid becoming airborne. The key is to avoid relying solely on brakes — aft cyclic must also be used to prevent the nose from pitching forward under braking. Taxi speed should be kept to a walking pace or slower in all conditions.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 9 – Basic Flight Maneuvers

questions.question: During a ground taxi demonstration, you notice the student has raised the collective to slow the helicopter down instead of using brakes. What is the hazard with this technique, and what is the correct procedure?
questions.answer: Raising the collective to slow ground taxi speed is incorrect and dangerous because it partially unloads the landing gear, making the helicopter light on its wheels and susceptible to inadvertent liftoff — especially in gusty wind conditions. If the helicopter becomes airborne unexpectedly at low altitude without the pilot being prepared for flight, the risk of loss of control is significant. The correct technique is to use the wheel brakes as the primary speed-reduction tool, supplemented with aft cyclic to reduce disk tilt, while keeping collective low and stable throughout the taxi.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 9 – Basic Flight Maneuvers

questions.question: A crosswind is blowing from the left while you are taxiing forward on wheel-type gear. How does this affect your cyclic inputs, and what are you trying to prevent?
questions.answer: In a left crosswind during ground taxi, the rotor disk tends to be pushed downward on the upwind (left) side, and the retreating blade experiences reduced lift. The pilot should apply into-the-wind (left) cyclic to level the rotor disk and prevent the upwind skid or wheel from rising. Without this correction, the helicopter could begin to weathervane into the wind, develop a lateral rolling tendency, or in extreme cases tip over. The cyclic must continuously compensate for crosswind effects throughout the taxi to keep the rotor disk level and maintain directional control.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 9 – Basic Flight Maneuvers

questions.question: During a practical test, a candidate taxies the wheel-equipped helicopter at an excessive speed and then brakes abruptly while simultaneously pulling the cyclic aft. The helicopter's nose pitches up aggressively and the main rotor comes dangerously close to the tail boom. What caused this, and what is the correct recovery and preventive technique?
questions.answer: Abrupt aft cyclic combined with hard braking creates an additive nose-up pitch moment — braking transfers weight forward onto the nose gear, but the aggressive aft cyclic simultaneously tilts the rotor disk rearward, driving the tail of the helicopter down and pitching the nose up sharply. This can result in main rotor blade contact with the tail boom, which is a catastrophic outcome. The correct technique is to apply brakes gradually and smoothly, while using only a moderate aft cyclic input proportional to the deceleration needed — never an aggressive pull. Taxi speed must be kept slow (walking pace) so that braking demands are minimal and control inputs remain small. Prevention is key: maintain appropriate taxi speed from the start so emergency braking is never required.
questions.follow_up: If the main rotor blade does strike the tail boom during a ground taxi incident, what are the immediate actions and what airworthiness concern exists before any further flight?
questions.follow_up_answer: Immediately shut down the engine and secure the helicopter. Do not attempt flight.
