It is a precursor to controlled flight into terrain or settling with power.

questions.question: During your steep approach briefing, you identify a potential distraction — a passenger who tends to ask questions during critical phases. What task prioritization principle should guide how you handle this?
questions.answer: Aviate, Navigate, Communicate — in that order. The pilot must maintain aircraft control first. Passenger communication is a non-critical task and should be deferred until a stabilized hover or ground contact is achieved. Briefing passengers before the approach begins is the proper mitigation: inform them that there will be no communication during the approach and that questions should wait until after landing.

questions.question: You are on a steep approach to a mountaintop pinnacle when ATC calls with a new transponder code and requests a readback. You are passing through 200 feet AGL at a high rate of descent. How should you prioritize this situation?
questions.answer: Aviate first — do not reach for the transponder or respond to ATC until you have stabilized the approach or transitioned to a go-around. If workload allows, a brief 'standby' call is appropriate, but no head-down task should be performed during this critical phase. After landing or going around and reaching a stable condition, respond to ATC. Attempting to dial a transponder code on a steep approach at 200 feet AGL is exactly the kind of distraction that breaks the error chain link leading to CFIT.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (ADM, Error Chain); 14 CFR 91.123 (ATC compliance)

questions.question: On a steep approach over unfamiliar terrain, you become uncertain whether you have cleared the obstacle at the top of the approach path. You think the rotor will 'probably' clear it. According to sound ADM principles, what should you do and why?
questions.answer: The word 'probably' is a red flag in aeronautical decision-making. If the pilot cannot confirm obstacle clearance, the correct action is to go around and re-evaluate — either by performing a high reconnaissance to verify obstacle height, or by choosing an alternate approach path. The FAA's ADM guidance specifically cautions pilots to avoid choosing an action that will only 'probably' work; instead, select the option known to work. Continuing when uncertain is a classic error chain link.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (ADM, Trescott Tip on 'probably'); Chapter 10 (Pinnacle/Confined Area Reconnaissance)

questions.question: You are flying a steep approach into a confined area at dusk with sloping terrain on both sides. Halfway down the approach, you realize you have lost your visual reference to the landing zone due to shadowing. Describe the risks present and your response.
questions.answer: This scenario combines spatial disorientation risk, loss of situational awareness, and potential CFIT — a compounding error chain. The risks include: inability to judge descent rate visually, misjudging slope angle, and inadvertent terrain contact. The correct response is to immediately execute a go-around using instrument cross-check to maintain controlled flight while climbing away from terrain. Do not continue a steep approach without a clear visual reference to the landing zone. Post-go-around, reassess the approach with improved lighting or choose an alternate site.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10 (Confined Area Operations, Go-Around Decision); Chapter 11 (CFIT Awareness); Chapter 13 (ADM)

questions.question: During a steep approach with a student pilot on the controls, the student becomes task-saturated and fixated on the landing point while airspeed decays well below ETL with rotor RPM beginning to droop. As the instructor, how do you recognize this specific situational awareness failure, and at what point must you intervene?
questions.answer: The student has fallen into 'target fixation' — a form of loss of situational awareness where one parameter (landing spot) consumes all attentional resources while other critical parameters (airspeed, Nr, collective position) go unmonitored. Recognition cues include: no pilot-induced corrections to airspeed decay, absence of collective increase despite slowing below ETL, and Nr droop audible or visible on the tachometer. Intervention must occur before the situation becomes unrecoverable — in practice, the moment Nr begins to droop below the green arc on a steep approach with insufficient altitude for recovery, the instructor must take controls immediately. The rule is: never let a training situation deteriorate to the point where a safe recovery requires exceptional skill. Verbalize the takeover: 'I have the controls,' then execute a go-around.
questions.follow_up: After the go-around, the student asks why you intervened 'so early' — how do you explain the recovery window concept specific to steep approaches?
questions.follow_up_answer: On a steep approach, the helicopter is operating at a high descent rate, low airspeed, and high power demand simultaneously. If Nr droops and collective must be raised to arrest descent, you are simultaneously demanding more power from an already-loaded system and reducing the aerodynamic force driving the rotor. The recovery window — the combination of altitude, airspeed, and Nr available to execute a safe go-around — shrinks extremely rapidly on a steep approach. Unlike a normal approach where gradual parameter decay gives more time, a steep approach can transition from manageable to unrecoverable within seconds. Early intervention preserves options; late intervention eliminates them.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10 (Steep Approach); Chapter 11 (Low Rotor RPM/Rotor Stall); Chapter 13 (ADM, Error Chain); 14 CFR 61.195 (Flight Instructor Responsibilities)

questions.question: You are conducting a solo steep approach to a remote helipad. You have the landing zone in sight, but you notice the wind sock is no longer visible due to your approach angle and ambient lighting. You realize you are unsure of the current wind direction at the pad level. Describe how this loss of situational awareness could cascade into a serious incident, and what risk mitigation steps should have been taken before and during the approach.
questions.answer: Loss of wind awareness at pad level on a steep approach creates a cascading risk: if the surface wind has shifted, you may be unknowingly flying a downwind or crosswind steep approach. A tailwind on final increases groundspeed and effective approach angle, reduces ETL effectiveness, and may require more power than anticipated — potentially exceeding OGE hover power available, especially at elevation or on a hot day. Disorientation can compound if the hover drift at the pad is opposite to expectation. Mitigation steps that should have been taken: (1) Pre-approach reconnaissance — observe the wind sock and other wind indicators at a known angle before committing to the approach; (2) Determine the approach corridor that allows an abort path and is aligned with the wind; (3) Establish a 'no-go' decision point with defined abort criteria including unexpected drift or power demand; (4) If wind confirmation is lost mid-approach, treat it as an unknown hazard and go around to reassess.
questions.follow_up: If you arrive at the hover point and realize you have a tailwind of approximately 10 knots, what aerodynamic and performance consequences must you immediately account for?
questions.follow_up_answer: A 10-knot tailwind at the hover means translational lift is working against you — the rotor is operating in less efficient airflow, increasing induced power requirement. You are effectively in a degraded OGE hover condition because the relative wind is reducing disk efficiency rather than enhancing it. Additionally, any attempt to transition forward to go around requires accelerating into the headwind direction first, which may mean climbing over terrain or obstacles in the tailwind direction. Power margins must be immediately verified against the AFM OGE hover chart for current conditions. If power margins are insufficient, the pilot is in a performance trap — unable to hover efficiently or depart safely — underscoring why wind confirmation before committing to a steep approach is non-negotiable.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10 (Steep Approach, Confined Area Reconnaissance, Abort Planning); Chapter 11 (LTE, Loss of Tail Rotor Effectiveness in Tailwind); Chapter 13 (ADM, Risk Management)

questions.question: What is loss of tail rotor effectiveness (LTE), and what does the term mean in plain language?
questions.answer: LTE is a condition in which the tail rotor is generating thrust but that thrust is insufficient to maintain directional control of the helicopter. The tail rotor is still turning and producing some thrust — it has not failed — but aerodynamic forces are overpowering it, causing uncommanded yaw. In a counterclockwise-main-rotor helicopter (most American designs), LTE results in an uncommanded right yaw. LTE is not a mechanical failure; it is an aerodynamic phenomenon.

questions.question: What is the immediate pilot action when an uncommanded right yaw begins and LTE is suspected at low altitude?
questions.answer: The immediate recovery action is: (1) Apply full left pedal simultaneously with (2) moving the cyclic forward to increase airspeed (above 30 KIAS ETL restores aerodynamic directional stability), and (3) if altitude permits, reduce collective to decrease torque demand on the tail rotor. If rotation cannot be stopped and ground contact is imminent, execute a hovering autorotation or run-on landing with the aircraft in a wings-level attitude. The key priority is arresting the yaw before it becomes uncontrollable.

questions.question: You are conducting a steep approach into a confined area. Wind is from your 10 o'clock position at 12 knots. As you slow through translational lift and begin to increase collective, you notice a slow right yaw developing. What specific risk factors present in this scenario are compounding to increase your LTE susceptibility?
questions.answer: Multiple LTE risk factors are stacking in this scenario: (1) Loss of ETL during the steep approach reduces aerodynamic anti-torque contribution and increases tail rotor workload; (2) Increased collective to maintain approach profile increases engine torque, demanding more tail rotor thrust at the exact moment its effectiveness may be degraded; (3) The wind from the 10 o'clock position (roughly 300°–330° relative) places you in or near the tail rotor vortex ring state azimuth band (285°–315°), where the tail rotor can begin ingesting its own vortex; (4) Low airspeed and low altitude reduce your margin for recovery. The combination of high power demand, loss of ETL, and an adverse wind azimuth creates the classic LTE setup.
questions.regulatory_ref: AC 90-95; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10 (steep approach) and Chapter 11 (LTE)

questions.question: How does high density altitude increase LTE risk during a steep approach, and what preflight risk mitigation strategies should a pilot consider?
questions.answer: At high density altitude, air is less dense, which reduces tail rotor thrust output for a given pitch angle — the tail rotor must work harder to produce the same anti-torque force. Additionally, the engine produces less power, meaning the pilot may demand a higher percentage of available tail rotor authority just to maintain level hover or a stabilized approach. This narrows the margin before LTE occurs. Preflight mitigations include: (1) Perform a performance calculation to confirm OGE hover capability — if OGE hover is marginal, the approach is high-risk; (2) Plan the approach heading to avoid the three adverse LTE wind azimuths; (3) Minimize time at low airspeed and high power settings; (4) Select approach paths that allow an escape route or run-on landing option if yaw control is lost; (5) Brief the abort point before committing to the confined area.
questions.regulatory_ref: AC 90-95; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10 and Chapter 11; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 7 (performance planning)

questions.question: A student pilot argues that LTE cannot happen during a steep approach because 'the wind is helping the helicopter slow down.' How would you correct this misunderstanding, and what does wind direction during a steep approach actually mean for LTE risk?
questions.answer: The student is confusing headwind value (its contribution to airspeed and deceleration) with wind azimuth relative to the tail rotor. A headwind may help slow the helicopter aerodynamically, but the direction the wind strikes the tail rotor assembly is what determines LTE susceptibility — not whether the wind is a headwind from the pilot's perspective. If the wind is from the left front quarter (approximately 285°–315° relative), it enters the tail rotor disc from the leading edge, promoting tail rotor vortex ring state regardless of whether the pilot perceives it as a headwind. Additionally, as the helicopter decelerates on a steep approach and loses ETL, the effective wind contribution to directional stability diminishes, and tail rotor demand increases. Wind is not an LTE-prevention tool — it can be a contributing cause depending on its azimuth.

questions.question: During a checkride steep approach, your applicant correctly slows to an appropriate final approach airspeed but then uses left pedal aggressively to align with the landing area centerline just before transitioning to a hover. The wind is approximately 15 knots from the left rear (about 210°–240° relative). What specific LTE mechanism are you concerned about, and why does the pedal input at this phase make the situation more dangerous — not less?
questions.answer: The wind azimuth of 210°–240° places the helicopter in the main rotor tip vortex interference zone, where main rotor vortices are carried rearward into the tail rotor disc, disrupting its efficiency and reducing effective thrust. At this point, the tail rotor is already operating in degraded aerodynamic conditions. When the applicant applies aggressive left pedal to align with the centerline, they are demanding increased tail rotor pitch and thrust output at exactly the moment the tail rotor's aerodynamic environment is already compromised. Additionally, during the transition to hover, ETL is being lost, removing the aerodynamic stabilizing contribution to directional control. The aggressive pedal application increases the blade angle on the tail rotor, which can further destabilize airflow over the blades — potentially worsening vortex ingestion. The correct technique is smooth, anticipatory pedal inputs early in the approach so that large control demands are not required at the most vulnerable phase: low, slow, and high-power.
questions.follow_up: If the applicant's right yaw begins to accelerate and full left pedal alone is not arresting the rotation at 30 feet AGL over the landing spot, what is the decision hierarchy at that point, and what control input mistake must be avoided?
questions.follow_up_answer: At 30 feet AGL with an accelerating right yaw that full left pedal cannot stop, the priority is to get the helicopter on the ground in a survivable attitude before rotation rate increases further. The pilot should simultaneously lower the collective to reduce torque demand (if ground contact is seconds away), allow the nose to continue rotating as needed to align with a safe touchdown attitude, and accept a firm but controlled landing. The critical mistake to avoid is pulling collective in an attempt to cushion the landing or 'buy time' — increasing collective at this point increases engine torque and actively worsens the yaw, accelerating rotation and potentially resulting in a high-energy rollover or dynamic rollover on ground contact. The FAA and AC 90-95 both emphasize that adding collective during LTE recovery at very low altitude is a known fatal error pattern.

questions.question: A highly experienced pilot tells you they never worry about LTE because their helicopter has a fenestron (shrouded tail rotor) and claims it is 'immune to LTE.' How do you evaluate this claim, and what nuanced risk factors remain even with a fenestron design?
questions.answer: The claim is an oversimplification. While fenestron designs do offer meaningful advantages — the shroud reduces tip losses, provides some protection from ground strike, and the enclosed airflow can reduce susceptibility to external vortex interference — fenestron-equipped helicopters are not immune to all LTE mechanisms. Specifically: (1) The weathercock stability effect (wind from approximately 210°–330°) still acts on any helicopter regardless of tail rotor design, because it is a fuselage aerodynamic phenomenon, not a rotor phenomenon; (2) At very high power demands and low airspeeds, any tail rotor system — fenestron included — can be overpowered if the aerodynamic anti-torque demand exceeds available thrust; (3) At high density altitudes, fenestrons suffer the same thrust degradation as conventional tail rotors due to reduced air density. The pilot's confidence in equipment is itself an ADM risk factor — overconfidence based on a specific design feature can lead to placing the aircraft in situations that exceed even the fenestron's enhanced margins. Each aircraft must be operated within its specific RFM limitations regardless of tail rotor design.
questions.follow_up: What ADM concept best describes the risk this experienced pilot is demonstrating, and how would you address it in a preflight briefing context?
questions.follow_up_answer: This pilot is demonstrating 'invulnerability' — one of the classic hazardous attitudes identified in FAA ADM doctrine — combined with equipment-specific overconfidence. They believe a specific technology makes them exempt from a known risk. In a preflight briefing, the appropriate approach is to acknowledge the genuine advantages of the fenestron design (to maintain credibility), then redirect to the specific scenarios and conditions where LTE risk remains real for that aircraft type, referencing the aircraft's RFM and the applicable wind azimuth diagrams. Framing it around the specific performance limits of the aircraft model — rather than a general LTE lecture — is more likely to be received by an experienced pilot and aligns with SRM principles: use all available resources (including the RFM) to inform risk decisions.
questions.regulatory_ref: AC 90-95; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11 and Chapter 13 (ADM/hazardous attitudes); aircraft-specific RFM

questions.question: What is a Degraded Visual Environment (DVE), and give two examples specific to helicopter operations during a steep approach?
questions.answer: A Degraded Visual Environment (DVE) is any condition that reduces a pilot's ability to perceive visual cues needed for safe flight and obstacle avoidance. Examples specific to steep approaches include: blowing dust or sand kicked up by rotor wash during a confined area approach, snow or water spray obscuring the landing zone, smoke or haze reducing contrast near the touchdown point, and flat light conditions over featureless terrain such as snow-covered or desert surfaces. DVE is particularly hazardous during steep approaches because the pilot relies heavily on visual depth perception and slope/obstacle cues during the high rate of descent phase.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10 and Chapter 11; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (ADM/SRM)

questions.question: What is flat light, and why is it especially dangerous during the final portion of a steep approach to a pinnacle or ridgeline?
questions.answer: Flat light is a phenomenon that occurs when an overcast sky or uniform lighting eliminates shadows and contrast, making it nearly impossible to perceive terrain features, surface texture, slope, and depth. It is especially dangerous during the final portion of a steep approach to a pinnacle or ridgeline because the pilot needs accurate visual reference to judge height above the surface, identify obstacles, and assess slope angle. Without shadow or contrast, the pilot may misjudge the landing surface as level when it is sloped, fail to see rocks or brush, or flare too high or too low. This can result in dynamic rollover, main rotor/tail rotor strikes, or a hard landing.

questions.question: During a steep approach in DVE conditions, what is the significance of losing Effective Translational Lift (ETL) at a higher altitude than a normal approach?
questions.answer: During a steep approach, the helicopter transitions through ETL at a higher altitude above the ground than during a normal approach due to the steeper angle of descent. This means the pilot must increase collective power earlier to compensate for the loss of ETL-induced lift. In DVE or flat light conditions, the pilot may not have reliable visual cues to judge when this altitude is being reached or how quickly the helicopter is descending, making it difficult to time the power addition correctly. This increases the risk of an uncontrolled descent into terrain or arriving at the landing zone with insufficient power to arrest the descent, especially if already near OGE hover power limits.

questions.question: You are conducting a steep approach to a snow-covered ridgeline in overcast conditions. As you descend through 200 feet AGL, flat light makes the surface indistinguishable from the sky. What risk management actions should you take before and during this approach?
questions.answer: Before the approach: (1) Perform a thorough high and low reconnaissance to memorize landmark references such as rocks, trees, or color variations that can help judge height and slope in flat light. (2) Identify abort decision points and an escape route. (3) Calculate OGE hover power requirement and verify power available exceeds it. (4) Brief yourself on expected rate of descent and power cues to substitute for degraded visual references. During the approach: (1) Use instrument references (VSI, radar altimeter if equipped, torque gauge) to supplement or replace degraded visual cues. (2) Slow the approach as early as possible to maximize control response time. (3) If visual reference is lost entirely, initiate a go-around immediately — do not continue into a deteriorating visual environment. (4) Use any available contrast markers (ground crew, surveyor stakes, colored tape on the LZ) to maintain orientation. The key ADM principle: if the situation will 'probably' be okay, choose the option you know will work — in this case, a go-around.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10 (Reconnaissance Procedures, Steep Approach); Chapter 13 (ADM, Trescott Tip)

questions.question: During a steep approach to a confined area at dusk, rotor wash begins kicking up dust and reduces visibility to near zero just before touchdown. Walk me through your decision-making process using the SRM framework.
questions.answer: Using Single-Pilot Resource Management (SRM): (1) Situational Awareness — recognize immediately that visual cues for height, drift, and obstacles have been lost; this is a DVE emergency, not a minor inconvenience. (2) Risk Management — the risk of continuing blind into an unknown surface with obstacles far outweighs the risk of initiating a go-around; the error chain has begun (dusk + dusty LZ + steep approach = accumulating risks). (3) Workload Management — prioritize aircraft control first: stop any descent, maintain coordinated flight, and transition to instrument references (VSI, airspeed, torque) while executing the go-around. (4) CFIT Awareness — the greatest threat is controlled flight into terrain or obstacles obscured by the dust cloud; arrest the descent before attempting any lateral movement. (5) Decision — execute a go-around immediately, climb to a safe altitude, and re-evaluate. Do not attempt to 'feel' for the ground. Reassess whether an alternative LZ or delay until conditions improve is warranted.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (SRM, ADM, Error Chain); Chapter 10 (Confined Area Operations)

questions.question: A pilot argues that because they know the landing zone well from previous visits, flat light conditions during a steep approach are not a significant risk. How would you challenge this reasoning from a risk management standpoint?
questions.answer: Familiarity with a landing zone does not eliminate the hazards of flat light — it may actually increase risk by creating overconfidence. The dangers of flat light are not about knowing the location but about the loss of real-time visual depth perception and contrast needed to judge height, slope, and surface conditions at the moment of approach. Surface conditions change: snow depth varies, ice forms, new obstacles appear. Even an experienced pilot cannot mentally substitute for absent visual cues at the critical moment of flare and touchdown. Additionally, pilot error and poor decision-making contribute significantly to aviation accidents, and dismissing a known hazard because of familiarity is itself a poor decision that creates an error chain. The correct approach is to treat DVE/flat light as an objective environmental risk that requires mitigation regardless of experience at that specific site.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (ADM, Human Factors, ~80% pilot error statistic); Chapter 10 (Steep Approach)

questions.question: During a steep approach in DVE, a pilot transitions their scan entirely to the instrument panel and loses situational awareness of a power line crossing the approach path. What does this scenario illustrate about the limitations of using instruments as a DVE mitigation strategy during a steep approach, and what should the pilot have done differently?
questions.answer: This scenario illustrates the critical limitation of instrument scanning as a DVE mitigation strategy during low-altitude visual flight operations: instruments provide attitude, power, and rate data, but they cannot substitute for obstacle avoidance, which requires outside visual reference. In DVE, the correct strategy is not to abandon the outside scan in favor of instruments, but to integrate instrument cues to supplement — not replace — whatever outside visual references remain. The pilot should have: (1) completed a thorough low reconnaissance at a safe altitude to identify and memorize obstacle locations, including the power line, before beginning the approach; (2) established a mental model of the approach corridor so that even degraded visual cues could be cross-referenced against known obstacles; (3) maintained a divided scan — using instruments to manage descent rate and power while continuing to scan outside for obstacles at the expected position; (4) positioned a ground guide if available to identify obstacles in real time. The fundamental principle is that in DVE, risk management begins with the reconnaissance and abort decision, not with the approach itself.
questions.follow_up: If during the low reconnaissance you couldn't clearly see the power line due to flat light, at what point in your decision-making process should the steep approach have been abandoned?
questions.follow_up_answer: The steep approach should have been abandoned during the reconnaissance phase, before ever committing to the approach. If a hazard as significant as a power line cannot be positively identified and located during reconnaissance due to DVE or flat light, the landing zone has not been adequately assessed and the approach does not meet the standard required for safe operations. The reconnaissance is the risk management tool — if it fails to produce sufficient situational awareness, the answer is not to proceed anyway. The pilot should either delay until lighting conditions improve, request a ground guide to physically mark the power line, approach from a different direction that avoids the obstacle corridor, or select an alternate landing zone. Proceeding with an approach when a known obstacle cannot be confirmed is an unacceptable risk regardless of operational pressure.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10 (Reconnaissance Procedures, Confined Area, Pinnacle Operations); Chapter 13 (ADM, SRM, Error Chain)

questions.question: A helicopter pilot is authorized under BasicMed and has been hired to fly a film crew into a mountain location requiring a steep approach over snow-covered terrain. Flat light conditions are forecast. What are the regulatory and risk management concerns specific to this scenario?
questions.answer: There are both regulatory and risk management concerns here. Regulatory: BasicMed under 14 CFR Part 68 and 61.113(i) prohibits operations for compensation or hire. Flying a film crew who has hired the pilot constitutes compensation or hire, making BasicMed invalid for this operation — the pilot would require a valid FAA medical certificate (at minimum a Third Class). If the pilot proceeds under BasicMed for this paid operation, they are operating illegally. Risk Management: Assuming the regulatory issue is resolved with a proper medical, the DVE/flat light concern for a steep approach over snow-covered mountain terrain is significant. Risk mitigation should include: (1) thorough high and low reconnaissance before committing to approach; (2) identification of abort decision points and escape routes; (3) verification that OGE hover power is available at that altitude and density altitude; (4) use of instrument references to supplement degraded visual cues; (5) go/no-go criteria established before flight — not in the moment under passenger or mission pressure; (6) recognizing that operational pressure from a film crew is a hazardous attitude (invulnerability/machismo) that must be consciously countered. The combination of compensation-driven pressure and DVE conditions is a classic accumulating error chain scenario.
questions.follow_up: If this pilot holds a valid Third Class medical and proceeds with the flight, at what point in deteriorating flat light conditions should the approach be categorically abandoned rather than modified?
questions.follow_up_answer: The approach should be categorically abandoned — not merely modified — when the pilot can no longer positively identify the landing surface, slope, and obstacle environment with sufficient confidence to execute a safe steep approach and go-around if needed. Specifically: if during the low reconnaissance the surface texture, slope angle, and obstacle positions (trees, rocks, wires) cannot be determined; if the horizon is indistinguishable from the terrain surface; or if the pilot cannot identify at least one reliable external reference point to use as a height-above-ground cue during final approach. Modification (slower approach speed, earlier power addition, instrument integration) is appropriate when DVE is partial and manageable. Categorical abandonment is required when the visual information needed to safely arrest descent and avoid obstacles is simply not present. No modification of technique compensates for the absence of the visual data the technique depends on.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR Part 68; 14 CFR 61.113(i) (BasicMed); FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10 (Reconnaissance, Steep Approach); Chapter 13 (ADM, Hazardous Attitudes, Error Chain)

questions.question: Before beginning a steep approach to a confined area, which checklist should you complete, and at what point in the sequence do you typically run it?
questions.answer: You should complete the before-landing checklist prior to commencing the approach. This is typically accomplished during the high reconnaissance or while still at a safe altitude with time to review items without becoming task-saturated close to the ground. The checklist ensures fuel is on the correct tank, mixture/governor is set, landing light is on if required, and any other aircraft-specific items are confirmed before committing to the approach.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10; POH/RFM Before Landing Checklist

questions.question: What is the purpose of completing checklists before a steep approach rather than relying on memory alone?
questions.answer: Checklists exist because human memory is fallible, especially under the increased workload and stress of a demanding maneuver like a steep approach. Reading and responding to a printed checklist ensures that no critical configuration items — such as fuel selector position, throttle friction, governor setting, or warning systems — are missed. Skipping a checklist step could result in an aircraft not configured correctly at a critical phase of flight where power demands and pilot workload are both high.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (ADM/SRM); POH/RFM General Operating Procedures

questions.question: During a steep approach, at what point is it generally NOT appropriate to be running a paper checklist, and why?
questions.answer: Once you are established on final and inside the critical portion of the steep approach — particularly as you are losing ETL and increasing collective to manage your descent rate — is not an appropriate time to be reading from a paper checklist. This phase requires both hands and full visual attention outside the aircraft. Checklists should be completed before the approach begins, during the reconnaissance phase or on downwind/base, so the pilot is heads-up and hands-free during the most critical portion of the maneuver.

questions.question: You are flying a steep approach into a mountain pinnacle. During your high reconnaissance you are managing airspeed, wind assessment, and obstacle identification. When exactly do you fit in your before-landing checklist, and how do you ensure it actually gets done?
questions.answer: The before-landing checklist should be completed during the high reconnaissance before committing to the approach. A practical method is to complete it while still at reconnaissance altitude and a safe distance from the landing area — for example, while orbiting and observing the site. To ensure it gets done, verbalize each item aloud (even single-pilot), use a finger to track your position on the checklist card, and confirm completion before descending for the low reconnaissance or approach. If interrupted, restart the checklist from the beginning rather than guessing where you left off.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10 (Pinnacle/Ridgeline Operations, Steep Approach); Chapter 13 (SRM/Workload Management)

questions.question: You complete your before-landing checklist and begin a steep approach. Midway through the approach, you realize you did not select the correct fuel tank per your checklist. What is the safest course of action and what does this scenario reveal about checklist technique?
questions.answer: The safest action is to go around immediately while you still have altitude and energy to do so, reconfigure correctly, rerun the checklist, and re-attempt the approach only when properly configured. Continuing a steep approach with a known configuration error adds unnecessary risk at one of the most demanding phases of flight. This scenario reveals that a checklist completed but not verified — where items are marked off without actually confirming the action — is just as dangerous as not using a checklist. The 'do-verify' method, where you perform the action and then confirm its state, is the correct technique.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10 (Steep Approach, Go-Around); POH/RFM Fuel System Procedures

questions.question: How does the required power check — confirming you have sufficient power available for an OGE hover — relate to the checklist process before a steep approach, and what happens if you skip it?
questions.answer: The power check is a performance verification step that should be integrated into your pre-approach planning, often referenced in or alongside the before-landing checklist items. For a steep approach into a confined area or pinnacle, you must confirm that OGE hover power is available, since ETL is lost at a higher altitude than in a normal approach and you may need to hover OGE at the landing point. If you skip this check and attempt the approach without sufficient power, you may arrive at the termination point unable to stop the descent, unable to hover, and without adequate altitude or airspeed to safely go around — a potentially fatal situation. The Helicopter Flying Handbook explicitly states OGE hover power is required for steep approach operations.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10 (Steep Approach — power check requirement); Chapter 10 (Confined Area Operations)

questions.question: You are flying a turbine helicopter with a crew member who calls out checklist items while you fly. On final for a steep approach, your crew member is distracted by a radio call and stops at item four of a seven-item checklist. You believe the remaining items were already set from the previous flight leg. How do you handle this, and what principle does it demonstrate?
questions.answer: You should verbally advise the crew member that the checklist was interrupted and direct them to resume from item four or restart from the top once they are off the radio. You must not assume the remaining items are in the correct configuration simply because they were set on a previous leg — configuration can change due to inadvertent contact with switches, different phase-of-flight requirements, or previous emergency procedures. The principle demonstrated is challenge-and-response checklist discipline: no item is considered complete until both crewmembers have confirmed it in the current operation. If the approach cannot be safely delayed, execute a go-around and complete the checklist properly before re-attempting.
questions.follow_up: What is the specific danger of assumption-based checklist completion in a multi-crew helicopter environment, and how does CRM address it?
questions.follow_up_answer: Assumption-based completion — where a pilot assumes items are already done without verification — is a leading contributor to configuration-related accidents. In a multi-crew environment, each pilot may assume the other has confirmed an item, leading to a situation where neither pilot actually verified it. CRM addresses this through defined crew roles (pilot flying vs. pilot monitoring), explicit verbal challenge-and-response protocols, and cross-check culture where both crew confirm safety-critical items. The FAA's ADM framework identifies this as a form of complacency — one of the hazardous attitudes — and training programs specifically target assumption-based behavior as an accident precursor.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (ADM, Hazardous Attitudes, SRM/CRM); FAA Advisory Circular AC 120-71B (Standard Operating Procedures and Checklists)

questions.question: During a practical test, you complete the before-landing checklist correctly before a steep approach, but after landing I ask you which specific items on that checklist are most critical to a steep approach as opposed to a normal approach, and why. Walk me through your reasoning.
questions.answer: While all checklist items must be completed, items of heightened criticality for a steep approach compared to a normal approach include: (1) Fuel selector — a fuel interruption during the high-power demand at ETL loss on a steep approach could be fatal with little altitude or airspeed to recover; (2) Governor/throttle friction — the steep approach requires precise collective management through a high-power transition as ETL is lost at a higher altitude; a stiff or improperly set throttle can cause rotor droop; (3) Emergency landing area identification — although not always a printed checklist item, confirming your abort point and go-around path is operationally critical because the go-around from a steep approach is more demanding than from a normal approach; (4) Any OGE power verification step — confirming you have adequate power before committing to a point of no return. The underlying principle is that steep approaches reduce your margins for error at every phase, so items affecting power, fuel, and emergency egress carry greater weight than in a standard approach.
questions.follow_up: If the POH checklist does not specifically include a power check before a steep approach, are you still required to perform one? Why or why not?
questions.follow_up_answer: Yes — performing a power check before a steep approach into a confined or high-elevation area is a sound operational practice required by the Helicopter Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-21B) regardless of whether the POH explicitly lists it. The POH represents the minimum manufacturer requirements for normal operations, but the pilot in command is responsible under 14 CFR 91.3 for the safe operation of the flight. FAA-H-8083-21B clearly states that OGE hover power must be confirmed available for steep approaches. A pilot who skips a power check because 'it wasn't on the checklist' and subsequently cannot stop the descent at the landing point has still exercised poor judgment. Checklists are a tool — they do not replace aeronautical knowledge or judgment. The PIC must integrate handbook procedures with checklist discipline.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10 (Steep Approach); 14 CFR 91.3 (PIC Responsibility); POH/RFM General

questions.question: When conducting a steep approach to an uncontrolled airport, at what point in the approach would you make your radio calls, and what information should those calls include?
questions.answer: At an uncontrolled airport, you should make position calls on CTAF at key points in the traffic pattern: downwind, base, and final. A general informational call at 10 miles is good practice for situational awareness, but the primary regulatory guidance in AIM 4-1-9 focuses on position calls within the pattern. Each call should include: your aircraft type and identifier, current position in the pattern (downwind, base, or final), altitude, intentions (e.g., landing steep approach runway XX), and the airport name. Example: 'Riverside traffic, Helicopter 4 Lima Bravo, downwind runway 27, 2,500 feet, landing, Riverside.'

questions.question: What radio frequency would you use for position calls during a steep approach to a controlled airport's helipad that is within the airport's Class D airspace?
questions.answer: You would use the tower frequency for that controlled airport. You must establish two-way radio communication with the tower before entering Class D airspace. The tower will issue clearances and instructions. You should not switch to CTAF or UNICOM — all calls during the approach at a Class D airport go through the control tower on the tower frequency unless instructed otherwise (e.g., switching to ground after landing).

questions.question: During a steep approach at an uncontrolled airport, what radio call should you make when you are on final and committed to the landing?
questions.answer: You should broadcast your final call on the CTAF, stating your aircraft type and identifier, that you are on final for the specific runway or landing area, and the airport name. For example: 'Riverside traffic, Helicopter 4 Lima Bravo, final, steep approach runway 27, Riverside.' This alerts other traffic in the pattern and on the ground to your position and intentions, which is especially important since a steep approach brings you in at a steeper, less conventional angle that other pilots may not anticipate.

questions.question: You are conducting a steep approach to a confined area landing zone on private property outside of any airport environment. There is no control tower, and no CTAF is published. How do you handle radio communications during this approach, and what is the purpose of any calls you make?
questions.answer: Outside of an airport traffic area with no published CTAF, there is no regulatory requirement to make radio calls. However, best practice is to self-announce on the area's designated frequency if one exists, or on 122.9 MHz (multicom), especially if other aircraft are known to be operating in the area. The purpose shifts from ATC compliance to collision avoidance and situational awareness — alerting any other pilots in the vicinity of your position, altitude, and intentions. You should also coordinate directly with any ground personnel using radio or other means. If operating under Part 135 or company operations specifications, follow your company's communication protocols.

questions.question: You are on a steep approach to a helipad at a hospital located within Class B airspace. You received your clearance before departure but now the radio goes silent — you are not getting any response from approach control and you are inside the Class B shelf. What are your communication and procedural obligations at this point?
questions.answer: If you experience two-way radio communication failure inside Class B airspace, you must follow 14 CFR 91.185 procedures for lost communications. Squawk 7600 on the transponder immediately to indicate radio failure. If you are already in VMC, continue the flight under VFR, land as soon as practicable, and notify ATC as soon as possible after landing. If you received a clearance, you may continue as cleared since you had established two-way communication prior to entering the airspace. Immediately attempt to restore communication on all appropriate frequencies, including guard frequency 121.5 MHz. Continue attempting communication attempts throughout the flight. Document everything for post-flight ATC notification.

questions.question: During a steep approach to an uncontrolled airport, you hear another pilot report they are on a 3-mile final for the same runway you are approaching. Your steep approach will bring you in much steeper and slower — meaning you will likely arrive at the threshold around the same time. What radio call do you make, and what action do you take?
questions.answer: You should immediately broadcast on CTAF to establish situational awareness with the other pilot. State your position, that you are conducting a steep approach to the same runway, and ask the other traffic to confirm their position and intentions. For example: 'Riverside traffic, Helicopter 4 Lima Bravo, steep approach runway 27, currently [position/altitude], traffic on 3-mile final, please advise.' Based on their response, coordinate visually and verbally to sequence your arrivals — you may need to extend, orbit, or yield right-of-way. Under 14 CFR 91.113, the lower aircraft on final generally has right-of-way, but the helicopter pilot must exercise good judgment. Do not assume the other aircraft sees you — steep approaches place you in an unconventional position that may not be expected.

questions.question: During a steep approach to an off-airport landing zone, your workload is extremely high — you are managing a high rate of descent, anticipating the loss of ETL, and monitoring engine instruments. A student pilot argues that making radio calls during this critical phase is a distraction and should be skipped. How do you evaluate this argument, and how should radio call timing be structured around the steep approach profile to minimize distraction?
questions.answer: The student's concern reflects poor workload management, not a valid reason to skip radio calls. The solution is to plan radio calls proactively — before entering the high-workload phase. Best practice is to complete all required position reports before beginning the final descent on a steep approach. Make your final radio call at the top of the approach before you begin the steep descent, when workload is manageable. Once committed to the steep approach, your hands and attention are on cyclic, collective, and anti-torque pedals — this is not the time for lengthy transmissions. Cockpit resource management (CRM) and single-pilot resource management (SRM) both emphasize anticipating workload peaks and front-loading tasks. Skipping radio calls entirely is not acceptable because it degrades traffic awareness and situational awareness for other pilots. The proper answer is smarter timing, not omission.
questions.follow_up: If you did fail to make a radio call during the high-workload phase and landed safely, what is the appropriate action after landing?
questions.follow_up_answer: After landing and securing the aircraft, broadcast your position and intentions on CTAF if still relevant (e.g., taxiing, or if traffic may be inbound). More importantly, conduct a personal debrief or crew debrief to identify the workload management breakdown. If operating under Part 135 or in a training environment, report the communication lapse to the appropriate supervisor or log it for training purposes. Recurring omissions of radio calls should be treated as a systems issue — the pilot's briefing or scan flow likely needs restructuring to build radio call checkpoints into the approach profile before the high-workload phase begins.

questions.question: You are flying a steep approach to a rooftop helipad in a congested urban area. The helipad has no published frequency, it is not within controlled airspace, and there are multiple nearby airports and helipads on different CTAF frequencies. How do you determine what frequency to use for radio calls, and what content should those calls include given the non-standard environment?
questions.answer: First, consult the Chart Supplement (formerly A/FD) and any Notices to Airmen (NOTAMs) for the helipad — some rooftop and hospital helipads have published frequencies. The safest and primary approach is to contact the helipad facility directly (by phone or radio prior to flight) to confirm the preferred frequency and any local traffic advisories. If the helipad has a published frequency in the Chart Supplement, use that. If no published frequency exists and direct facility coordination is not possible, 123.025 MHz is a designated helicopter-to-helicopter communication frequency per AIM 4-1-3 and may be monitored by other helicopter operators in the area. In the absence of any other guidance, 122.9 MHz (multicom) is acceptable as a true fallback. Radio call content should include: aircraft type and identifier, current position and altitude, intended approach direction and helipad name, and ETA. Because the environment is non-standard, calls should be more descriptive than at a typical airport — other pilots may not know the helipad's location. After landing, broadcast clear of the helipad to alert inbound traffic.
questions.follow_up: What reference document would you consult to determine if a specific rooftop helipad has a published advisory frequency, and where would you find NOTAM information relevant to that helipad?
questions.follow_up_answer: You would consult the FAA Chart Supplement (formerly Airport/Facility Directory) for the relevant region, which lists heliports and helipads with published data including frequencies when available. You would also check the FAA NOTAM system at notams.faa.gov or through your EFB/dispatch service — NOTAMs are issued by facility identifier, so you need the helipad's identifier if it has one. For unlisted private helipads, the FAA Sectional Aeronautical Chart or helicopter route chart may show the location, and you would coordinate directly with the operator or facility prior to flight. Part 135 operators must also comply with operations specifications that may require specific pre-approach communication procedures.
questions.regulatory_ref: AIM 4-1-9; AIM 4-1-3; FAA Chart Supplement; 14 CFR 91.103

questions.question: Before beginning a steep approach to a confined area, what three site factors must you evaluate?
questions.answer: You must evaluate wind direction and conditions, the landing surface, and obstacles. Wind tells you the preferred approach path and affects ETL loss timing. The landing surface determines whether a skid, run-on, or hover landing is appropriate and identifies hazards like slopes, soft ground, or debris. Obstacles define your approach angle and dictate whether a steeper-than-normal angle is even required.

questions.question: Why is a steep approach typically flown into the wind rather than with a tailwind or crosswind?
questions.answer: Flying into the wind reduces groundspeed for a given airspeed, which shortens the ground track and provides more control authority. It also maximizes the benefit of effective translational lift (ETL) as long as possible during the descent and makes the helicopter more responsive to collective and cyclic inputs. A tailwind increases groundspeed, compresses the approach, and can push the helicopter into obstacles on final.

questions.question: What is the purpose of identifying the landing surface condition before committing to a steep approach?
questions.answer: The landing surface condition determines what type of termination is safe. A soft or uneven surface may not support a run-on landing, requiring a hover or vertical landing. Slopes may require slope landing technique. Debris, rocks, or loose material can create FOD hazards to the tail rotor. Identifying these conditions in advance allows the pilot to select an appropriate approach termination and abort criteria before entering a profile that limits options.

questions.question: You are conducting a high reconnaissance of a mountain landing zone. The wind sock at the lower elevation indicates a westerly wind, but you notice dust swirling in multiple directions near the LZ on the ridgeline. How does this affect your approach planning?
questions.answer: Swirling dust at the LZ indicates mechanical turbulence or variable wind caused by terrain features — the surface wind at the LZ may differ significantly from the lower-elevation indicator. You cannot rely on the lower windsock for approach direction. Plan your approach based on direct observation at LZ altitude: look for dust movement, vegetation movement, or smoke if available. You should also anticipate gusty, variable conditions during the final phase of the approach when ETL is lost, which increases the power demand unpredictably. Consider an abort point and ensure you have OGE hover power available before committing.

questions.question: During a low reconnaissance of a confined area, you identify that the only clear approach path is a 20-degree angle over a tree line on the upwind end, but the only departure path is the same direction — meaning you'll land with obstacles directly on your intended go-around path. How does this factor into your steep approach decision?
questions.answer: This scenario means you have no clear abort path once inside the obstacle ring, which significantly changes your risk profile. Before committing, you must confirm you have sufficient power for OGE hover at that altitude and density altitude so a vertical or near-vertical departure is possible if needed. You should also positively identify a departure path — even if it's a different direction than the approach. If the only usable path is through the same obstacle corridor, you must evaluate whether you can safely reverse course using a climbing pedal turn or similar technique. If no safe abort or departure path exists, the correct decision may be to not land.

questions.question: On final approach to a steep approach LZ, you notice the surface is a sloped gravel pad tilted approximately 10 degrees downslope to the left. The obstacle-clear approach path brings you in from directly upslope. How does the slope affect your landing termination and what specific technique do you apply?
questions.answer: A 10-degree slope requires slope landing technique. You should not attempt to simultaneously touch all skids — instead, land the uphill skid first while maintaining a level fuselage with lateral cyclic into the slope. Once the uphill skid is firmly on, gradually lower collective to settle the downhill skid while maintaining cyclic pressure into the slope to prevent dynamic rollover. Throughout this, keep the tail rotor clear of the surface and monitor lateral roll rate carefully. Gravel introduces additional risk of FOD to the tail rotor, so approach direction, rotor clearance from terrain, and touchdown point precision are all critical.

questions.question: During a steep approach on a calm, hot day at high density altitude, you cross the obstacle threshold with adequate power but notice your collective is significantly higher than expected while still 50 feet above the LZ with airspeed already below ETL. What does this indicate and what is your required action?
questions.answer: This indicates you are in or approaching the region of reversed command at low airspeed, below ETL, with power demand higher than anticipated — likely because OGE hover power at this density altitude is near or exceeding your available power margin. You are now in a situation where further deceleration will require even more power, which you may not have. The required action is to immediately initiate a go-around: apply full available power, lower the nose to regain airspeed and ETL, and execute a climbing departure over or around the obstacles if possible. Do not continue the approach — attempting to power through a hover at this energy state risks settling with power or dynamic stall of the rotor system. This situation underscores why verifying OGE hover capability during reconnaissance is mandatory before committing to a steep approach.
questions.follow_up: If you had verified OGE hover power was available before starting the approach, why might you still find yourself in this situation on short final?
questions.follow_up_answer: Several factors could cause this discrepancy: density altitude may have increased since the power check (rising temperature during the day); fuel burn may have reduced weight slightly but not enough to offset DA changes; wind could have decreased on short final, reducing effective translational lift earlier than expected and increasing power demand sooner; or the pilot may have flown a shallower angle than planned, arriving at the termination point with more airspeed bleed-out needed in a shorter distance. Additionally, the power check hover may have been performed OGE but at a slightly different altitude than the actual LZ elevation. All of these reinforce that the power check is a minimum standard — the pilot must also monitor power margins continuously throughout the approach and be prepared to go around at any point.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapters 10 and 11; FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 4 (region of reversed command)

questions.question: A pilot conducts a high and low reconnaissance, identifies the wind direction, surface, and obstacles, then commits to a steep approach. Midway through the approach, a large truck parks at the far end of the LZ, partially blocking the intended termination point. Walk me through your real-time decision-making process.
questions.answer: This is a dynamic obstacle change requiring immediate reassessment mid-approach. First, determine if the remaining landing area is still large enough to safely terminate — if yes, evaluate whether the new obstacle is within rotor blade clearance distance. If the area is still usable and rotor clearance is adequate, continue with heightened precision to the adjusted touchdown point. If the obstacle now blocks the only usable surface, or if rotor clearance is questionable, initiate a go-around immediately — do not attempt to problem-solve inside the obstacle ring at low airspeed. The key principle from ADM is: if an option will only 'probably' work, choose the known-safe option, which is the go-around. After the go-around, communicate with ground personnel, reassess the LZ, and re-plan if the area is cleared.
questions.follow_up: At what point in the steep approach does your go-around option become significantly limited, and what does that mean for how early you should make this decision?
questions.follow_up_answer: The go-around option becomes significantly limited at or below ETL on a steep approach, typically around 15–20 knots airspeed, because at that point you are fully reliant on OGE hover power to climb and have minimal kinetic energy to trade for altitude. On a steep approach, ETL is lost at a higher altitude than a normal approach due to the steeper descent angle, meaning this critical decision point arrives earlier than pilots expect. Therefore, the go-around decision should be made while still above ETL — ideally at the obstacle threshold — so the helicopter can accelerate, regain ETL, and climb away safely. Waiting until below ETL inside the obstacle ring greatly increases the risk that available power is insufficient to arrest the descent and clear the obstacles.

questions.question: When selecting a termination point for a steep approach, what is the primary surface characteristic you are looking for before committing to that spot?
questions.answer: The primary surface characteristic is that the termination point must be firm and capable of supporting the aircraft's weight without sinking, settling, or significant shifting. Secondary considerations include being level enough to prevent dynamic rollover risk, free of obstacles that could interfere with the tail rotor or main rotor, and sized appropriately to accommodate the helicopter's footprint. For a steep approach specifically, the pilot should also confirm that the termination point allows a hover or near-hover stop before touchdown, since the approach angle is steeper than normal and ETL is lost at a higher altitude.

questions.question: Why is it important to identify your termination point before beginning the steep approach rather than during the descent?
questions.answer: Once you begin the steep approach, your workload increases significantly — you are managing a higher-than-normal approach angle, anticipating early ETL loss, and making precise collective adjustments. If you have not already identified and committed to a specific termination point, you will be dividing attention at the most critical phase of the maneuver. Pre-selecting the point during the high and low reconnaissance allows you to fly a stabilized approach to a known, evaluated spot rather than making real-time decisions under high workload.

questions.question: What does it mean to 'terminate' a steep approach, and what are the two acceptable termination options available to the pilot?
questions.answer: Terminating a steep approach means bringing the helicopter to a controlled stop at the selected point. The two acceptable termination options are: (1) a hover termination — the pilot decelerates to a stabilized hover at a safe altitude above the surface where control is positive and confirmed, then performs a controlled descent to the surface; or (2) a run-on or roll-on landing — where the helicopter contacts the surface with some forward speed while maintaining control. In confined or pinnacle operations where OGE hover power may not be available, a hover termination followed by a controlled vertical descent to the surface is the most common method for steep approaches.

questions.question: You are conducting a high reconnaissance of a pinnacle and you identify two possible termination points: one on the upwind, level crown of the pinnacle, and one slightly downslope on the leeward side which has more flat area. Which do you select and why?
questions.answer: Select the upwind, level crown of the pinnacle. Terminating on the leeward side exposes the helicopter to turbulence and downdrafts created by wind flowing over the pinnacle — this is especially hazardous during the critical deceleration phase when you need precise control. Additionally, landing downslope on the leeward side increases dynamic rollover risk if the terrain is uneven. The upwind approach also means you can execute a go-around into clear air if needed, whereas aborting from the leeward side could put you into obstacle or terrain conflict. The FAA Helicopter Flying Handbook specifically notes that approaches to pinnacles should be made into the wind and that the leeward side produces turbulent, unreliable air.

questions.question: During your low reconnaissance of a confined area, you identify a termination point near the center of the clearing. When you check your hover power during the reconnaissance, you find you can only marginally achieve OGE hover. How does this affect your termination point selection and the type of termination you plan?
questions.answer: Marginal OGE hover power is a significant constraint for termination point selection. If you can only barely achieve OGE hover, you need to select a termination point that allows you to transition to OGE as briefly as possible — ideally terminating directly on the surface without an extended hover. You should look for a termination point that (1) is closest to the approach path so you are not hovering sideways or repositioning, (2) has the most level surface to avoid dynamic rollover, and (3) if possible, allows a roll-on or run-on landing to eliminate the OGE hover requirement entirely. You should also confirm your abort point before beginning the approach, since power margins are critical during the deceleration phase when ETL is lost earlier than a normal approach.

questions.question: You are on final for a steep approach and your pre-selected termination point now has a person walking into it from the treeline. At what point in the approach profile is it still safe to go around, and what factors determine that decision?
questions.answer: The go-around decision must be made as early as possible — ideally before ETL is lost. On a steep approach, ETL is lost at a higher altitude than a normal approach because the steeper angle means slower translational speed earlier in the descent. Once ETL is lost and you are deep in the approach with collective nearly full up, a go-around becomes very difficult and may not be possible with available power. The factors that determine whether a go-around is safe include: current altitude and airspeed (do you have enough energy to accelerate through ETL?), available power margin, obstacle clearance in the go-around direction, and rotor RPM status. If the person enters the LZ while you still have translational lift and power margin, initiate the go-around immediately by adding collective, applying forward cyclic, and transitioning to a climbing turn toward clear air. Do not continue if the termination point is compromised.

questions.question: A student pilot selects a termination point at the far end of a confined area during a steep approach, reasoning that it gives the most room to decelerate. As their instructor, explain what is wrong with this reasoning and what the correct termination point selection logic should be.
questions.answer: The student's reasoning reverses the correct logic. Selecting a termination point at the far end of the confined area is problematic for several reasons: (1) If the approach becomes unstabilized or power is insufficient, you have the least room to execute a go-around — you are approaching the most confined, obstacle-laden boundary. (2) The far end is typically where trees or obstacles are closest after the clearing ends, meaning a tail rotor strike or main rotor clearance becomes a concern if you slightly overshoot. (3) On a steep approach, the steeper angle means you are descending nearly vertically near the termination point — being at the far end reduces the safety buffer if you are slightly long. The correct logic is to select a termination point that: maximizes obstacle clearance during the approach, allows the abort to be into clear air, is reachable well before the obstacles at the far end, and gives the most usable ground around it for emergency repositioning. The termination point should be on the upwind side of the clearing, closest to the approach corridor, not the far end.
questions.follow_up: If the ideal termination point is on the upwind end of the confined area but the surface there is soft and muddy, how do you resolve the conflict between the aerodynamically preferred spot and the unsuitable surface?
questions.follow_up_answer: This is a classic risk management tradeoff. If the surface at the aerodynamically ideal point is unsuitable, you have several options: (1) Select the next best termination point that balances surface suitability with approach geometry — perhaps slightly deeper into the clearing on firmer ground — and adjust your approach angle accordingly. (2) Consider whether a hover taxi to firmer ground after a hover termination at the preferred aerodynamic point is feasible and safe. (3) Evaluate whether the entire confined area operation is viable at all — if no termination point combines acceptable surface and acceptable approach geometry, the correct decision may be to not land there. The hazard chain is critical: a soft surface causing dynamic rollover or a stuck skid may be a greater risk than a slightly longer hover transit, but you must have the power to support that decision. Never compromise both the approach path and the surface — one of them must be acceptable.

questions.question: During a checkride, a candidate selects what appears to be an excellent termination point during reconnaissance — level, firm, upwind, and obstacle-free. However, during the approach, they fixate on the termination point and fail to notice a deer running into the LZ at 50 feet AGL. They continue and land. How do you evaluate this from an ACS standpoint, and what is the underlying skill deficiency?
questions.answer: From an ACS standpoint, the candidate demonstrated poor situational awareness and inadequate risk management during the final phase of the approach. While the initial termination point selection was technically sound, the skill of 'selecting a suitable termination point' is not a one-time decision made during reconnaissance — it is a continuous evaluation that must be maintained throughout the approach. The ACS standard implies that the pilot must verify the termination point remains suitable up to and including the moment of touchdown. A deer in the LZ presents a dynamic rollover risk, tail rotor strike hazard, and potential loss of control on ground contact. The underlying skill deficiency is target fixation — the candidate locked onto the pre-selected point and stopped actively evaluating it. A competent pilot maintains a scan that includes the termination point throughout the descent and is prepared to execute a go-around if the LZ status changes. This would likely constitute an unsatisfactory performance under risk management standards related to recognizing and mitigating hazards.
questions.follow_up: The candidate argues that at 50 feet AGL on a steep approach, there was not enough power to go around safely. How do you assess that argument, and what should have been done differently?
questions.follow_up_answer: The argument may have some merit if power was genuinely marginal — a go-around at 50 feet AGL after ETL has been lost on a steep approach in a high-density altitude environment can be extremely difficult or impossible. However, this actually reinforces the deficiency rather than excusing it: if the aircraft is in a condition at 50 feet where a go-around is not safely available, then the pilot has already entered a critical phase where the termination point must be available and clear. The correct mitigation should have occurred earlier — either during reconnaissance by establishing a strict abort decision altitude (e.g., 'if anything compromises the LZ above 100 feet AGL I go around, below that I land'), or by selecting a termination point with greater power margins available for a later go-around decision. Additionally, a proper scan during final — not fixating on the point itself — would have identified the deer at a higher altitude when a go-around was still viable. The FAA Helicopter Flying Handbook's discussion of steep approaches specifically calls out early power increases as ETL is lost, which means there may have been a brief window of available power earlier in the descent that the pilot missed by fixating.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13; Helicopter ACS HI.IX.D

questions.question: During a steep approach, at what point does the helicopter lose effective translational lift (ETL), and how does that differ from a normal approach?
questions.answer: During a steep approach, ETL is lost at a higher altitude above the touchdown point than during a normal approach. This is because the steeper flight path causes the helicopter to slow through ETL airspeed (approximately 16-24 knots) while still well above the surface. The pilot must anticipate this earlier and begin increasing collective sooner to compensate for the loss of translational lift efficiency.

questions.question: How does a pilot visually establish the correct steep approach angle and assess proper rate of closure to the landing point?
questions.answer: The pilot establishes the steep approach angle by selecting a reference point at the intended touchdown zone and ensuring that point remains at a consistent high angle in the windshield — significantly steeper than a normal approach. Proper rate of closure is assessed by monitoring the apparent size growth of the landing area and the speed at which objects in the peripheral scene move. The landing point should appear to move steadily upward in the windshield as the helicopter descends steeply. Airspeed and vertical speed instruments supplement visual cues to verify the angle and closure rate are within limits.

questions.question: You are established on a steep approach at approximately 13° and notice your rate of closure to the landing point is increasing — the touchdown area is growing rapidly in size. What is the most likely cause, and what control inputs do you make?
questions.answer: An increasing rate of closure on a steep approach indicates the helicopter is descending too rapidly or airspeed is too high for the approach angle, causing the pilot to overshoot the intended profile. The most likely cause is insufficient collective or excessive forward cyclic allowing the airspeed and descent rate to build. The correct response is to simultaneously increase collective to arrest the excessive descent rate and apply aft cyclic to reduce airspeed, effectively shallowing the approach angle or reducing closure rate. The pilot must be cautious not to over-correct, which could cause the approach to go low on power or inadvertently enter a vortex ring state if descent rate remains high with low airspeed.

questions.question: You are conducting a steep approach into a confined area. Midway through the approach at 13° you realize you are consuming power rapidly and approaching OGE hover power limits before reaching the landing point. What factors are contributing to this and what are your options?
questions.answer: On a steep approach, ETL is lost at a higher altitude than normal, which means the rotor transitions from efficient translational lift to less efficient hovering flight earlier in the approach. Without sufficient OGE hover power to complete the landing, the pilot faces a serious hazard. Contributing factors include high density altitude, high gross weight, or the approach being steeper than necessary. Options include: (1) executing a go-around immediately while still at a safe airspeed and altitude — the safest choice if power margins are inadequate; (2) attempting to use a running landing if the surface permits; or (3) if OGE hover power is marginally available, accepting a steeper than planned final few feet into the confined area. The pilot should have confirmed OGE hover power was available during the reconnaissance before committing to the approach.

questions.question: During a steep approach at 12° you are holding a consistent angle and the landing point appears stable in your windshield, but you notice your airspeed has decayed well below ETL and your descent rate is still 600 FPM. What hazard is developing and what is your immediate action?
questions.answer: This combination of low airspeed below ETL, high descent rate, and low collective application describes the onset conditions for vortex ring state (settling with power). The rotor is operating in its own downwash, reducing lift efficiency as the helicopter descends through the recirculating vortex. If the pilot adds collective to stop the descent, the condition may worsen. Immediate action is to execute a go-around by applying full available power, lowering the nose to gain translational airspeed, and flying clear of the disturbed air. If altitude permits, moving laterally while accelerating can also help escape vortex ring state. This situation emphasizes why the pilot must maintain a sufficient airspeed component — even on a steep approach — to preserve rotor inflow and avoid power settling.

questions.question: A student pilot consistently establishes the correct 12° steep approach angle on entry but tends to flatten the approach significantly in the last 100 feet, arriving over the touchdown point at nearly a normal approach angle. What is the most likely cause of this habit, and how would you evaluate whether it represents a standards deficiency on the checkride?
questions.answer: The most likely cause is the student subconsciously reacting to the sensation of high descent rate and the rapidly growing appearance of the landing zone by pulling aft cyclic and adding collective earlier than necessary — effectively reverting to a normal approach profile in the critical final phase. This is a common transition error driven by spatial disorientation or inadequate training on controlling the visual picture during the steep final. On the checkride, this represents a skills deficiency under HI.IX.D.S5 because the standard requires the pilot to establish AND MAINTAIN the steep approach angle throughout the approach, not just initially. If the angle is consistently flattened to normal in the final phase, the maneuver is not being executed to standards. The practical test should result in the examiner noting the failure to maintain the approach angle and, depending on severity, it could constitute an unsatisfactory performance if the deviation is repeated or uncorrected.
questions.follow_up: If the student argues that flattening the approach at 100 feet AGL was a safety measure because they were running out of power, how do you evaluate that justification?
questions.follow_up_answer: If the student was genuinely approaching power limits, that would be a legitimate and correct decision — recognizing a safety hazard and modifying the approach or executing a go-around is always appropriate. However, the examiner must determine whether the power concern was real or rationalized. A genuine power issue should have been identified earlier during reconnaissance and the pilot should have elected a different approach profile or landing site. If the student had adequate power margin but avoided the steep angle out of discomfort or poor visual management, the justification is invalid and the deficiency stands. The examiner should debrief this by reviewing the power indications recorded or recalled, and discuss why reconnaissance before committing to the approach exists precisely to prevent this scenario from arising unexpectedly on short final.
