If maintaining normal climb airspeed requires power that exceeds engine or transmission limits (torque, TGT, or MGT redlines), power limits always take priority — you must not exceed published limits. The correct technique is to set power at or just below the applicable limit, then adjust cyclic to fly whatever airspeed the helicopter will sustain at that power setting. This may mean climbing at a speed slightly different from 'normal' but still within a safe envelope. The pilot should reference the RFM for hot-and-high climb charts and consider whether a rolling takeoff was the appropriate technique given the conditions. Additionally, the ACS ±5-knot tolerance applies to normal climb speed when it is achievable — but never at the expense of exceeding aircraft limitations.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.9; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10; Aircraft RFM Performance Charts

questions.question: During the transition to normal climb airspeed after a rolling takeoff, a student consistently overshoots the target speed by 10–12 knots before correcting back. As an examiner, what underlying skill deficiency does this pattern reveal, and what training technique would you prescribe?
questions.answer: This pattern reveals poor pitch attitude reference and over-reliance on the airspeed indicator rather than establishing the correct visual attitude first. The student is likely 'chasing' the airspeed needle reactively rather than proactively setting a climb attitude and trimming. This suggests a deficiency in attitude flying and instrument cross-check discipline. The underlying issue is that by the time the airspeed indicator reflects the deviation, the helicopter is already well outside the tolerance band. The prescribed training technique is to practice attitude-based climbs: establish and hold a known pitch attitude for normal climb (using the horizon reference), set power, then verify airspeed. Repeated practice of pitch attitude awareness — including partial-panel exercises to reduce over-fixation on instruments — combined with slow-flight and climb transition drills will build the anticipatory control inputs needed.
questions.follow_up: If this same student then begins under-correcting and staying 6–8 knots slow in the climb, what changed and what does it tell you about their learning progression?
questions.follow_up_answer: The student has now over-corrected their previous error and is over-applying aft cyclic in an effort to avoid the high-speed deviation. This is actually a positive sign — it indicates the student is now aware of the error and attempting to correct proactively, but their pitch attitude reference is not yet calibrated. They are in the 'overcorrection phase' of skill acquisition. The instructor should reinforce a specific pitch attitude reference (a visual picture of the nose relative to the horizon at normal climb), use a consistent landmark or attitude reference, and have the student verbally call out their attitude before checking airspeed. This phase should resolve with repetition as the student builds a reliable mental model of the correct climb picture.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 9 (attitude flying); FAA-H-8083-3C Airplane Flying Handbook attitude concepts (cross-applicable principle)

questions.question: A pilot executing a rolling takeoff in a turbine helicopter transitions to climb and sets what appears to be correct climb power, but the helicopter is climbing significantly slower than expected even though airspeed is within ±5 knots of normal climb speed. The temperature and pressure altitude are within normal operating range. What systematic check should the pilot run, and what are the two most likely power-related causes?
questions.answer: The pilot should systematically check: (1) actual torque or power instrument reading versus the published climb power value, (2) rotor RPM — if Nr is low, the rotor system is not producing rated thrust even at the correct power setting, and (3) engine instruments for any anomaly (TGT, N1/N2 split on a twin, fuel flow). The two most likely power-related causes are: First, the power instruments may show correct numbers, but the collective has inadvertently been set to a value yielding less torque than required — the pilot may have misread the instrument or confused MAP and torque. Second, and more concerning, rotor RPM may be drooping slightly below the normal operating range due to insufficient collective or a governor that is not holding Nr correctly, meaning the rotor is not converting all available engine power into lift efficiently. A slight Nr droop is easily missed but significantly degrades climb performance. The pilot should verify Nr is in the green arc, confirm power setting against the published value, and troubleshoot from there.
questions.follow_up: If Nr is confirmed in the green arc and power is set correctly but climb performance is still degraded, what external and aircraft system factors should the pilot now consider?
questions.follow_up_answer: With Nr and power confirmed normal, the pilot should consider: (1) Fuel — is the aircraft heavier than planned due to fuel load miscalculation or passengers/cargo, reducing available excess power for climb? (2) Bleed air — on turbine helicopters, are engine bleed air systems (air conditioning, anti-ice) drawing power and reducing available shaft horsepower? These should be reduced or turned off if not required. (3) Wind — is there a tailwind component that reduces effective translational lift and climb efficiency? (4) Rotor blade or airframe icing — even light icing on rotor blades dramatically increases drag and reduces lift. (5) A developing engine or fuel control anomaly that has not yet triggered an indicator but is causing subtle power loss. The pilot should consult the RFM abnormal/emergency section and consider whether continuing the flight is appropriate.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10 and Chapter 11; Aircraft RFM Systems Description and Performance sections

questions.question: After liftoff from a rolling takeoff, what control input do you use to maintain a straight ground track when there is a crosswind from the right?
questions.answer: After liftoff, you apply RIGHT cyclic (into the wind) to bank the helicopter into the crosswind. This counteracts the wind's tendency to push the helicopter to the left and maintains a straight ground track. Use pedals to keep the nose aligned with the ground track and maintain coordinated flight. The principle is to establish a wind correction angle by banking into the wind with cyclic so that the fuselage track remains aligned with the intended departure path.

questions.question: At what point during a rolling takeoff should you begin applying crosswind correction to maintain your ground track?
questions.answer: Crosswind correction should begin at liftoff — the moment the skids or wheels leave the ground and the helicopter transitions from ground contact to free flight. During the ground roll, directional control is maintained with pedals and cyclic aligned with the takeoff path. Once airborne, you must immediately apply cyclic into the crosswind to prevent drift and maintain the intended ground track, since the surface is no longer providing lateral restraint.

questions.question: What is the difference between a crab and a slip when correcting for crosswind after liftoff from a rolling takeoff, and which technique applies to helicopters?
questions.answer: A crab correction points the nose of the aircraft into the wind so the flight path remains over the intended ground track — used primarily by fixed-wing aircraft. A slip (or side-slip) involves banking into the wind while keeping the nose aligned with the runway using opposite rudder. Helicopters use a slip-like technique: apply cyclic into the crosswind to create a lateral tilt that offsets drift, while using pedals to keep the nose pointed along the intended ground track. This combination of into-wind cyclic and coordinated pedal input is the standard helicopter crosswind correction technique after liftoff.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 9, Basic Flight Maneuvers; Chapter 10

questions.question: You are departing from a narrow taxiway with trees on both sides. The wind is 15 knots from the left at a 45-degree angle to your takeoff heading. After liftoff, you apply left cyclic to correct for the crosswind but notice you are drifting toward the trees on the right side. What is the most likely cause, and how do you correct it?
questions.answer: The wind from the left is pushing the helicopter to the right. You applied left cyclic (correct direction), but the input was insufficient in magnitude to fully counteract the 15-knot crosswind component. To correct, increase the left cyclic input further until lateral drift stops and the helicopter's ground track aligns with the taxiway centerline. You may also need to increase collective slightly to maintain climb performance while holding the correction angle, since tilting the rotor disk reduces the vertical component of total rotor thrust. Additionally, verify pedal inputs are keeping the nose coordinated and not allowing yaw to compound the drift. In a confined area with obstacles, this correction must be made immediately — delay increases the risk of contact with trees on the right.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10, Advanced Flight Maneuvers; Chapter 9

questions.question: During a rolling takeoff at an unfamiliar airstrip, you lift off and immediately notice the wind has shifted — the crosswind is now stronger and from a slightly different direction than you briefed. Describe how you prioritize your control inputs to maintain ground track while also managing obstacle clearance.
questions.answer: Immediate priorities in order: (1) Maintain aircraft control — apply cyclic into the new crosswind direction promptly to stop lateral drift; (2) Ensure continued climb — confirm collective is set for best climb performance and do not sacrifice altitude to chase the ground track; (3) Maintain ground track — once drift is arrested, fine-tune cyclic and pedals to track the intended departure path; (4) Assess obstacles — if the combination of altered wind and drift has compromised obstacle clearance, consider an abort if still low and slow enough to stop safely, or commit to the climb and accept a slightly offset track if obstacles allow. Throughout, maintain coordinated flight with pedals. The key risk here is fixating on the ground track at the expense of climb rate near obstacles — altitude and obstacle clearance take priority over precise centerline tracking in this scenario.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10, Advanced Flight Maneuvers; Chapter 13, ADM

questions.question: You complete a rolling takeoff and are climbing out with a left crosswind correction applied. As airspeed increases through ETL and beyond, how should your crosswind correction input change, and why?
questions.answer: As indicated airspeed increases above translational lift (ETL, approximately 16–24 knots), the wind correction angle required to maintain your ground track decreases. This occurs because the 15-knot crosswind component becomes a smaller proportion of your total airspeed — for example, at 20 knots TAS the wind correction angle is steep, but at 60 knots TAS the same 15-knot crosswind requires only a shallow bank angle. Continuously monitor your ground track against a reference (a road, runway edge, or distant landmark) and apply progressively smaller, smooth cyclic corrections to maintain alignment with the intended departure track. Avoid over-correcting, which could introduce lateral oscillations or allow the helicopter to drift to the opposite side.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 9 and Chapter 10; translational lift discussion

questions.question: A student pilot consistently drifts downwind after liftoff on rolling takeoffs even when applying what they think is the correct crosswind correction. As an instructor, what are the three most likely skill deficiencies causing this, and how would you specifically address each one during remediation?
questions.answer: Three most likely deficiencies: (1) Timing error — the student delays applying crosswind correction until drift is already visible, rather than anticipating and applying correction at the moment of liftoff. Remediation: Use ground references and brief the student to begin cyclic into-wind input as wheels leave the surface, not after drift begins. (2) Magnitude error — the student underestimates the required cyclic displacement, applying insufficient into-wind tilt to fully counteract the wind. Remediation: Have the student verbalize the wind direction and expected drift before each takeoff, and practice hovering in crosswind conditions to build feel for the required input. (3) Coordination error — the student applies cyclic but neglects pedal inputs, causing the nose to yaw into the wind (creating an uncoordinated slip that degrades lift and increases drag). Remediation: Emphasize that cyclic and pedal are used together — cyclic corrects drift, pedals maintain heading alignment with the ground track. Practice coordinated crosswind hover taxiing before attempting rolling takeoffs in crosswind conditions.
questions.follow_up: If the student correctly identifies and applies the crosswind correction but still drifts after liftoff, what external factor might you investigate that is unrelated to their control inputs?
questions.follow_up_answer: The most likely external factor is that the wind conditions at the surface during the ground roll differ from the wind at rotor height just after liftoff — a phenomenon common near tree lines, buildings, or terrain features that create wind shadow zones at ground level but allow full crosswind exposure at rotor height. Additionally, a gusty or variable wind condition could mean the correction applied at liftoff is appropriate for the initial wind but the wind suddenly increases or shifts just after wheels-off. The instructor should review the ATIS/AWOS for gust spread, observe windsocks at multiple points if available, and consider whether surface obstacles are sheltering the takeoff roll area while exposing the departure path to full crosswind after liftoff. This demonstrates the value of pre-flight wind analysis and situational awareness rather than relying solely on technique.

questions.question: During a rolling takeoff checkride at a private airstrip, the applicant lifts off cleanly and applies crosswind correction, but the examiner notices the tail is slowly weathervaning into the wind, the nose is pointing slightly downwind, and the helicopter is tracking straight. Is this an acceptable technique, and what is the underlying control problem?
questions.answer: No, this is not acceptable technique. What the examiner is observing is an uncoordinated control input — the applicant is using pedals to yaw the nose into the wind (creating a crab-like correction) rather than using cyclic to bank into the wind while keeping the nose aligned with the ground track. While the ground track may appear straight momentarily, this technique creates a skid condition where the tail is being pushed by the wind and the pedal input is masking it. In helicopter terms, a skid occurs when the rate of turn or yaw is greater than appropriate for the bank angle — the helicopter is pointed into a yaw while not banking into the wind with cyclic. This is aerodynamically inefficient, creates asymmetric loading, and fails to demonstrate proper crosswind correction technique per the ACS. The correct technique is cyclic into the wind to tilt the rotor disk and arrest drift, with pedals used only to maintain coordinated, trimmed flight with the nose pointing along the intended ground track.
questions.follow_up: What instrument in the cockpit would confirm to you as an examiner that the applicant's pedal-dominant crosswind correction is producing an out-of-trim or skid condition?
questions.follow_up_answer: The ball in the inclinometer (slip/skid indicator), part of the turn-and-slip indicator, would confirm this. In a proper crosswind correction with into-wind cyclic, the ball should be centered, indicating coordinated flight. If the applicant is using excess pedal to yaw the nose into the wind without corresponding cyclic bank, the ball will deflect — in this case toward the downwind side (out toward the skid side), indicating a skid. The examiner would direct the applicant's attention to the ball and ask them to apply cyclic pressure to center it, which would prompt the correct corrective action of banking into the wind rather than yawing into it.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 9 (slips and skids); Chapter 10 (rolling takeoff technique); FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 4 (adverse yaw, coordination)

questions.question: Before beginning a rolling takeoff from a runway intersection, what clearance must you have from ATC, and what does that clearance authorize you to do?
questions.answer: You must have an explicit takeoff clearance from ATC before entering the runway or crossing the hold short line. A clearance to 'taxi to' a runway does not authorize entry onto that runway. An intersection takeoff also requires ATC to specifically offer or approve the intersection departure; the pilot should confirm the available runway length from that point. The clearance authorizes you to enter the runway and initiate the takeoff roll, nothing more — it does not authorize crossing an active runway unless specifically stated.

questions.question: What does the term 'runway incursion' mean, and what are the four categories used to classify their severity?
questions.answer: A runway incursion is any occurrence at an aerodrome involving the incorrect presence of an aircraft, vehicle, or person on the protected area of a surface designated for landing and takeoff. The FAA classifies them by severity: Category A — a serious incident in which a collision was narrowly avoided; Category B — an incident with significant potential for collision requiring an abrupt maneuver to avoid; Category C — an incident characterized by ample time/distance to avoid collision; Category D — an incident that meets the definition with little or no chance of collision but rules were still violated.

questions.question: What does a hold short line look like on the runway surface, and what does it mean for a helicopter pilot preparing for a rolling takeoff?
questions.answer: The runway holding position marking consists of four yellow lines — two solid and two dashed — running perpendicular to the taxiway centerline. The solid lines are on the side where you must hold; the dashed lines face the runway side. For a helicopter pilot, you must stop and hold at this line unless you have explicit ATC clearance to enter or cross the runway. During a rolling takeoff, you should not cross this line until takeoff clearance is received and any potential conflicts on the runway or final approach path are visually confirmed clear.

questions.question: You are cleared for takeoff on Runway 27. During your rolling takeoff ground roll, you notice a light aircraft on short final that does not appear to be going around. Tower has not issued a go-around instruction to that aircraft. What do you do?
questions.answer: Despite holding a valid takeoff clearance, you must exercise pilot-in-command authority under 14 CFR 91.3. If the aircraft on final poses a genuine collision threat and tower has not resolved the conflict, you have three options depending on your position and energy state: (1) if still slow enough and runway permits, abort the takeoff and hold clear; (2) if you have sufficient energy to safely become airborne immediately and climb clear, expedite liftoff and turn to avoid the conflict while immediately notifying tower; (3) if you cannot safely remain on the runway or safely lift off, exit the runway via the nearest available taxiway. Immediately advise ATC of your action in all cases. Your clearance does not relieve you of the responsibility to see and avoid.

questions.question: You are at a non-towered airport preparing for a rolling takeoff on Runway 18. There is no active CTAF traffic visible and no radio responses to your calls. Walk me through the specific runway incursion avoidance steps you take before entering the runway.
questions.answer: At a non-towered airport, the responsibility is entirely on the pilot. Before entering Runway 18: (1) Make a position and intentions broadcast on CTAF — state the airport name, your tail number, location, and that you are departing Runway 18; (2) Visually scan final approach, base, and crosswind legs for traffic — do not rely solely on radio calls; (3) Check ASOS/AWOS or wind indicators to confirm wind direction and verify 18 is the appropriate runway; (4) Taxi to the hold short line and perform a full 360-degree visual scan looking down the runway in both directions, including the far departure end for anyone backtracking; (5) Scan for vehicles, personnel, or wildlife on the runway surface; (6) Make a final broadcast before entering — 'departing Runway 18'; (7) Enter the runway and commence the ground roll only after visually confirming it is clear.

questions.question: During taxi to the runway for a rolling takeoff at a towered airport at night, ground control instructs you to 'hold short of Runway 9L.' You hear tower issue a landing clearance to a Boeing 737 for that same runway. Moments later, ground clears you to cross Runway 9L. What is the correct action and why?
questions.answer: You should NOT cross Runway 9L until you visually confirm the 737 has landed and cleared the runway, even though you received a crossing clearance from ground control. ATC errors and miscommunications occur. Your responsibility under 14 CFR 91.3 as PIC means you retain authority and accountability for safe operation. At night, you must use all available lighting cues — approach lights, PAPI, landing light reflections — to confirm the runway is clear. If there is any doubt, query ATC: 'Confirm 737 has cleared 9L?' It is always safer to ask and confirm than to proceed on a potentially conflicting clearance. This scenario illustrates why runway incursion awareness requires active pilot participation, not passive compliance.

questions.question: A student pilot you are evaluating initiates a rolling takeoff and, partway down the runway, realizes they taxied onto the wrong runway — Runway 25 instead of the cleared Runway 23. They have not yet lifted off. As the examiner, I want you to tell me: what should they do immediately, and what is the regulatory exposure for operating on an unauthorized runway?
questions.answer: Immediately, the pilot should abort the rolling takeoff, bring the helicopter to a stop safely, and advise ATC immediately: 'Tower, [callsign], we are on Runway 25, not 23 — holding.' Do not attempt to hover-taxi or lift off to reposition without clearance. The regulatory exposure is significant: 14 CFR 91.129 requires compliance with ATC clearances and instructions at towered airports. Operating on an unauthorized runway is a runway incursion and may constitute a violation of 91.129 and potentially 91.13 (careless and reckless operation) depending on risk created. The FAA may initiate a certificate action. If the pilot self-reports via NASA ASRS within 10 days, they may receive immunity from certificate suspension or civil penalty under 49 U.S.C. § 44709(d), provided the violation was inadvertent, did not involve an accident, criminal conduct, or deliberate misconduct. However, ASRS does not protect against revocation (which requires a finding of incompetency or deliberate conduct), criminal charges, or violations involving accidents. ASRS also provides confidentiality protection — the report itself cannot be used as evidence in FAA enforcement proceedings.
questions.follow_up: If the pilot self-reports through ASRS within 10 days, what specific protection does that provide, and is there anything it does NOT protect against?
questions.follow_up_answer: A timely NASA ASRS report filed within 10 days of the incident provides immunity from certificate suspension or civil penalty for a first-time, inadvertent violation — but only if the violation was not deliberate, did not involve an accident, and did not involve a criminal act. It does NOT protect against: certificate revocation (which requires deliberate or egregious conduct), violations involving accidents, criminal charges, or violations of 49 U.S.C. 44702 (fraudulent airman certificates). The ASRS report also does not shield against suspension if the FAA determines the act was not inadvertent. The report is confidential and cannot be used as evidence in enforcement proceedings — that is the key legal protection it provides.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.129; 14 CFR 91.13; NASA ASRS Advisory Circular AC 00-46F

questions.question: Unlike fixed-wing aircraft, a helicopter can enter a runway from essentially any position and angle, hover-taxi across hold short lines, or reposition laterally mid-runway. How does this unique helicopter capability create runway incursion risks that fixed-wing pilots and ATC controllers may not anticipate, and how do you mitigate those risks during a rolling takeoff?
questions.answer: Helicopters are uniquely capable of entering runway protected areas from non-standard directions — hovering over, landing on taxiways adjacent to runways, or crossing hold-short points while in ground effect at low altitudes that may not register on airport surface detection equipment (ASDE). This creates several specific risks: (1) ATC may not have situational awareness of a helicopter that hovered into a runway environment from an off-taxiway position; (2) Fixed-wing pilots on final may not expect a helicopter to be positioned sideways or diagonally on the runway; (3) Hovering behind hold-short lines can create visual ambiguity for fixed-wing pilots and tower controllers about whether the helicopter has crossed; (4) During a rolling takeoff, early forward movement may appear to fixed-wing traffic as if the helicopter has departed when it has not. Mitigation: always obtain explicit verbal clearance before entering ANY part of the runway protected area regardless of how you arrive there; positively confirm your position with ATC using runway designator and position descriptions; use landing lights and strobes to maximize conspicuity; when in doubt about your position relative to hold-short lines, query ATC; and treat every runway as active until confirmed otherwise, even during hover-taxi repositioning.
questions.follow_up: At airports with ASDE-X or ASDE-3 surface detection equipment, can the controller always see your helicopter on their display, and what does this mean for your personal runway incursion responsibilities?
questions.follow_up_answer: No — ASDE systems have limitations that may prevent reliable display of helicopter targets in some conditions. Helicopters flying at very low altitudes in ground effect, those without operating transponders, or those hovering in areas near taxiway intersections may not produce consistent or accurate returns. ASDE-X uses a combination of radar and transponder data; if your transponder is off or in standby, your ground track may not display at all or may be intermittent. ASDE-3 relies purely on radar and may have blind spots or ground clutter masking in some areas. This means you cannot assume the controller sees you simply because ASDE is installed. PIC responsibility under 14 CFR 91.3 remains absolute — technology assists controllers but does not transfer responsibility to the system. You must always verify your own position, obtain explicit clearances, and maintain visual situational awareness independent of what ATC's equipment may or may not be showing.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.3; 14 CFR 91.129; FAA AC 91-73B; AIM 4-3-18; FAA Runway Safety Program

questions.question: What is the most common collective management error pilots make during a rolling takeoff, and what is the immediate result if that error occurs?
questions.answer: The most common error is raising the collective too rapidly or too aggressively before sufficient translational lift has been achieved. This causes the helicopter to lift off prematurely—before adequate airspeed is established—essentially converting the rolling takeoff into an attempted vertical or semi-vertical departure without the power margin to support it. The result can be an uncommanded drift, loss of directional control, or settling back onto the surface with insufficient runway remaining.

questions.question: A student performing a rolling takeoff consistently allows the helicopter to veer left during the ground roll. What is the most likely cause of this?
questions.answer: The most likely cause is insufficient right pedal input to compensate for the increase in torque as power is added during the ground roll. As the collective is raised and engine power increases, torque reaction tends to yaw the nose to the left in a counterclockwise rotor system. The pilot must anticipate this with right pedal to maintain directional control. A secondary cause could be crabbing into a crosswind without proper correction.

questions.question: Why is it a critical error to attempt a rolling takeoff if the helicopter cannot be momentarily hovered at the beginning of the maneuver?
questions.answer: The FAA Helicopter Flying Handbook states that a running or rolling takeoff should not be attempted if the helicopter cannot be hovered at least momentarily. If the helicopter cannot hover, it means available power is insufficient for OGE hover. Without that baseline power margin, the pilot has no reliable way to abort the takeoff and transition back to a stable hover if something goes wrong during the roll. It also indicates the helicopter may not have adequate performance to clear obstacles after liftoff.

questions.question: During a rolling takeoff training flight, your student lifts off at the correct airspeed but immediately begins a steep climb attitude right after leaving the surface. What error is being made and what are the risks if uncorrected?
questions.answer: The student is raising the nose too aggressively immediately after liftoff, likely pulling aft cyclic to climb before sufficient airspeed and translational lift are fully established. This can cause the airspeed to decay, moving the helicopter back toward the region below effective translational lift (ETL). If power available is marginal, the helicopter could settle back toward the surface. It also increases the risk of entering a low-airspeed, high-power-demand condition close to the ground. The correction is to maintain a shallow climb attitude and allow airspeed to build before transitioning to a normal climb.

questions.question: You observe a student consistently allowing the skids or wheels to skip or bounce during the ground roll phase of a rolling takeoff before liftoff. What is causing this and how should it be corrected?
questions.answer: Skipping or bouncing during the ground roll is caused by raising the collective to a level that unloads most—but not all—of the helicopter's weight onto the landing gear, then allowing small cyclic or collective oscillations that alternately load and unload the gear. The correction is to apply collective smoothly and continuously, transitioning through the ground contact phase without hesitation. The pilot should maintain a slight forward cyclic to keep the nose attitude level and prevent the helicopter from trying to rotate prematurely. Any cyclic inputs during the roll should be smooth and deliberate.

questions.question: A pilot completes a rolling takeoff and climbs out on a straight path but notices the ball on the slip/skid indicator is consistently deflected throughout the climbout. What common error likely caused this and how is it corrected?
questions.answer: A deflected ball during climbout after a rolling takeoff typically indicates the pilot has not properly coordinated pedal inputs with power changes throughout the takeoff sequence. As torque increases during the roll and liftoff, the nose yawed but the pilot compensated with bank rather than pedal, or failed to neutralize a pedal input that was appropriate during the roll but not during climbout. The correction is to use pedals to maintain trim—keeping the ball centered—throughout every phase of the maneuver, and to scan the ball regularly rather than fixating on ground track or attitude alone.

questions.question: A student with 60 hours of helicopter time consistently performs the rolling takeoff with no errors individually—correct collective timing, good directional control, smooth liftoff—but the overall maneuver still looks rushed and uncoordinated when observed as a whole. As an instructor, how do you diagnose what is actually going wrong, and what is your corrective strategy?
questions.answer: When individual components are correct but the integrated maneuver looks uncoordinated, the underlying issue is almost always task saturation and poor scan prioritization. The student is performing each input reactively rather than anticipating the sequence. At 60 hours total time, the student likely has not yet developed automaticity for basic control inputs, so managing collective, cyclic, pedals, and external visual reference simultaneously exceeds their working memory capacity. The corrective strategy is to first have the student verbalize the maneuver sequence aloud before flying it, building a mental model of anticipation rather than reaction. Then break the maneuver into two phases—ground roll and liftoff/climb—and practice each phase in isolation, talking through transitions. Finally, reintegrate with a deliberate scan pattern: outside for directional control, instruments for airspeed cue, outside for obstacle clearance. Research in the HFH Chapter 13 context supports that accident risk is significantly elevated below 100 hours in type; task saturation at this stage is expected and addressed through structured repetition.
questions.follow_up: If this same student is about to go on a checkride and still shows this pattern under workload, what specific standard from the ACS would the evaluator use to determine whether a disapproval is warranted, and what would the evaluator be looking for?
questions.follow_up_answer: The evaluator would apply the general ACS task completion standards, which require the applicant to complete the task within the tolerances specified and to demonstrate single-pilot resource management and workload management throughout. Specifically, the evaluator would observe whether the applicant maintains positive aircraft control at all times, applies smooth and coordinated control inputs, and follows the correct sequence as described in the POH/RFM and HFH. If the lack of coordination results in deviation from heading exceeding ACS tolerances, failure to maintain proper airspeed during climbout, or any unsafe condition such as uncontrolled drift or skipping liftoff, the evaluator has grounds to disapprove. The evaluator is also assessing whether the applicant can self-identify and self-correct errors in real time—the S11 standard explicitly requires analyzing and correcting common errors, not just avoiding them.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10 and Chapter 13; ACS HI.IX.E.S11

questions.question: During a rolling takeoff on a narrow taxiway with obstacles on both sides, a student drifts left during the ground roll, overcorrects with right cyclic, briefly touches the right skid/wheel harder than the left, then lifts off in a right bank before recovering. Walk me through every error in that sequence and explain which one created the greatest risk.
questions.answer: Error 1 — Left drift during ground roll: Caused by insufficient right pedal to counter torque as power was applied. Error 2 — Overcorrection with right cyclic: The student confused directional control (a pedal function) with lateral bank (a cyclic function). Cyclic should not be used to correct heading drift on the ground; pedals are the correct input. Error 3 — Uneven weight on right gear: The right cyclic overcorrection loaded the right gear asymmetrically, creating a dynamic rollover risk. This is the greatest risk in the sequence. Dynamic rollover can occur when one gear becomes a pivot point and the rolling moment exceeds the pilot's ability to arrest it with opposite cyclic. On a narrow surface with obstacles, a rollover is catastrophic and non-recoverable once the critical rollover angle is exceeded. Error 4 — Liftoff in a right bank: The pilot lifted off with a bank angle already established, meaning the helicopter was not in a stable attitude at the moment of ground separation. This increases the risk of a tip-over or obstacle strike. The corrective strategy for the whole sequence is: anticipate torque with right pedal before adding power, never use cyclic to correct yaw during the ground roll, and if a significant bank develops before liftoff, abort the takeoff and return to a stable hover before reattempting.
questions.follow_up: At what point during that sequence should the student have recognized the situation was no longer recoverable and initiated an abort, and what does that abort look like in a rolling takeoff?
questions.follow_up_answer: The abort decision point was the moment the student recognized the right cyclic overcorrection was loading the right gear—before liftoff occurred. Once an asymmetric gear load begins in a confined-width area, continuing to liftoff compounds the risk of dynamic rollover. To abort a rolling takeoff, the pilot simultaneously reduces collective to settle the helicopter firmly and equally onto all gear, neutralizes cyclic to level the skids/wheels, and uses pedals to stop yaw. The helicopter should come to a controlled stop or return to a stable hover. Importantly, the abort must happen while there is still runway/surface ahead and before an unsafe bank angle develops. After aborting, the pilot should not reattempt until the cause of the drift is identified and corrected, and should verify no structural damage occurred from the asymmetric gear loading.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10 and Chapter 11 (Dynamic Rollover); ACS HI.IX.E.S11

questions.question: What is the primary reason a pilot would choose a running or roll-on landing over a normal hover landing in a helicopter?
questions.answer: A running or roll-on landing is used when the helicopter cannot develop enough power to hover out of ground effect (OGE) at the intended landing site. This most commonly occurs when operating at high density altitudes, high gross weights, or both — conditions where available power is insufficient to sustain a hover but may be sufficient to maintain translational lift during a low-speed approach and use the landing surface to decelerate.

questions.question: According to the Helicopter Flying Handbook, what is the key power check a pilot must perform before committing to a running or roll-on takeoff — and how does that same principle apply when planning a running landing?
questions.answer: Before a running or rolling takeoff, the pilot must verify that the helicopter can be hovered at least momentarily — if it cannot hover even briefly, the running takeoff should not be attempted. This same logic applies in reverse for a running landing: if the helicopter cannot hover at the destination, the pilot must plan for a running or roll-on landing rather than attempting a hover that exceeds available power. The ability to hover, even momentarily, is the threshold check.

questions.question: How does landing surface texture affect a running or roll-on landing, and what types of surfaces are most problematic?
questions.answer: Landing surface texture directly affects the friction and deceleration available to the helicopter after touchdown. Hard, smooth surfaces such as pavement provide predictable friction but can be slippery if wet or contaminated with fuel, oil, or ice. Soft surfaces like mud, sand, or tall grass may grab skids or wheels unevenly, creating a dynamic rollover risk or causing the helicopter to stop abruptly. Uneven or sloped terrain can cause a lateral roll tendency. Ideal surfaces are firm, flat, and free of obstructions. Pilots must assess surface conditions before committing to a running landing because loss of directional control or sudden deceleration on an unsuitable surface can be catastrophic.

questions.question: You're flying a skid-equipped helicopter at a mountain site at 9,500 feet density altitude, near max gross weight, and the POH shows your OGE hover ceiling is 8,200 feet. The landing zone is a wide, firm dirt road. Walk me through how you determine whether a running landing is appropriate and what your go/no-go criteria are before you begin the approach.
questions.answer: Since the density altitude (9,500 ft) exceeds the OGE hover ceiling (8,200 ft) at current gross weight, a normal hover landing is not feasible — a running or roll-on landing is the appropriate technique. Before committing, the pilot should: (1) Verify the landing surface is firm, flat, and free of loose debris, ruts, or hidden obstacles that could catch a skid; (2) Confirm the surface is long enough to allow full deceleration to a stop without running off the end or into obstacles; (3) Assess crosswind component — excessive crosswind can cause skids to drag laterally and induce a rollover; (4) Confirm an abort path is available if the approach deteriorates; (5) Verify the POH does not prohibit running landings on skids under any specific condition (e.g., some manufacturers limit skid landings on slopes). If the surface is firm, long, into the wind, and clear of obstacles, proceed. If any of those conditions cannot be met, reconsider the landing site.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 10; POH/RFM performance section

questions.question: During a shallow approach for a running landing, at what point does the helicopter transition out of effective translational lift (ETL), and how does the timing of that transition differ from a normal approach — and what control inputs does that require from you?
questions.answer: Effective translational lift is achieved as the helicopter accelerates through approximately 16–24 knots and is fully lost as airspeed decays near zero at touchdown. On a shallow approach, the helicopter maintains a higher forward speed throughout the descent and therefore transitions through the ETL range (16–24 knots) at a higher altitude above the ground compared to a steep approach. On a steep approach, the greater descent rate keeps the helicopter in the ETL envelope longer, so the transition through ETL occurs closer to touchdown. As the helicopter slows below approximately 10–15 knots and loses ETL-derived efficiency, induced power requirements increase sharply. The pilot must anticipate this power spike, smoothly increase collective to maintain rotor RPM, and apply forward cyclic as needed to manage the descent rate and maintain the desired approach path. The helicopter will exhibit a nose-pitch tendency as ETL breaks, requiring coordinated cyclic input.

questions.question: A helicopter with wheel-type landing gear versus one with skid-type landing gear — how does the landing gear configuration affect technique and risk during a running or roll-on landing, particularly regarding lateral stability and directional control?
questions.answer: Wheel-equipped helicopters are generally more forgiving during running landings because wheels allow the helicopter to roll in any direction with less resistance, reducing the risk of a skid catching and initiating a dynamic rollover. Directional control with wheels can be maintained using differential braking if equipped, or by keeping slight forward cyclic during rollout. Skid-equipped helicopters are more sensitive: if a skid catches on uneven terrain, a rut, or soft ground, it can abruptly stop that side of the helicopter while the other side continues, creating a rapid roll moment that can lead to dynamic rollover — particularly if the rotor disk is tilted in the wrong direction at that moment. For skid-equipped aircraft, keeping the cyclic centered or slightly into any crosswind during rollout and keeping the collective low (but not slammed down) is critical to prevent a skid-induced rollover. Manufacturers may also publish specific restrictions on skid running landings in the RFM.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 10 and Chapter 11 (dynamic rollover); POH/RFM

questions.question: A student tells you: 'As long as the landing area is long enough and I can keep it straight, a running landing on wet grass is no more risky than pavement.' What is wrong with that reasoning, and what specific hazards does wet grass present that could make it more dangerous than the student recognizes?
questions.answer: The student is oversimplifying a genuinely hazardous surface combination. Wet grass presents several risks that pavement does not: (1) Non-uniform deceleration — grass can vary in height, density, and moisture content across a short distance, causing one skid or wheel to experience more drag than the other, inducing an unplanned yaw or lateral roll; (2) Hidden terrain irregularities — grass conceals ruts, holes, rocks, and soft spots that a skid can catch, potentially triggering dynamic rollover; (3) Reduced friction at high speed but sudden grip at low speed — wet grass may be slippery initially, causing the pilot to carry more speed than intended, then the surface may suddenly grip a skid causing abrupt deceleration; (4) Skid-sink risk — wet or soft ground beneath grass can allow skids to dig in during rollout rather than sliding cleanly. None of these hazards are easily visible from the cockpit on approach. Pavement, while offering less cushion, is at least predictable and uniform. A pilot should specifically assess and recce the grass surface condition (wet, soft, uneven) before committing, and recognize that wet grass on skids is one of the higher-risk running landing surface combinations.
questions.follow_up: If during the rollout on wet grass one skid catches and the helicopter begins to roll rapidly, what is the immediate correct control response and why?
questions.follow_up_answer: The immediate response is to lower the collective fully and apply cyclic away from the direction of roll (toward the high side) to reduce the rolling moment. The collective must come down quickly to reduce rotor thrust, which is the force driving the rollover — without reducing rotor lift, the cyclic correction alone may be insufficient because the rotating disk continues to generate a moment that overcomes the pilot's input. This is the core of dynamic rollover recovery: collective reduction is the priority because it removes the energy source driving the roll. Delaying collective reduction even by one or two seconds dramatically reduces the chance of successful recovery as the aircraft approaches the critical rollover angle.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 10 (running landings) and Chapter 11 (dynamic rollover)

questions.question: Your helicopter's RFM does not specifically address running landings, but density altitude at the destination exceeds your OGE hover ceiling by 1,200 feet. What is your authority to perform a running landing, and what aircraft limitations must you still comply with even if the RFM is silent on the specific procedure?
questions.answer: The absence of a specific prohibition in the RFM does not mean the maneuver is unrestricted — it means the manufacturer has not addressed that specific procedure. Under 14 CFR 91.9, no person may operate an aircraft in excess of its limitations, and the RFM/POH constitutes the controlling document for those limitations. The pilot must still comply with all published limitations including maximum gross weight, center of gravity envelope, maximum airspeed (particularly at touchdown — some RFMs define maximum ground speed for landing), and any landing gear specific limits. Additionally, the pilot is responsible under 14 CFR 91.103 to become familiar with all available information appropriate to the flight, which includes performance data. Even with a silent RFM, the pilot should: (1) calculate whether forward speed at touchdown will be within any published airspeed or ground speed limits; (2) ensure the maneuver does not require exceeding any power or torque limit to maintain controlled flight on approach; (3) apply the general airmanship principle that the maneuver must remain within the aircraft's demonstrated safe operating envelope. If the pilot cannot determine from the RFM that the maneuver is safe within all known limitations, consulting the manufacturer directly or deferring to a more suitable landing site is the appropriate conservative action.
questions.follow_up: If a running landing results in a hard touchdown that you believe may have exceeded the aircraft's structural limits, what is your regulatory obligation before flying the aircraft again?
questions.follow_up_answer: Under 14 CFR 91.7, the pilot in command is responsible for determining the airworthiness of the aircraft before flight. A hard landing that may have exceeded structural design limits creates an airworthiness concern that must be resolved before the next flight. The pilot must ground the aircraft and have it inspected by a certificated mechanic in accordance with the manufacturer's hard-landing inspection requirements (typically published in the maintenance manual). Many helicopter manufacturers specify specific inspection criteria following hard landings, including rotor head, mast, skid gear, and airframe inspections. Flying without this inspection could expose the pilot to violation of 91.7 and potentially 14 CFR 91.9 for operating in a potentially unairworthy condition. The pilot should document the event in the aircraft maintenance logbook and contact the operator or owner immediately.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.7, 14 CFR 91.9, 14 CFR 91.103; FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 10; POH/RFM

questions.question: During a running/roll-on landing, how does a headwind affect the ground roll distance required to decelerate to a stop?
questions.answer: A headwind reduces the ground roll distance required. Because a headwind increases the airspeed over the rotor for any given groundspeed, the helicopter reaches effective translational lift (ETL) and becomes aerodynamically effective at a lower groundspeed. This means less forward momentum must be dissipated through ground friction and braking, so the helicopter stops in a shorter ground distance compared to a calm-wind or tailwind condition.

questions.question: Why is a running/roll-on landing technique used when a helicopter is operating at a high gross weight or in high density altitude conditions?
questions.answer: At high gross weight or high density altitude, the helicopter may not have sufficient power to hover out of ground effect (OGE) or even in ground effect (IGE). A running or roll-on landing uses translational lift gained from forward airspeed to supplement rotor lift, reducing the total power required to maintain controlled flight throughout the approach and landing. This allows the pilot to complete a safe landing even when hover power is unavailable.

questions.question: What is density altitude, and name two conditions that would produce a high density altitude on an otherwise mild day?
questions.answer: Density altitude is pressure altitude corrected for non-standard temperature — it represents the altitude at which the aircraft 'performs' regardless of actual elevation. Two conditions that would produce high density altitude on a mild day are: (1) High field elevation above sea level, which reduces air pressure and therefore air density. (2) High ambient temperature, which causes air to expand and become less dense, raising the density altitude above the pressure altitude. High humidity also contributes, as moist air is less dense than dry air at the same pressure and temperature.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 10; FAA-H-8083-25B Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, Chapter 4

questions.question: You're planning a shallow approach and running landing at a mountain airport (elevation 6,500 ft) on a hot afternoon with an outside air temperature of 35°C. The wind is calm. Walk me through how you would evaluate whether a running landing is the right technique and what specific performance concerns you'd have.
questions.answer: First, I'd calculate density altitude using the POH performance charts or the formula (approximately pressure altitude + [120 × (OAT – ISA temp)]). At 6,500 ft elevation with 35°C, density altitude could easily be 9,500–10,000 ft or higher. Next, I'd check the helicopter's hover charts to determine if OGE or even IGE hover is possible at the current gross weight. If OGE hover is not available, a running/roll-on landing is mandatory — I cannot execute a go-around to a stationary hover. Specific concerns include: (1) Increased approach airspeed needed to maintain translational lift, (2) Reduced power margin throughout the approach making precise airspeed and collective management critical, (3) Longer ground roll due to calm wind (no headwind component to help decelerate), (4) Engine and rotor performance degraded — I must monitor turbine temps and rotor RPM closely, and (5) A go-around may not be possible, so the approach must be fully committed and the landing surface adequate for ground roll.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 10; POH performance charts

questions.question: During a shallow approach to a running landing, you notice a direct crosswind. How does the crosswind affect your technique and what control inputs must you plan for during the ground roll?
questions.answer: A crosswind during a running landing requires lateral correction throughout the approach and ground roll. During the approach, I'll use a crab or side-slip technique to maintain track alignment with the landing surface. As I touch down, I must transition to a slip (upwind cyclic) to prevent the helicopter from drifting laterally — the skids or wheels must contact the surface aligned with the direction of travel to avoid a dynamic rollover tendency. During the ground roll, I apply upwind cyclic to keep the disc tilted into the wind, preventing the wind from rolling the helicopter. Excessive crosswind can make a running landing unsafe because lateral ground forces on the skids during the roll can induce dynamic rollover, particularly if one skid catches or brakes unevenly. I must know the crosswind limitation for running landings from the POH.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 10; Aircraft POH/RFM

questions.question: Your helicopter is loaded near maximum gross weight for the day's mission. How does this weight affect the approach airspeed you should fly on a shallow approach, and what happens to your power margin as you transition through ETL on the way to touchdown?
questions.answer: At maximum gross weight, approach airspeed should be flown per the normal procedure for the aircraft type; weight itself does not change the recommended approach speed. However, at high gross weight the helicopter operates higher on the power required curve, leaving reduced power margin for corrections and the final deceleration to hover. As the helicopter decelerates below approximately 16–24 knots and transitions out of effective translational lift near touchdown, induced power requirements increase sharply because the rotor must generate all lift through induced flow rather than translational flow. At maximum gross weight, particularly when operating near OGE or IGE hover power limits, this power spike can consume remaining available power, leaving little margin. If power is insufficient during this critical transition, the pilot may be unable to arrest the sink rate smoothly and could experience a hard landing or rotor RPM loss. This is why confirming available OGE and IGE hover power before the approach is essential at high weights.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapters 5 and 10

questions.question: A pilot argues that on a cool, high-humidity day at sea level, density altitude is essentially a non-issue for a running landing and full hover power should be readily available. Is this reasoning entirely sound, and what factors might still drive the decision to use a running landing even at sea level on a cool day?
questions.answer: The reasoning is partially correct — at sea level on a cool, low-humidity day, density altitude will be near or below standard, meaning engine and rotor performance is at or near book values. However, the decision to use a running landing is not driven by density altitude alone. Other valid reasons include: (1) Gross weight — even at sea level with ideal density altitude, a heavily loaded helicopter may not achieve OGE hover, and a running landing is the appropriate technique. (2) Obstacle environment — a shallow approach with a running landing may be operationally preferred at certain sites regardless of performance. (3) Engine health — a degraded engine may not produce rated power even at favorable density altitude. (4) Rotor system condition — worn blades or altered pitch links can reduce actual hover capability below published performance. The pilot should always consult the hover charts for the specific gross weight and conditions rather than relying on a general assumption about density altitude being 'not a factor.'
questions.follow_up: If a pilot confirms from the hover chart that the helicopter can hover OGE at the current weight and conditions, does that mean a running landing is never necessary at sea level on a cool day?
questions.follow_up_answer: Not necessarily. Even with confirmed OGE hover power available, a running landing may still be the best technique if the landing area is a prepared surface long enough to accommodate a roll-out, the surface conditions make a hover approach risky (e.g., blowing dust, brownout, whiteout), or operational efficiency requires minimizing hover time (e.g., frequent stops in a confined area). Additionally, if the hover chart was based on standard atmospheric data and engine anti-ice or bleed air is in use, actual power available may be less than charted — always account for any power extraction before trusting hover performance data.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 10; Aircraft POH/RFM performance section

questions.question: During a shallow approach and running landing in a tailwind condition, what are the compounding effects of a tailwind combined with high density altitude, and at what point does the combination of these factors make the attempt unsafe?
questions.answer: A tailwind increases groundspeed for a given airspeed, meaning the helicopter arrives at the landing surface with significantly more forward momentum than in calm or headwind conditions — the ground roll distance increases substantially. Combined with high density altitude, the effects compound in several dangerous ways: (1) Power required is already elevated due to reduced air density, leaving less margin for collective adjustments during approach. (2) Translational lift is lost at a higher groundspeed in a tailwind (the rotor 'sees' relative wind based on airspeed, but touchdown occurs at a higher groundspeed), so the helicopter hits the surface faster. (3) The ground roll is longer at high density altitude because there is less aerodynamic braking (thinner air) and potentially higher touchdown speed. (4) Go-around capability may be severely limited or nonexistent at high density altitude — committing to a tailwind/high-DA approach with inadequate landing surface length is a serious hazard. The combination becomes unsafe when: the calculated touchdown groundspeed combined with the available ground roll distance exceeds the landing surface, when the helicopter cannot be confirmed to maintain positive control through the full roll-out, or when any engine or power anomaly during the approach would leave no recovery option. The pilot must consult performance charts for the specific combination of weight, OAT, pressure altitude, and wind, and apply appropriate go/no-go criteria before beginning the approach.
questions.follow_up: If you arrive at the approach and realize the tailwind is stronger than expected and density altitude is higher than planned, what is your immediate decision priority and what options remain?
questions.follow_up_answer: Immediate decision priority: do not continue the approach if a safe running landing and roll-out cannot be guaranteed — go around immediately while energy and altitude still allow. Options remaining depend on power available: (1) If power permits, climb, fly to an alternate landing site with a headwind orientation or a longer surface. (2) If the site has no headwind option, consider whether a hover landing is possible — check if hover power exists at current weight and DA; if so, a hover/vertical landing eliminates the tailwind ground roll problem entirely. (3) If power is marginal and a go-around is questionable, the pilot should not have begun the approach — this underscores the critical importance of pre-approach performance planning and having an abort point identified before committing to descent. Continuing a tailwind approach into a high-DA site without adequate surface length or a confirmed abort plan is an error chain that should have been broken much earlier.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapters 10 and 13; Aircraft POH/RFM

questions.question: What is the most common airspeed error pilots make during the shallow approach phase of a running/roll-on landing, and why is it dangerous?
questions.answer: The most common airspeed error is allowing airspeed to decay too rapidly during the approach, which can result in the helicopter arriving over the touchdown point with insufficient translational lift and excessive sink rate. Since a running/roll-on landing is specifically used when the helicopter cannot hover OGE, losing airspeed prematurely eliminates the translational lift advantage the maneuver depends on, potentially leading to a hard landing or settling with power if power margins are insufficient.

questions.question: During a roll-on landing, what is the typical error a pilot makes with the collective at touchdown, and what hazard does it create?
questions.answer: A common error is raising the collective at or after touchdown in an attempt to cushion the landing or out of instinct. This is dangerous because it increases lift and torque demands at a moment when the helicopter is transitioning to ground contact, which can cause the helicopter to become airborne again momentarily with little airspeed, leading to a loss of directional control, dynamic rollover tendency, or a hard re-contact with the ground. The correct technique is to gradually lower the collective as the skids or wheels make contact to settle the helicopter firmly.

questions.question: What common glide path error occurs during a shallow approach, and how does it differ from the same error made during a normal approach?
questions.answer: A common glide path error during a shallow approach is flying the descent angle too shallow, which causes the helicopter to arrive over the landing surface at a lower altitude and farther down the runway, requiring an extended ground roll to stop. Conversely, flying the descent angle too steep can result in an excessive sink rate that cannot be arrested without available power. The shallow approach is more sensitive to glide path deviations than a normal approach because the power margin is already limited (OGE hover power may not be available), leaving less tolerance for corrections. A steep glide path deviation in particular can result in a sink rate that exceeds the aircraft's power capability to arrest, making early recognition and a go-around decision critical.

questions.question: You are on short final for a running landing and notice you are high and fast. You attempt to steepen the descent by lowering collective. What error are you at risk of committing, and what is the correct recovery technique?
questions.answer: By lowering collective aggressively on short final to steepen the descent when already low to the ground, you risk allowing rotor RPM to decay if the engine cannot respond quickly enough, and you also risk arriving at the touchdown point with excessive sink rate and insufficient airspeed to arrest it through ground effect. Additionally, rapidly decreasing collective can cause an abrupt nose pitch-up if not coordinated with forward cyclic. The correct technique is to recognize the high/fast condition early enough to execute a go-around rather than attempting to salvage the approach. If within limits, a coordinated reduction of collective with slight aft cyclic can control the descent, but the pilot must be prepared to execute a go-around immediately if parameters cannot be met by the decision point.

questions.question: During a running landing rollout, the helicopter begins to veer to one side. What are two common pilot errors that can cause this, and how should each be corrected?
questions.answer: First, improper pedal trim during the approach and touchdown causes the helicopter to have a yaw tendency upon ground contact, which the pilot must then correct with rudder/pedal — but the correction is often too aggressive, causing overcorrection and swerving. The fix is to establish proper pedal trim before touchdown. Second, unequal application of cyclic during rollout — either holding lateral cyclic input or failing to keep the cyclic centered — causes one skid or wheel to bear more weight, creating directional instability. The fix is to maintain coordinated, centered cyclic during rollout and use smooth pedal inputs for directional control. On wheeled helicopters, nose wheel steering must be coordinated with pedal inputs.

questions.question: A student pilot consistently attempts running landings even when the performance charts indicate OGE hover is available. Why is this a significant error in judgment, and what is the correct decision-making process?
questions.answer: This is a significant error because the running/roll-on landing is specifically a performance-limited maneuver, used when OGE hover power is not available. Defaulting to running landings when unnecessary reduces the pilot's proficiency with normal hover techniques, removes the option to abort and reposition prior to landing, and may result in the pilot developing a habit that leads to attempting running landings in unsuitable terrain where ground roll is impossible. The correct process is to check performance charts, compute OGE hover power required versus available, and select the appropriate landing technique based on actual performance data, obstacle clearance requirements, and landing surface suitability — not habituation.

questions.question: A pilot completes a running landing that appears successful, but during the rollout the helicopter experiences a dynamic rollover tendency. The pilot's instinct is to raise the collective to lift off. Why is this response potentially catastrophic, and what should have been done to prevent this error chain from starting?
questions.answer: Raising the collective during a dynamic rollover tendency during rollout is extremely dangerous because it increases both lift and torque asymmetrically — the side with the pivot point (a caught skid, slope, or uneven surface) acts as a fulcrum, and adding collective accelerates the roll rate beyond the point where cyclic input can arrest it. The helicopter can roll inverted in less than one second once dynamic rollover begins. The correct immediate response is to lower collective completely to the ground stop, not raise it. The error chain should have been broken earlier: the pilot should have assessed the landing surface for hazards before touchdown, maintained proper airspeed through translational lift to ensure a controlled touchdown, kept the cyclic neutral during rollout, and been alert to any lateral force or asymmetric ground contact cue. Attempting to fly out of a dynamic rollover after initiation is almost always fatal.
questions.follow_up: At what roll angle is dynamic rollover generally considered unrecoverable, and does that threshold change based on the direction of roll relative to the tail rotor?
questions.follow_up_answer: Dynamic rollover is generally considered unrecoverable at approximately 5–8 degrees of bank angle once rollover rate is established, which is well within normal-appearing bank angles — the pilot often has no perception of danger until it is too late. The threshold does change based on roll direction: rolling toward the tail rotor side (right roll on counterclockwise-rotor helicopters) is more critical because the tail rotor thrust contributes to the rolling moment. Rolling away from the tail rotor side allows slightly more recovery margin because tail rotor thrust opposes that roll direction. This is why pilots must be especially alert during right side slope operations or right crosswind conditions on standard U.S. helicopters.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 11; Chapter 10

questions.question: During a shallow approach in deteriorating wind conditions, a pilot fails to recognize that the headwind has shifted to a quartering tailwind. What compounding errors are likely to follow, and how does this scenario relate to Loss of Tail Rotor Effectiveness?
questions.answer: When a headwind shifts to a quartering tailwind on short final, several compounding errors commonly occur: (1) The pilot may not recognize the airspeed decay because the groundspeed reference looks normal — airspeed drops without obvious visual cues; (2) Loss of translational lift occurs earlier and at a higher altitude than expected, requiring more power than was planned; (3) The pilot may attempt to continue the approach rather than go around, entering a low-airspeed, high-power demand state; (4) At low airspeed with high power, the tailwind or right quartering wind condition creates an LTE-susceptible environment, particularly at the 210–330 degree relative wind sector for counterclockwise-rotor helicopters, where the tail rotor vortex ring state can reduce antitorque authority. The pilot who fails to anticipate this compound hazard may find themselves simultaneously dealing with insufficient power margin, loss of ETL, and degraded directional control — all on short final. The correct response is to go around at the first indication of an unplanned wind shift, replan the approach for actual conditions, and maintain awareness of the LTE risk sectors during any low-airspeed, high-power operation.
questions.follow_up: If you are already in the landing flare at low airspeed and notice an uncommanded yaw beginning, is it better to execute a go-around or complete the running landing? What factors determine this decision?
questions.follow_up_answer: This is a time-critical decision with no universal answer — it depends on the available power margin, altitude, ground speed, the rate and direction of the yaw, and the suitability of the landing surface ahead. If the yaw is slow and controllable with pedal input and the landing surface ahead is clear, completing the landing may be the safer option because a go-around requires applying full power, which increases torque demand and can worsen the yaw if antitorque is already compromised. However, if yaw rate is increasing despite full pedal input, the helicopter is at altitude, or the landing surface is unsuitable for rollout, an immediate go-around with aggressive acceleration to restore translational lift and pedal authority is warranted. The key decision factor is whether pedal authority is being regained or lost — if it is being lost, the situation will not improve at low airspeed and the go-around must be executed immediately, accepting the transient yaw during power application.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 10; Chapter 11 (LTE section)

questions.question: When planning a shallow approach and running landing, why is wind direction the first factor you consider when selecting your approach path?
questions.answer: Wind direction determines the effective lift and translational lift available during the approach. A headwind reduces groundspeed at any given airspeed, shortens the landing roll, and increases lift — all of which improve performance margins. A tailwind does the opposite: it increases groundspeed, extends the landing roll, and reduces effective lift, requiring more power and a longer landing area. Selecting an into-the-wind approach path directly reduces the risk of running out of performance or landing area.

questions.question: What is the primary reason a pilot uses a running or roll-on landing instead of a normal approach to a hover?
questions.answer: A running or roll-on landing is used when the helicopter cannot hover out of ground effect (OGE) — meaning the aircraft does not have sufficient power to sustain a hover outside the ground effect cushion. This typically occurs at high density altitude, heavy gross weight, or high temperature conditions. The running landing takes advantage of translational lift and ground effect throughout the landing roll, allowing the aircraft to operate safely even when hover power is unavailable.

questions.question: Before committing to a shallow approach and running landing, what aircraft performance check should you complete to confirm the maneuver is appropriate for current conditions?
questions.answer: You should verify whether the helicopter can be hovered — even momentarily — in ground effect (IGE). Per the Helicopter Flying Handbook, a running or rolling takeoff or landing should not be attempted if the helicopter cannot be hovered at least momentarily. This check confirms you have enough power to maintain directional control at the slow-speed transition during the landing roll. Additionally, you should reference the POH/RFM performance charts for hover IGE capability at the current gross weight, pressure altitude, and temperature.

questions.question: You are operating at a high-altitude airport on a hot day with a 15-knot crosswind. The only suitable landing area is a paved surface oriented 90 degrees to the wind. Walk me through how you would evaluate whether this approach path is acceptable for a shallow approach and running landing.
questions.answer: First, determine the helicopter's actual performance capability by checking hover IGE power available versus power required from the POH charts at current gross weight, pressure altitude, and OAT. If hover IGE is marginal, a running landing may still be viable — but the crosswind introduces additional risk. Evaluate the crosswind component against any demonstrated or published crosswind limitations in the RFM. During a running landing with a 90-degree crosswind, the helicopter will weathervane into the wind, creating a directional control challenge and potential for dynamic rollover as the skids or wheels touch down asymmetrically. Consider whether a longer, lower approach into the wind — even if it requires obstacle clearance adjustment — is possible. If the crosswind component exceeds aircraft limits or crew capability, the approach should not be attempted on that path. Always have a go-around point identified before committing.

questions.question: During your shallow approach setup, you realize the selected landing path has a slight downslope. How does slope affect your risk assessment for a running landing, and would you continue?
questions.answer: A downsloping landing surface reduces the effective stopping distance available because gravity assists acceleration during the roll-out instead of helping decelerate the aircraft. This means the helicopter will travel farther before coming to a stop, increasing the risk of running off the end of the usable surface or colliding with obstacles. Additionally, on a downslope, if the collective is raised prematurely during the roll-out, the helicopter may become airborne again in an uncontrolled manner. You must assess whether the usable length of the landing surface — accounting for the slope — is sufficient for the expected groundspeed at touchdown given current wind conditions. If the combination of slope, groundspeed, and surface length creates unacceptable stopping distance risk, select an alternate path or landing area. The decision point (abort point) should be moved closer to the approach end.

questions.question: You've selected an approach path for a running landing, but midway through the approach a gust shifts the wind 30 degrees and increases 10 knots. At what point does this new information require you to reassess your approach path selection, and what is your decision-making process?
questions.answer: Wind changes must trigger an immediate reassessment any time they affect your planned touchdown point, groundspeed at touchdown, or landing roll-out. In this scenario, a 30-degree shift combined with a 10-knot increase introduces both a crosswind component that wasn't planned and a change in your approach energy. First, evaluate: does the aircraft now have a crosswind component that exceeds limits or comfortable handling margins? Second, has your planned touchdown point shifted due to the changed headwind component — are you now arriving faster or slower than planned? Third, is there still adequate landing surface remaining given the new parameters? If any of these create doubt, execute a go-around immediately and re-evaluate from a stabilized position. The Helicopter Flying Handbook supports the principle that if the action will only 'probably' work out, choose an option known to work — a go-around is always the conservative and correct choice when in doubt during a running landing approach.

questions.question: A pilot argues that selecting a slightly tailwind approach path for a running landing is acceptable because the surface is long enough to accommodate the extra roll. As an examiner, what specific performance and risk factors would you probe to determine whether this reasoning is sound or fatally flawed?
questions.answer: This reasoning requires deep scrutiny. While a long surface theoretically compensates for increased groundspeed, the actual risk factors go beyond stopping distance. First: at what point during the approach does loss of translational lift (ETL) occur, and does the tailwind component reduce the airspeed at which ETL is lost, forcing the collective up earlier and at a higher groundspeed? Second: what is the available power margin? With a tailwind, effective airspeed is lower at any given groundspeed — the helicopter may require more collective during the approach to maintain glide path, reducing power margin. Third: what happens if a go-around is required late on the approach? Initiating a go-around with a tailwind at low airspeed places the aircraft in a low-airspeed, high-power-demand regime that may not be recoverable given the performance environment.
