FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 emphasizes that if an action will only 'probably' work out, the pilot should choose an option that is known to work. As the instructor, the correction is to replace 'probably' reasoning with a concrete decision rule: if there is doubt, the go-around is always the known-safe action. The student should be taught to establish personal minimums and stabilized approach criteria, and to treat any deviation from those criteria as an automatic go-around trigger — removing subjective probability assessment from the decision entirely. This structured approach prevents fatigue, pressure, and wishful thinking from influencing critical decisions at the most vulnerable flight phase.
questions.follow_up: How do personal minimums help a pilot avoid this type of 'probably' reasoning during approach, and what elements should a helicopter pilot include in their personal approach minimums?
questions.follow_up_answer: Personal minimums remove in-flight judgment from pre-defined go/no-go criteria, replacing subjective probability with predetermined thresholds. For helicopter approaches, personal minimums should include: (1) Maximum allowable sink rate on final (e.g., no more than 500 FPM below 200 AGL); (2) Airspeed range at key gates; (3) Power setting within defined limits at defined altitudes; (4) Maximum crosswind component; (5) Minimum visibility for the type of approach; (6) Whether the aircraft is trimmed and stable at a defined gate height. If any criterion is not met at the defined gate, the go-around is executed automatically — no further judgment required. This structure prevents the pilot from being influenced by fatigue, pressure, or wishful thinking at the most critical phase of flight.

questions.question: During an IFR approach in a helicopter, you reach the missed approach point (MAP) with the runway not in sight. You are fatigued, low on fuel, and the alternate is 45 minutes away. Walk me through how you would make the go-around decision, and what physiological and cognitive factors are working against you at this moment.
questions.answer: The go-around at the MAP when the runway is not in sight is not a decision — it is a regulatory requirement under 14 CFR 91.175(c): the pilot may not descend below MDA or DH unless the runway environment is clearly visible and the aircraft is in a position to make a normal landing. Therefore, the go-around must be executed regardless of fuel or fatigue. The physiological and cognitive factors working against the pilot include: (1) Fatigue degrades attention, working memory, and risk assessment — the pilot may underestimate how low fuel truly is or overestimate aircraft performance; (2) Fuel pressure creates urgency bias — the pilot may rationalize continuing below minimums; (3) The sunk-cost fallacy ('I've already come this far') can override sound judgment; (4) Continuation bias — the strong tendency to continue a plan already in motion rather than divert. The correct action is immediate initiation of the published missed approach procedure, squawk 7700 if fuel is emergency status, declare an emergency with ATC to receive priority handling, and divert to the nearest suitable airport — not necessarily the filed alternate.
questions.follow_up: If fuel state is now truly emergency and the alternate is too far, what regulatory authority does the pilot have, and what actions should be taken immediately?
questions.follow_up_answer: Under 14 CFR 91.3(b), the pilot-in-command may deviate from any rule to the extent necessary to meet an emergency. This means the pilot may request an immediate approach to any available airport, may declare an emergency with ATC (which triggers priority handling and emergency services), and may request a special instrument approach or visual approach if conditions permit. The pilot should: (1) Declare the emergency immediately — 'MAYDAY, MAYDAY, MAYDAY' — to obtain priority; (2) Request radar vectors to the nearest suitable airport with instrument or visual approach capability; (3) Advise ATC of fuel remaining in time (not gallons) and souls on board; (4) After the flight, submit a report to the FAA Administrator if deviation from an FAA regulation occurred, as required by 91.3(c). Waiting too long to declare degrades options — early declaration is always the right call.

questions.question: What is the most common cyclic error a pilot makes when initiating a go-around from a low, slow approach in a helicopter?
questions.answer: The most common cyclic error is applying abrupt or excessive forward cyclic to accelerate, which can cause the nose to pitch down aggressively and reduce ground clearance. The correct technique is a smooth, coordinated cyclic input to establish a climbing attitude while simultaneously adding collective and adjusting pedals for torque. Abrupt inputs can also lead to rotor RPM fluctuations and loss of situational awareness.

questions.question: During a go-around, a student pilot fails to add right pedal when rapidly increasing collective in a counterclockwise-rotor helicopter. What is the likely result of this error?
questions.answer: When collective is increased rapidly, engine torque increases and causes the nose to yaw left. Failure to apply right pedal (antitorque input) to compensate will cause the helicopter to yaw left, disrupting directional control and potentially leading to an uncoordinated, skidding climb. This is one of the most common pedal errors during a go-around and can result in loss of heading control.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 9, Basic Flight Maneuvers; Chapter 11, Helicopter Emergencies

questions.question: What collective-related error is commonly seen when a pilot executes a go-around and what instrument should be monitored to catch it early?
questions.answer: A common collective error is raising collective too rapidly, which can cause rotor RPM to decay below the normal operating range as the rotor system absorbs the increased pitch demand faster than the engine can supply power. Pilots should monitor the tachometer (rotor/engine RPM gauge) closely during the go-around to ensure rotor RPM stays within the green arc. A slow, smooth collective increase coordinated with throttle (if applicable) is the correct technique.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 9, Basic Flight Maneuvers; Chapter 11 (Low Rotor RPM)

questions.question: You are on short final at a confined area at 300 feet AGL, slow airspeed, and in a high power condition. You decide to go around. Describe two errors specific to this scenario that could make the go-around more hazardous than the original approach.
questions.answer: First, initiating the go-around too late when already in a high power, low-airspeed condition may leave little power margin remaining to climb, especially if the helicopter is near its maximum gross weight or at high density altitude — the pilot may attempt the go-around but be unable to achieve a positive rate of climb. Second, abrupt cyclic forward to accelerate while simultaneously pulling collective could place the helicopter dangerously close to the height-velocity (avoid) curve, increasing the risk of an unsurvivable power failure. Additionally, fixating on the go-around without scanning for obstacles or terrain in the climb-out path is a common attentional error in confined area operations.

questions.question: A student executing a go-around from an instrument approach in IMC climbs away from the MDA but then starts drifting off the published missed approach course. What two common errors likely led to this situation?
questions.answer: The first error is task saturation — the pilot is managing the physical demands of the go-around (collective, cyclic, pedals, power) and neglects immediate transition to the published missed approach procedure, particularly the required heading and altitude. The second error is failure to brief the missed approach procedure before commencing the approach, which is a standard pre-approach task. Without a mental plan, the pilot defaults to visual instincts rather than instrument scan, leading to heading deviations. Both errors reflect poor single-pilot resource management (SRM) and workload prioritization.

questions.question: During a go-around, your examiner notices the helicopter entered a left skid throughout the climb transition. Walk me through the two most likely control errors that produce a skid in this phase of flight.
questions.answer: A skid occurs when the pilot applies excessive rudder (pedal input) relative to the bank angle, causing the nose to yaw faster than the turn rate dictates — the helicopter's velocity vector points toward the inside of the turn. In a go-around, two common causes are: (1) Excessive right pedal input during the power application phase — the pilot over-corrects for torque and over-rotates the nose right, then the helicopter skids left as the pedal is released or as the pilot attempts to recover; and (2) Failure to maintain coordinated flight during a climbing turn if one is required — applying too much pedal relative to bank angle will produce a skid. You can detect a skid by observing the inclinometer ball moving toward the outside of the turn. The pilot should monitor the ball throughout the maneuver to ensure coordinated flight and apply pedal input appropriate to the bank angle and rate of turn.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 9 (Slips and Skids); FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 4

questions.question: A pilot successfully executes the physical go-around but after the fact admits they hesitated for several seconds after recognizing an unstabilized approach before deciding to go around. What cognitive error pattern does this reflect, and how can it contribute to an accident even when the go-around itself is successful?
questions.answer: This reflects the 'plan continuation bias' (also called get-there-itis or press-on-itis), where a pilot continues an established course of action — landing — despite cues indicating it should be abandoned. The hesitation represents the pilot's cognitive resistance to deviating from the original plan. Even when the go-around is ultimately executed, the delayed decision compresses the safety margin: altitude is lower, airspeed may be further decayed, and the helicopter may have entered a more critical point in the height-velocity envelope. The FAA's error chain concept from ADM states that accidents rarely result from a single error — this hesitation can be the link that converts a manageable situation into a fatal one if any additional factor (mechanical, environmental) occurs during the delay window.
questions.follow_up: If this pilot repeatedly shows plan continuation bias across multiple approaches during the checkride, what does that tell you as an examiner, and is that a disqualifying performance issue?
questions.follow_up_answer: Repeated plan continuation bias is a significant safety concern that indicates a systemic ADM deficiency, not an isolated control error. As an examiner, it suggests the pilot has not internalized the go-around as a normal, expected maneuver but rather as an admission of failure — a dangerous mindset. Per the ACS, unsatisfactory performance in risk management or ADM is grounds for discontinuation of the practical test. The examiner is not limited to evaluating stick-and-rudder skills; a pilot who consistently demonstrates poor judgment or fails to manage risk effectively cannot be certificated, regardless of how smooth their control inputs are.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (ADM, Plan Continuation Bias, Error Chain); ACS Risk Management Standards

questions.question: During a practice go-around from a simulated instrument approach, your student rapidly raises collective, applies forward cyclic to accelerate, and the rotor RPM begins to decay. The student responds by lowering collective slightly, but the RPM continues to drop. What compounding error has the student likely made, and what is the correct recovery sequence?
questions.answer: The student has likely made the compounding error of simultaneously applying forward cyclic aggressively while the rotor RPM is already decaying — the forward cyclic attitude change increases the blade pitch requirement on the advancing side and can actually accelerate rotor RPM decay in some situations, particularly if the nose pitch-down attitude is causing the rotor to unload. Additionally, the student may have failed to verify throttle is at the full open/flight detent position before manipulating collective. The correct recovery sequence is: (1) immediately verify throttle is full open, (2) lower collective smoothly to allow RPM to recover into the green arc, (3) maintain a level or slightly nose-high attitude with cyclic to prevent altitude loss during recovery, and (4) once RPM is restored, gradually reapply collective to establish the go-around climb. The FAA is explicit that rotor stall in a helicopter is not recoverable — early recognition and immediate corrective action are imperative.
questions.follow_up: At what point in this scenario should the student have recognized the RPM decay was occurring, and what is the first instrument they should have scanned after initiating the go-around?
questions.follow_up_answer: The student should have been monitoring the tachometer (dual-needle RPM gauge showing both rotor and engine RPM) as the first instrument scan after initiating the go-around power application, even before verifying climb attitude on the attitude indicator. The tachometer needle split or rotor needle dropping below the green arc is the immediate trigger for corrective action. In helicopters with governor systems, a split between engine and rotor RPM needles is an early warning that the rotor is being loaded faster than the engine can follow. The student's scan order error — prioritizing attitude or airspeed over RPM — is itself a common error in the go-around that the ACS expects candidates to recognize and correct.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11 (Low Rotor RPM / Rotor Stall); Chapter 9 (Basic Flight Maneuvers)

questions.question: What is a go-around, and at what point in an approach should a pilot be prepared to execute one?
questions.answer: A go-around is the decision to abandon a landing approach and transition back to climbing flight. A pilot should be prepared to execute a go-around at any point during the approach, but the decision becomes most critical when the helicopter is below a safe abort altitude, is not stabilized on the approach, or conditions on or near the landing area are unsafe. The fundamental principle is that a go-around is always an option until the helicopter is firmly on the ground with power reduced.

questions.question: Name at least four conditions that should trigger the recognition of a need for a go-around during a helicopter approach.
questions.answer: Conditions that should trigger recognition of a go-around include: (1) an unstabilized approach — improper airspeed, rate of descent, or approach angle that cannot be corrected in time; (2) an unexpected obstacle or hazard in the landing zone; (3) another aircraft or vehicle on the intended landing area; (4) loss of visual reference or sudden deterioration of visibility; (5) excessive crosswind or wind shear causing loss of control; (6) low rotor RPM that cannot be corrected before touchdown; (7) a mechanical issue or abnormal indication identified during final; (8) the landing zone surface appearing unsuitable (soft ground, debris, slope greater than published limits).
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapters 9 and 11

questions.question: Why is recognizing the need for a go-around considered a risk management skill rather than simply a technical flying skill?
questions.answer: Recognizing the need for a go-around is fundamentally a risk management skill because it requires the pilot to evaluate accumulating risk factors, make a timely aeronautical decision, and resist the psychological pressure to continue a bad approach — often called 'get-there-itis' or 'press-on-itis.' According to the FAA, approximately 80% of aviation accidents are caused by human factors and poor decision-making. The go-around decision requires situational awareness, honest self-assessment, and the willingness to choose the known safe option over continuing an approach that will 'probably' work out — the FAA explicitly cautions against relying on 'probably' when a safer alternative exists.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 13; ADM principles

questions.question: You are on a steep approach to a confined area. At 50 feet AGL you notice the intended touchdown spot is smaller than it appeared from altitude, rotor wash is kicking up significant dust, and your airspeed has bled below the recommended approach speed. How do you evaluate whether a go-around is needed, and what factors are you weighing?
questions.answer: This scenario presents multiple simultaneous risk factors that together strongly indicate a go-around is needed. The evaluation should consider: (1) Airspeed below recommended approach speed means energy management is compromised — if the aircraft is already slow and descending, there is reduced margin to arrest sink rate without entering a low-G situation or exceeding power limits; (2) The dust cloud reduces visual reference to the landing surface, creating a risk of brownout and spatial disorientation; (3) A landing zone smaller than anticipated increases the risk of rotor blade or skid contact with obstacles. No single factor alone may be decisive, but the combination of unstabilized airspeed, reduced visibility, and a revised LZ assessment creates a compounding risk chain. Per ADM principles, when multiple factors are stacking up negatively, the correct decision is to break the error chain early — execute the go-around rather than commit to a landing that will 'probably' work out.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapters 9 and 13

questions.question: A student pilot says, 'I didn't go around because I thought I could salvage the approach — I almost had it.' As an instructor, what specific risk management concept does this statement illustrate, and how would you address it?
questions.answer: The student's statement illustrates the concept of 'continuation bias' combined with the hazardous attitude of 'invulnerability' — the belief that poor outcomes happen to other pilots, not to them. It also reflects a failure to apply the FAA's ADM principle that 'probably' is not an acceptable standard when a safe alternative exists. As an instructor, I would address this by: (1) reinforcing that a go-around is not a failure — it is the correct decision; (2) discussing how accidents typically result from a chain of multiple poor decisions, not one single mistake, and that continuing a bad approach adds links to that chain; (3) establishing personal minimums for stabilized approach criteria — specific airspeed, glide path, and visual reference thresholds — so the go-around decision is pre-planned rather than made under pressure; (4) referencing that accidents correlate with experience in a specific aircraft type and that newer pilots especially should default to conservative decision-making.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 13; ADM/SRM principles

questions.question: You are shooting an IFR approach in a helicopter and break out of the clouds at minimums. The runway environment is in sight, but you notice your rate of descent is excessive and you are significantly high on the VASI. You have approximately 8 seconds to reach the threshold. Walk me through how you recognize whether a go-around is required.
questions.answer: At minimums with an excessive rate of descent and a high VASI indication, the approach is not stabilized. The recognition process is: (1) Assess whether the deviation can be corrected with normal control inputs in the available distance and time — being high on VASI with excessive descent rate simultaneously often indicates a dive-and-drive approach that places the aircraft in an energy state where either a hard landing or undershoot is likely; (2) Determine whether correcting one problem (reducing descent) will create another (floating past the touchdown zone); (3) Apply the stabilized approach standard — if the approach cannot be brought into tolerance by 200 feet AGL, a go-around is required. With only 8 seconds to the threshold and two simultaneous deviations, the honest assessment is that corrective action will not result in a safe landing. The go-around must be recognized and initiated immediately. Delaying recognition while attempting a correction that 'probably' will work is the exact scenario the FAA cautions against in ADM guidance.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapters 9 and 13; FAA-H-8083-15B Instrument Flying Handbook, Chapter 1

questions.question: A pilot executes every approach with a personal rule: 'If I am not stabilized by 300 feet AGL on a normal approach, I go around — no exceptions.' During a checkride, the examiner observes the pilot initiate a go-around at 290 feet AGL on an approach that appeared nearly stable. The examiner questions the decision. How would you evaluate whether this pilot's decision-making reflects sound risk management or excessive conservatism, and what does this reveal about the nature of pre-planned go-around criteria?
questions.answer: This pilot's decision reflects sound risk management, not excessive conservatism. Pre-planned personal minimums — such as a stabilized approach gate at 300 feet AGL — are a cornerstone of proactive ADM. Their value lies precisely in removing in-the-moment judgment from a high-workload, high-pressure environment. When a pilot commits in advance to a binary criterion ('stable by 300 feet or go around'), they eliminate the cognitive trap of real-time rationalization ('I can probably fix this'). The fact that the approach appeared 'nearly stable' is irrelevant — 'nearly stable' is not stable, and the pilot correctly applied their pre-established standard. From a risk management perspective, a go-around executed at 290 feet on a nearly-stable approach carries essentially zero risk, while continuing a 'probably fixable' approach carries compounding risk. The examiner's question is legitimate, however, because it tests whether the applicant can articulate the rationale — not just follow a rule. The correct answer reveals that pre-planned criteria are most effective when the pilot understands why the standard exists, not just that it exists.
questions.follow_up: If this same pilot always goes around at the slightest deviation and never lands on the first attempt during training, is there a point at which this pattern itself becomes a risk management concern?
questions.follow_up_answer: Yes. While conservative go-around decisions are generally encouraged, a pattern of consistent inability to complete approaches to landing can indicate a skill deficiency in approach technique or aircraft control rather than genuinely good ADM. If a pilot never lands on the first attempt, it may signal that they lack the precision to fly a stabilized approach in the first place — a different category of risk. A true risk manager develops both the discipline to go around when needed AND the skill to fly approaches that meet stabilized criteria consistently. Instructors and examiners should distinguish between a pilot who goes around because of genuine instability and one who uses the go-around as an avoidance behavior to mask poor approach technique. The goal of pre-planned criteria is to remove judgment from borderline situations, not to substitute for developing competency.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 13; ADM/SRM principles

questions.question: During a night approach to an offshore platform, a helicopter pilot is on short final when the helideck crew signals 'clear to land.' The pilot notices a slight lateral drift, marginal airspeed, and the deck appears to be rising and falling approximately 2–3 feet with swell. The pilot is fatigued after a long duty day. Walk me through all the risk factors present and explain how the recognition of a go-around need must be evaluated differently at night and over water versus a standard land approach.
questions.answer: This scenario involves multiple compounding risk factors that individually might be manageable but together strongly suggest a go-around: (1) Lateral drift on short final — indicates the approach is not stabilized laterally, increasing risk of striking the deck edge or superstructure; (2) Marginal airspeed — reduced energy state limits ability to arrest descent or correct drift without exceeding power limits; (3) Moving deck — a 2–3 foot heave cycle requires precise timing for touchdown; misjudging the phase can result in hard landing, dynamic rollover, or structural damage; (4) Night conditions — reduced visual cues make lateral drift and closure rate harder to judge accurately, and depth perception over water is severely degraded; (5) Pilot fatigue — impairs reaction time, decision-making quality, and the ability to recognize developing hazards, all of which are compounded at night. The evaluation at night over water differs from a land approach because: visual illusions are more prevalent (black hole effect, featureless water), there is no go-around terrain reference, and the consequence of an in-water ditching is immediately life-threatening. The recognition threshold for a go-around should therefore be lower — any single significant factor at night over water should prompt the same go-around decision that might require two or three factors on a daytime land approach. Fatigue specifically degrades the pilot's ability to recognize the need for a go-around, which is itself the primary risk management threat in this scenario.
questions.follow_up: You execute the go-around. Now you have a fatigued pilot at night over water with limited fuel. How does the recognition that a go-around was necessary change the decision-making framework for the next approach attempt?
questions.follow_up_answer: The go-around itself is data. The pilot must now perform an honest self-assessment: Why was the approach unstabilized? Was it fatigue, technique, environmental conditions, or aircraft factors? If fatigue is the root cause, a second attempt under the same conditions with less fuel creates a higher-risk scenario, not a lower one. The correct framework is: (1) Establish a higher altitude orbit to allow time for deliberate planning; (2) Communicate with the platform crew about deck movement and request a status update; (3) Honestly assess whether personal performance is degraded enough to require diverting to an alternate (ship or land base) rather than continuing; (4) Apply the ADM principle that the 'error chain' is already active — a go-around from fatigue-induced instability, now with reduced fuel, is a chain with multiple links already formed. Adding another approach attempt without addressing the root cause adds another link. The pilot should brief themselves aloud: 'If I am not fully stabilized at 100 feet, I divert — no second chances.' This pre-commitment is the correct SRM response to a known degraded state.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapters 11 and 13; ADM/SRM principles; offshore operations guidance

questions.question: When executing a go-around in a helicopter, what is the primary risk associated with applying full power too abruptly during the initial power application?
questions.answer: Applying full power too abruptly on a helicopter with a counterclockwise-rotating main rotor (most American helicopters) creates a sudden and large torque reaction to the right. If the pilot fails to anticipate and apply sufficient left pedal simultaneously, the nose will yaw sharply right, potentially leading to loss of directional control. Additionally, rapid collective application can cause rotor RPM to decay if the engine cannot spool up fast enough to match the increased blade pitch demand.

questions.question: During a go-around from a low approach, what is the coordinated sequence of flight control inputs required when transitioning from a descent to a climb?
questions.answer: The coordinated sequence is: (1) simultaneously apply collective to arrest the descent and add power, (2) apply left pedal to counteract the increased torque from higher power, (3) apply forward cyclic as needed to accelerate toward best rate-of-climb airspeed and prevent the nose from pitching excessively high as the collective is raised, and (4) maintain a positive rate of climb and clear all obstacles. All inputs must be coordinated and smooth — abrupt or out-of-sequence inputs risk yaw excursions, rotor RPM fluctuations, or loss of positive aircraft control.

questions.question: What is the risk of applying aft cyclic aggressively during a helicopter go-around initiated at low altitude and low airspeed?
questions.answer: Aggressive aft cyclic at low altitude and low airspeed risks inducing a low-G pushover recovery or exceeding aft cyclic limits. More critically at low speed with power being applied, excessive aft cyclic combined with high collective and possible out-of-trim conditions can place the helicopter in a tail-low, nose-high attitude that may exceed torque limits and reduce forward obstacle clearance. There is also a risk of the tail rotor striking the ground if the nose pitches excessively high near the surface.

questions.question: You are on a steep confined-area approach at reduced airspeed and you decide to go around just as you cross the approach threshold. The collective is already near mid-range to control descent rate. What specific risk exists with power application at this point, and how do you mitigate it?
questions.answer: At reduced airspeed near a confined area, the helicopter is operating in a high-induced-drag, low-translational-lift environment. Applying full collective quickly may cause the rotor RPM to decay if engine response is not immediate, especially in turbine helicopters with slight spool-up lag. There is also a high risk of settling — the helicopter may continue to descend momentarily even after collective is raised due to power settling or low inertia rotor systems. Mitigation: apply collective firmly but smoothly, cross-check rotor RPM, ensure the collective does not exceed engine torque limits, simultaneously apply appropriate pedal and cyclic, and establish a positive climb attitude before maneuvering toward a departure path. Do not attempt to turn back into the confined area until a positive rate of climb is confirmed.

questions.question: During an instrument approach in IMC, you reach the decision altitude and the runway environment is not in sight. You initiate a go-around. What is the risk of delaying power and cyclic inputs even by one or two seconds at this point, and what does that mean for control priorities?
questions.answer: In IMC at decision altitude, the helicopter is in a stabilized descent configuration — delay in go-around power and flight control inputs means continued descent below a safe altitude, potentially below obstacle clearance height. Even one to two seconds at a 500 ft/min descent rate equates to 15–17 feet of additional altitude loss. The immediate priority is: collective up to stop the descent, coordinated pedal to maintain trim, and cyclic to establish a climb attitude — all referenced to flight instruments rather than visual cues. A delayed or incomplete power application risks controlled flight into terrain (CFIT). The pilot must also guard against transitioning to visual references too early if momentarily breaking out of the base of the cloud layer.

questions.question: You are executing a go-around from a running landing attempt that has gone unstable. As you apply collective to transition back to flight, a left yaw begins. You apply right pedal to correct. What risk have you just introduced, and what is the proper corrective action?
questions.answer: On a counterclockwise-rotor helicopter, increased power during the collective application creates increased engine torque, which naturally induces left yaw. The correct antidote is LEFT pedal to counteract this torque-induced yaw. By applying RIGHT pedal instead, you reduce tail rotor thrust at the exact moment when high power is being demanded — this is the low-airspeed, high-power environment where Loss of Tail Rotor Effectiveness (LTE) risk is greatest. Improper pedal input in this condition can trigger rapid uncommanded rotation at low altitude. The proper corrective action is to apply LEFT pedal to control the torque-induced yaw, maintain coordinated flight through the inclinometer, and accelerate airspeed through translational lift to reduce power and pedal demands.

questions.question: A student pilot consistently applies power correctly during go-arounds but always lags on the pedal input, allowing the nose to yaw 10–15 degrees before correcting. Explain the compounding risks this error creates at low altitude and what underlying concept the student is failing to apply.
questions.answer: A 10–15 degree yaw excursion at low altitude during a go-around creates several compounding risks: (1) the nose yaw changes the direction of the climb, which in a confined or obstacle-rich environment could vector the helicopter toward terrain or obstructions; (2) the yaw destabilizes the flight path just as the pilot is workload-saturated managing collective, cyclic, and outside references; (3) the delayed correction often results in an overcorrection, creating a pendulum yaw oscillation that further degrades control; (4) at high power settings, a right yaw (for counterclockwise rotor systems) is actually a reduction in tail rotor thrust, which at the wrong airspeed and power combination can enter an LTE onset condition. The underlying concept the student is failing to apply is anticipatory — or proactive — flight control coordination. The pedal correction must be applied simultaneously with, not after, the collective increase, because torque is instantaneous with power application. This reflects a broader ADM and workload management deficiency where the student is reacting rather than anticipating.
questions.follow_up: If this student also tends to fixate on the airspeed indicator during the go-around transition instead of outside visual references or attitude, what additional risk does that cross-cockpit fixation create, and how would you address it as their instructor?
questions.follow_up_answer: Fixating on the airspeed indicator during the low-altitude, high-workload go-around transition delays detection of developing yaw, pitch excursions, and obstacle awareness. Airspeed builds relatively slowly in the initial go-around; the pilot fixating on the instrument is likely to see little immediate change, which increases dwell time inside the cockpit precisely when terrain and obstacle avoidance demand outside attention. This is a classic example of channelized attention — one of the hazardous human factors addressed in ADM. As the instructor, I would address this through scenario-based training where I identify and verbalize the fixation in debrief, then have the student practice go-arounds with emphasis on an instrument scan that prioritizes attitude and power instruments first, with airspeed as a secondary cross-check. I would also use the Trescott Tip principle: if the student's go-around will 'probably' be okay with delayed pedal and instrument fixation, that is not an acceptable margin — we must train to the standard that is known to work every time.

questions.question: During a checkride go-around from a simulated instrument approach at 200 feet AGL, the applicant raises collective, applies left pedal, but then pulls aft cyclic aggressively to climb over a 'simulated' obstacle. The helicopter pitches nose-high, airspeed decays to near hover, and the low-RPM warning activates briefly. Walk me through every risk that just manifested and what the chain of events could become if not immediately corrected.
questions.answer: This scenario presents a cascading error chain with multiple simultaneous risks: (1) Aggressive aft cyclic at 200 AGL in a high-power, low-airspeed condition risks transitioning through translational lift in an uncontrolled manner — the helicopter may enter an exaggerated nose-high, tail-low attitude where the tail rotor approaches ground proximity; (2) The nose-high attitude with high collective demand causes rotor RPM decay, evidenced by the low-RPM caution — this is the onset of a rotor stall condition, which in helicopters is not recoverable once fully developed; (3) At near-hover airspeed with high power, the helicopter is deep in the region of reversed command — any further airspeed decay requires even more power, which the rotor system may not be able to sustain at reduced RPM; (4) The loss of translational lift at this stage means induced power requirements spike, worsening the RPM decay; (5) If the low-RPM condition is not corrected immediately by reducing collective to allow RPM recovery, and simultaneously lowering the nose to accelerate, the situation can progress to a main rotor stall from which there is no recovery. The pilot must immediately: lower collective to recover rotor RPM, lower the nose with forward cyclic, allow airspeed to build through ETL, and re-establish a stabilized climb. The 'simulated obstacle' never justifies a maneuver that risks rotor stall at low altitude.
questions.follow_up: If the applicant argues that the Pilot's Operating Handbook shows the helicopter has a maximum continuous power setting and they were 'within limits,' how do you explain why rotor RPM decay still occurred?
questions.follow_up_answer: Engine torque limits and rotor RPM are related but separate parameters. The engine may be producing its rated torque at or below the maximum continuous power limit, but if collective pitch is raised faster than the engine can respond — particularly with turbine spool-up lag — the rotor blades are demanding more energy than the engine is delivering instantaneously. This creates a rotor RPM decay that is independent of whether the torque gauge is in the green. Additionally, the aggressive aft cyclic increased the effective angle of attack across the disk, increasing induced drag on the rotor system simultaneously with the high collective demand, further burdening the rotor. Being 'within engine limits' does not mean the rotor RPM will remain in the green — the pilot must monitor rotor RPM as a separate and critical parameter, especially during aggressive or abrupt control inputs at low speed and high power.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 9, Chapter 11; specific POH/RFM for aircraft in use

questions.question: During a go-around from a helicopter instrument approach, what are the primary collision hazard categories you need to account for?
questions.answer: The primary collision hazard categories during a go-around are: (1) terrain and obstacles — towers, wires, trees, and terrain in the missed approach corridor; (2) other traffic — aircraft on the runway, in the pattern, or on parallel approaches; and (3) vertical obstructions not depicted on approach plates or easily overlooked at low visibility, such as power lines and antenna towers. The pilot must immediately establish a positive climb, follow the published missed approach procedure, and contact ATC to obtain traffic separation. Situational awareness of all three hazard categories must be maintained simultaneously.

questions.question: Why are wire strikes a particularly serious collision hazard during a helicopter go-around in IMC compared to a fixed-wing aircraft go-around?
questions.answer: Helicopters frequently operate at much lower altitudes than fixed-wing aircraft, and their published decision altitudes and missed approach climb gradients may still result in the helicopter passing through altitude bands where distribution lines, communication wires, and fence wires exist. Additionally, helicopter instrument approaches often serve sites in rural or industrial areas where unlighted or charted-but-hard-to-locate wires are common. Wires are rarely depicted on instrument approach plates and are nearly invisible in low-visibility or night conditions. The helicopter's slower airspeed during transition also increases exposure time in the hazardous altitude band.

questions.question: What role does ATC communication play in managing collision hazards during an unexpected go-around on an instrument approach?
questions.answer: ATC provides traffic separation and sequencing for IFR aircraft, so declaring a missed approach to ATC as early as possible is critical. When the pilot initiates a go-around, ATC must be notified so that: (1) any following traffic on the same approach can be sequenced safely; (2) departing traffic from the airport can be held or re-sequenced; and (3) the pilot can receive missed approach clearance instructions, including radar vectors if available. Failure to communicate promptly increases the risk of a mid-air collision, particularly in low-visibility conditions when visual separation is not possible. Per AIM guidance, the pilot should fly the published missed approach procedure until receiving ATC instructions.

questions.question: You are flying a GPS approach to a remote helipad in mountainous terrain and break out of the clouds at MDA with a 200-foot ceiling. You determine the helipad is not in sight and initiate a go-around. Describe how you manage terrain collision hazards from this point forward.
questions.answer: Immediately upon initiating the go-around: (1) Apply full power and establish a positive climb attitude — for a helicopter the transition from near-hover or slow flight to climb must be positive and deliberate; (2) Climb at Vy or the best rate speed specified in the missed approach procedure to maximize terrain separation as quickly as possible; (3) Follow the published missed approach procedure exactly — the protected obstacle clearance area is only guaranteed if you fly the published course and climb gradient; (4) Do not attempt to visually navigate around terrain — in marginal VMC below MDA/DA you may be tempted to maneuver visually, but mountainous terrain can rapidly lead to a box canyon or inadvertent IMC situation; (5) Communicate with ATC immediately; (6) Do not re-attempt the approach until conditions improve above minima. The greatest terrain collision risk occurs if the pilot deviates from the published missed approach track while trying to maintain visual contact with the ground.

questions.question: You are on a visual approach to a hospital helipad when a ground vehicle enters the landing zone and you execute a go-around. The hospital is surrounded by buildings and light poles. How does your go-around execution differ from a standard runway go-around in terms of collision hazard management?
questions.answer: A helipad go-around in a confined urban environment involves significantly higher collision hazard complexity than a runway go-around. Key differences: (1) There is no clear runway environment — obstacles surround the helipad on multiple sides; the pilot must know the pre-planned escape route before beginning any approach (this should be briefed during the approach setup); (2) The go-around must be executed along the pre-briefed egress path, not simply 'straight ahead' as in a fixed-wing go-around; (3) Building-induced turbulence and rotor wake can create control challenges during the climb-out; (4) Light poles, antennas, and HVAC equipment on nearby rooftops are collision hazards that may be very close to the go-around flight path; (5) There may be other aircraft or helicopters operating near a busy medical facility. The pre-approach brief must include: the go-around direction, specific obstacles to avoid, and a minimum altitude to be reached before any turn.

questions.question: During a go-around at night in VMC, you lose situational awareness of your exact position relative to nearby tall tower obstacles that were on your approach chart. What risk management strategies should you apply to prevent a collision?
questions.answer: Risk management strategies: (1) Climb immediately to a safe altitude — if there is any doubt about obstacle clearance, climb above the maximum charted obstacle height for the sector before maneuvering; (2) Use instrument references — even in VMC at night, towers and obstacles are often invisible without lights; treat the situation as if it were IMC until obstacle clearance is confirmed; (3) Contact ATC and request radar vectors or position assistance — ATC radar can identify your position relative to known terrain and obstacles; (4) Reference the approach chart's missed approach procedure — the published procedure accounts for the charted obstacles in the area; (5) Avoid descending or maneuvering laterally until positive situational awareness is re-established; (6) Use GPS moving map if available to confirm position relative to charted obstacles. The error chain concept from ADM applies here — loss of situational awareness combined with continued maneuvering at low altitude is a classic fatal accident chain; breaking it requires climbing and slowing the decision tempo.

questions.question: A pilot flying a helicopter ILS approach in actual IMC initiates a go-around at DA but continues to descend an additional 50 feet below DA before the climb is established, due to the transition time from approach configuration to climb configuration. How does this relate to collision hazard risk, and what technique reduces this specific vulnerability?
questions.answer: This scenario illustrates the 'decision altitude undershoot' — a well-documented risk in instrument approaches where the mechanical delay between reaching DA and establishing a positive climb can result in the aircraft momentarily descending below published obstacle clearance height. At DA the obstacle clearance surface comes to a point; any descent below DA while maneuvering puts the aircraft in uncharted obstacle territory. In a helicopter this risk is amplified because: (1) helicopters have different pitch inertia and power response characteristics than fixed-wing aircraft; (2) the transition from approach attitude to climb attitude is not instantaneous; (3) a helicopter at slow approach speed may have a longer time-to-climb than anticipated. Risk reduction techniques: (1) Brief a 'decision altitude + buffer' — mentally trigger the go-around decision slightly above DA to allow for reaction time; (2) Maintain approach power settings that allow a rapid transition — avoid being at a very low power setting at DA; (3) Practice the go-around transition under the hood in training to reduce reaction time; (4) In a simulator, measure your actual descent during go-around initiation and account for it in your personal minimums.
questions.follow_up: If your helicopter's published approach category allows you to use a higher MDA rather than a DA, does this change the collision hazard calculus during a go-around?
questions.follow_up_answer: Yes, significantly. A DA is a decision point — you must have begun the missed approach by that point, and the obstacle protection surface accounts for continued flight to the missed approach point. An MDA is a minimum altitude that must not be descended below; the pilot is expected to remain at MDA until reaching the missed approach point (MAP) before initiating the climb. This means at an MDA-based approach, the pilot may be flying level at MDA with no additional climb buffer built in at the MAP — the obstacle clearance protection ends at the MAP. If the pilot delays initiating the go-around until the MAP and then has a climb transition delay, they are again vulnerable to being at or below obstacle clearance altitude. The risk mitigation is to initiate the go-around slightly before reaching the MAP if not in a position to land, rather than waiting until the MAP itself.

questions.question: You are conducting a go-around from a published instrument approach and ATC instructs you to turn to a heading immediately that takes you off the published missed approach procedure track. What is the collision hazard risk in complying, and how should you respond?
questions.answer: Immediately departing the published missed approach procedure at low altitude at ATC's request introduces significant collision hazard risk because: (1) the published missed approach track is the only course with guaranteed obstacle clearance at the specified climb gradient — lateral deviations off that track place you in uncharted obstacle territory; (2) ATC radar does not have the resolution to guarantee obstacle clearance — ATC provides traffic separation, not terrain/obstacle separation; (3) ATC may be unaware of unlighted obstacles or recent additions in the area. The correct response is to comply with ATC's instruction ONLY after reaching a safe altitude that ensures obstacle clearance for the new heading. Per 14 CFR 91.175(e), the pilot should climb on the published missed approach course until reaching a safe altitude before complying with ATC vectors. The pilot should tell ATC: 'Unable immediate turn, will comply when obstacle clearance altitude is reached, climbing on published missed approach.' ATC generally understands and accepts this. If ATC insists for traffic conflict reasons, the pilot must use judgment — pilot-in-command authority under 14 CFR 91.3 allows deviation from ATC instructions when necessary for safety.
questions.follow_up: What specific climb gradient is typically required by published missed approach procedures, and what happens if your helicopter cannot meet that gradient on a single engine during a go-around?
questions.follow_up_answer: The standard required obstacle clearance for a missed approach procedure assumes a 200 feet per nautical mile climb gradient unless a higher gradient is published on the approach plate. If a higher gradient is required, it will be noted with a climb via notation or in the procedure notes. If your helicopter cannot achieve the published climb gradient — for example due to engine failure, high density altitude, or heavy gross weight — the published obstacle clearance is not guaranteed. In a single-engine failure scenario during a go-around, the pilot must: (1) follow emergency procedures for the aircraft; (2) declare an emergency with ATC; (3) be aware that the published missed approach may not be safely achievable; (4) consider an immediate landing on or near the runway or helipad if conditions allow, rather than attempting a climb-out that cannot be executed. Aircraft flight manuals for multiengine helicopters typically publish OEI (one engine inoperative) performance charts that allow the pilot to determine if the missed approach gradient can be maintained, and this should be part of the pre-approach performance planning.

questions.question: During a go-around in a helicopter, what does 'loss of situational awareness' mean, and why is it particularly dangerous at low altitude?
questions.answer: Loss of situational awareness (SA) means the pilot no longer has an accurate mental picture of the aircraft's position, altitude, speed, and environment. During a go-around — which is a high-workload, low-altitude transition — losing SA can result in controlled flight into terrain (CFIT), collision with obstacles, or failure to climb away safely. At low altitude there is minimal margin for error before terrain or obstacles become a factor, and the time available to recognize and correct a problem is extremely compressed.

questions.question: Name the four risk factors listed in ACS element HI.X.B.R4 that can affect a pilot during a helicopter go-around.
questions.answer: The four risk factors are: (1) Distractions — anything that diverts the pilot's attention from flying the helicopter; (2) Task prioritization — failing to manage the sequence of actions correctly during the go-around transition; (3) Loss of situational awareness — no longer having an accurate picture of aircraft state and environment; and (4) Disorientation — becoming spatially or positionally confused, especially likely when transitioning from a visual approach to a climb in degraded conditions.

questions.question: What is the correct task priority sequence a helicopter pilot should follow immediately after deciding to execute a go-around?
questions.answer: The first priority is always to fly the aircraft — establish a positive climb attitude and apply go-around power with the collective while maintaining heading and airspeed control with cyclic and pedals. Second, configure the helicopter as required (e.g., adjust attitude for Vy or obstacle clearance speed). Third, communicate with ATC or CTAF. Finally, complete any required checklists or configuration changes. Aviate, Navigate, Communicate is the correct hierarchy. Attempting to communicate or complete checklists before establishing aircraft control is a common prioritization error.

questions.question: You are on final approach to a confined area helipad when ATC suddenly issues a frequency change and a new routing clearance. You are 200 feet AGL and recognize you need to go around. How should you manage this distraction to avoid losing situational awareness?
questions.answer: Immediately prioritize flying the aircraft over responding to ATC. Initiate the go-around by applying collective for climb power, establishing a positive climb attitude with cyclic, and controlling heading with pedals. Do not touch the radio until the helicopter is climbing safely and aircraft control is confirmed. If needed, advise ATC with a brief 'going around' call, but only after aircraft control is established. The new routing clearance can be copied once you are established in the climb and workload permits. Attempting to copy a clearance while simultaneously transitioning from approach to climb at 200 feet AGL is a classic distraction-induced SA breakdown scenario — the error chain begins when you divide attention from flying.

questions.question: A student pilot you are flying with misses a confined-area approach and you take the controls to perform a go-around. During the climb, the student starts asking questions about what went wrong and pointing at the instruments. Describe how this scenario creates a risk of disorientation and what you do to mitigate it.
questions.answer: The student's verbal interaction and physical gestures toward the panel create a cockpit distraction that competes for the instructor's visual and cognitive attention precisely when control inputs and obstacle clearance demand full focus. In low-altitude, high-workload phases like a go-around, even brief periods of head-down time or divided attention can cause the pilot to lose track of aircraft pitch, bank, altitude, and proximity to terrain — the definition of disorientation and SA loss. To mitigate: clearly state 'I have the controls' and direct the student to be quiet until clear of the area ('Hold all questions until we're established in the climb'). Maintain outside visual reference, cross-check altimeter and VSI, and do not engage in any discussion until at a safe altitude and away from obstacles. Debriefing the approach is a ground task, not an in-flight task at low altitude.

questions.question: You are flying a night go-around at an unlit rural helipad. After initiating the climb, you notice you are unsure whether you are in a left or right bank. What risk factor is this, and what is the correct recovery action?
questions.answer: This is spatial disorientation — specifically, the inability to determine aircraft attitude without reliable outside visual references at night. During a night go-around, the absence of visual horizon creates ideal conditions for vestibular illusions. The correct action is to immediately transition to instrument flying: cross-check the attitude indicator for bank angle, the altimeter for altitude trend, and the VSI for climb rate. Do not rely on seat-of-the-pants sensations. Establish a wings-level, positive-climb attitude on instruments and climb to a safe altitude before attempting to reorient visually. This scenario illustrates why night or low-visibility go-arounds require instrument proficiency even for VFR-rated pilots.

questions.question: The FAA states that approximately 80% of aviation accidents are caused by human factors, and that the 'error chain' typically involves multiple poor decisions. Walk me through how a single go-around decision in a helicopter can deteriorate into a fatal accident through accumulated SA loss and poor task prioritization, identifying at least three links in that chain.
questions.answer: A representative error chain might look like this: Link 1 — The pilot delays the go-around decision, allowing the approach to deteriorate further before acting, meaning the go-around is initiated lower and slower than ideal. Link 2 — During the go-around, the pilot attempts to simultaneously copy an ATC frequency change, splitting attention between radio and aircraft control; collective application is delayed and climb rate is insufficient. Link 3 — The pilot becomes distracted by a passenger question or cockpit alert, goes heads-down briefly, and loses awareness of a rising terrain feature or obstacle off the departure end. Link 4 — Now disoriented as to position relative to the obstacle, the pilot makes a reactive cyclic input that reduces climb performance at the critical moment. The accident occurs not because any single error was catastrophic but because each poor decision degraded the margin for error. Breaking any one link — deciding earlier, deferring radio work, briefing passengers before flight — could change the outcome. This is the core principle of error chain awareness in ADM.
questions.follow_up: You mentioned the pilot delayed the go-around decision. What specific cues during a helicopter approach should trigger an immediate go-around decision before the situation deteriorates further?
questions.follow_up_answer: Go-around triggers include: unstabilized approach (excessive sink rate, speed not on target, heading not aligned by a defined gate altitude); loss of a clear landing zone view due to obstacles or dust/debris; mechanical anomaly indication (unusual vibration, warning light); traffic or obstacle in the landing area; ATC instruction; wind shear or sudden unexpected turbulence disrupting the approach; and any condition where the pilot's mental model of the approach no longer matches what they are seeing. The earlier the decision is made, the higher the altitude and the more options exist. Waiting until committing to land and then aborting at low hover altitude is the highest-risk scenario. The FAA Helicopter Flying Handbook emphasizes that a go-around is always a valid option and should be made without hesitation when any doubt exists.

questions.question: What is a runway incursion, and why is a go-around a critical phase of flight for this risk?
questions.answer: A runway incursion is any occurrence at an aerodrome involving the incorrect presence of an aircraft, vehicle, or person on the protected area of a surface designated for the landing and takeoff of aircraft. During a go-around, the pilot is simultaneously managing a sudden configuration change, increased power, aircraft attitude, and ATC communications — all while the aircraft remains at low altitude near active runways and taxiways. This high workload phase increases the risk of misidentifying the correct runway or runway crossing clearances.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA AC 91-73B; 14 CFR 91.129; FAA Runway Safety Program

questions.question: What are the four categories of runway incursion severity defined by the FAA, and which represents the greatest risk of collision?
questions.answer: The FAA categorizes runway incursions from Category A through D. Category A is the most severe — a serious incident where a collision was narrowly avoided. Category B involves significant potential for collision requiring a drastic response. Category C has ample time and distance to avoid a collision but with a reduced safety margin. Category D is an incursion that meets the definition but presents little or no immediate safety consequence. A Category A incursion represents the greatest risk of collision.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA Runway Safety Program; FAA AC 91-73B

questions.question: When ATC clears you to land and you execute a go-around, what is your immediate communication responsibility to reduce the risk of a runway incursion by other traffic?
questions.answer: You must immediately notify ATC that you are executing a go-around. The tower may have issued a takeoff clearance to another aircraft based on your expected landing, or may have traffic crossing the runway. Prompt communication allows ATC to issue revised instructions and prevent conflicting traffic from entering the runway environment. Failure to promptly advise ATC of the go-around is a leading contributing factor to runway incursions during this phase.

questions.question: You are executing a go-around at a towered airport and ATC instructs you to make an immediate left turn to avoid traffic on the parallel runway. During the turn, you become uncertain whether you are now positioned over an active taxiway used by a departing aircraft. Walk me through how you manage the runway incursion risk in that moment.
questions.answer: First, comply with the ATC instruction and maintain aircraft control — do not fixate on the uncertainty at the expense of flying the helicopter. Immediately request clarification from ATC: 'Tower, [callsign], confirm I'm clear of [runway/taxiway designation].' Use all available positional cues — runway markings, lighting (hold short bars, REILs, PAPIs), moving map if equipped, and visual traffic scan. Do not descend below a safe maneuvering altitude while positional awareness is uncertain. If you have any reason to believe a collision is imminent, climb and maneuver aggressively while advising ATC. The priority hierarchy is: aviate, navigate, communicate — but in this scenario all three must happen nearly simultaneously.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.113; AIM 4-3-13; FAA AC 91-73B; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (ADM/SRM)

questions.question: You're conducting instrument approaches at an unfamiliar towered airport at night. After a missed approach, ATC clears you to re-intercept the final approach course, but the heading takes you toward what appears to be a lit runway crossing. What runway incursion risk factors are stacking up here, and how do you manage them?
questions.answer: Multiple risk factors are stacking: night operations reduce visual cues, unfamiliar airport increases positional uncertainty, instrument approach workload is high, and the heading given by ATC may route you over an active surface. Risk factors from the ADM error chain concept include task saturation, unfamiliarity, and low-visibility environment. Manage by: (1) slowing down mentally — request clarification or a delay vector if needed; (2) pulling up the airport diagram on an EFB or chart to confirm the layout; (3) querying ATC for traffic advisories and confirming any crossing clearances explicitly; (4) not descending below the published missed approach altitude until positionally certain. Never assume a clearance covers runway crossings unless explicitly stated.
questions.regulatory_ref: AIM 4-3-18; FAA AC 91-73B; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (error chain/ADM); 14 CFR 91.129

questions.question: How does a helicopter's go-around differ from a fixed-wing go-around in terms of runway incursion risk, specifically regarding where the aircraft goes after the maneuver is initiated?
questions.answer: A fixed-wing go-around typically results in the aircraft climbing out along the runway extended centerline or following a published missed approach segment, keeping it within a predictable corridor. A helicopter, however, has the unique capability — and sometimes the operational need — to break off an approach and transition laterally or even hover in close proximity to taxiways or other runways. This lateral flexibility, combined with low-altitude maneuvering, can place the helicopter over surfaces where ATC expects no aircraft. Pilots must be explicit with ATC about their intended flight path after a go-around and must not assume that standard fixed-wing missed approach routing applies to their helicopter operation.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 9 (Basic Flight Maneuvers); AIM 4-3-13; FAA AC 91-73B

questions.question: A pilot flying a Part 135 EMS helicopter executes a go-around at a busy regional airport. In the high-workload transition, the pilot fails to read back a hold-short instruction and inadvertently crosses Runway 28L — resulting in a runway incursion. From a risk management standpoint, what systemic factors likely contributed, and what mitigation strategies should be in place before the flight ever begins?
questions.answer: Systemic contributors likely include: task saturation during go-around transition (power, trim, attitude, climb), insufficient sterile cockpit discipline, inadequate pre-briefing of airport layout and hot spots, failure to use read-back/hear-back procedures, and possibly crew/individual complacency from familiarity with the airport. Pre-flight mitigations include: reviewing airport diagrams and published hot spots (noted on FAA Hot Spot list and approach plates), briefing go-around procedures and anticipated ATC instructions, committing to verbal hold-short readbacks regardless of workload, using crew resource management (CRM) or SRM discipline to protect critical communications, and setting automation (moving map) prior to descent so it can serve as a positional cue. The ADM error chain concept from FAA-H-8083-21B underscores that this incursion was the result of multiple compounding decisions, not a single failure — breaking any one link would likely have prevented it.
questions.follow_up: After the incursion, the crew reports that they had been to this airport many times and felt very comfortable with the layout. How does familiarity specifically increase runway incursion risk rather than reduce it?
questions.follow_up_answer: Familiarity breeds complacency — a recognized human factors hazard in ADM. When pilots feel they 'know' an airport, they are less likely to actively scan for changed runway configurations, NOTAMs regarding temporary runway closures or construction, or unfamiliar ATC instructions that deviate from the expected flow. Research cited in FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 shows that accident rates correlate more strongly with hours in a specific aircraft and environment than total flight hours, and that overconfidence in a familiar environment reduces vigilance. Familiar pilots also tend to anticipate ATC clearances rather than waiting for and reading back explicit instructions — a direct cause of runway incursions. The FAA recommends treating every airport arrival as if it were the first time, regardless of experience there.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (ADM/SRM/error chain); FAA AC 91-73B; AIM 4-3-18 (Hot Spots); 14 CFR 135.81; 14 CFR 91.129

questions.question: During a go-around in low IMC at a towered airport, ATC issues a heading that conflicts with what the pilot believes is a published missed approach procedure. The pilot is uncertain whether the new heading will take the helicopter over an occupied runway. How should the pilot resolve this conflict, and what is the regulatory basis for the action taken?
questions.answer: The pilot must comply with the ATC instruction if it does not create an immediate safety hazard — ATC radar vectors supersede published procedures when issued in a controlled environment. However, if the pilot has genuine safety concerns about a runway conflict, they are authorized under 14 CFR 91.3 to deviate from any rule or ATC clearance to the extent necessary to meet an emergency or safety-of-flight need, and must notify ATC immediately. In this scenario: (1) execute the vector while querying ATC simultaneously — 'Tower, [callsign], confirm we're clear of Runway XX on this heading'; (2) if ATC cannot provide immediate assurance and the aircraft is at low altitude with imminent runway conflict, climb and deviate as necessary, then advise ATC; (3) file an ASRS report after landing regardless of outcome. The AIM states that when a clearance is not understood or appears unsafe, the pilot should request clarification immediately. Silence is not compliance — it is a hazard.
questions.follow_up: If this same situation occurred under actual IFR conditions and the pilot deviated from the ATC vector without declaring an emergency, what are the potential regulatory and certificate consequences, and how does filing an ASRS report affect that outcome?
questions.follow_up_answer: Deviating from an ATC clearance without declaring an emergency is a violation of 14 CFR 91.123, which requires pilots to comply with ATC clearances and instructions unless an emergency exists. The FAA could initiate certificate action (suspension or revocation) or civil penalty proceedings. However, filing a NASA Aviation Safety Reporting System (ASRS) report within 10 days of the incident provides the pilot with immunity from certificate suspension (though not from revocation in cases of criminal activity or lack of qualification) under FAA Order 8900.1 and the ASRS program rules. The report does not prevent an investigation, but it demonstrates good faith and contributes safety data. Importantly, the pilot should also consider whether to declare a pilot deviation report proactively with ATC — this is distinct from the ASRS report and demonstrates transparency.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.3; 14 CFR 91.123; AIM 4-4-11; FAA ASRS Program (NASA); FAA Order 8900.1

questions.question: At what point during an instrument approach should you make the decision to execute a go-around if the runway environment is not in sight?
questions.answer: The decision must be made at or before reaching the Decision Altitude (DA) on a precision approach, or the Minimum Descent Altitude (MDA) on a non-precision approach. If the runway environment is not in sight by that point, a missed approach must be initiated immediately. Continuing below DA/MDA without the required visual references is not permitted.

questions.question: What are the required visual references that must be distinctly visible and identifiable before you can descend below MDA or continue below DA on an instrument approach?
questions.answer: Under 14 CFR 91.175(c), the pilot must have one of the following in sight and be able to make a normal landing: approach light system (ALS), threshold, threshold markings, threshold lights, runway end identifier lights (REIL), visual approach slope indicator (VASI), touchdown zone, touchdown zone markings, touchdown zone lights, runway, runway markings, or runway lights. Flight visibility must also be at or above the published minimum.

questions.question: When flying a helicopter instrument approach, what is the correct sequence of control inputs when executing a go-around from a low-airspeed, near-hover condition at minimums?
questions.answer: Apply collective to increase power and arrest any descent, simultaneously apply forward cyclic to establish a climb attitude and accelerate to best rate of climb airspeed (Vy), use appropriate antitorque pedal input to maintain trim throughout the power increase, and transition smoothly to the published missed approach procedure. Avoid abrupt collective increases which can cause rotor RPM decay or dynamic rollover risk. Follow the published missed approach instructions immediately.

questions.question: You are flying an ILS approach in IMC and break out of the clouds at 300 feet AGL — 100 feet above your DA. The runway appears to be slightly left of centerline and you are behind on your descent. You are not in a position to make a normal landing. What do you do, and why?
questions.answer: Execute a go-around immediately. Even though the runway is in sight and you are still above DA, the approach is unstabilized — you are off centerline and behind on the descent profile. A timely decision means recognizing that continuing will not result in a safe landing. Pressing on from an unstabilized position is a classic link in the error chain. Apply collective, establish climb attitude, and fly the published missed approach. The ACS specifically requires a timely decision; waiting until touchdown becomes unavoidable is too late.

questions.question: During a helicopter RNAV (GPS) approach, you arrive at MDA with the runway environment in sight, but you are in a high right quartering tailwind that has you drifting across final at 15 knots. You believe you can correct. Should you continue or go around? Explain your reasoning.
questions.answer: You should execute a go-around. Although the runway is in sight and you are at MDA, the ability to make a normal landing is in question — 14 CFR 91.175(c) requires the flight visibility and the ability to execute a normal landing, not just runway contact. A right quartering tailwind means the wind has both a tailwind component and a right crosswind component. During deceleration to hover and landing, this configuration increases LTE risk (particularly with the left-rear quartering wind pattern) and makes recovery from a drift more difficult. The inability to execute a normal landing safely — meaning you cannot reliably control your descent path and touch down aligned with the runway — mandates a go-around per 14 CFR 91.175(c).

questions.question: The evaluator calls 'go around' just as you cross the final approach fix inbound at 2,000 AGL — well above MDA. You are fully established on course. How do you respond, and are there any helicopter-specific considerations at this stage of the approach?
questions.answer: Respond immediately by acknowledging the call, applying collective to maintain or climb from current altitude, adjusting power as needed, and transitioning to the published missed approach procedure. At this stage you are at normal cruise or approach airspeed, so the go-around is aerodynamically straightforward — no risk of low-G or mast bumping if inputs are smooth. Comply with the missed approach routing on the chart immediately; do not continue inbound. At a towered field, advise ATC you are executing the missed approach. Helicopter-specific consideration: ensure rotor RPM remains in the green arc and antitorque inputs match the power change to prevent yaw excursion.

questions.question: A pilot reports they hesitated to go around at DA because they saw approach lights and 'felt' they could make the runway if they descended just a bit further. They landed hard and off the runway edge. Using the ADM framework, identify what decision-making failure occurred and how the ACS standard for 'timely decision' addresses it.
questions.answer: This is a textbook example of plan continuation bias — also called 'get-there-itis' — and the 'error chain.' Seeing approach lights satisfies part of 14 CFR 91.175(c), but the pilot did not assess whether a NORMAL landing was possible, which is also required. The ACS standard 'make a timely decision' means the go-around must be initiated at or before DA, not after the pilot has already descended past the legal limit hoping for improvement. ADM teaches that 'probably' is not good enough — if you are only probably going to make it, the known-safe option (go around) must be chosen. Every second of continued descent below DA without a clear, achievable landing path deepens commitment to an unsafe outcome and removes the ability to go around safely.
questions.follow_up: If the approach lights are in sight at DA but the runway itself is not visible, can you legally continue descending below DA?
questions.follow_up_answer: Yes, but only to 100 feet above the touchdown zone elevation (TDZE), and only when using approach lights as the visual reference. Under 14 CFR 91.175(c)(1), if the only visual reference is the approach lighting system — without red terminating bars or red side row bars — you may not descend below 100 feet above TDZE. If you then gain sight of additional runway environment elements, you may continue. If not, a go-around is mandatory at that 100-foot floor.

questions.question: You are executing a go-around from very close to the surface in a turbine helicopter — nearly hover speed and height — when you experience a momentary yaw to the right as you aggressively raise collective. What is happening, and how does it affect your go-around technique?
questions.answer: A rapid collective increase demands more torque from the main rotor, which increases the reactive torque force on the airframe. In a counterclockwise rotor system (most American helicopters), this causes an uncommanded yaw to the right. Additionally, rapid collective increase at low airspeed can induce Loss of Tail Rotor Effectiveness (LTE) conditions, particularly if wind is from certain directions (left rear quartering in particular). The correct technique is to increase collective smoothly — not abruptly — while simultaneously applying left antitorque pedal to counteract torque increase, then establish climb attitude with forward cyclic. Abrupt collective input at low airspeed and low altitude is one of the most dangerous moments in helicopter IFR operations and must be practiced until it is instinctive.
questions.follow_up: If you are at near-hover speed during the go-around and the yaw becomes uncontrollable, what is the appropriate emergency action?
questions.follow_up_answer: If antitorque authority is lost or insufficient during a go-around at very low altitude, the priority is to reduce power to reduce torque demand — lower the collective — and execute an immediate landing on the available surface before the yaw becomes a ground contact or rollover event. If altitude permits, attempt to accelerate into translational lift which improves tail rotor efficiency. This is consistent with antitorque failure procedures in FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11: maintain control, reduce power if necessary, and land as quickly as safely possible.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11 (LTE, antitorque failures); Chapter 9 (go-around technique)

questions.question: When executing a go-around from an instrument approach, what is the correct sequence of control inputs to stop the descent and initiate a climb?
questions.answer: The correct sequence is: (1) simultaneously apply collective to increase power and arrest the descent, (2) apply forward cyclic as needed to establish a climb attitude, and (3) use antitorque pedals to maintain trim as torque increases with the power application. The collective drives the initial power increase and rotor thrust change, while cyclic transitions the helicopter from approach attitude to climb attitude. All inputs should be smooth and coordinated to prevent rotor RPM excursions.

questions.question: During a go-around, what instrument do you primarily reference to confirm that rotor RPM is remaining within normal limits as you raise the collective?
questions.answer: The primary instrument is the tachometer, specifically the rotor RPM gauge (Nr).
