What options does the pilot have to manage the excess altitude, and what is the risk of each?
questions.answer: The pilot has several options: (1) S-turns — gentle left/right track deviations to bleed off altitude and distance while maintaining autorotation airspeed. Risk: S-turns at low altitude become increasingly dangerous; below 300 feet AGL they should not be initiated. (2) Increase airspeed — flying faster steepens the glide and burns altitude faster but may arrive at flare height with higher airspeed, increasing flare difficulty. Risk: excessive speed at flare height can result in hard landing or rotor RPM overspeed. (3) Reduce airspeed below best autorotation speed — steepens descent but at the cost of a higher rate of descent and reduced rotor RPM margin. Risk: rotor RPM decay with insufficient altitude to recover. (4) Execute a go-around (power recovery) and re-enter from an appropriate altitude. This is the safest option if altitude management has become compromised — a go-around is never a failure if executed safely and timely. The examiner is looking for recognition that continuing a mis-managed approach to an unsafe touchdown is more dangerous than executing a power recovery and trying again.
questions.follow_up: At what point during the approach is it too late to safely execute a go-around from an autorotation, and what must the pilot do instead?
questions.follow_up_answer: Once the pilot has begun the flare and rotor RPM has been significantly increased through flare attitude, a go-around may not be safely achievable because: (1) The aircraft is at very low altitude (typically below 100 feet AGL); (2) Forward airspeed may have been reduced below translational lift; (3) Engine spool-up time (turbine) or throttle response (piston) may not provide power fast enough to arrest the descent before ground contact. At this point, the pilot must commit to the landing — apply collective smoothly to cushion the touchdown using stored rotor RPM energy. Attempting a go-around from deep in the flare at very low altitude risks dynamic rollover, settling with power at low airspeed/low altitude, or loss of tail rotor effectiveness during the power application. The ACS requires the pilot to recognize that a go-around decision must be made early — not after the flare has been initiated.

questions.question: You are flying a turbine helicopter with a known low-inertia rotor system. How does rotor inertia specifically affect your entry altitude selection for a straight-in autorotation, and what is the consequence of selecting an entry altitude that is too low with this type of system?
questions.answer: Low-inertia rotor systems store less kinetic energy in the rotor blades due to lower blade mass. When the engine fails or is reduced to idle, rotor RPM decays much faster than in a high-inertia system. This means the pilot has a significantly shorter window — often only 1–2 seconds — to lower collective and establish autorotation before RPM decays below a recoverable range. The consequence for entry altitude selection is: (1) Entry must occur at sufficient altitude that even with a brief pilot reaction delay, RPM can still be recovered within the green arc before impact; (2) Low-altitude entry (e.g., below 300–400 feet AGL) may not allow enough time to stabilize RPM, establish glide airspeed, and execute a proper flare; (3) The FAA states that rotor stall in a helicopter is not recoverable — if RPM decays to blade stall, the helicopter will not fly regardless of remaining altitude. Therefore, for low-inertia systems, a conservative (higher) entry altitude is essential, and the RFM limitations on height-velocity diagrams must be strictly observed to ensure any power loss occurs within the recoverable envelope.
questions.follow_up: What is the height-velocity (H-V) diagram, and how does it directly inform your entry altitude decision for autorotation training in a low-inertia helicopter?
questions.follow_up_answer: The Height-Velocity (H-V) diagram — also called the 'dead man's curve' — is a chart in the RFM that defines combinations of altitude AGL and airspeed from which a successful autorotation landing cannot be made following sudden engine failure. It has two avoid regions: a high-altitude/low-airspeed region (the main 'dead man's curve' upper left) and a low-altitude/high-airspeed region (lower right, related to insufficient height for flare). For a low-inertia helicopter, the avoid regions are typically larger than for high-inertia systems because RPM decays faster, giving the pilot less margin. When selecting entry altitude for practice autorotations, the pilot must ensure the entry point is OUTSIDE the H-V avoid area — meaning either sufficient altitude with adequate forward airspeed, or airspeed high enough that a roll-on landing is feasible at low altitude. Flying within the H-V avoid area during training without reason is contrary to the RFM and represents an unacceptable risk.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; Aircraft RFM H-V diagram

questions.question: When practicing a straight-in autorotation, what is the generally accepted altitude and position at which you should begin the maneuver?
questions.answer: The standard entry point for a straight-in autorotation practice is typically 500 feet AGL while on the approach path leading to the intended landing point (not abeam it). This entry position and altitude provide sufficient height to complete the full autorotation profile — decelerate from cruise airspeed, stabilize rotor RPM in the green arc, establish a stable autorotation glide, and complete the flare and landing — without exhausting rotor inertia. The exact entry altitude and distance from the landing area should follow the aircraft's POH/RFM and the instructor's guidance, but 500 feet AGL on approach is the commonly recommended baseline for training helicopters.

questions.question: What is the first flight control action you must take the moment you initiate a straight-in autorotation entry from cruise flight?
questions.answer: The first and most critical action is to immediately lower the collective to the full down position. This reduces blade pitch angle, decreases lift and drag on the rotor blades, and allows upward airflow through the rotor disk to maintain and recover rotor RPM. Simultaneously, aft cyclic is applied to reduce airspeed and increase airflow up through the disk, and the throttle is rolled to idle. Pedal input is adjusted to maintain trim. Delaying the collective reduction — even briefly — allows rotor RPM to decay rapidly, especially in low-inertia rotor systems.

questions.question: What visual cues or ground references do you use to determine the correct point to initiate a straight-in autorotation to a specific landing zone?
questions.answer: The pilot should assess the position of the intended touchdown point relative to the helicopter's current position and altitude, ensuring there is a proper glide path angle — typically 200 to 300 feet per 1,000 feet of horizontal distance, depending on helicopter type and wind. The touchdown point should initially appear in a fixed or slightly rising position in the windshield as the approach is established. A point that appears to be rising on the windshield means you are undershooting; one that is dropping means you are overshooting. Wind direction and speed also directly affect where the entry point should be — headwinds allow a shorter, steeper approach while tailwinds require a longer, shallower entry with more forward distance from the landing point.

questions.question: You are on a training flight and your instructor tells you to practice a straight-in autorotation. You are 800 feet AGL, directly over the intended landing point, with a 15-knot tailwind. Describe how this wind condition affects when and where you should initiate the maneuver.
questions.answer: A 15-knot tailwind significantly affects the autorotation profile. Because the tailwind increases your ground speed, the helicopter will cover MORE horizontal distance per foot of altitude lost during the descent — the glide angle over the ground is shallower. You should initiate the autorotation at a point much farther upwind (before/behind the landing zone), at a greater distance from the landing area than you would use in calm or headwind conditions. Additionally, a tailwind increases the ground speed during the approach, requiring a more aggressive flare to dissipate that energy. If you initiate from directly over the landing point at 800 feet AGL with a 15-knot tailwind, you will overshoot the landing zone. The proper initiation point would be to reposition farther upwind before beginning the autorotation, to account for the extended ground distance that will be covered during descent.

questions.question: During a straight-in autorotation, you initiate the maneuver but notice your rotor RPM has already decayed into the caution range before you established the autorotation glide. What does this tell you about your initiation point or technique, and what are the immediate implications?
questions.answer: Rotor RPM decay into the caution range prior to establishing a stable autorotation glide indicates either a delayed collective reduction at entry — the most common cause — or that the entry was initiated at too low an altitude or too low an airspeed to allow rotor RPM recovery before impact. A delayed collective is dangerous because the rotor stores kinetic energy that depletes quickly when blades are producing high lift/drag with no engine power. Immediate implications include reduced flare effectiveness, reduced cushioning capability at the bottom of the autorotation, and potential for a hard landing or loss of control. The pilot must immediately ensure collective is fully down and allow rotor RPM to recover within the normal operating range before proceeding. This scenario is a critical teaching point — the FAA Helicopter Flying Handbook states that rotor stall in helicopters is not recoverable, making early recognition imperative.

questions.question: You are flying a Robinson R44 at 1,000 feet AGL and 80 knots when the engine fails. Compared to a heavier helicopter with a high-inertia rotor system, how does the low-inertia rotor system of the R44 affect your window of time to initiate autorotation and get the collective down?
questions.answer: Low-inertia rotor systems, such as those found in lighter helicopters like the Robinson R44, have significantly less stored kinetic energy in the rotor blades compared to high-inertia systems on heavier turbine helicopters. This means that once the engine fails and collective is not reduced immediately, the rotor RPM decays very rapidly — within one to two seconds in some cases. The initiation must be nearly instantaneous; there is virtually no margin for hesitation. In contrast, a heavy helicopter with a high-inertia rotor may give the pilot several seconds before RPM decays to a critical level. For the R44 and similar light helicopters, the POH/RFM limitations and training emphasis focus on immediate collective reduction as the survival-critical action. Delayed entry in a low-inertia helicopter can result in an RPM deficit that cannot be recovered before ground contact.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; POH/RFM for specific helicopter model

questions.question: A student consistently initiates the straight-in autorotation too late — always arriving low and fast with insufficient altitude to complete a proper flare. As their instructor, what are the three most likely root causes of a late initiation point, and how would you correct each one?
questions.answer: The three most likely root causes are: 1) Misjudging the glide path angle — the student may not have developed the visual picture of where the helicopter should be relative to the touchdown point for a given altitude. Correction: use ground reference drills and have the student identify the 'aim point' behavior on the windshield during normal approaches before combining that judgment with power-off flight. 2) Hesitation due to anchoring on airspeed or altitude numbers rather than the visual picture — students often wait until they reach a memorized altitude before initiating, rather than responding to their position relative to the landing zone. Correction: teach them to recognize the correct approach angle visually first, then correlate altitude. 3) Delayed collective reduction adding to the effective late initiation — even if position was correct, RPM decay and altitude loss during a slow entry compounds the 'too low' arrival. Correction: emphasize the simultaneous nature of the entry — position selection and the physical control inputs must happen together without hesitation. Repetition at altitude with power recovery and instructor coaching the entry point decision is the best corrective training.
questions.follow_up: If this student's late initiation pattern is consistently occurring despite repeated corrections, at what point does this become a training versus a standards issue, and what documentation obligation do you have as the instructor?
questions.follow_up_answer: If a student cannot correct a recurring, pattern-based deficiency after multiple instructional attempts with documented debriefs and varied teaching methods, this transitions from a normal training progression issue to a potential qualification concern. As a flight instructor, you are obligated to document each lesson's content, what deficiencies were noted, what corrective instruction was given, and the student's response, in accordance with 14 CFR 61.189. If the student cannot consistently demonstrate the skill to ACS standards after a reasonable training period, it would be inappropriate to endorse them for a checkride. If a stage check or end-of-course check reveals the pattern, it should be documented and additional training assigned before any endorsement is issued. The instructor must not falsify or omit material information in logbook endorsements per 14 CFR 61.51 and 61.189.

questions.question: During an actual engine failure at 600 feet AGL over mountainous terrain with no ideal landing zone directly ahead, how does the principle of initiating the autorotation at the 'proper point' change when there is no defined landing zone — and what factors now govern your initiation decision?
questions.answer: When there is no defined landing zone, the concept of 'proper initiation point' shifts from optimizing a glide to a specific target to maximizing energy management options. At 600 feet AGL in mountainous terrain, the pilot must immediately lower the collective and establish a stabilized autorotation while simultaneously scanning for any usable landing area within the glide range. The initiation is still immediate — rotor RPM preservation is non-negotiable — but now heading selection and airspeed become the primary tools. The pilot should establish best glide airspeed (per POH/RFM) to maximize horizontal distance and use cyclic heading changes to steer toward the best available surface, even if imperfect. The 'proper point' in this context means: collective down immediately upon failure, airspeed at the manufacturer's recommended autorotation speed, and the earliest possible selection and commitment to a survivable landing area rather than searching too long. Delayed decision-making at low altitude in mountainous terrain is more dangerous than committing to an imperfect landing zone. ADM and SRM principles apply — the best available option, even if suboptimal, is chosen decisively rather than continuing to search.
questions.follow_up: You commit to a small clearing on a hillside slope and realize during the flare that the ground slopes uphill away from you at approximately 15 degrees. What adjustment do you make to your flare and touchdown technique, and what is the primary hazard?
questions.follow_up_answer: On an upslope landing during autorotation, the pilot must time the flare to account for the rising terrain — the effective ground distance closes faster than on flat terrain, so the flare must begin earlier and at a higher altitude than normal to avoid flying into the hillside. The touchdown should be made with the upslope skid contacting first, followed by the downslope skid, to prevent dynamic rollover. The primary hazard is dynamic rollover: if the uphill skid catches on terrain while the helicopter still has lateral or translational momentum, the rotor thrust line will pivot over the contact point and can roll the helicopter before the pilot can react with corrective collective reduction. Collective must be reduced smoothly through touchdown, and if any rolling tendency develops, immediate full collective reduction is the only effective recovery action. Shutdown on the ground must also account for main rotor blade clearance on the low side of the slope.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 9 (dynamic rollover); FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (ADM/SRM)

questions.question: What does it mean to have the helicopter 'trimmed' during an autorotation glide, and why does it matter?
questions.answer: A trimmed helicopter has no uncoordinated forces acting on it — the ball is centered, there is no slip or skid, and the fuselage is aligned with the relative wind. In autorotation, an untrimmed condition creates additional drag, disrupts smooth airflow through the rotor disk, and produces yaw that makes the approach less predictable. Trim is primarily managed with the antitorque pedals to keep the nose aligned without yaw, and cyclic to maintain the desired glide attitude. A trimmed glide also reduces pilot workload so attention can shift to the landing zone.

questions.question: What is the primary flight control used to establish and maintain autorotation airspeed during the power-off glide, and what is the tolerance allowed on the practical test?
questions.answer: Cyclic pitch controls autorotation airspeed. Aft cyclic raises the nose and decreases airspeed; forward cyclic lowers the nose and increases airspeed. The pilot selects and holds the attitude that produces the autorotation airspeed published in the Rotorcraft Flight Manual (RFM) for the specific helicopter. The ACS tolerance is plus or minus 5 knots of the recommended autorotation airspeed.

questions.question: Why is the collective immediately lowered upon entry into autorotation, and what happens to rotor RPM if you delay that input?
questions.answer: Lowering the collective reduces the blade pitch angle, which decreases the drag on the rotor blades and allows upward airflow through the disk to sustain and restore rotor RPM. If the collective is not lowered promptly, the pitch angle remains high, the rotor blades continue to produce lift against engine resistance that is no longer there, and rotor RPM decays rapidly. On low-inertia rotor systems this decay can happen in just seconds. A rotor stall in a helicopter is not recoverable, so immediate collective reduction is critical.

questions.question: You are flying a straight-in autorotation and notice your airspeed is 12 knots above the published autorotation speed. You're also slightly high on the approach profile. Walk me through your control inputs to correct both deviations simultaneously.
questions.answer: Being 12 knots fast and high indicates the nose is too low (shallower glide). Apply gentle aft cyclic to raise the nose, which reduces airspeed and steepens the glide path toward the landing zone. In autorotation with collective fully down, rotor RPM is self-regulating — the upward airflow through the disk maintains RPM as long as airspeed is controlled. The cyclic correction will change airspeed first, and the glide path will adjust accordingly. Monitor the landing zone position and airspeed trend; make small inputs to avoid overshooting the target altitude. Do not raise the collective — that will reduce RPM and destabilize the descent rate needed for energy management during the flare.

questions.question: During a straight-in autorotation entry from cruise, your helicopter has a counterclockwise main rotor system. As you lower collective and apply aft cyclic at entry, what do you expect the helicopter to do yaw-wise, and how do you correct for it?
questions.answer: In a counterclockwise rotor system (viewed from above, which is the American convention), the tail rotor produces thrust to the right to counteract main rotor torque. When collective is lowered at autorotation entry, main rotor torque drops significantly because the engine is no longer driving the system. The tail rotor thrust that was opposing torque is now excessive for the reduced torque condition, causing the nose to yaw left. The pilot must reduce left pedal (reduce tail rotor pitch) to maintain coordinated, trimmed flight. The exact pedal adjustment depends on the aircraft, but failure to make this correction results in a slipping, uncoordinated glide that adds drag and complicates the approach.

questions.question: Your RFM lists best glide autorotation speed as 65 knots and minimum rate of descent speed as 52 knots. You are on a straight-in autorotation to a confined landing zone and you are slightly short of the intended touchdown point. Which speed would you select, and why?
questions.answer: To stretch the glide and reach a landing zone that is slightly beyond your current projected touchdown point, you should fly closer to best glide speed (65 knots in this case). Best glide speed produces the flattest glide angle, covering the most horizontal distance per foot of altitude lost. Minimum rate of descent speed (52 knots) descends more slowly in terms of feet per minute but produces a steeper glide angle, meaning you will not cover as much ground — it would actually land you shorter, making the problem worse. Unless there is also a concern about rotor energy storage, flying the best glide speed is the correct choice to extend range in a straight-in autorotation.

questions.question: During an oral debrief after a checkride, a candidate argues that minor out-of-trim condition during the autorotation glide is acceptable as long as airspeed stays within the ±5-knot band. How would you respond, and does the ACS support or contradict that reasoning?
questions.answer: The candidate's reasoning is incorrect. The ACS skill element HI.XII.B.S7 explicitly requires the helicopter to be trimmed AND at autorotation airspeed within ±5 knots — these are two separate, concurrent requirements, not alternatives. An out-of-trim glide, even at correct airspeed, adds parasitic yaw drag, produces uneven airflow through the rotor disk, and degrades rotor system efficiency. More critically, arriving at the flare point in an out-of-trim condition means the pilot is already behind the aircraft and managing a cross-coupled control problem during the most demanding phase of the maneuver. In a real emergency, an untrimmed autorotation compounds the hazard. The examiner should note the failure to maintain trim as a discrepancy, separate from any airspeed tolerance issue.
questions.follow_up: If a candidate consistently flies out of trim during autorotations but always hits the airspeed tolerance, which FAA judgment standard applies, and could that alone be a basis for disapproval?
questions.follow_up_answer: Yes. Under the ACS, a single-element failure within a task can be the basis for disapproval if it represents a safety-of-flight issue or a consistent inability to meet a stated standard. HI.XII.B.S7 is one combined skill standard — trim AND airspeed. Consistently flying uncoordinated demonstrates incomplete mastery of the task. Furthermore, under the broader ADM and risk management standards, a candidate who normalizes uncoordinated flight is demonstrating a hazardous attitude (invulnerability or complacency). The examiner has discretionary authority under 14 CFR 61.43 to disapprove based on consistent failure to demonstrate a required skill element to the ACS standard.

questions.question: A pilot transitioning from a high-inertia piston helicopter to a low-inertia turbine helicopter asks why they need to be more aggressive lowering the collective at autorotation entry in the new aircraft. Explain the aerodynamic and mechanical reason in detail.
questions.answer: Rotor inertia determines how long the rotor system can sustain RPM through the entry transient before airflow through the disk takes over. High-inertia rotors (heavy blade systems, large diameter) have significant stored kinetic energy — they resist RPM decay and give the pilot several seconds to establish the glide. Low-inertia rotors (lighter, smaller) lose RPM very quickly when pitch angle remains high and there is no engine torque driving them. At entry, if the collective is not lowered promptly in a low-inertia system, blade pitch remains high, induced drag is high, and rotor RPM decays below the recoverable threshold in as little as one to two seconds. Once rotor RPM drops into a stall condition, no control input can recover it. The FAA Helicopter Flying Handbook explicitly states that rotor stalls in helicopters are not recoverable. The transitioning pilot must recalibrate their muscle memory to treat collective reduction at autorotation entry as an immediate, aggressive action — not the measured response that worked in the high-inertia aircraft.
questions.follow_up: If a pilot enters autorotation from a low-speed, low-altitude condition in a low-inertia helicopter and notices rotor RPM has already dropped to the low end of the green arc, what options remain and what are the risks of each?
questions.follow_up_answer: Options are extremely limited. The pilot could attempt to lower collective further if it is not already at full down — this reduces blade pitch and allows maximum autorotative airflow to recover RPM, but at low altitude there may not be enough altitude to allow recovery before ground contact. If airspeed is available, a slight forward cyclic input increases airflow through the disk and can help recover RPM, but this exchanges altitude for rotor energy. Pulling aft cyclic to flare early may be attempted to arrest descent, but if RPM is insufficient, the flare will not be effective and collective application at the bottom will stall the rotor completely. The honest answer is that the situation is likely not survivable if RPM has significantly decayed at low altitude — which is precisely why early recognition and immediate entry technique is non-negotiable in low-inertia systems. The FAA handbook states rotor stalls are not recoverable.

questions.question: During a straight-in autorotation, what is the primary flight control used to maintain rotor RPM (Nr) within the normal operating range?
questions.answer: The collective pitch control is the primary control for managing Nr during autorotation. Lowering collective reduces blade pitch and drag on the rotor system, allowing airflow up through the disk to accelerate rotor RPM. Raising collective increases blade pitch and drag, which slows Nr. The pilot must continuously monitor the tachometer and make small collective adjustments to keep Nr within the green arc.

questions.question: What does the green arc on the tachometer represent during an autorotation, and why is it critical to stay within that range?
questions.answer: The green arc on the tachometer represents the normal operating range for main rotor RPM (Nr). During autorotation, staying within the green arc ensures the rotor blades are generating adequate lift for a controlled descent and that sufficient energy is stored in the rotor system for the flare and cushioning maneuver at the bottom. Operating below the green arc risks rotor stall — which is not recoverable — and operating above risks structural overspeed damage to the rotor system.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B, Chapter 11; aircraft-specific Rotorcraft Flight Manual (RFM)

questions.question: At autorotation entry from cruise airspeed, what three simultaneous control inputs are required, and how does each affect Nr?
questions.answer: At entry from cruise airspeed the pilot simultaneously applies: (1) Down collective — reduces blade pitch and drag, allowing upward airflow to sustain and build Nr; (2) Aft cyclic — increases upward airflow through the rotor disk, contributing to Nr recovery and slowing forward airspeed to autorotation glide speed; (3) Pedal trim — adjusts as needed to maintain coordinated flight since torque demand drops immediately. The combined effect establishes the autorotative glide and arrests Nr decay before it falls below the normal range.

questions.question: You are established in a straight-in autorotation at the recommended glide speed and notice Nr is slowly creeping toward the top of the green arc. What could be causing this and what corrective action would you take?
questions.answer: Nr trending toward the top of the green arc during an established autorotation typically indicates the aircraft is gliding at a speed slightly higher than the recommended autorotation airspeed, the collective is lower than required for the conditions, or external factors such as strong updrafts are affecting rotor energy. Note that a tailwind increases groundspeed but does not increase descent rate relative to the air mass; descent angle through still air remains unchanged. Corrective action: Raise collective slightly to increase blade pitch and load the rotor, which will add drag and bring Nr back into the mid-green range. If airspeed is excessive, apply gentle aft cyclic to reduce forward speed.

questions.question: During the flare phase of a straight-in autorotation, how does aft cyclic input affect Nr, and what is the pilot's responsibility at that moment?
questions.answer: During the flare, applying aft cyclic tilts the rotor disk rearward, which increases the upward component of relative airflow through the disk. This effectively increases the angle of attack on the blades and can cause Nr to rise, sometimes rapidly. The pilot must monitor the tachometer and, if Nr approaches the top of the green arc or the yellow caution range, apply a small amount of collective to load the rotor and arrest the RPM increase. The flare simultaneously reduces descent rate and forward groundspeed — the pilot is managing both Nr and the energy exchange to set up for a safe landing while not allowing Nr to exceed limits or decay below the green arc before touchdown.

questions.question: A student pilot delays lowering the collective at engine failure and Nr decays to the bottom of the green arc before they react. Walk me through how you would coach them to recover Nr to mid-green without overshooting the top of the range.
questions.answer: With Nr at the bottom of the green arc, the priority is immediate, brisk — but not abrupt — collective reduction to fully flat pitch, combined with aft cyclic to increase upward airflow and help spool the rotor back up. Coach the student to watch the tachometer needle closely: as Nr climbs back through the lower third of the green arc, begin slowly raising collective in small increments to moderate the rate of Nr increase and avoid overshooting into the yellow or red arc. Simultaneously, establish the correct autorotation glide speed with cyclic. The key coaching point is that Nr recovery requires anticipation — the student must lead the collective increase slightly before Nr reaches the desired mid-green value, because rotor inertia will carry it a little further after inputs are made. Emphasize that low-inertia rotor systems decay and recover faster, requiring quicker and more precise inputs.

questions.question: During a straight-in autorotation, a pilot executes the flare correctly but then delays the collective pull-up at the bottom of the flare for nearly two seconds. Explain the aerodynamic sequence that unfolds with Nr during those two seconds and the likely outcome if no corrective action is taken.
questions.answer: After the flare arrests descent rate and decelerates forward airspeed, the helicopter begins to settle again as translational energy is depleted. Without the collective pull-up, the rotor is no longer being loaded to trade stored rotational energy for lift, and as the disk loading decreases (no collective input) the rotor may actually begin to overspeed briefly as inflow increases with the renewed descent — or Nr may decay depending on the specific energy state. More critically, as the aircraft settles toward the ground with insufficient collective loaded, Nr may drop below the green arc because the upward airflow alone cannot sustain it without the disk angle established in the flare. The pilot now has little Nr energy left to cushion the landing. If Nr falls below the stall threshold, the blades lose the ability to produce lift, and a hard landing or catastrophic rotor stall results. The FAA specifically states that rotor stalls in helicopters are not recoverable, making the timing of collective application at the bottom of the flare one of the most critical skill elements in autorotation.
questions.follow_up: If this scenario occurred and you had Nr at the very bottom of the green arc just two feet above the ground with forward groundspeed still present, what are your options and what are the tradeoffs?
questions.follow_up_answer: With Nr at the bottom of the green arc, two feet AGL, and residual forward groundspeed, the pilot's options are extremely limited. Pulling collective aggressively is the only way to cushion the landing, but doing so will further load and rapidly decay Nr — meaning only one attempt is available before rotor energy is gone. The tradeoff is accepting a firm touchdown in exchange for preventing a catastrophic rotor stall. The pilot should pull collective as smoothly and fully as the remaining Nr allows to cushion vertical descent, accept the hard-ish landing, and keep the skids aligned with the direction of travel to prevent dynamic rollover. If a go-around is attempted (power available), application of throttle and collective simultaneously must occur before Nr decays further. The broader lesson is that there is no recovery option that fully compensates for a delayed collective pull — the pilot must execute the collective application at the correct moment during the flare/level-off transition.

questions.question: You are evaluating a candidate on a straight-in autorotation and notice that throughout the entire maneuver they never once look at the tachometer — they successfully complete the autorotation with Nr staying in the green arc the whole time. Is this acceptable performance? How would you evaluate it as an examiner?
questions.answer: This is a nuanced evaluator judgment. On one hand, an experienced pilot who has developed proprioceptive and auditory cues for Nr management — rotor noise, vibration, control feedback — may fly an acceptable autorotation without fixating on instruments. On the other hand, as an examiner evaluating whether a pilot can maintain Nr within normal limits, the concern is: did the pilot know Nr was in limits, or were they simply lucky? The ACS skill standard requires the pilot to demonstrate maintenance of Nr within normal limits, which implies situational awareness of the actual Nr value, not just an acceptable outcome. A candidate who cannot articulate that they were monitoring Nr through alternative cues, or who cannot identify where Nr was at key phases (entry, mid-glide, flare, touchdown), raises a risk management concern. The correct examiner response is to debrief the candidate and ask them to describe what Nr was doing at each phase. If they can accurately describe it, they may have internalized the monitoring. If they cannot, it is a deficiency. In marginal conditions — density altitude, high-inertia versus low-inertia rotor systems — relying on feel alone without instrument cross-check is inadequate and should not be signed off as meeting the standard.
questions.follow_up: Under what conditions would relying solely on auditory and tactile cues for Nr monitoring during autorotation be most dangerous, and why?
questions.follow_up_answer: Relying solely on auditory and tactile cues for Nr is most dangerous in: (1) High-density altitude operations — where the reduced air density changes the 'feel' and sound of rotor performance, making learned cues unreliable; (2) Low-inertia rotor systems — which decay very rapidly (seconds), giving little tactile warning before Nr drops below stall threshold; (3) High-workload or distraction environments — cockpit noise, passenger communication, or emergency stress can mask auditory cues; (4) Unfamiliar aircraft type — pilots transitioning to a new model have not yet calibrated their sensory cues to that aircraft's rotor behavior. In all these scenarios, active tachometer cross-check is not optional — it is the only reliable method to confirm Nr is within limits before it is too late to recover.

questions.question: During a straight-in autorotation, what is the primary effect of a direct headwind on your glide range, and how should you account for it when selecting your touchdown point?
questions.answer: A headwind reduces your groundspeed while your airspeed and descent rate remain essentially the same. This means your glide distance over the ground is shorter than it would be in calm conditions. You should plan to aim for a point FARTHER away than you would in calm wind, to compensate for the reduced ground coverage caused by the headwind. The key is recognizing that a headwind requires selecting a touchdown point farther down range to achieve the same effective glide range.

questions.question: In a straight-in autorotation with a direct tailwind, will you tend to overshoot or undershoot your selected landing area, and what is the correct control response?
questions.answer: A tailwind increases your groundspeed without increasing your rotor RPM or changing your aerodynamic glide profile, so you will tend to overshoot your selected landing area. The correct response is to either select an aim point farther down the landing area to account for the extra ground coverage, or manage your energy by adjusting glide speed with cyclic — flying a slightly slower airspeed reduces groundspeed and glide distance. Flaring earlier and more aggressively can also help arrest the overshoot during the flare phase.

questions.question: What is the standard best glide (autorotation) airspeed used for in relation to wind compensation during a straight-in autorotation, and can you fly a different airspeed to manage your energy to the landing area?
questions.answer: The best glide airspeed — also called the autorotation airspeed — is published in the helicopter's Rotorcraft Flight Manual and provides the maximum glide distance in still air. It is the baseline speed around which you adjust. Yes, you can intentionally fly slightly faster than best glide to extend your range (such as when undershooting in a headwind) or fly slightly slower to shorten your distance (such as when overshooting in a tailwind), within the rotor RPM limits. Cyclic controls airspeed in autorotation, and small adjustments are the primary tool for range correction.

questions.question: You are established in a straight-in autorotation at 1,000 feet AGL with a 20-knot direct headwind. Halfway down the approach you realize you are going to land well short of your intended touchdown point. Walk me through your control inputs to correct for the undershoot.
questions.answer: Recognizing an undershoot early gives you the most options. First, lower the nose slightly with forward cyclic to increase airspeed above best glide — this trades some altitude for increased glide distance over the ground by taking better advantage of the headwind component. Second, verify collective is fully down to maintain rotor RPM. Third, reassess the aim point — you may need to accept a landing point shorter than originally planned if the correction is insufficient. Avoid the instinct to raise collective to stretch the glide, as this will bleed rotor RPM and leave you with less energy for the flare and cushion. If the undershoot cannot be corrected, use available rotor inertia to cushion the landing even if short of the intended area.

questions.question: You are on a straight-in autorotation approach and there is a 15-knot crosswind from your left. How does this crosswind affect your approach path and landing point, and what adjustments do you make to stay on track for your selected area?
questions.answer: A crosswind from the left will continuously push you to the right of your intended approach path, causing lateral drift away from your selected landing area. If uncorrected, you will land downwind of — and displaced laterally from — your intended point. To compensate, use a crab angle into the wind (left cyclic input) to maintain the desired ground track toward the landing area. As you approach the flare point, transition to a side slip or kick straight with pedal so the helicopter is aligned with the direction of travel at touchdown to avoid a lateral ground contact. Your glide distance (descent rate ÷ altitude loss) remains unchanged by the crosswind; the crosswind causes lateral displacement of your ground track, so mental aim point adjustment is needed to account for this lateral offset, not for reduced range.

questions.question: You've entered an autorotation from cruise flight and you notice the wind is at your back — a direct tailwind of about 15 knots. Your selected landing zone is a small clearing. Describe how your approach profile and timing of the flare need to change compared to a calm-wind autorotation.
questions.answer: With a tailwind, your groundspeed is higher than your indicated airspeed, so you are covering more ground per unit of altitude lost. The approach will appear flatter and faster over the ground, and the tendency is to overshoot the clearing. To compensate: select an aim point at the near edge or even short of the clearing rather than the center; consider flying a slightly slower airspeed to reduce groundspeed; and initiate the flare earlier than you would in calm wind because you have more kinetic energy to dissipate. The flare must also be more aggressive to arrest the higher groundspeed before touchdown. Rotor RPM will increase during the flare due to the higher inertia energy — be ready to manage it with collective during the cushion. Tailwind autorotations demand precise planning because errors compound quickly near the ground.

questions.question: A student pilot consistently undershoots on straight-in autorotations even in calm wind. When you add a headwind to the scenario, the undershoot becomes more pronounced and the student increases collective early to try to stretch the glide. As the evaluating instructor, what specific misunderstanding is the student demonstrating, and what is the correct technique and its physiological risk?
questions.answer: The student is demonstrating a fundamental misunderstanding of energy management in autorotation — specifically, the belief that raising collective will extend the glide. In fact, raising collective increases blade pitch, which increases drag on the rotor system and causes rotor RPM to decay. This bleeds the stored inertial energy in the rotor before it is needed for the flare and cushion, resulting in a harder landing with less rotor energy available. The correct technique to extend glide distance is to lower the nose slightly with forward cyclic to increase airspeed, which flattens the glide angle and covers more ground. The headwind further penalizes groundspeed, so the student must also revise the aim point closer. The physiological risk is the 'instinct to survive' — pulling up (collective) feels intuitively like it will arrest the descent, but it is precisely the wrong action. This is a critical training point because a student who pulls collective prematurely in a real emergency may reach the ground with insufficient rotor RPM to cushion the landing.
questions.follow_up: If this student enters the flare with rotor RPM already below the bottom of the green arc due to premature collective application, what are their remaining options and what is the likely outcome?
questions.follow_up_answer: Options are extremely limited. With rotor RPM below the green arc, the blades have lost the inertial energy needed to generate the lift required to arrest the descent during the flare and collective application at the bottom. The pilot can attempt to apply collective to use whatever remaining inertial energy exists, but the cushion will be partial at best. The likely outcome is a hard landing with high vertical velocity — potentially resulting in structural damage to the landing gear or fuselage, and risk of injury to occupants. This is why the FAA Helicopter Flying Handbook states that rotor stall in helicopters is not recoverable; early recognition and correct RPM management throughout the entire autorotation are imperative. There is no 'save' available once RPM is critically low near the ground.

questions.question: During a practical test, a candidate enters a straight-in autorotation with a quartering tailwind from the right rear. The candidate drifts left of the intended landing area and is now lined up with rough terrain. What combination of errors likely occurred, and how should the candidate have used wind awareness from the entry point to prevent this outcome?
questions.answer: A quartering tailwind from the right rear has two components: the tailwind component pushes the helicopter forward and increases groundspeed (overshoot tendency), and the crosswind component from the right pushes the helicopter to the left (lateral drift). The likely errors are: (1) failing to identify and account for the crosswind component at entry — no left crab was established to counteract rightward-to-left drift; (2) possibly fixating on the aim point without monitoring lateral track; and (3) not pre-planning an adjusted aim point for the tailwind component. From entry, the correct procedure is to recognize the full wind vector — both magnitude and direction — and immediately establish a crab angle to the right to counteract leftward drift while simultaneously accounting for the extended groundspeed by selecting a near-edge aim point. Continuous track monitoring throughout the descent is required, with cyclic corrections to stay on centerline. In a quartering wind scenario, no single correction is enough — the pilot must actively manage both the lateral track and the longitudinal energy simultaneously. Waiting until short final to notice the drift is too late in a power-off approach because options for lateral repositioning are severely limited without engine power.
questions.follow_up: If the candidate recognizes the drift late — say at 200 feet AGL — what specific actions are available to attempt a lateral correction toward better terrain, and what are the risks of each?
questions.follow_up_answer: At 200 feet AGL in autorotation, options are limited but not zero. The candidate can apply lateral cyclic (right cyclic in this case) to arrest the leftward drift and re-establish a ground track toward better terrain, but this tilts the rotor disk and reduces the vertical component of lift, increasing the descent rate. Additionally, any sideward movement at touchdown increases the risk of dynamic rollover due to lateral groundspeed at skid contact. The candidate might also attempt a slight turn to align with a new, safer aim point within the available terrain — but turns in autorotation below 200 feet AGL are high-risk because the resulting loss of altitude may be insufficient to complete even a gentle turn and still have energy for a proper flare and cushion. The safest option at this point is to accept the best available landing area within the current flight path, focus on executing a proper flare and cushion to minimize vertical and lateral velocity at contact, and be prepared for a possible roll-over or rough landing. This scenario underscores why wind analysis and aim point selection must happen at entry, not at 200 feet.

questions.question: During a straight-in autorotation, what is the primary purpose of applying aft cyclic during the deceleration flare?
questions.answer: Aft cyclic during the flare tilts the rotor disk rearward, which increases the angle of attack of the rotor blades, builds rotor RPM, decelerates forward airspeed, and converts forward kinetic energy into rotor energy. This deceleration also pitches the nose up, which automatically raises the tail boom away from the ground — a critical safety factor for preventing tail boom strike.

questions.question: At what point in a straight-in autorotation do you begin applying collective pitch to cushion the landing, and what is the risk if you apply it too early?
questions.answer: Collective pitch application for cushioning typically begins when the helicopter is approximately 8 to 15 feet above the surface (depending on aircraft type and conditions) after the flare is complete and the nose is leveled. Applying collective too early dissipates rotor RPM prematurely, leaving insufficient rotor energy to arrest the final descent rate — resulting in a hard landing or possible structural damage.

questions.question: What specific tail boom strike hazard does the nose-high attitude during the flare create, and how does leveling the nose before touchdown address it?
questions.answer: During the flare, the nose-high attitude places the tail boom geometrically lower relative to the ground ahead. If the pilot fails to level the nose before touchdown, the helicopter's continued descent will contact the tail boom or tail rotor with the surface before the skids. Leveling the nose — typically by applying forward cyclic as altitude decreases through 8–15 feet — returns the fuselage to a near-level attitude, ensuring the skids contact the ground first and the tail clears the surface with adequate clearance.

questions.question: You are performing a straight-in autorotation and realize at 200 feet AGL that your airspeed is 20 knots above the recommended autorotation airspeed. How does this affect your flare timing and collective application, and what is the specific risk to the tail boom?
questions.answer: Excess airspeed at 200 feet AGL means you are carrying more forward kinetic energy than intended. You will need to initiate the flare earlier and/or apply more aggressive aft cyclic to bleed off the excess speed. If the flare is initiated at the normal altitude but with excess airspeed, the deceleration will be incomplete by touchdown altitude — meaning the nose may still be in a high pitch attitude when you begin leveling and applying collective. This creates a compounded risk: the tail may be lower and closer to the ground during the level-off, and the forward speed remaining could cause the aircraft to contact the surface with the tail boom before the skids.

questions.question: A student applies collective pitch aggressively at 30 feet AGL during a straight-in autorotation in an attempt to slow the descent, but the helicopter still touches down hard. Walk me through exactly what happened to rotor RPM and tail boom clearance during that sequence.
questions.answer: When collective was applied aggressively at 30 feet — well above the recommended cushion altitude of 8–15 feet — it rapidly increased blade pitch angle, causing a large increase in induced drag. This bled rotor RPM quickly. By the time the helicopter reached the surface, rotor RPM had decayed to a point where the blades could no longer generate sufficient lift to arrest the descent rate, resulting in a hard landing. The tail boom strike risk is compounded because low RPM reduces tail rotor authority and cyclic effectiveness, leaving insufficient control to maintain proper attitude (level nose) and skid-first contact through touchdown. The hazard is RPM decay and loss of control authority, not a downward pitch swing from the collective itself.

questions.question: You are flying a low-inertia rotor system helicopter and must perform a straight-in autorotation. How does the rotor system's low inertia specifically change your approach to deceleration and collective pitch application to maintain tail boom clearance?
questions.answer: Low-inertia rotor systems store significantly less kinetic energy in the rotating blades, meaning rotor RPM decays very rapidly once lift demand increases. This requires the pilot to manage the entire sequence with greater urgency and precision. Specifically: (1) the flare must be well-timed and smooth — a delayed or shallow flare leaves less rotor energy for cushioning; (2) collective pitch application must be delayed until the lowest safe point because any premature collective increase rapidly depletes the available RPM; and (3) there is less margin for error — if the nose is not leveled promptly and the collective pulled at the correct instant, the combination of low RPM and tail-low attitude can result in both a hard landing and tail boom strike simultaneously. The pilot's technique must be crisp and practiced specifically in that aircraft type.

questions.question: During an examiner-observed straight-in autorotation, the applicant performs a textbook flare but then applies forward cyclic aggressively to level the nose while still at 20 feet AGL, then immediately pulls full collective. The landing appears smooth, but you observed the tail boom pass within about 18 inches of the surface during the level-off. Did the applicant pass or bust this element, and what is the precise technical failure demonstrated?
questions.answer: This is a borderline situation requiring examiner judgment, but the described technique contains a demonstrable technical deficiency. By aggressively applying forward cyclic at 20 feet to level the nose, the applicant caused the tail to arc downward rapidly — a pendulum effect — while still at a height where that arc brought the tail boom dangerously close to the surface. The safe outcome (18-inch clearance) was more fortuitous than the result of good technique. The correct technique is to initiate nose leveling smoothly and progressively as altitude decreases through the flare, so the fuselage reaches a near-level attitude by the time the helicopter is at cushion altitude (8-15 feet), without an abrupt forward cyclic input that swings the tail downward. The fact that smooth collective application then produced a 'smooth' landing does not validate the dangerous intermediate step. Whether this constitutes a bust depends on whether the examiner judges the tail clearance margin to have been truly unsafe — ACS standards require the applicant to 'permit safe clearance between the aircraft tail boom and the surface.' 18 inches on a typical helicopter is marginal at best and may not meet that standard.
questions.follow_up: If the applicant argues that the tail never actually contacted the surface and the landing was smooth, how do you respond as the examiner?
questions.follow_up_answer: A near-miss does not validate unsafe technique. The ACS standard is not 'avoid tail boom contact' — it is 'use proper deceleration and collective pitch application that permits safe clearance.' The word 'proper' means the technique itself must be correct, not just that the outcome was acceptable. An applicant who gets a good outcome through poor technique has demonstrated luck, not proficiency. The examiner's role is to evaluate technique, not just result. Additionally, on a different day — different wind, different gross weight, slightly higher approach — that same technique may result in a tail strike. The standard exists precisely to ensure the pilot has a reliable, repeatable technique with adequate margin, not one that barely avoids contact.

questions.question: A pilot has correctly flared and is leveling the nose at 10 feet AGL when a sudden 15-knot tailwind gust is encountered. How should the pilot adjust deceleration and collective pitch application at this point to maintain tail boom clearance, and what makes this scenario particularly dangerous?
questions.answer: A sudden tailwind gust at 10 feet AGL during the level-off phase of autorotation is one of the most dangerous moments to encounter it. The tailwind reduces effective translational lift and decreases the airflow through the rotor disk, causing a rapid decrease in rotor RPM and lift — exactly when the pilot needs rotor energy to cushion the landing. The correct response: (1) Do not apply additional forward cyclic to chase the gust — this will swing the tail downward toward the surface. (2) Accept the aircraft's attitude and immediately apply collective pitch to use whatever rotor RPM remains to arrest the descent rate, understanding the landing may be firmer than desired. (3) Prioritize skid-first contact over trying to soften the touchdown. What makes this scenario especially dangerous is the compounding effect: the tailwind simultaneously degrades rotor RPM, reduces available lift, and increases the rate of descent — all at an altitude too low to flare again and with insufficient altitude for any recovery. The pilot has essentially no option except to use collective immediately to protect the tail boom and accept a harder-than-normal skid contact rather than risk a tail boom strike from trying to 'fix' the attitude.
questions.follow_up: How would this scenario differ in terms of tail boom risk if the gust occurred during the flare at 100 feet AGL versus at 10 feet AGL during level-off?
questions.follow_up_answer: At 100 feet AGL during the flare, the pilot has altitude and time to respond. The tailwind gust would reduce rotor inflow and RPM, but the pilot can adjust flare attitude, manage collective carefully, and still have enough altitude to complete the energy exchange over the remaining 100 feet. The tail boom is also in a higher position relative to the ground during the nose-high flare attitude, so the immediate tail strike risk is lower. At 10 feet during level-off, the pilot has no altitude margin and no time — the tail boom is near its lowest point relative to the ground precisely because the nose is being leveled, and any attempt to re-flare or adjust attitude risks swinging the tail into the surface. The 10-foot scenario is objectively more dangerous because it combines minimal altitude, low rotor energy state, and the tail boom at its geometrically most vulnerable position relative to the terrain.

questions.question: During a straight-in autorotation, at approximately what height above the ground do you initiate the power recovery, and what is the first control input you make?
questions.answer: Power recovery is typically initiated between 40 and 100 feet AGL, depending on the specific helicopter's flight manual guidance. The first input is a gradual increase of collective to arrest the descent rate while simultaneously adding throttle (or allowing the governor to respond) to restore rotor RPM and engine power. Cyclic is used to control forward speed throughout the recovery.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; specific altitude per helicopter POH/RFM

questions.question: When executing a full touchdown autorotation to the surface, what is the purpose of the flare, and how does it affect rotor RPM?
questions.answer: The flare — aft cyclic input made typically between 75 and 100 feet AGL — decelerates forward airspeed and reduces the descent rate. It also increases the angle of attack of the rotor blades, which increases airflow up through the rotor disk and causes rotor RPM to increase. This stored rotor energy is then used during the cushion/collective pull to arrest the final descent for touchdown.

questions.question: What happens to tail rotor effectiveness and directional control during an autorotation power recovery as you restore engine power?
questions.answer: During autorotation, the main rotor torque is low, so minimal left pedal is needed. As engine power is restored during recovery, main rotor torque increases significantly. The pilot must anticipate this by adding left pedal (counterclockwise rotor system) to counteract the increased torque and maintain coordinated flight and heading control. Failure to add left pedal can result in an uncontrolled right yaw.

questions.question: You are on a straight-in autorotation approach and the evaluator tells you 'power recovery' at 75 feet AGL. You begin raising the collective, but you notice the rotor RPM has decayed to the lower limit of the green arc. Walk me through exactly how you manage this situation.
questions.answer: With rotor RPM at the low end of the green arc, I must be careful not to over-pull collective, which would further decrease RPM and risk rotor stall. I would: (1) ensure the throttle is being advanced (or governor is engaged and responding) to restore engine power; (2) raise collective gradually — not abruptly — allowing RPM to recover as engine torque is restored; (3) use aft cyclic to help increase inflow through the disk if RPM continues to lag; (4) use left pedal to counter increasing torque; and (5) closely monitor the RPM gauge to keep it within the green arc throughout the recovery. If RPM continues to drop, I would prioritize completing the autorotation to a landing rather than risk a rotor stall.

questions.question: The evaluator briefed you for a full touchdown autorotation, but during the approach you realize you are going to land significantly short of the intended landing spot. At 200 feet AGL, you still have sufficient airspeed. What options do you have and what are your decision priorities?
questions.answer: At 200 feet AGL with sufficient airspeed, options include: (1) initiating a power recovery to go-around if the engine is available and the evaluator confirms this is permitted; (2) shallowing the approach glide angle by reducing the flare or adding slight forward cyclic to increase forward speed and glide distance; or (3) if the area short of the intended spot is a suitable landing surface, accepting that landing point. The priority is: first ensure a safe landing surface is available, then attempt to stretch the glide only if airspeed and altitude allow without sacrificing rotor RPM. Forcing a stretch glide that depletes rotor RPM is never acceptable. The evaluator's brief determines whether power recovery is authorized.

questions.question: During a power recovery from a straight-in autorotation, you restore engine power and begin climbing away. The helicopter starts drifting to the right. What is most likely causing this and what is the correct corrective action?
questions.answer: The rightward drift is most likely caused by insufficient left antitorque pedal input during the power restoration. As engine torque increases, the main rotor torque reaction tends to yaw the nose right (in a counterclockwise rotor system). The pilot should add left pedal to coordinate the recovery. Additionally, if there is a right crosswind or if the cyclic has inadvertently been displaced, those factors should be checked and corrected. The fix is to add left pedal proportional to power applied while keeping the cyclic coordinated to maintain heading and track.

questions.question: You are flying a low-inertia rotor system helicopter and executing a straight-in autorotation. The evaluator calls 'power recovery' at 50 feet AGL. How does the low-inertia rotor system change the urgency and technique of your power recovery compared to a high-inertia system, and what specific error are you most guarded against?
questions.answer: Low-inertia rotor systems store significantly less kinetic energy in the rotor blades compared to high-inertia systems. This means rotor RPM decays much more rapidly during autorotation — particularly if the collective is not lowered promptly at entry and during the descent. During power recovery, the window of time to restore engine power before RPM decays to an unrecoverable level is much shorter. The technique requires: (1) initiating recovery at a slightly higher altitude to allow more margin; (2) advancing throttle and raising collective smoothly but without delay; (3) closely monitoring RPM throughout. The most critical error to guard against is pulling collective before the engine has restored sufficient torque — this can rapidly drive RPM below the minimum and result in a rotor stall, which is unrecoverable. Timing of collective and throttle must be precisely coordinated.
questions.follow_up: If the rotor RPM drops below the minimum safe RPM during a power recovery and cannot be recovered, what is your only remaining option and why?
questions.follow_up_answer: If rotor RPM drops below the minimum safe RPM during an attempted power recovery and cannot be restored, the only option is to immediately lower the collective to unload the rotor and attempt to recover RPM from whatever inflow is available, then execute the best possible landing with whatever rotor energy remains. The FAA Helicopter Flying Handbook states that rotor stall in a helicopter is not recoverable — once the blades stall, lift is lost and the helicopter will descend uncontrollably. This underscores why early recognition and prevention are the only effective strategies; there is no recovery procedure once a full rotor stall occurs.

questions.question: During a straight-in autorotation with a briefed full touchdown, you complete the flare and begin the collective pull at 10 feet AGL to cushion the landing, but the helicopter is still moving forward at approximately 15 knots and the skids contact the ground while forward speed remains. What hazard does this create and what should you have done differently during the approach to prevent it?
questions.answer: Landing with significant forward speed on skids creates the risk of dynamic rollover. If one skid contacts the ground while forward speed remains, it can create a pivot point. If the pilot then pulls additional collective or applies lateral cyclic, the helicopter can roll over that pivot point faster than the pilot can correct — especially if the center of gravity is displaced toward the grounded skid. The proper prevention is to adequately decelerate during the flare so that forward speed is near zero at touchdown. If forward speed remains at cushion height, the pilot should continue the flare, use the remaining collective energy to slow the helicopter, and if necessary accept a slightly firmer touchdown rather than land with excessive groundspeed. Additionally, after skid contact with any residual speed, the pilot should keep the cyclic neutral, not pull additional collective, and allow the helicopter to slide to a stop rather than attempting to become airborne again.
questions.follow_up: Under what specific conditions does dynamic rollover become most dangerous during an autorotation touchdown, and what is the critical rollover angle for most helicopters?
questions.follow_up_answer: Dynamic rollover is most dangerous when: (1) one skid or wheel is caught on an obstacle, a rut, or soft terrain while the other remains free; (2) a crosswind creates a lateral drift at touchdown; (3) the pilot applies an abrupt or excessive lateral cyclic input after skid contact; or (4) the collective is raised while one skid is grounded. The FAA Helicopter Flying Handbook states that most helicopters have a critical rollover angle of approximately 5 to 8 degrees — beyond that angle, the rolling moment exceeds the corrective capability of the cyclic and rollover becomes unrecoverable. This is why smooth, near-zero-groundspeed touchdowns and immediate awareness of any lateral drift are essential skills in autorotation landings.

questions.question: When terminating a straight-in autorotation to a hover, at approximately what height above the ground should you begin applying collective to cushion the landing?
questions.answer: The collective cushion typically begins during the flare recovery phase, generally between 8 and 15 feet AGL (varies by helicopter model), as the forward speed is arrested and the helicopter transitions to a vertical descent. The pilot applies collective gradually to use remaining rotor RPM inertia to arrest the descent rate and establish a stabilized hover. The exact height depends on the specific helicopter's POH/RFM and rotor inertia characteristics.

questions.question: What is the ACS accuracy standard for terminating a straight-in autorotation to a designated point on the surface?
questions.answer: The ACS requires the pilot to terminate the autorotation to the surface within 100 feet of the designated point. If terminating to a hover instead, the hover must be stabilized — meaning the helicopter is in a steady, controlled hover with no excessive drift or altitude oscillation.

questions.question: What does it mean for a hover to be 'stabilized' at the termination of an autorotation, and why is this specifically required in the ACS standard?
questions.answer: A stabilized hover means the helicopter is at a controlled, steady altitude (typically 2–5 feet AGL), with minimal lateral or fore/aft drift, consistent heading, and no excessive power fluctuations. The ACS requires this because an unstabilized hover following autorotation indicates the pilot did not properly manage collective application, cyclic attitude control, or remaining rotor RPM — all of which reflect precision and safety in the recovery. An unstabilized hover increases risk of dynamic rollover, hard landing, or rotor RPM decay.

questions.question: You are on final in a straight-in autorotation and realize you are going to land approximately 150 feet short of your designated point. You still have sufficient altitude to make an adjustment. What options do you have, and what are the trade-offs of each?
questions.answer: To extend the glide and reach the designated point, the pilot has several options: (1) Reduce the flare intensity or delay the flare slightly to maintain more forward speed and cover more ground — however, this reduces the time available to arrest descent rate and may result in a harder touchdown. (2) Reduce collective if it was prematurely applied, which restores rotor RPM and extends the glide, but requires adequate altitude margin. (3) Adjust the glide by reducing the nose-high pitch attitude if excess back cyclic was applied too early. Each option requires careful management of rotor RPM, forward speed, and remaining altitude. Attempting aggressive corrections at low altitude increases risk significantly. If the adjustment cannot be safely made, the pilot should commit to a safe landing short of the point rather than sacrifice the quality of the termination.

questions.question: During the termination phase of a straight-in autorotation, you notice your rotor RPM is at the lower limit of the green arc just as you begin your collective pull to cushion the landing. How does this affect your termination technique and what is the primary hazard?
questions.answer: Low rotor RPM at the start of the collective cushion is a serious situation. The collective pull further reduces RPM because increased blade pitch adds drag to the rotor system. With RPM already at the low end of the green arc, there is very little inertia energy available to arrest the descent rate. The pilot must apply collective smoothly but with less total input than normal, accepting a firmer touchdown to avoid driving RPM below the stall threshold. The primary hazard is rotor stall — if RPM decays to the point where the blades can no longer produce adequate lift, recovery is not possible. The FAA states that rotor stalls in helicopters are not recoverable, making early recognition and prevention critical. The pilot should have identified the low RPM earlier in the descent and corrected by reducing collective to allow RPM recovery.

questions.question: You are practicing straight-in autorotations and consistently overshoot the designated point by 80–120 feet. Your instructor asks you to self-analyze the problem. What are the most likely technique errors causing consistent overshoot, and how would you correct each one?
questions.answer: Consistent overshoot typically results from one or more of the following technique errors: (1) Flare initiated too late or insufficient flare angle — the helicopter carries excessive forward speed into the termination. Correction: begin the flare slightly earlier and increase the aft cyclic input. (2) Collective applied too early during the flare, which arrests the descent too high and allows the helicopter to float forward before touchdown. Correction: delay collective application until airspeed has bled off sufficiently. (3) Entry airspeed too high, resulting in a flatter glide path that covers more ground. Correction: ensure proper entry airspeed per the RFM before reducing collective. (4) Approach angle too shallow — the helicopter has too much ground to cover. Correction: steepen the initial approach by establishing a proper autorotation glide slope. All corrections should be made incrementally and evaluated over multiple practice approaches.

questions.question: During a straight-in autorotation to the surface in a high-inertia rotor system helicopter, a student pilot applies collective aggressively at 20 feet AGL and the helicopter balloons up to 35 feet before beginning to settle again with rapidly decaying rotor RPM. As the examiner, how do you evaluate this situation, and what does it reveal about the student's understanding of energy management in the termination phase?
questions.answer: This scenario reveals a fundamental misunderstanding of rotor energy management. In a high-inertia rotor system, stored kinetic energy in the rotor is substantial, and aggressive collective application converts that rotational energy into lift rapidly — causing the balloon effect. Once the helicopter climbs unexpectedly, the student has essentially wasted the stored energy on an unintended altitude gain rather than arresting the descent rate at the intended point. The subsequent RPM decay is because that energy has been spent, and the engine is not running to replenish it. The student is now in a degraded energy state at an unplanned altitude with reduced rotor RPM — a potentially dangerous combination. This demonstrates the student does not understand that collective during autorotation termination must be applied smoothly and in proportion to the remaining rotor RPM and descent rate. The evaluation would likely result in a discontinuation of the maneuver if RPM continues to decay, and a discussion of energy management, the relationship between collective input rate and RPM decay, and the importance of using the flare — not just collective — to arrest both forward speed and descent rate.
questions.follow_up: If the student had been in a low-inertia rotor system instead of a high-inertia system during this same aggressive collective application, how would the outcome likely differ?
questions.follow_up_answer: In a low-inertia rotor system, the same aggressive collective application would cause RPM to decay much faster because there is significantly less stored kinetic energy in the rotor to draw from. Rather than ballooning up to 35 feet, the rotor RPM would likely drop rapidly below safe limits almost immediately, potentially reaching the rotor stall threshold before the pilot could react. The balloon effect may be less pronounced or absent, but the RPM decay would be more severe and immediate. This is why low-inertia rotor systems demand even more precise collective timing and technique during autorotation termination — the margin for error is substantially smaller, and the FAA emphasizes that since rotor stalls are not recoverable, early recognition and prevention are imperative.

questions.question: A pilot successfully lands within 100 feet of the designated point but touches down with significant lateral drift — approximately 10 knots of sideward movement to the left. The landing is otherwise smooth. Does this meet the ACS standard for HI.XII.B.S12, and what are the real-world safety implications of accepting a drifted surface landing during autorotation?
questions.answer: This does not fully meet the ACS standard. While the 100-foot accuracy requirement for point of touchdown may technically be satisfied, the ACS also requires the maneuver to demonstrate controlled, precise technique consistent with safe operations. A 10-knot lateral drift at touchdown represents a significant loss of directional control and is not consistent with a satisfactory termination. The ACS standard for surface landings implies a controlled, wings-level, minimal-drift touchdown — not merely geographic proximity to the point. In real-world operations, a 10-knot lateral drift during an autorotation touchdown creates multiple hazards: dynamic rollover risk is high because ground contact with lateral momentum can cause the skid or wheel to catch, creating a rolling moment the collective and cyclic may not be able to counter quickly enough; blade strike risk increases if the helicopter rolls; and in off-airport or confined-area scenarios, lateral drift could place the helicopter into obstacles. The pilot failed to correct the drift with cyclic inputs during the flare and termination, which is a fundamental control coordination failure. This would be evaluated as an unsatisfactory performance element despite the accuracy of the landing point.
questions.follow_up: What specific control input during the flare phase, if made earlier or more precisely, would most directly have prevented the left lateral drift at touchdown?
questions.follow_up_answer: Right cyclic input during the flare and transition to the hover or surface should have been used to counter the left lateral drift. Lateral drift during autorotation termination is typically caused by either a crosswind component not being corrected, or incorrect cyclic trim during the descent that allows the helicopter to develop sideward velocity. The pilot should have identified the drift during the approach and applied corrective cyclic to zero it out before reaching the critical low-altitude phase. Additionally, proper heading control throughout the autorotation — using pedals for yaw and cyclic for translational control — would have addressed the drift well before it became a problem at touchdown. Waiting until the last moment to correct lateral movement at low altitude is ineffective because there is insufficient time and altitude to complete the correction safely.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; ACS HI.XII.B.S12; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 9 (dynamic rollover discussion)

questions.question: What is one of the most common errors a pilot makes at the entry point of a straight-in autorotation, and what is the immediate consequence if it is not corrected?
questions.answer: Failing to lower the collective immediately upon engine failure is one of the most common entry errors. If collective is not lowered promptly, blade pitch remains high, rotor RPM decays rapidly due to increased drag on the blades with no engine power driving them. On low-inertia rotor systems, RPM can decay to an unrecoverable level within seconds. The pilot must simultaneously lower collective, apply aft cyclic to slow to best glide airspeed, and apply pedal to maintain trim.

questions.question: During the autorotation glide, a student pilot is flying with rotor RPM consistently at the top of the green arc or slightly above. What common control error is likely causing this, and how should it be corrected?
