Because the main rotor is still turning — now driven by autorotative airflow rather than engine torque — the tail rotor remains functional throughout the descent, allowing the pilot to correct and hold heading.

questions.question: Why does heading tend to drift immediately after an engine failure at a hover, and in which direction does it typically yaw on a helicopter with a counterclockwise-rotating main rotor?
questions.answer: When the engine fails, torque from the main rotor suddenly disappears. The tail rotor, which was producing thrust to counteract that torque, now has excess thrust relative to the new zero-torque condition. On a helicopter with a counterclockwise-rotating main rotor (most US designs), the nose will yaw left because tail rotor thrust was pushing the tail to the right; once engine torque is removed, right pedal input is needed to prevent the nose from swinging left.

questions.question: You are performing a simulated engine failure at a hover and notice your heading has already drifted 8° left before you begin your descent. What does this tell the examiner about your control inputs, and how do you recover while still meeting the ±5° standard?
questions.answer: An 8° heading deviation before the descent begins indicates the pilot was slow on right pedal input after the simulated torque loss — the tail rotor's residual thrust caused the left yaw. To recover, apply right pedal smoothly and promptly to stop the yaw and return to within 5° of the original heading. Meeting the ±5° standard requires anticipating the yaw tendency at the moment of failure and making an immediate, coordinated pedal correction rather than chasing the heading reactively after it has already drifted beyond tolerance.

questions.question: During a checkride hover autorotation, the wind is 12 knots from your 3 o'clock position. How does a crosswind from the right affect your heading control challenge during the maneuver, and what adjustments do you anticipate?
questions.answer: A right crosswind at hover creates a weathervaning tendency that will try to push the nose into the wind (right). As rotor RPM and collective change throughout the autorotation descent, the net yaw forces also change. You must be prepared to use more left pedal than you would in a no-wind condition to counteract both the weathervaning effect and any residual right-pedal trim from the original hover. Additionally, a right crosswind reduces tail rotor effectiveness slightly because it partially opposes tail rotor thrust, requiring closer attention to heading throughout. Anticipate these forces and apply smooth, proactive pedal inputs to stay within ±5°.

questions.question: A student tells you that during hover autorotations they focus entirely on collective management for cushioning the landing and frequently exceed the ±5° heading standard. What is the fundamental control prioritization error they are making, and how would you correct it?
questions.answer: The student is treating collective as the highest-priority input and letting heading management become an afterthought. In a hover autorotation, all four controls must be coordinated simultaneously — not sequentially. Heading is a continuous task managed with the pedals throughout the entire maneuver, not something addressed only after cushioning. The correction is to train the student to divide attention equally across collective, cyclic, pedals, and overall aircraft position from the moment of failure to touchdown. In the pattern of a hover autorotation, the pedal input to counter the sudden loss of torque should actually be one of the first instinctive corrections, occurring at the same time as the collective is lowered.

questions.question: During the checkride, you perform a hover autorotation and touch down exactly on heading — but I observed you were 7° off heading at mid-maneuver before recovering at the last second. Is the ±5° standard met, and what does that mid-maneuver deviation tell me as your examiner?
questions.answer: No — the ±5° standard is not met. The ACS language states the pilot must maintain heading ±5° 'throughout the maneuver,' meaning the standard applies continuously, not just at touchdown. A 7° deviation at any point during the maneuver constitutes a failure of this task element, even if the pilot recovers to the correct heading before touchdown. As an examiner, the mid-maneuver deviation tells me the pilot lacks proactive pedal coordination at the moment of failure and is reacting to heading drift rather than preventing it. This is likely a training deficiency in internalizing the immediate pedal response needed when torque is suddenly removed.
questions.follow_up: If a pilot consistently recovers to heading by touchdown but always drifts beyond ±5° in the middle of hover autorotations, what specific training technique would you use to break that reactive habit?
questions.follow_up_answer: I would have the student practice the pedal input in isolation by simulating the torque-loss yaw on the ground or during hover practice without committing to the full autorotation — focusing exclusively on the speed and magnitude of the pedal correction. I would also use slow-motion verbal callouts: as the throttle is reduced, the student calls 'pedal' before calling 'collective' to reinforce the priority and simultaneity of the pedal input. Additionally, I'd review the Helicopter Flying Handbook Chapter 11 discussion of tail rotor behavior during power loss so the student understands the aerodynamic reason for the yaw tendency, building anticipation rather than reaction.

questions.question: You're conducting a hover autorotation in a turbine helicopter with a low-inertia rotor system. How does low rotor inertia specifically increase the difficulty of maintaining the ±5° heading standard compared to a high-inertia rotor system, and what must the pilot do differently?
questions.answer: In a low-inertia rotor system, rotor RPM decays very rapidly after engine failure — within seconds. This rapid RPM decay directly reduces tail rotor thrust because tail rotor output is proportional to main rotor RPM (the tail rotor is driven off the main rotor transmission). As RPM drops quickly, the pilot has significantly less time before tail rotor effectiveness is substantially reduced, meaning heading control authority degrades faster than in a high-inertia system. The pilot must lower collective immediately and more aggressively to preserve RPM, while simultaneously applying the correct pedal input. Any delay in lowering collective accelerates RPM decay, which in turn reduces the pedal authority needed to maintain heading within ±5°. The pilot must internalize that collective and pedal are effectively linked through RPM — protecting rotor RPM is also an act of protecting heading control authority.
questions.follow_up: If rotor RPM has decayed to the point where tail rotor effectiveness is severely reduced mid-hover-autorotation, what is the likely outcome, and is there a recovery option?
questions.follow_up_answer: If tail rotor thrust is severely reduced due to low RPM, the helicopter will yaw rapidly in the direction of main rotor rotation (left on a counterclockwise-rotation helicopter) and heading control will be effectively lost. At hover altitude with very low RPM, there is essentially no recovery option — the FAA Helicopter Flying Handbook states explicitly that rotor stall in helicopters is not recoverable and early recognition is imperative. The outcome is likely a hard landing with uncontrolled heading and the real possibility of a rollover or dynamic rollover if the helicopter contacts the ground while yawing. This is why the immediate collective reduction at power loss is non-negotiable in low-inertia aircraft — it is both an RPM preservation action and a heading control preservation action.

questions.question: When an engine fails in a hover and you execute a hovering autorotation, why is rearward movement at touchdown specifically prohibited while sideward movement is only minimized rather than eliminated?
questions.answer: Rearward movement at touchdown is prohibited because the pilot cannot see what is directly behind the helicopter, creating a collision hazard with obstacles, personnel, or terrain features. Rearward ground contact also increases the risk of tail boom or tail rotor strike and can cause the aircraft to tip rearward. Sideward movement at touchdown is minimized rather than fully eliminated because small amounts of sideward drift may be unavoidable during the settling process, but it must be kept to the absolute minimum to prevent dynamic rollover and maintain skid/wheel integrity.

questions.question: During a hovering autorotation following engine failure, which flight control is primarily responsible for arresting sideward movement just before touchdown?
questions.answer: The cyclic is primarily responsible for arresting sideward movement before touchdown. The pilot uses lateral cyclic inputs to stop any sideward drift and center the helicopter over the intended touchdown point. Proper cyclic coordination ensures the helicopter is tracking straight down with minimal lateral movement at the moment of ground contact.

questions.question: At what hover height does an engine failure most commonly occur during training, and why does that height influence how much sideward drift you can correct before touchdown?
questions.answer: Training hovering autorotations are typically practiced from a normal hover altitude of approximately 2 to 3 feet skid height above the ground. At this low altitude, the time available to detect and correct sideward drift is extremely limited—often only one to two seconds from failure to ground contact. This short time window means any pre-existing sideward drift at the moment of engine failure may be difficult or impossible to fully arrest before touchdown, which is why the standard requires minimum rather than zero sideward movement.

questions.question: You are practicing hovering autorotations and notice that each time the engine fails, you are touching down with consistent left sideward movement. What is the most likely cause, and how would you correct it?
questions.answer: Consistent left sideward drift during hovering autorotations typically indicates the helicopter was already drifting left during the hover before the simulated failure, or the pilot is applying excessive right pedal during the descent which yaws the nose right and allows the left skid to contact first, inducing a leftward roll tendency. Correction requires ensuring the helicopter is trimmed and stationary in the hover before simulating the failure, and during descent, using cyclic to actively neutralize any sideward movement detected early in the settling phase. The pilot must also check that the hover itself is stable with no pre-existing drift before the failure is introduced.

questions.question: During a hovering autorotation, the helicopter develops a slight rearward movement just as you lower the collective. You still have about 1.5 feet of altitude remaining. Walk me through the exact corrective actions you take to prevent rearward touchdown.
questions.answer: With 1.5 feet of altitude remaining and rearward movement developing, apply forward cyclic immediately to stop the rearward drift — the input must be smooth and deliberate to avoid over-correcting into a forward pitch. Simultaneously use the remaining rotor RPM and collective cushion available to manage the rate of descent. The priority is to arrest rearward movement before ground contact; even accepting a slightly firm landing is preferable to any rearward ground contact. If rearward movement cannot be fully arrested in time and a rearward touchdown appears imminent, the pilot should consider whether a go-around is still possible depending on rotor RPM status. Do not allow rearward contact under any circumstances due to tail boom/tail rotor strike risk.

questions.question: How does wind direction and speed during a hover affect your ability to achieve a touchdown with minimum sideward movement during a hovering autorotation, and what pre-hover positioning technique helps mitigate this risk?
questions.answer: A crosswind during a hover creates a tendency for the helicopter to drift downwind, which translates directly to sideward movement during a hovering autorotation. The stronger the crosswind, the greater the drift tendency during the short settling time available. To mitigate this, the pilot should position the helicopter into the wind before any hover work — hovering with the nose into the wind minimizes sideward drift because any wind effect becomes a headwind component rather than a lateral force. If a crosswind is unavoidable, the pilot must pre-position with cyclic leaned slightly into the wind during the hover to prevent drift, so that at the moment of engine failure the helicopter is already neutralized and does not carry sideward momentum into the descent.

questions.question: During a hovering autorotation evaluation, a student touches down with the left skid contacting first due to slight leftward movement. The aircraft remains upright with no damage. How do you assess this performance against the ACS standard, and at what point does sideward movement at touchdown transition from a deficiency to a potential unsatisfactory performance item?
questions.answer: ACS standard HI.XIII.A.S8 requires touchdown with minimum sideward movement and no rearward movement. A single-skid-first touchdown caused by lateral drift represents a deviation from the standard. As an examiner, I assess whether the movement was truly minimal — a very slight, momentary drift that resulted in a clean, controlled landing with no dynamic rollover tendency or loss of aircraft control would be evaluated differently than a pronounced lateral skid or a repeated pattern of drifting. The transition to unsatisfactory occurs when sideward movement is significant enough to create a dynamic rollover risk, results in loss of aircraft control, causes aircraft damage or simulated damage, or becomes a repeated pattern indicating the pilot lacks the skill to correct drift. A single minor deviation with an otherwise stable approach and landing could be noted as a deficiency requiring discussion; however, any sideward movement that places the helicopter or occupants in jeopardy is an unsatisfactory performance.
questions.follow_up: The student insists the leftward touchdown was acceptable because the skids didn't slide. How do you explain why that reasoning misses the point of the standard?
questions.follow_up_answer: The standard is not about what happens after the skids contact the ground — it's about controlled placement during the approach and at the moment of touchdown. A skid that contacts firmly without sliding may still have imposed asymmetric load on the landing gear, created a dynamic rollover risk in a higher wind condition, or indicated the pilot was not in full control of aircraft lateral positioning during the most critical phase. In a real engine failure with obstacles, personnel, or uneven terrain nearby, that same leftward drift could have been catastrophic. The goal of the standard is to demonstrate precise aircraft control throughout the maneuver, not just survivable contact with the ground.

questions.question: A low-inertia rotor system helicopter experiences an engine failure in a hover at a high-density altitude airport. How does rotor system inertia interact with the time available to correct sideward and rearward movement before touchdown, and what technique adjustments are required compared to a standard sea-level practice environment?
questions.answer: Low-inertia rotor systems decay RPM much faster following an engine failure than high-inertia systems, as described in FAA-H-8083-21B. At high-density altitude, the rotor is already operating at a higher blade pitch angle to generate the same lift in less dense air, meaning the blade drag is already elevated and RPM decay will be even more rapid. This dramatically compresses the time available to make cyclic corrections for sideward and rearward drift — the effective correction window may be reduced by 30-50% compared to sea-level conditions. Technique adjustments required include: (1) ensuring the hover is completely stationary with zero drift before any maneuver; (2) lowering collective even more aggressively at failure recognition to unload the rotor and slow RPM decay; (3) accepting that the correction envelope is extremely narrow and that any pre-existing drift at failure onset will almost certainly translate to ground movement at touchdown; and (4) recognizing that the margin for error that exists at sea level essentially disappears at high-density altitude with a low-inertia system, making preflight stabilization of the hover even more critical.
questions.follow_up: Given these limitations, should this maneuver even be practiced at high-density altitude in a low-inertia system, and what does the pilot need to know before attempting it?
questions.follow_up_answer: Whether to practice hovering autorotations at high-density altitude in a low-inertia system depends on the specific aircraft's RFM (Rotorcraft Flight Manual) guidance and operator procedures. Some manufacturers restrict or provide specific procedures for hovering autorotations at altitude. Before attempting the maneuver, the pilot must know the aircraft's rotor RPM decay rate at that density altitude, the minimum RPM at which collective cushioning is still effective, and whether the RFM authorizes the maneuver under those conditions. The pilot should also ensure the rotor RPM is at the top of the green arc before any failure is simulated, and the instructor must be prepared to intervene immediately if RPM decays to a level where a safe landing is no longer achievable. Operating outside the RFM envelope to demonstrate a maneuver is never acceptable.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; applicable aircraft RFM; 14 CFR 91.9

questions.question: During a hovering autorotation, which flight control is primarily responsible for cushioning the touchdown, and what is the general timing for its application?
questions.answer: The collective is the primary control used to cushion the touchdown. As the helicopter descends through the final few feet, the pilot applies upward collective to increase blade pitch, which increases lift and slows the rate of descent just before ground contact. This collective application must be timed to coincide with the final few feet of descent — applying it too early depletes rotor RPM before touchdown, while applying it too late results in a hard landing.

questions.question: Why must the pilot lower the collective immediately upon engine failure during a hover before eventually using it to cushion the touchdown?
questions.answer: Upon engine failure in a hover, the collective must be immediately lowered to reduce blade pitch and decrease drag on the rotor system. This allows the residual rotor inertia to maintain rotor RPM during the descent rather than rapidly decaying. If the collective is not lowered promptly, the rotor RPM bleeds off and there will be insufficient rotor energy stored to execute a collective pull for cushioning the touchdown.

questions.question: What role does cyclic play in cushioning the touchdown during a hovering autorotation from a low hover?
questions.answer: The cyclic is used to keep the helicopter level and to control any lateral or fore-aft drift during the descent and at touchdown. Drift at touchdown significantly increases the risk of dynamic rollover or skid damage. The cyclic should be held to maintain a wings-level, minimal-drift attitude so that the collective cushion is applied while the helicopter is essentially vertical over the landing surface. It does not directly provide the cushioning effect, but its proper use ensures the collective can be effective.

questions.question: You are practicing hovering autorotations at 3 feet AGL. On one practice attempt, you notice the rotor RPM is at the lower limit of the green arc just as you reach ground level. How does this affect your cushioning technique and what is the likely outcome if you still attempt a full collective pull?
questions.answer: With rotor RPM already at the bottom of the green arc at ground level, there is very little stored rotor energy remaining. Attempting a full collective pull at this point will further load the rotor and rapidly decay RPM below the stall threshold, providing very little actual lift or rate-of-descent reduction. The result will likely be a hard landing. The correct response is to recognize low RPM early, accept a firmer-than-desired landing with a reduced collective application, and focus on maintaining a level skid attitude with the cyclic to avoid dynamic rollover. This scenario reinforces why rotor RPM management throughout the entire descent — not just at the bottom — is critical.

questions.question: During a hovering autorotation to an unimproved surface, the skids contact an unseen slope just as you apply collective to cushion. One skid touches first, tilting the helicopter. Describe the correct cyclic and collective inputs to prevent dynamic rollover at this moment.
questions.answer: The instant one skid contacts a slope and the helicopter begins to tilt, the pilot must move the cyclic into the slope — toward the low side — to counteract the rolling tendency. Simultaneously, the collective should be reduced if the RPM allows, to reduce the lifting force that is amplifying the roll. The goal is to get the second skid on the ground quickly with a level attitude. If the roll rate exceeds the cyclic's ability to arrest it, the pilot must aggressively reduce collective and accept a potential rollover rather than allow the dynamic rollover to complete with full rotor energy. Dynamic rollover can occur rapidly and the cyclic must never be moved away from the slope during ground contact.

questions.question: You are hovering at 8 feet AGL when the engine fails. Compare the collective cushioning technique required from this height versus a failure at 2 feet AGL, specifically addressing rotor RPM management.
questions.answer: From 8 feet AGL, the helicopter has more time and vertical distance in which to descend, meaning the rotor has more time to potentially decay RPM during the descent. The pilot must lower collective aggressively upon failure to preserve RPM, and then time the cushioning pull at the correct height — approximately 1 to 2 feet AGL — to convert that stored rotor energy into lift. From 2 feet AGL there is very little descent time, so RPM decay is less of a concern, but the timing window for the cushioning pull is extremely short and less rotor energy is available. In both cases, the pilot should not begin the cushioning pull until the last possible moment, but the higher failure demands more precise RPM management throughout the descent.

questions.question: A student consistently applies the collective cushion too early during hovering autorotations, resulting in the rotor RPM decaying to the bottom of the green arc before touchdown and a hard contact. As the instructor, what is your diagnosis of the underlying control habit causing this, and what specific corrective technique or training emphasis would you use to fix it?
questions.answer: The root cause is typically a startle or anxiety response — the student sees the ground approaching and instinctively pulls collective to arrest the descent before reaching the optimal initiation point. This is compounded by a lack of ground reference depth perception at low altitude. The corrective technique involves several approaches: First, develop the student's ability to judge height above the surface by practicing stationary hovers at varying heights to calibrate their visual references. Second, have the student verbally call out their height during descents ('four feet, three feet, two feet') to slow down their mental processing and delay the pull. Third, practice the maneuver from a very low hover — one to two feet — so the student can feel what an appropriate last-second pull feels like. Finally, emphasize that rotor RPM is the fuel for the cushion — pulling early spends that fuel before it's needed. The student must trust the rotor inertia and commit to a later application.
questions.follow_up: If you've tried all of those corrective techniques and the student still consistently pulls too early, at what point do you make a training record entry or consider whether this student can meet the ACS standard, and what documentation is required?
questions.follow_up_answer: If a student consistently demonstrates an inability to correct a specific maneuver after multiple training sessions with varied corrective techniques, the instructor has a responsibility to document the deficiency in the student's training record with specific dates, descriptions of the maneuver failures, and the corrective actions taken. Under 14 CFR 61.189, the instructor must maintain records of flight training provided. If the instructor endorses the student for a checkride, they are certifying the student is prepared; endorsing a student who cannot reliably perform this skill would be inappropriate and potentially expose the instructor to certificate action. The instructor should consider additional training, possibly with a different instructor perspective, before making any endorsement decision. If the student cannot meet the ACS standard after documented good-faith training effort, the endorsement should be withheld.

questions.question: You are conducting a hovering autorotation in a helicopter with a low-inertia rotor system versus one with a high-inertia rotor system. How does rotor inertia fundamentally change the timing and magnitude of the collective cushion input, and what does this mean operationally when transitioning between aircraft types?
questions.answer: In a high-inertia rotor system, the rotor stores significantly more kinetic energy due to the greater mass of the blades. This means RPM decays more slowly after engine failure, giving the pilot more time during the descent and more stored energy available for the cushioning pull. The cushioning collective application can be slightly more deliberate and the margin for timing error is greater. In a low-inertia rotor system, RPM decays rapidly after engine failure — sometimes within a second or two — meaning the pilot must lower the collective immediately and the timing window for the cushioning pull is extremely narrow. The magnitude of the available lift from the cushion is also reduced because there is less kinetic energy stored. Operationally, a pilot transitioning from a high-inertia type to a low-inertia type must recalibrate their response speed — what feels like an adequate reaction time in one aircraft may result in an unsalvageable RPM decay in the other. This is a significant safety consideration during type transitions and contributes to the FAA statistic that accident rates decrease substantially after 100 hours in type.
questions.follow_up: Given this RPM decay rate difference, is there a scenario where a pilot in a low-inertia helicopter could actually have a worse outcome from a higher hover AGL than from a lower one during an engine failure, and why?
questions.follow_up_answer: Yes. In a low-inertia helicopter, a failure at a higher hover height — say 6 to 8 feet — can actually be more dangerous than a failure at 1 to 2 feet in some circumstances. The additional time in the air, while seemingly advantageous, allows the rotor RPM to decay to a dangerously low level before the helicopter reaches the ground. If the pilot lowers collective promptly, RPM may still decay significantly over the longer descent time. The pilot may then be forced to choose between pulling collective too early (spending remaining RPM too high) or arriving at the ground with insufficient RPM for any meaningful cushion. At 1 to 2 feet, the time available is short, but so is the RPM decay — a quick collective pull can still be effective. This phenomenon is part of the 'dead man's curve' concept for low-inertia helicopters and underscores why hovering height and power management are critical safety considerations in those aircraft types.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 2 (rotor inertia and aerodynamics)

questions.question: After an autorotation touchdown following a hover power loss, what is the correct sequence of control actions?
questions.answer: After touchdown, the pilot must immediately lower the collective fully to the down position and then neutralize all flight controls — cyclic to a neutral/centered position and pedals to a neutral, feet-flat position. Lowering the collective reduces rotor blade pitch to minimize any remaining lift and prevent the helicopter from becoming airborne again or rolling. Neutralizing the cyclic prevents the rotor disk from tilting and causing blade contact with the tailboom or ground. Pedal neutralization prevents any yawing tendency from residual tail rotor thrust.

questions.question: Why is it critical to lower the collective immediately after touchdown in a hover autorotation — not just slow it down, but fully lower it?
questions.answer: After touchdown, residual rotor RPM still generates lift if the collective is left in a raised position. If the collective is not fully lowered, that remaining lift can partially unload the skids, allowing the helicopter to shift, skid, or even become briefly airborne — potentially leading to dynamic rollover or a hard secondary contact. Fully lowering the collective removes blade pitch, eliminates lift production, and keeps the helicopter firmly on the ground while the rotor spools down safely.

questions.question: What does 'neutralize flight controls' mean in the context of post-touchdown actions after a hover power loss, and which specific controls are included?
questions.answer: Neutralizing flight controls means returning each control to its neutral, no-input position after touchdown. This includes: (1) Cyclic — centered so the rotor disk is level and not tilted in any direction, preventing blade flap toward the airframe or ground; (2) Antitorque pedals — centered or relaxed to a neutral position so no yaw input is applied and the tail does not swing; (3) Collective — already fully lowered as the primary post-touchdown action. The goal is to remove all aerodynamic forces and let the helicopter settle statically on the landing gear.

questions.question: You've just completed a simulated hover power loss to touchdown on the practice pad. The examiner notices you lowered the collective but your cyclic drifted slightly aft after contact. What's the risk of that specific control error?
questions.answer: Allowing the cyclic to drift aft after touchdown tilts the rotor disk rearward. With any residual rotor RPM remaining, this rearward disk tilt can lift the nose of the skids, causing the helicopter to rock back onto the tailboom skid or, on a sloped surface, initiate a rearward tip-over. In extreme cases with sufficient rotor energy, it could cause the aft rotor blades to strike the tailboom. Proper technique requires the cyclic to be centered promptly and held there until the rotor fully decelerates. Additionally, aft cyclic with collective down during roll-out is the correct technique during a running landing autorotation, but not after a hover auto touchdown where the aircraft must be held stationary.

questions.question: During a hover power loss practice at 3 feet AGL, your helicopter drifts slightly left just before touchdown and lands with the left skid contacting first. How does this affect the priority and execution of your post-touchdown collective lowering and control neutralization?
questions.answer: An asymmetric touchdown with the left skid contacting first increases the risk of dynamic rollover. In this situation, the pilot must still lower the collective immediately and aggressively — there is no delay. If the collective is held or raised while the helicopter is in a lateral tilt with one skid on the ground, the rotor thrust will add to the overturning moment and rollover can occur rapidly. Simultaneously, the cyclic must be moved to counter any rolling tendency — slight right cyclic input may be needed momentarily to level the disk before fully neutralizing — and pedals should be centered. The critical point is that collective down is the priority regardless of the landing attitude; it is the single most important action to prevent rollover. Recovery cyclic can be applied, but raising collective to 'save' the landing at this stage would likely worsen the rollover risk.

questions.question: A student pilot asks why they need to neutralize the antitorque pedals after touchdown in a hover power loss — 'the aircraft is on the ground, why do the pedals matter?' How do you explain this?
questions.answer: Even after touchdown, the tail rotor is still spinning and producing thrust as long as rotor RPM exists and collective isn't fully flat-pitched. If a pedal input is held, that tail rotor thrust creates a yaw moment about the contact point between the skid and the ground. This can cause the helicopter to pivot or swing on the landing surface, especially on a slippery or smooth surface. Additionally, on a helicopter with skids, a hard yaw input after one skid is planted can induce a rolling tendency. Neutralizing the pedals removes this risk and allows the helicopter to remain stationary and settled until the rotor coasts to a stop. The habit is also critical — in a real engine failure, the pilot must land safely AND secure the aircraft; any residual control input after touchdown adds unnecessary risk.

questions.question: On the checkride, the applicant executes a hover power loss, touches down cleanly, but then hesitates approximately one second before lowering the collective — the rotor RPM decays normally and nothing bad happens. Is this a unsatisfactory performance element, and what's the underlying aerodynamic reason the one-second delay is actually a significant error?
questions.answer: Yes, this is an unsatisfactory performance element because the ACS standard explicitly requires lowering the collective after touchdown — 'after' meaning immediately upon contact, not as a delayed action. The aerodynamic reason the delay is critical: at hover, the collective may be anywhere from mid to near-full pitch to cushion the descent. During that one second of hesitation, the rotor disk is still producing meaningful lift at reduced — but not zero — rotor RPM. The helicopter's skids are on the ground but the rotor is still attempting to fly the aircraft. This is the exact condition that precedes dynamic rollover: one or both skids are in contact with a surface that provides a pivot point, and any lift, wind gust, or control input can generate enough overturning moment to exceed the critical rollover angle (which can be as low as 3–8° depending on the helicopter model). The examiner should note this hesitation as a failure to demonstrate the full skill as described in HI.XIII.A.S10.
questions.follow_up: If the applicant argues that lowering the collective 'too fast' could cause rotor RPM to spike and damage the transmission, how would you respond?
questions.follow_up_answer: This concern conflates two different phases of flight. Aggressively lowering collective rapidly during autorotation entry can cause transient rotor RPM overspeed, but after touchdown, rotor RPM is already decaying and the rotor is no longer being driven by engine power. Lowering the collective at touchdown does not spike RPM — it reduces blade pitch and removes lift. The transmission is no longer under load at this point. There is no aerodynamic or mechanical basis for hesitating to lower the collective after the helicopter has contacted the ground. The student has confused the engine-failure entry technique with the post-touchdown action.

questions.question: You're evaluating an applicant on a hover power loss to a confined, sloped landing area where the upslope skid touches first. After touchdown, you observe the applicant lower the collective fully but then apply forward cyclic to keep the nose from rising with the slope. Is this correct technique — should cyclic truly be 'neutralized' to a centered position, or should it be adjusted for the terrain?
questions.answer: This is a nuanced situation. The ACS standard says to neutralize flight controls, which in a flat-pad, controlled training environment means centering the cyclic. However, on a sloped surface, strict mechanical centering of the cyclic may not be appropriate — the pilot should maintain cyclic input sufficient to keep the rotor disk parallel to the slope and prevent the helicopter from rolling downhill on the skids. The intent of 'neutralize' in the context of HI.XIII.A.S10 is to remove any pilot inputs that could cause the helicopter to become airborne again or tip over — not necessarily to move the cyclic to a geometric center point regardless of terrain. A competent pilot recognizes that on a slope, the cyclic should be held into the slope (upslope cyclic) to prevent the high-skid side from rising. The examiner should credit the applicant who lowers collective immediately and then manages cyclic appropriately for terrain, rather than one who rigidly centers the cyclic on a slope and allows the helicopter to roll.
questions.follow_up: What is the maximum recommended slope angle for most single-engine training helicopters during slope landings, and where would you find that limitation?
questions.follow_up_answer: Maximum slope landing angles are helicopter-model specific and are found in the Rotorcraft Flight Manual (RFM) for each aircraft — there is no single universal FAA standard. Many light training helicopters have limits in the range of 5–10 degrees, but this varies significantly. For example, some Robinson R44 operating guidance references slope limitations, while military-derived helicopters may have different values. The pilot must reference the specific RFM for the aircraft being flown. The examiner should expect the applicant to know that this is an RFM limitation, not a generic FAA regulation, and to be able to reference where it's found.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 9 (Slope Landings); ACS HI.XIII.A.S10; Aircraft RFM (model-specific)

questions.question: What is the most common initial error pilots make when experiencing a powerplant failure during a hover, and why is it so dangerous?
questions.answer: The most common initial error is freezing on the controls — failing to immediately lower the collective. When engine power is lost in a hover, rotor RPM decays rapidly. Delaying collective reduction allows rotor RPM to bleed below the power-on RPM range, and since low-inertia rotor systems decay especially fast, even a brief hesitation can result in an unrecoverable low-rotor-RPM condition. The helicopter will settle and contact the ground with insufficient rotor energy to cushion the landing.

questions.question: During a simulated hover autorotation, what common error do students make with the cyclic, and what is the correct technique?
questions.answer: A common error is allowing the cyclic to drift — either pulling back to arrest the descent or pushing forward inadvertently when startled. The correct technique is to maintain a level attitude with cyclic throughout the settling. The pilot should hold the cyclic in a position that keeps the helicopter level or very slightly nose-up, preventing a forward tip or tail-low attitude on ground contact. Overcorrecting with aft cyclic can cause a tail-strike.

questions.question: What pedal error commonly occurs during a powerplant failure in a hover, and what causes it?
questions.answer: When the engine fails in a hover, engine torque is suddenly removed. The pilot must promptly reduce left pedal input (in a counterclockwise-rotor helicopter) to maintain heading, because the engine torque that was previously present no longer exists and no longer needs to be countered by antitorque pedal input. Failing to reduce left pedal promptly causes the nose to yaw left (in the direction of rotor rotation). The correct response is to reduce left pedal input proportionally to the loss of torque to maintain heading. Over-applying right pedal is also a common overcorrection error.

questions.question: A student consistently lands with excessive lateral drift during simulated hover engine failures. As their instructor, how would you diagnose the root cause and correct this error?
questions.answer: Lateral drift usually results from one of two causes: (1) the student is not maintaining a wings-level (laterally level) attitude with cyclic during the descent, allowing the helicopter to track sideways, or (2) the student is not hovering directly over a reference point at the start, so any lateral displacement at hover altitude is amplified during settlement. The correction involves pre-flight reinforcement of maintaining a stable hover position before the failure is introduced, followed by training the student to make small, prompt lateral cyclic corrections during the descent to arrest drift before ground contact. Practicing at lower hover heights first helps reduce the time available for drift to accumulate.

questions.question: During a checkride, a candidate correctly lowers collective immediately on the simulated engine failure but then raises it again before touchdown, resulting in a hard landing. What error chain led to this outcome, and how should it be corrected?
questions.answer: The candidate likely panicked as the ground approached and instinctively pulled up collective to arrest the descent rate — a 'cushion pull' that depletes what little remaining rotor RPM was available. This error often stems from inadequate training at recognizing the proper moment for a final collective application, if any, versus the inappropriate early application that dissipates rotor energy. Correction involves teaching the student to trust the descent rate during a low hover autorotation (which is relatively gentle from a low hover), focusing their attention on aircraft attitude rather than rate of descent, and using surface reference to judge when — or if — a slight collective input is warranted. In most helicopters, a hover autorotation from a standard 3–5 ft hover requires minimal or no cushion pull.

questions.question: A pilot has 500 total flight hours but only 20 hours in the specific helicopter model they are flying. How does this experience gap increase their risk of making control errors during a hover engine failure, and what does FAA guidance say about accident risk in new aircraft types?
questions.answer: FAA guidance and accident data show that accident risk correlates more strongly with hours in a specific aircraft model than with total flight hours. Significant proficiency improvements typically occur within the first 50–100 hours in type, though the precise threshold varies by aircraft and pilot. A pilot with limited hours in type will have less ingrained muscle memory for that aircraft's specific control sensitivity, rotor inertia characteristics, and power response. During a high-stress, time-critical event like a hover engine failure, they are more likely to over- or under-correct on collective, apply incorrect pedal inputs, or hesitate — all common errors. Mitigations include type-specific training, simulator time if available, and deliberate practice of emergency procedures early in the transition.

questions.question: A pilot performs a hover engine failure correctly in all respects — immediate collective reduction, proper attitude, heading maintained — but still experiences a dynamic rollover on contact. Walk me through the error analysis: what specific mistake caused this outcome, and how would you detect it during debriefing?
questions.answer: Dynamic rollover on an otherwise correct hover autorotation typically indicates the pilot allowed one skid to contact the ground before the other, creating a pivot point. Once the low-side skid is on the ground and the helicopter is still moving laterally — even slightly — the combination of rotor lift, lateral momentum, and a fixed pivot point can drive a rollover faster than the pilot can correct. During debriefing, you would review whether: (1) the helicopter had lateral drift at touchdown, (2) the collective was held at a position that maintained partial lift on one side during ground contact, or (3) the helicopter was not laterally level at touchdown. Video review or a debrief using exaggerated slow-motion verbal replay of the sequence helps identify which of these occurred. The fix is coordinated cyclic to eliminate all lateral drift before contact and ensuring both skids touch simultaneously.
questions.follow_up: At what point during a dynamic rollover does the situation become unrecoverable, and what does the FAA say about the critical angle?
questions.follow_up_answer: According to FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11, dynamic rollover becomes unrecoverable when the helicopter reaches the critical rollover angle — approximately 5–8 degrees depending on the aircraft — at which point the center of gravity moves outside the pivot point and gravity accelerates the rollover faster than full opposite cyclic can counter. The FAA emphasizes that the only effective recovery is immediate, aggressive opposite cyclic AND lowering the collective simultaneously to reduce lift and eliminate the rolling moment. Above the critical angle, the collective must be reduced to the floor; attempting to fly out of it with cyclic alone is ineffective once the CG passes the tipping point.

questions.question: A candidate on an instrument helicopter checkride successfully executes a hover engine failure during the practical test but admits they were simply 'reacting by habit' without consciously processing each control input. As an examiner, why does this concern you from an ADM and SRM standpoint, and how would you probe deeper?
questions.answer: Reacting purely by conditioned habit without conscious processing is a risk in novel or degraded conditions — such as an engine failure at an off-airport site, in crosswind, over uneven terrain, or during an instrument approach to a hover. If the pilot's habit loop was trained in a sterile environment, they may apply the correct response in a standard scenario but fail when the situation deviates. From an SRM perspective, the pilot is not actively managing situational awareness or applying the decision-making process — they are pattern-matching, which is brittle under stress or novel conditions. To probe deeper, I would present a scenario variation: 'What if the engine failure occurred while you were in a crosswind hover over a confined area with one skid already lower than the other — walk me through your exact inputs and decision process.' This forces articulation of conscious decision-making rather than habit recall.
questions.follow_up: The FAA Helicopter Flying Handbook states that approximately what percentage of aviation accidents are caused by pilot error, and how does this apply to a pilot who relies on habit-based responses during emergencies?
questions.follow_up_answer: The FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 states that approximately 80% of aviation accidents are attributed to pilot error and human factors. A pilot who relies on pure habit-based responses without conscious ADM processing is more vulnerable to the 'error chain' — a series of compounding poor decisions or missed cues that leads to an accident. Habit-based responses bypass the evaluation step in ADM, meaning the pilot may not recognize when the situation has evolved beyond what their habitual response addresses. The handbook emphasizes that breaking even one link in the error chain can change the outcome, and that requires active awareness — something a purely reactive pilot may lack when the scenario deviates from training.

tasks.title: Task B. Powerplant Failure at Altitude in a Single-Engine Helicopter

questions.question: When an engine fails at altitude in a single-engine helicopter, what is the very first control input you must make, and why?
questions.answer: The first input is to immediately lower the collective to the full-down (or minimum pitch) position. This reduces the pitch angle on the rotor blades, decreasing lift and drag. With the engine no longer driving the rotor, reducing blade pitch allows the upward airflow through the descending rotor disk to maintain or recover rotor RPM through autorotation. Delaying this input allows rotor RPM to decay rapidly, and low-inertia rotor systems in particular can reach a stall condition before recovery is possible.

questions.question: After an engine failure at altitude, what happens to tail rotor authority and heading control during autorotation?
questions.answer: During autorotation, the main rotor continues to turn because it is being driven by upward airflow through the descending rotor disk. The tail rotor remains connected to the main rotor through the transmission and continues to produce thrust. Therefore, heading control with the antitorque pedals is maintained normally throughout the autorotative descent, just as it is in powered flight.

questions.question: Name the three simultaneous control inputs required at the moment of engine failure when a helicopter is in cruise flight at altitude.
questions.answer: At the moment of engine failure from cruise airspeed, the pilot must simultaneously apply: (1) down collective — to reduce blade pitch and preserve rotor RPM; (2) aft cyclic — to decelerate from cruise speed to the best autorotation airspeed and to increase upward airflow through the rotor disk, which also helps sustain rotor RPM; and (3) appropriate pedal input (typically right pedal in most helicopters with counterclockwise rotor systems) — to compensate for the sudden loss of torque and maintain trim.

questions.question: You are cruising at 3,500 feet AGL when your engine quits. You have adequate rotor RPM and the helicopter is in a stable autorotative descent. Walk me through the three distinct phases you must manage between now and touchdown.
questions.answer: The three phases of an autorotative descent from altitude are: (1) Entry and steady-state descent — After the initial inputs (collective down, aft cyclic, trim with pedals), establish the manufacturer's recommended autorotation airspeed (typically near best glide or minimum rate of descent speed per the RFM). This maximizes your glide distance and time available. (2) Deceleration (flare) — As you approach the landing area, apply aft cyclic to flare the helicopter. This converts forward momentum and some rotor energy into reduced rate of descent and adds lift, slowing both forward speed and vertical speed. Rotor RPM will increase during the flare due to increased airflow and blade pitch changes. (3) Touchdown/cushion — Level the helicopter with forward cyclic to arrest the nose-high attitude, then apply collective to use stored rotor energy to cushion the landing and reduce the final rate of descent to a survivable level. Timing is critical — applying collective too early depletes rotor energy before touchdown.

questions.question: Your helicopter has a low-inertia rotor system and the engine fails at altitude. How does this change the urgency of your response compared to a high-inertia system, and what does this mean practically?
questions.answer: Low-inertia rotor systems store significantly less kinetic energy in the rotor blades due to lighter blade mass. When the engine fails, rotor RPM decays much more rapidly than in a high-inertia system. This means the pilot has a much smaller time window — sometimes only one to two seconds — to lower the collective before rotor RPM drops into the stall range. A rotor stall in a helicopter is not recoverable. Practically, this means the pilot of a low-inertia helicopter must react immediately and instinctively, with no hesitation. High-inertia systems provide a longer window due to the greater energy stored, giving the pilot slightly more time to assess the situation before taking action. Pilots must know which type of rotor system their specific helicopter has and train accordingly.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B, Chapter 11 (Helicopter Emergencies and Hazards); Rotorcraft Flight Manual (RFM) for specific aircraft

questions.question: During an engine failure at altitude, a student applies aft cyclic during the entry. Besides slowing the helicopter, what aerodynamic effect does aft cyclic have on rotor RPM, and why?
questions.answer: Applying aft cyclic during autorotation entry tilts the rotor disk aft, which increases the angle at which air flows upward through the rotor disk. This increased upward airflow acts on the rotor blades and produces a greater driving force on the blade sections in the autorotative region of the blade. The result is an increase — or at minimum, preservation — of rotor RPM. This is one reason aft cyclic is a simultaneous input at autorotation entry rather than a secondary concern: it works together with the down-collective input to protect rotor RPM from decaying during the transition from powered flight to autorotation.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B, Chapter 11 (Helicopter Emergencies and Hazards); Chapter 2 (Aerodynamics of Flight)

questions.question: An applicant tells you that during a power failure at altitude, they would first assess the situation to determine whether it is truly an engine failure before lowering the collective — to avoid an unnecessary autorotation. How do you respond, and what does the FAA say about this type of decision-making?
questions.answer: This is a dangerous mindset. The Helicopter Flying Handbook is explicit: upon recognizing an engine failure at altitude, the pilot must immediately lower the collective — there is no time for deliberation, especially in low-inertia rotor systems where rotor RPM can decay to the stall point in one to two seconds. The FAA's guidance on ADM specifically warns against the word 'probably' — if an action will only 'probably' work out, choose an option known to work. Hesitating to lower collective because it is 'probably' just a temporary issue is exactly the kind of error chain decision that leads to accidents. The correct response is: lower collective immediately to protect rotor RPM, then — once in a stable autorotative descent with adequate altitude — assess whether a restart is possible per the RFM. Protecting rotor RPM is always the priority; everything else is secondary.
questions.follow_up: You've established a stable autorotation with good rotor RPM and plenty of altitude. The RFM includes an air restart checklist. At what point during the descent would you attempt a restart, and what is the limiting factor that determines whether you pursue it?
questions.follow_up_answer: An air restart should only be attempted if there is sufficient altitude remaining to complete the restart procedure AND still execute a safe autorotative landing if the restart fails. The pilot must never sacrifice the autorotation setup — including the flare and cushion phases — for a restart attempt. The limiting factor is having enough altitude to safely abort the restart attempt and still reach the intended landing area with adequate rotor RPM and airspeed. If there is any doubt about having that altitude margin, the restart is abandoned and all attention goes to the landing. The RFM for the specific helicopter will define the minimum altitude for restart attempts, and that limitation must be respected.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B, Chapter 11 (Emergencies) and Chapter 13 (ADM); Rotorcraft Flight Manual (RFM)

questions.question: Explain the aerodynamic relationship between induced drag and rotor RPM during autorotation, and how this relationship affects the pilot's management of rotor RPM throughout the descent and flare.
questions.answer: During autorotation, the rotor disk can be divided into regions based on aerodynamic effect: the driving region (mid-span, where relative wind produces a forward-acting aerodynamic force that sustains rotation) and areas near the hub and tip with different loading characteristics. Induced drag increases with blade angle of attack and opposes rotor rotation. In the descent phase, the pilot maintains rotor RPM in the green arc by adjusting collective pitch to balance the driving force against drag forces. As airspeed decreases toward the flare, the forward airflow that sustains the driving force diminishes. During the flare, aft cyclic increases the angle of the relative wind through the rotor disk, which temporarily increases the driving force. If rotor RPM climbs toward the top of the green arc during the flare, the pilot can make a small upward collective input to increase blade pitch angle, which increases induced drag and load, slowing the rotor back into the normal range. This must be done cautiously in small increments because: (1) raising collective consumes stored rotor energy needed for the cushion at touchdown, and (2) aggressive collective input can disrupt flare geometry. The pilot must balance RPM control with preserving sufficient rotor energy for the landing.
questions.follow_up: If rotor RPM climbs toward the top of the green arc during the flare, what is the correct control response, and why must you be cautious about how aggressively you apply it?
questions.follow_up_answer: If rotor RPM is approaching the top of the green arc during the flare, the pilot can make a small upward collective input to increase blade pitch angle, which adds induced drag and load to the system, slowing the rotor RPM back into the normal range. However, this must be done carefully and in small increments because: (1) raising collective consumes stored rotor energy that is needed for the cushion at touchdown — spending it prematurely reduces the energy available to arrest the final rate of descent; and (2) an aggressive collective increase during the flare can cause the nose to pitch, disrupting the flare geometry and approach path. The pilot must balance RPM control with preserving rotor energy for the landing itself.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B, Chapter 2 (Aerodynamics of Flight) and Chapter 11 (Helicopter Emergencies and Hazards)

questions.question: What does 'Nr' stand for, and why is it specifically important during a powerplant failure in a single-engine helicopter?
questions.answer: Nr stands for 'rotor RPM' — specifically the rotational speed of the main rotor. During a powerplant failure, the engine is no longer driving the rotor, so Nr will begin to decay immediately. Maintaining Nr within the green arc is critical because the rotor is now the helicopter's only source of lift and control. If Nr decays below the minimum limit, the rotor can stall, which is not recoverable. The pilot must immediately lower the collective to reduce blade pitch, allowing aerodynamic forces (autorotation) to sustain rotor speed.

questions.question: What is the immediate effect on main rotor RPM (Nr) if a pilot fails to lower the collective promptly after an engine failure at cruise altitude?
questions.answer: If the collective is not immediately lowered after engine failure, the existing blade pitch angle creates high drag on the rotor system with no engine power to sustain it. Nr will decay rapidly. As Nr decreases, lift decreases and the helicopter will begin to descend uncontrollably. If Nr decays below the minimum RPM threshold, the rotor blades can stall — a condition that is not recoverable. Low-inertia rotor systems decay especially rapidly, leaving very little time for correction.

questions.question: During an autorotation following engine failure, what rotor RPM range should the pilot maintain, and where is that range indicated on the cockpit instruments?
questions.answer: The pilot must maintain Nr within the green arc on the tachometer (or dual-needle tachometer showing both engine RPM and rotor RPM). The specific green arc limits vary by helicopter make and model and are defined in the Rotorcraft Flight Manual (RFM). During autorotation, collective pitch is the primary control for managing Nr — raising collective increases blade drag and reduces Nr, while lowering collective decreases blade drag and allows Nr to increase. The pilot must continuously monitor the rotor tachometer to keep Nr in the safe operating range through the entire autorotation.

questions.question: You experience an engine failure at 3,000 feet AGL in cruise flight at 90 knots. As you enter autorotation, you notice Nr is climbing above the top of the green arc toward the red line. What caused this, and what is your corrective action?
questions.answer: Nr climbing above the green arc during autorotation entry from cruise airspeed (90 knots) is primarily caused by the high forward airspeed providing efficient upward airflow through the rotor disk combined with the immediate collective reduction necessary to enter autorotation. The high inflow rate accelerates rotor RPM rapidly. Excessive aft cyclic during entry can exacerbate this tendency by further increasing the angle of the relative wind. To correct overspeed, the pilot should gradually raise the collective to increase blade pitch and induce drag, which absorbs rotor energy and brings Nr back into the green arc. This correction must be applied in small, controlled increments while maintaining coordinated cyclic inputs to control airspeed and descent profile. Lowering collective further would allow rotor RPM to increase even more, worsening the overspeed condition.

questions.question: How does rotor system inertia (high-inertia vs. low-inertia rotors) affect the pilot's time margin to establish autorotation and recover Nr after an engine failure?
questions.answer: High-inertia rotor systems (typically those with heavier blades or greater blade mass) store more kinetic energy and therefore decay more slowly after engine failure, giving the pilot more time — sometimes several seconds — to recognize the failure and lower the collective. Low-inertia rotor systems lose RPM very rapidly after power loss, sometimes in just one to two seconds, leaving almost no margin for delayed reaction. This is why immediate and automatic collective-down response is drilled so extensively during training. Pilots transitioning to a low-inertia helicopter must recalibrate their reaction time expectations accordingly. The RFM will identify characteristics of the rotor system, and training will establish appropriate response times for that specific aircraft.

questions.question: A student pilot asks why Nr tends to decrease during the flare portion of an autorotation if the pilot doesn't compensate. Explain the aerodynamic reason and what the pilot should do.
questions.answer: During the flare, as forward airspeed decreases, the rotor loses some of the efficient upward airflow that sustained rotor RPM during the descent at cruise speeds. Additionally, as airspeed approaches zero and the helicopter transitions toward hover, the rotor loses the aerodynamic benefit of forward-speed airflow, and the driving force diminishes because the relative wind angle and efficiency of the driving region change. The aft cyclic input during flare increases the angle of the relative wind temporarily, which can slow the rate of Nr decrease, but it does not prevent the fundamental loss of driving force caused by low airspeed. The pilot must monitor Nr closely during the flare and be prepared to adjust collective slightly to maintain Nr in the green arc as airspeed reduces. When rotor RPM is still within the usable range near the bottom of the flare, the pilot raises collective to cushion the landing and arrest the final rate of descent. This final collective application must be made before Nr decays below a usable threshold for generating adequate lift.

questions.question: During a simulated autorotation practice, your student consistently allows Nr to decay to the bottom of the green arc during the approach phase before the flare. What specific aerodynamic and pilot technique factors could be causing this, and what are the real-world consequences if this pattern occurs in an actual engine failure?
questions.answer: Low Nr during the approach phase of autorotation is most commonly caused by: (1) insufficient initial collective reduction at entry — the pilot did not lower collective enough to fully establish autorotative airflow through the disk; (2) excessive glide airspeed — flying too slow (below best glide speed for that aircraft) reduces the inflow velocity needed to sustain rotor RPM; (3) flying too steep a glide angle without adjusting airspeed, which reduces relative inflow; or (4) delayed recognition and response to decaying Nr. Contributing factors may include distractions, a tendency to 'ride' the collective up slightly during the approach phase without realizing it, or inadequate instrument scan. In a real engine failure, entering the flare or raising collective for the cushion with Nr already at the bottom of the green arc is extremely dangerous — there is minimal stored rotor energy remaining. The collective application for the flare or cushion will rapidly consume that energy, and if Nr decays below the minimum, rotor stall occurs with no recovery option. The helicopter will hit the ground at an uncontrolled rate of descent.
questions.follow_up: If you saw this student's Nr touch the red line at the bottom of the green arc just as they began their flare, would you intervene? At what exact point during an autorotation is it no longer safe to continue to the landing, and what would you do instead?
questions.follow_up_answer: Yes — a trained instructor must intervene if Nr reaches the red line (minimum limit) at the initiation of the flare because there is insufficient rotor energy stored to complete a safe cushioned landing. The decision point to abort a practice autorotation and execute a power recovery is typically defined by the specific aircraft's RFM and the operator's training program, but the general principle is: if at any point Nr decays below the green arc, a power recovery should be initiated immediately. For a real emergency where power is not available, the pilot would need to accept a hard landing or attempt to arrest descent with whatever Nr remains — emphasizing why practicing with adequate Nr margin is essential. In training, the instructor should have already applied throttle to recover before Nr reached the red line, and this incident should trigger a full debrief about why Nr was allowed to decay and how to prevent it on the next attempt.

questions.question: At high density altitude, how does the aerodynamic environment change the way a pilot must manage Nr during an autorotation compared to the same autorotation performed at sea level on a standard day?
questions.answer: At high density altitude, the air is less dense, which has several compounding effects on Nr management during autorotation: (1) Induced velocity is reduced — the rotor must move a greater volume of air to generate the same lift, meaning the rotor disk angle of attack effectively decreases. This reduces the aerodynamic force that sustains rotor RPM, so Nr tends to decay more readily. (2) To maintain the same lift, the pilot may need to fly at a higher indicated airspeed or accept a higher rate of descent, both of which affect Nr maintenance. (3) The flare and cushion are more challenging because less dense air means less aerodynamic braking from the flare and less lift available from a given collective position — the pilot has less margin for error in timing. (4) The collective 'cushion' at the bottom will be less effective, meaning the helicopter will require more Nr and more precise timing to arrest the descent. Overall, at high density altitude the pilot must be especially diligent about maintaining Nr in the upper portion of the green arc throughout the approach to preserve adequate stored rotor energy for the flare and touchdown. Best autorotation airspeed may need to be adjusted per the RFM performance charts for density altitude.
questions.follow_up: If your RFM shows a best autorotation airspeed of 65 knots at sea level standard conditions, and you're conducting a real engine failure autorotation at 8,000 feet density altitude, should you fly faster, slower, or the same airspeed? Why?
questions.follow_up_answer: Some RFMs specify airspeed corrections for density altitude, and the pilot should always refer to those first. In general, at higher density altitude, the indicated airspeed for best autorotative glide may remain similar (since the airspeed indicator reads indicated, not true), but the pilot should be aware that the true airspeed is higher than indicated — meaning the helicopter is actually moving faster through the air and covering more ground distance per altitude lost. This can be an advantage for glide range but requires awareness for the flare. If the RFM does not specify, pilots are typically taught to use the published indicated airspeed since the aerodynamic forces on the rotor depend on indicated airspeed, not true. However, the reduced air density means rotor thrust and braking efficiency during the flare are degraded, so the pilot must be even more precise. The key takeaway is always to consult the aircraft-specific RFM for density altitude autorotation guidance and to practice at the altitudes and conditions relevant to where the helicopter is operated.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B, Chapter 11; Aircraft RFM performance section (model-specific)

questions.question: How does a headwind affect your autorotation glide during a powerplant failure at altitude?
questions.answer: A headwind reduces your groundspeed while maintaining the same airspeed, which decreases the total horizontal distance you can cover over the ground relative to a no-wind condition. However, a headwind increases your time aloft over a given ground reference point, giving you more time to identify and set up a landing zone. A headwind also reduces your groundspeed at touchdown, which is preferable for landing. The key trade-off is that a headwind reduces forward reach but improves your ability to land safely within a closer area. Always consider wind direction when selecting an autorotation landing zone immediately after engine failure, preferring to land into the wind when possible to minimize impact speed.

questions.question: How does gross weight affect rotor RPM decay rate immediately following an engine failure at altitude?
questions.answer: A heavier gross weight increases the aerodynamic load on the rotor system, causing rotor RPM to decay more rapidly after engine failure. Higher weight means greater collective pitch is typically set to maintain flight, and that increased blade pitch creates more drag on the rotor. This makes immediate collective reduction even more critical in a heavy helicopter — you have less time before rotor RPM drops below the minimum safe operating range. Heavier aircraft also require higher descent rates during autorotation to maintain adequate rotor RPM.

questions.question: What effect does high density altitude have on autorotation performance following an engine failure?
questions.answer: High density altitude degrades autorotation performance in two significant ways. First, the thinner air produces less lift per unit of rotor RPM, so the rotor must work harder — meaning the descent rate required to maintain adequate rotor RPM increases. Second, thinner air reduces the effectiveness of the flare at the bottom of the autorotation, providing less aerodynamic braking. The result is a higher groundspeed and vertical velocity at touchdown compared to the same maneuver performed at sea level. Pilots must account for this by ensuring adequate airspeed and planning for longer landing distances.

questions.question: You experience an engine failure at 3,000 feet AGL on a hot summer day at a high-elevation mountain airport. There are two potential landing zones — one is directly into a 15-knot wind upslope, and one is downwind on flat terrain. Walk me through how weight, temperature, and wind would factor into your landing zone decision.
questions.answer: This scenario requires weighing several compounding factors. High temperature raises density altitude, increasing descent rate and reducing flare effectiveness — this argues for the flattest, most open terrain. The upslope zone into the wind offers two advantages: the headwind reduces groundspeed at touchdown, and landing upslope reduces effective groundspeed further. However, the slope itself introduces dynamic rollover risk, especially if the helicopter is heavy. If gross weight is high, rotor RPM will decay faster, so you need to commit to a landing zone quickly and ensure you're at best glide airspeed. The downwind flat terrain may require more total energy management but eliminates slope risk. Generally, flat terrain with even a partial headwind component is preferred when weight and density altitude are already degrading performance margins. The priority is a survivable touchdown — flat, firm, and into the wind as much as possible.

questions.question: Your helicopter's flight manual shows best glide autorotation airspeed as 65 KIAS at maximum gross weight. You are 500 pounds under max gross weight today. How does this affect the airspeed you should target during the autorotation glide, and why?
questions.answer: Always consult your specific Rotorcraft Flight Manual (RFM) for weight-adjusted autorotation airspeed guidance. Many RFMs specify the same best glide airspeed across the weight envelope because the aerodynamic optimum (best lift-to-drag ratio) is achieved at the same indicated airspeed regardless of weight. However, some RFMs do provide weight-adjusted values or tables. Never assume airspeed should be adjusted without explicit RFM guidance. Flying at the published best glide airspeed per your RFM ensures optimal glide distance and maintains adequate rotor RPM throughout the autorotation and flare.

questions.question: You're flying at 8,500 feet MSL on a calm, cold winter day. Your engine fails. Compare the autorotation performance you would expect versus if the same failure occurred on a calm, hot summer day at the same field elevation. Be specific about what changes and what stays the same.
questions.answer: On a cold winter day, the air density is higher than on a hot summer day at the same elevation. Higher air density means: (1) each blade revolution generates more lift, allowing the rotor to sustain adequate RPM at a lower descent rate; (2) the flare is more effective because denser air provides greater aerodynamic braking, reducing touchdown groundspeed and vertical velocity; (3) overall autorotative glide ratio is improved, giving you more horizontal distance. On the hot summer day, density altitude is significantly higher — lower air density means higher required descent rate to maintain rotor RPM, a less effective flare, and reduced glide distance. What stays the same is the geometric relationship between the helicopter and the terrain, the rotor system inertia characteristics, and the pilot's technique requirements. The cold day provides meaningfully better autorotation margins and a more forgiving flare window.

questions.question: A pilot argues that a strong tailwind during an autorotation at altitude is actually beneficial because it increases airspeed over the rotor and helps maintain rotor RPM. How would you correct this misunderstanding, and what is the actual risk of initiating or flying an autorotation with a significant tailwind?
questions.answer: This is a fundamental misunderstanding of the difference between airspeed and groundspeed. Rotor RPM during autorotation is maintained by airflow through the rotor disk driven by the helicopter's descent — not by horizontal wind direction. A tailwind does not increase airflow through the rotor disk in a meaningful way that improves autorotation RPM. The actual risk of a tailwind autorotation is significantly higher groundspeed at touchdown. Even with identical airspeed and vertical velocity, a 20-knot tailwind adds 20 knots of groundspeed to the landing, dramatically increasing the energy that must be dissipated at touchdown and greatly raising the risk of dynamic rollover, structural damage, or loss of control. Additionally, a tailwind reduces your effective glide distance over the ground — the wind is pushing you away from a headwind landing zone. Best practice after engine failure is to immediately assess wind direction and turn toward a headwind or crosswind component for the landing if altitude and distance permit.
questions.follow_up: If a pilot is committed to a tailwind autorotation because there is no time or altitude to turn around, what technique adjustments should be made?
questions.follow_up_answer: When committed to a tailwind autorotation, the pilot should: (1) plan for a significantly higher groundspeed at touchdown and select the longest available landing area; (2) use a lower approach angle if possible to allow more deceleration time; (3) initiate the flare slightly earlier and more aggressively to bleed off as much groundspeed as possible before touchdown, accepting that it may not fully compensate for the tailwind; (4) avoid any lateral drift at touchdown since combined groundspeed and sideward motion greatly increase dynamic rollover risk; (5) be prepared for a running landing or slide rather than a zero-groundspeed touchdown. The pilot should also understand that rotor RPM management remains the same — the tailwind does not change the timing of the flare or collective pull, only the groundspeed consequences.

questions.question: Explain how the compounding effects of high gross weight AND high density altitude simultaneously affect both the entry phase and the flare/touchdown phase of an autorotation following engine failure at altitude. Where is the greatest risk, and what does that demand of the pilot's technique?
questions.answer: At high gross weight and high density altitude simultaneously, the pilot faces compounding degradations at every phase of the autorotation. During entry: the higher blade pitch set for heavy-weight flight creates more rotor drag at the moment of failure, causing faster RPM decay — the pilot has less time to lower collective before RPM drops into the yellow or red arc. This demands an immediate, aggressive collective reduction. During the glide: the thinner air at high density altitude requires a steeper descent angle to sustain rotor RPM, meaning less horizontal glide distance is available — this is further compressed by the higher collective position needed to manage the heavier aircraft's lift requirements. The combination shrinks the autorotation glide envelope significantly. During the flare: this is where the greatest risk materializes. High density altitude reduces aerodynamic braking effectiveness, and high gross weight means more kinetic energy must be dissipated. The rotor has less stored inertia relative to the work demanded of it during the collective pull. The result is a narrow window for the final collective pull — too early and rotor RPM bleeds off before touchdown; too late and vertical velocity is not arrested.
