questions.answer: An ATD LOA contains two primary types of information: (1) the specific pilot-in-command (PIC) time credit allowances—meaning the maximum number of hours and the specific certificate or rating tasks for which the device may be credited toward pilot certification requirements—and (2) the limitations on that credit, such as the certificate level (e.g., private, commercial), aircraft category, and any operational restrictions. The LOA is issued in accordance with FAA Order 8900.1 and specifies exactly how the device may be used for training credit.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR Part 61; FAA ATD LOA policy

questions.question: Who issues the Letter of Authorization for an Aviation Training Device, and what is the significance of that LOA to a flight instructor using the device?
questions.answer: The FAA issues the LOA for an ATD. For a flight instructor, the LOA is significant because it legally defines what training credit the device may provide. An instructor cannot log or award pilot time credit in an ATD beyond what is specifically authorized in that device's LOA — using an unauthorized device or claiming unauthorized credit is a regulatory violation.

questions.question: You are a helicopter instrument student and your training facility just acquired a new Basic ATD. Your instructor tells you it can be used for all of your instrument currency requirements. How would you verify that claim before logging any time?
questions.answer: You should personally review the device's FAA-issued LOA. The LOA will specifically list what pilot time credit is authorized and any limitations. For a Basic ATD (BATD), 14 CFR 61.57(c)(3) allows up to 1 hour of the 6-hour instrument currency requirement per 6 calendar months, but only if the LOA authorizes that specific use. If the LOA doesn't list instrument currency credit or restricts it, the instructor's claim would be incorrect regardless of what the device is capable of performing technically.

questions.question: An ATD your school has used for years just reached the end of its 60-calendar-month LOA period. Can students continue training in it while the facility applies for renewal? What are the consequences if they do?
questions.answer: No. Once the 60-calendar-month LOA expires, the ATD is no longer authorized for pilot time credit. Any training time logged in the device after LOA expiration cannot be credited toward certificate, rating, or currency requirements. The FAA does not have an automatic grace period — the LOA must be renewed before the device is used for credited training. Logging time in an expired-LOA device could constitute falsification of logbook records if used to meet regulatory requirements.

questions.question: Two ATDs at your flight school look identical and are the same make and model. Does each device need its own individual LOA, or does one LOA cover all units of the same model?
questions.answer: Each individual ATD unit must have its own FAA-issued LOA. The LOA is device-specific — it is tied to the individual unit, not the make or model as a class. This is similar to how an aircraft airworthiness certificate is specific to a single aircraft by serial number. Before logging time, pilots and instructors should verify that the specific unit being used has a current, valid LOA on file.

questions.question: A helicopter instrument rating applicant presents a logbook showing 10 hours of ATD time used toward the 40-hour instrument experience requirement under 14 CFR 61.65. During the checkride, you ask to see the LOA for the ATD used. The applicant doesn't have it and says 'the school said it was approved.' How do you handle this as an examiner, and what is the applicant's responsibility?
questions.answer: As the examiner, you should not proceed with the practical test until the LOA can be produced or independently verified. The applicant bears the responsibility of ensuring that all logged training time meets regulatory requirements — 'the school said it was approved' is not a defense under 14 CFR 61.51 and 61.65. If the LOA cannot be verified, the ATD time may not count toward the instrument rating experience requirements, potentially making the applicant ineligible. The applicant should have confirmed the LOA before logging time, and the instructor who signed off the endorsement also shares responsibility for ensuring compliance.
questions.follow_up: If it turns out the ATD's LOA had expired six months ago and the applicant logged all 10 hours during that expired period, what specific regulatory violations may have occurred and who is potentially liable?
questions.follow_up_answer: Multiple violations may apply: (1) The applicant may have falsified logbook entries under 14 CFR 61.59 if they knowingly logged time that couldn't be credited as instrument time; (2) The flight instructor who provided the training and signed off the endorsement may have violated 14 CFR 61.195 by certifying training completed in an unauthorized device; (3) The training facility may have violated 14 CFR 61.4 by using a device without a valid LOA for credited training. The applicant would be ineligible for the rating until valid replacement hours are logged in an authorized device or actual IMC/authorized simulator/FTD time. FAA enforcement action against the instructor and facility is also possible.

questions.question: An ATD manufacturer claims their new helicopter-specific device can be used for up to 20 hours toward the instrument rating and for all IFR currency tasks. However, when you review the FAA-issued LOA for the unit at your school, it only authorizes 10 hours toward the rating and limits currency to 1 hour per 6-month period. Which document controls — the manufacturer's marketing claims or the LOA — and why?
questions.answer: The FAA-issued LOA controls absolutely. Manufacturer claims, brochures, or specifications carry no regulatory weight — only the LOA issued by the FAA for that specific device unit determines what credit is authorized. The FAA evaluates each device individually and may issue LOAs with limitations that are more restrictive than a manufacturer's design intent or marketing claims. Pilots, instructors, and examiners must rely solely on the LOA. Using the device beyond its LOA limitations — even if the manufacturer says it's capable — would mean that the excess time logged cannot legally be credited toward certificate or currency requirements.
questions.follow_up: Could a training facility petition the FAA to expand the LOA limitations on their existing ATD unit to match the manufacturer's claimed capabilities, and what process would that require?
questions.follow_up_answer: Yes, a training facility or the manufacturer can petition the FAA's Flight Standards Service to re-evaluate the device and potentially issue a revised LOA with expanded credit allowances. This typically requires a formal application to the FAA ATD evaluation program, a demonstration of the device's capabilities against FAA qualification standards, and an FAA inspection/evaluation of the unit. The FAA may issue an amended LOA if the device meets the standards for the expanded credit. Until a new LOA is issued, the existing LOA limitations remain in effect regardless of the manufacturer's capabilities documentation.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 61.4; FAA Flight Standards Service ATD qualification process; FAA ATD LOA policy

questions.question: Under 14 CFR Part 61, what is the maximum number of instrument flight training hours logged in an Aviation Training Device (ATD) that a private pilot applicant can apply toward the instrument experience requirement?
questions.answer: Under 14 CFR 61.109(a)(3), a private pilot applicant may log up to 2.5 hours of instrument flight training in an ATD toward the 3-hour instrument training requirement. The remaining time must be accomplished in an aircraft or flight simulator/flight training device.

questions.question: What is the maximum number of ATD training hours a helicopter instrument rating applicant can apply toward the 40-hour instrument experience requirement under 14 CFR Part 61?
questions.answer: Under 14 CFR 61.65(i), an instrument rating applicant may use up to 20 hours of instrument training logged in an ATD toward the required 40 hours of actual or simulated instrument time. An authorized instructor must conduct the ATD training.

questions.question: Does Part 141 place different limits on ATD training time compared to Part 61 for the same certificate or rating, and who must supervise ATD training in either case for it to count toward experience requirements?
questions.answer: Yes. Part 141 approved course curricula specify the maximum ATD hours permitted within each training course, and those limits may differ from Part 61 allowances. In both Part 61 and Part 141, ATD training must be conducted by an authorized instructor (a certificated flight instructor) for the time to be creditable toward experience requirements.

questions.question: You are a helicopter student pursuing your instrument rating under Part 61. Your instructor has been conducting all of your instrument training exclusively in an FAA-approved ATD. You have now logged 22 hours of ATD instrument time. How many of those hours can you legitimately apply toward your 40-hour instrument experience requirement, and what must you do with the remaining required hours?
questions.answer: Under 14 CFR 61.65(i), only 20 of those 22 ATD hours are creditable toward the 40-hour instrument experience requirement. The remaining 20 required hours must be logged in actual instrument meteorological conditions (IMC) or under simulated instrument conditions in an aircraft, flight simulator, or flight training device (FTD). The 2 excess ATD hours beyond the cap simply cannot be applied toward the rating requirements.

questions.question: A helicopter student is training at a Part 141 school for a commercial pilot certificate. The school's approved training course outline (TCO) allows a specific number of ATD hours. If that student later wants to switch to Part 61 training to finish the certificate, how does the ATD hour limit apply, and can they carry over ATD hours already logged?
questions.answer: When transitioning from Part 141 to Part 61 training, ATD hours already logged at the Part 141 school count as completed experience and reduce the remaining requirement. However, the Part 61 ATD hour cap (14 CFR 61.109(a)(3)—up to 10 of 20 required instrument hours for commercial pilot) is the absolute regulatory maximum that may be credited toward the certificate, regardless of the Part 141 TCO allowance. Previously logged ATD hours count against this cap. The student and instructor must verify that total ATD credit—both completed at Part 141 and any additional ATD hours planned under Part 61—does not exceed the Part 61 limit before the certificate can be issued.

questions.question: A helicopter CFI candidate is building the required 15 hours of instrument flight time needed for the flight instructor instrument (CFII) certificate. How much of that 15-hour requirement can be logged in an ATD?
questions.answer: Under 14 CFR 61.187(a), a CFII applicant must meet the instrument experience requirements of 14 CFR 61.65. Per 61.65(i), up to 20 hours of ATD time may be credited toward the total 40-hour instrument experience requirement for an instrument rating. Because the 15-hour CFII instrument requirement is part of the broader 40-hour experience requirement, the 20-hour ATD cap applies. Therefore, all 15 hours could theoretically be logged in an ATD, but doing so would consume 15 of the 20 allowable ATD hours, leaving only 5 ATD hours for any other instrument experience needs. The ATD must be authorized by a current Letter of Authorization (LOA), and the training must be conducted by a certificated flight instructor.

questions.question: A student argues that since the ATD is FAA-approved and the instructor is present for every session, there should be no regulatory cap on how many ATD hours count toward an instrument rating — the training quality is equivalent to a real aircraft. As an examiner, how do you respond, and what is the FAA's policy rationale for imposing these limits?
questions.answer: The FAA imposes ATD hour caps under 14 CFR 61.65(i) deliberately, regardless of the device's approval level or instructor presence. The policy rationale is that ATDs — even the most sophisticated — cannot fully replicate the sensory environment, physiological demands, actual aircraft handling characteristics, and real-world systems management that occur in flight. The regulations ensure that applicants gain a minimum threshold of actual flight experience in an aircraft or higher-level simulator where real-world factors like turbulence, true vestibular cues, and actual weather exposure are present. The 20-hour ATD cap for instrument ratings reflects a balance between leveraging the cost and safety benefits of ATD training while preserving the fidelity requirement that competency be demonstrated in conditions approximating actual flight.
questions.follow_up: If the FAA has already approved the ATD as a legitimate training tool and an instructor certifies the training was conducted properly, why can't those hours satisfy the full aeronautical experience requirement? What specifically in the regulations makes ATD hours a 'subset' rather than a full substitute?
questions.follow_up_answer: 14 CFR 61.65(a) requires a specific number of hours of 'actual or simulated instrument time' — and the regulatory definitions matter. 'Simulated instrument time' in an aircraft (under the hood) and time in an FAA-approved FTD or simulator can satisfy more of the requirement because those devices are qualified at a higher level (FSTD qualification levels) than an ATD. ATDs are qualified under Advisory Circular 61-136 but are not full Flight Simulation Training Devices (FSTDs) under 14 CFR Part 60. The regulations treat ATDs as a supplemental, lower-fidelity category specifically because Part 60 qualification standards for full simulators and FTDs are more rigorous. The hour caps are therefore tied directly to the device qualification level, not the instructor's judgment about training quality.

questions.question: During a checkride, you discover that an instrument rating applicant logged 25 hours in an ATD toward their 40-hour instrument requirement, but their logbook only shows the total ATD hours without separate entries specifying it was ATD time versus aircraft time. What are the logbook documentation requirements for ATD time, and what is the consequence of this recording deficiency?
questions.answer: Under 14 CFR 61.51(b), pilots must log flight time in a manner that allows a determination of the conditions of flight. Specifically, 14 CFR 61.51(g) requires that training time in a flight simulator, FTD, or ATD be logged separately and must indicate the type and approved identification number of the device used, as well as the name of the authorized instructor who conducted the training. If the applicant's logbook does not distinguish ATD hours from aircraft instrument time, the examiner cannot verify whether the 20-hour ATD cap was exceeded. This is a logbook deficiency that must be resolved before the checkride can proceed — the applicant may need to obtain a supplemental statement from their instructor or produce ATD session records to reconstruct accurate entries. An examiner has the authority to discontinue the practical test if required experience cannot be verified.
questions.follow_up: If the ATD hours were properly logged and it's confirmed the applicant used 25 ATD hours, but they still have the required total instrument hours when capping ATD at 20, are they eligible for the checkride? Walk me through the math.
questions.follow_up_answer: Yes, potentially eligible — but only if the remaining instrument experience requirements are met with non-ATD sources. The requirement under 14 CFR 61.65 is 40 hours of instrument time. With the ATD cap at 20 hours, the applicant can credit 20 of the 25 ATD hours. The remaining 20 required instrument hours must come from actual IMC, hood time in an aircraft, or time in a qualified FTD or full flight simulator (not an ATD). If those 20 non-ATD instrument hours are verified in the logbook, the applicant meets the 40-hour requirement. The 5 excess ATD hours simply cannot be applied. So the math: 20 creditable ATD hours + 20 verified aircraft/FTD instrument hours = 40 hours total, which satisfies 61.65(a)(6).

questions.question: What does 'LOA' stand for in the context of Aviation Training Devices, and who issues it?
questions.answer: LOA stands for Letter of Authorization. In the context of ATDs, it is issued by the FAA to the manufacturer of the training device, authorizing that specific device for use in meeting flight training and experience requirements. The LOA confirms the device meets the FAA's qualification standards for its designated level (Basic ATD or Advanced ATD).

questions.question: As an examiner conducting a helicopter instrument checkride, what specific document related to the ATD are you required to request from the applicant when they are using ATD flight training time toward minimum experience requirements?
questions.answer: The examiner is required to request a copy of the manufacturer's Letter of Authorization (LOA) for the ATD used. This document verifies that the specific training device has been authorized by the FAA and is qualified to log training time that may be credited toward the minimum experience requirements for the certificate or rating sought.

questions.question: Why is the manufacturer's LOA for an ATD specifically significant when an applicant wants to credit ATD time toward minimum experience requirements for a rating?
questions.answer: The manufacturer's LOA is the authoritative FAA document confirming that a particular ATD model meets the qualification standards required to log creditable training time under 14 CFR Part 61. Without a valid LOA, the device is not FAA-qualified, and any time logged in it cannot legally be applied toward the minimum aeronautical experience requirements for a certificate or rating. The LOA specifies the device's qualification level (BATD or AATD) and the conditions under which training time may be credited.

questions.question: You are about to conduct a helicopter instrument rating practical test. The applicant presents a logbook showing 10 hours of ATD time credited toward the 40-hour instrument experience requirement. They cannot produce a manufacturer's LOA for the ATD. How do you proceed, and what is the regulatory basis for your decision?
questions.answer: As the examiner, you must request and review the manufacturer's LOA before accepting ATD time as creditable toward minimum experience requirements — this is a direct ACS requirement (HI.XVIII.D.K6). If the applicant cannot produce the LOA, you cannot verify the ATD was FAA-qualified at the time the training was conducted. You should postpone or decline to conduct the practical test until the applicant provides the LOA or otherwise demonstrates the ATD time meets regulatory requirements. Under 14 CFR 61.65(i), a maximum of 20 hours of instrument time may be accomplished in an FAA-approved ATD for the helicopter instrument rating, but only when the device holds a valid LOA. Without the LOA, those hours may not be creditable, and the applicant may not meet the 40-hour minimum required by 14 CFR 61.65(a)(6).

questions.question: An applicant for a helicopter instrument rating used an ATD at a Part 141 flight school. The school's chief flight instructor signed off the ATD time in the applicant's logbook, but the LOA the applicant provides is for a different serial number than the device they actually trained on. Does this ATD time count toward the minimum experience requirements? Explain your reasoning.
questions.answer: No, this ATD time would not be creditable as logged. The FAA's LOA is issued to a specific device identified by make, model, and typically serial number. An LOA for a different serial number does not authorize the device the applicant actually trained on. As the examiner, HI.XVIII.D.K6 requires you to review the manufacturer's LOA and verify it corresponds to the device used. If it does not match, the examiner cannot confirm the training was conducted in an FAA-qualified ATD, and those hours cannot be applied toward the 14 CFR 61.65 minimum experience requirements. The applicant would need to obtain the correct LOA for the actual device used, or those hours may need to be made up in a verified qualified device or actual aircraft.

questions.question: A helicopter instrument applicant presents an LOA for a Basic ATD (BATD). Under 14 CFR 61.65, is there a limit to how many hours of BATD time can be credited toward the instrument rating minimum experience, and does the type of LOA — BATD versus AATD — matter when reviewing the applicant's qualifications?
questions.answer: Yes, the type of LOA matters significantly. Under 14 CFR 61.65(i), for a helicopter instrument rating, a maximum of 10 hours of instrument time in a BATD may be credited toward the required 40 hours of instrument flight time, while an AATD allows up to 20 hours of credit. The examiner reviewing the LOA must confirm not only that the LOA is valid and matches the device used, but also that the applicant has not exceeded the applicable credit limit for the device type. An applicant who logged 15 hours in a BATD can only credit 10 of those hours. The remaining hours must come from an AATD, flight simulator, or actual/simulated instrument conditions in an aircraft.

questions.question: As an examiner, you accept an applicant's manufacturer's LOA for an ATD and proceed with the practical test. After the test, you discover the LOA had actually expired or been revoked by the FAA prior to the test date, but neither you nor the applicant was aware of it. What are the potential implications, and what best practice should examiners follow to prevent this situation?
questions.answer: If the LOA was expired or revoked at the time the ATD training was conducted, then the device was not FAA-qualified during that period and the training hours may not be creditable toward minimum experience requirements — regardless of good faith on the part of the applicant or examiner. This could mean the applicant did not actually meet the minimum aeronautical experience requirements at the time of the test, which could create grounds for the certificate or rating to be invalid or subject to re-examination. Best practice for examiners is to verify the LOA's validity not just by reviewing the document presented, but by cross-referencing the FAA's publicly available list of approved ATDs (maintained on the FAA website) to confirm the device remains currently authorized. Examiners should also check the LOA's issuance date and any expiration provisions. The FAA may update or revoke LOAs, so relying solely on the paper document the applicant provides is insufficient due diligence.
questions.follow_up: If the certificate was issued based on ATD time that later turns out to be non-creditable due to an invalid LOA, what authority does the FAA have to address that situation?
questions.follow_up_answer: Under 14 CFR 61.19(c) and 14 CFR 61.63, the FAA has authority to reexamine any certificate holder if there is reason to believe minimum qualifications were not met. Under 49 U.S.C. 44709 (the 'reexamination' statute), the FAA Administrator may reexamine any civil airman and may suspend or revoke a certificate if the holder does not meet the applicable standards. If it is determined that required hours were not validly logged and the applicant did not actually meet minimum experience requirements, the FAA could initiate certificate action. This underscores why examiner diligence in verifying the manufacturer's LOA — including its current validity — is a critical safety and legal obligation.

questions.question: The ACS specifically requires examiners to request the manufacturer's LOA — not just any documentation. Why is the manufacturer's LOA specifically required rather than, say, a CFI endorsement or school records confirming ATD use? What does the LOA establish that those other documents cannot?
questions.answer: The manufacturer's LOA is the foundational FAA authorization document that establishes the device's qualification status. A CFI endorsement confirms only that training occurred and was satisfactory — it says nothing about whether the device itself was FAA-approved. School records confirm attendance and hours but also cannot substitute for device qualification. The manufacturer's LOA uniquely establishes: (1) the specific make, model, and configuration of the device that met FAA qualification standards under AC 61-136B; (2) the qualification level (BATD or AATD) which directly determines how many hours may be credited under 14 CFR 61.65(i); and (3) the FAA's affirmative authorization of that specific device for use in meeting regulatory training requirements. Without the LOA, no other document can confirm the device met the technical and functional standards required by the FAA at the time of manufacture and qualification. This is why the ACS places the obligation squarely on the examiner to request this specific document — it is the only document that closes the chain of regulatory authorization from FAA to manufacturer to device to applicant's logbook.
questions.follow_up: If a manufacturer updates or modifies an ATD after the LOA was issued, does the original LOA remain valid, or must a new LOA be obtained?
questions.follow_up_answer: Under AC 61-136B, if a manufacturer makes modifications to an ATD that affect its performance, capabilities, or the features for which it was qualified, the manufacturer is responsible for notifying the FAA and may be required to obtain a new or amended LOA. The original LOA is issued based on the device meeting specific qualification criteria at a point in time; material changes to the device that alter its compliance with those criteria could invalidate the original LOA. An examiner who notices discrepancies between the device as described in the LOA and the device as configured at the training facility should flag this issue and may not be able to accept the ATD time until the LOA status is clarified with the FAA. This is another reason examiners should review the LOA carefully and, when possible, verify current qualification status through the FAA's ATD approval database.

questions.question: What does LOA stand for in the context of Aviation Training Devices, and what FAA office issues it?
questions.answer: LOA stands for Letter of Authorization. It is issued by the FAA to approve a specific ATD for training purposes. The LOA identifies the device, its approved uses, and any limitations on how training time logged in that device may be credited toward certificate or rating requirements.

questions.question: Under 14 CFR Part 61, what is the general consequence if a pilot logs ATD flight time toward a certificate or rating requirement using a device whose LOA has expired?
questions.answer: Flight time logged in an ATD with an expired LOA cannot be credited toward any certificate, rating, or recency-of-experience requirement under 14 CFR Part 61. The FAA considers that time invalid for the intended purpose, meaning the pilot would not meet the prerequisite hours and could be found to have falsified training records if they apply for a certificate or rating claiming that time.

questions.question: What two things must you confirm about an ATD's LOA before you can legally credit training time in that device toward an instrument rating experience requirement?
questions.answer: You must confirm that (1) the LOA is current — meaning it has not expired — and (2) the LOA is applicable — meaning it specifically authorizes the type of training being conducted (e.g., instrument training, flight review credit, IPC) and is approved for use toward the specific certificate or rating requirement you intend to satisfy. An LOA for a Basic ATD (BATD) may not authorize the same hours as one issued for an Advanced ATD (AATD).

questions.question: You are a student preparing for your instrument rating and your CFI says you completed 10 hours in a local flight school's ATD. When you check the device, you find the LOA was issued for a fixed-wing AATD but contains no mention of rotorcraft or helicopter training. Can you apply those 10 hours toward your helicopter instrument rating requirements? Why or why not?
questions.answer: No. The LOA must be applicable to the specific training being conducted. If the LOA does not authorize the ATD for helicopter or rotorcraft instrument training, those hours cannot be credited toward a helicopter instrument rating. An ATD LOA specifies aircraft category and class for which the device is approved. Using hours from a device approved only for airplane training to satisfy rotorcraft requirements would not meet the intent of 14 CFR 61.4(c) and AC 61-136B. You would need to find an ATD with an LOA that specifically covers rotorcraft/helicopter instrument training.

questions.question: A flight school's ATD had a valid LOA when you completed 15 hours of instrument training in it six months ago. You are now applying for your instrument rating and discover the LOA expired two months ago. Are your previously logged hours still valid? What should you have done to protect yourself?
questions.answer: Yes — hours logged while the LOA was valid are generally still creditable, because the device was properly authorized at the time the training was conducted. The key risk management principle is to verify the LOA status before each training session, not just before applying for a rating. To protect yourself, you should have: (1) verified the LOA was current before every session, (2) retained copies of the LOA in effect at the time of training, and (3) had your CFI annotate logbook entries with the device's LOA number and expiration date. This documentation protects you if the LOA status is ever questioned.

questions.question: You show up at a training center to complete instrument proficiency hours in their ATD before your checkride. The device is set up and ready to go, but when you ask the instructor for the LOA, they say 'it's somewhere in the office, don't worry about it.' What is the risk management concern here, and what should you do?
questions.answer: The risk is that you may complete training in a device whose LOA has expired, been modified, or does not cover the specific type of training you need — meaning those hours would be invalid and you could show up to your checkride without the required experience. As a pilot in command of your own certificate process, you should refuse to begin training until the actual LOA document is produced, verified to be current, and confirmed as applicable to helicopter instrument training. This is a low-cost, high-value check that protects both your certificate application and your training investment. Accepting 'don't worry about it' is exactly the kind of passive decision-making that leads to the error chain described in ADM principles.

questions.question: A Part 141 helicopter flight school updates their ATD mid-course but retains the same LOA number, claiming the new device is 'equivalent.' A student is halfway through the approved course and has logged hours in both the old and new device. What is the risk, and who bears responsibility for verifying the LOA covers the replacement device?
questions.answer: The risk is significant: an LOA is issued for a specific device, identified by make, model, and serial number. When a school replaces the device — even with an ostensibly equivalent model — the existing LOA does not automatically transfer to the new device. The new device requires its own LOA from the FAA. Hours logged in the replacement device before a new LOA is issued are not creditable. Under Part 141, the school's chief instructor and the Director of Training bear primary responsibility for ensuring all training devices used in approved courses are covered by current, applicable LOAs. However, the student also bears risk management responsibility: they should verify the LOA covers the specific device serial number being used. For a Part 141 program, the training course outline (TCO) must identify approved training devices, and any substitution requires FAA approval.
questions.follow_up: If the student completes the course and discovers at the checkride that the replacement device never had a valid LOA, what recourse — if any — does the student have, and can the Part 141 school be held accountable?
questions.follow_up_answer: The student's immediate problem is that they cannot demonstrate the required aeronautical experience for the rating if those ATD hours are invalid — the checkride cannot proceed until the experience requirements are legitimately met through additional flight or properly authorized ATD time. Longer term, the student may file a complaint with the FAA against the Part 141 school, which could trigger a review or investigation of the school's operations under 14 CFR Part 141. The school's chief instructor may face certificate action for signing off on training conducted in an unauthorized device. However, regardless of the school's culpability, the FAA will not grant the rating based on improperly credited time — the student must still meet all regulatory requirements. This underscores that the burden of verification cannot be delegated entirely to an instructor or school; pilots must independently confirm LOA validity before crediting any ATD time.

questions.question: What document must you provide to an examiner when ATD flight training time has been used to meet minimum experience requirements for an instrument rating?
questions.answer: The pilot must provide evidence of the Letter of Authorization (LOA) for the Aviation Training Device—typically a copy obtained from the flight school or ATD facility. The LOA is issued by the FAA to the ATD manufacturer and confirms that the specific device has been approved for use in meeting training and experience requirements. The flight school normally retains the original LOA on file. Without verification that an unexpired, applicable LOA exists and covers the specific type of training (e.g., helicopter vs. airplane), the ATD time cannot be credited toward the rating.

questions.question: Who issues the Letter of Authorization (LOA) for an Aviation Training Device, and who is it issued to?
questions.answer: The FAA issues the LOA to the ATD manufacturer — not to a flight school or individual instructor. The LOA authorizes that specific make and model of device for use in meeting training requirements under 14 CFR Part 61. The flight school or pilot must obtain a copy of that manufacturer's LOA to document eligibility for credit.

questions.question: What is the maximum number of ATD training hours that can be applied toward the instrument rating aeronautical experience requirements under 14 CFR Part 61?
questions.answer: Under 14 CFR 61.65(i), a pilot may use up to 10 hours of training in an Advanced Aviation Training Device (AATD) toward the 40 hours of instrument time required for the instrument rating. Alternatively, up to 20 hours may be credited if the applicant is training under an approved Part 141 course that specifically allows it. Basic Aviation Training Devices (BATD) are limited to 10 hours under Part 61.

questions.question: You show up to your instrument helicopter checkride and tell the examiner that 8 of your 40 instrument hours were logged in an ATD at your training school. The examiner asks you to prove the device was qualified. You hand over your logbook. Is that sufficient, and what else do you need?
questions.answer: No, the logbook alone is not sufficient. The logbook may show the ATD hours and the instructor's endorsement, but it does not prove the device itself was FAA-authorized. You must also produce a copy of the manufacturer's LOA for that specific ATD. The LOA confirms the device model is approved by the FAA and eligible for training credit under 14 CFR Part 61. Without the LOA, the examiner cannot verify that the credited hours meet regulatory requirements, and the checkride may not proceed.

questions.question: Your flight school uses an ATD for instrument training but the school has misplaced the manufacturer's LOA. You have a checkride scheduled in two days. What are your options to still demonstrate the ATD time is creditable?
questions.answer: You have several options: First, contact the ATD manufacturer directly — they can provide a copy of their LOA since it was issued to them. Second, the LOA is also a matter of public record; FAA's ATD database or the FSDO that oversees the device may have a copy on file. Third, you can contact the FAA Flight Standards District Office (FSDO) for assistance in verifying the device's approval status. You should not proceed to the checkride claiming ATD credit without producing the LOA, as the examiner is required to verify it before accepting the hours.

questions.question: A CFI-I logs 6 hours of instrument instruction for you in a device that the school calls an 'ATD,' but neither of you produces the manufacturer's LOA at your checkride. The examiner determines the device was never FAA-authorized. How does this affect your eligibility to test?
questions.answer: If the device was never FAA-authorized via an LOA, those hours cannot be credited as ATD instrument time under 14 CFR 61.65(i). However, if those hours were flown under actual or simulated instrument conditions with a CFII and were logged appropriately, they may still count as instrument time if they were conducted in an actual aircraft under a hood or in actual IMC. If the device was used on the ground as a simulator substitute with no actual flight, the hours would be disqualified entirely. The examiner would need to determine whether the applicant still meets the minimum experience requirements without those credited hours before the checkride can proceed.

questions.question: You present the manufacturer's LOA for the ATD used during your training, but the examiner notices the LOA lists a specific model number that does not match the serial number placard on the device your school used. What is the significance of this discrepancy, and how should it be resolved?
questions.answer: This is a critical issue. The LOA is issued to a specific make and model of ATD — if the device used for training does not match the model listed on the LOA, the authorization does not apply to that device. FAA ATD authorization is model-specific, not school-specific or general. The hours logged in the non-matching device may not be creditable. Resolution requires contacting the ATD manufacturer to determine whether the device in question is covered under the same LOA (e.g., as a variant or updated model), or obtaining documentation from the FAA confirming coverage. If the discrepancy cannot be resolved, the examiner may not be able to accept those hours, and the applicant may not meet minimum experience requirements.
questions.follow_up: Suppose the manufacturer confirms in writing that the serial number in question is covered under their LOA because it is the same model — just a production unit with a slightly different internal designation. Is that manufacturer's letter alone sufficient for the examiner to accept the hours?
questions.follow_up_answer: The manufacturer's clarification letter provides useful context, but the definitive authority rests with the FAA LOA itself. The examiner should contact the local FSDO or the FAA's ATD approval office to verify whether that serial number is formally covered. A manufacturer's letter is not a regulatory document and does not carry the same legal weight as the FAA-issued LOA. The FSDO can make an official determination, and the examiner should defer to that guidance before accepting the hours. The checkride should be postponed if necessary until the matter is formally resolved.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 61.4(b); FAA Order 8900.2; FAA ATD LOA issuance process

tasks.title: Operational Requirements – VII. Hovering Maneuvers, Task E: Slope Operations

questions.question: When conducting slope operations, whose published limitations govern how the maneuver must be demonstrated?
questions.answer: The helicopter manufacturer's limitations govern slope operations. If the manufacturer has published specific limitations for slope operations — such as maximum allowable slope angle — the pilot must comply with those limitations. The ACS requires that demonstration of parallel slope operations be conducted in accordance with those published limitations.

questions.question: What does it mean when the ACS says manufacturer slope limitations apply 'if published'? What is your responsibility if no slope limitations are published in your Rotorcraft Flight Manual?
questions.answer: The phrase 'if published' means the requirement to follow those specific limitations only applies when the manufacturer has included them in the Rotorcraft Flight Manual (RFM) or Pilot's Operating Handbook (POH). If no slope limitations are published, the pilot must still exercise sound aeronautical judgment and follow general safe operating practices for slope operations as described in the FAA Helicopter Flying Handbook, being aware of dynamic rollover risk and the helicopter's structural limitations.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10; ACS HI.XVIII.E.K1; 14 CFR 27.1 (Normal Category Rotorcraft)

questions.question: In a parallel slope operation, how is the helicopter oriented relative to the slope, and why is this technique used?
questions.answer: In a parallel slope operation, the helicopter is positioned with its longitudinal axis (nose-to-tail) running parallel to the slope — the helicopter is oriented sideways to the slope rather than pointed uphill or downhill. This technique is used because it allows the pilot to touch down one skid at a time laterally, which is generally considered safer than a nose-up or nose-down approach to a slope, and may be required or preferred depending on the helicopter type and the manufacturer's published slope landing procedures.

questions.question: You are flying a Robinson R44 and your student wants to practice slope landings on a hillside that appears to be about 12 degrees. Where in your preflight planning would you find the maximum allowable slope angle, and what action is required before attempting this maneuver?
questions.answer: You must consult the R44 Pilot's Operating Handbook (POH) / Rotorcraft Flight Manual (RFM) to find the manufacturer's published slope limitation. Robinson publishes specific maximum slope angles for their aircraft. Before attempting the maneuver, you must verify the actual slope does not exceed that published limitation. If the slope exceeds the manufacturer's limit, the maneuver must not be attempted regardless of whether you believe the aircraft could physically handle it. The ACS specifically requires that slope operations be conducted within manufacturer-published limitations.

questions.question: During a checkride, an applicant begins a parallel slope landing on a hillside. The examiner knows the helicopter's RFM limits slope operations to 8 degrees, and the slope appears steeper than that. What is the examiner's concern from an ACS standards perspective, and what should the applicant have done before committing to the approach?
questions.answer: The examiner's concern is that the applicant is about to demonstrate slope operations outside the manufacturer's published limitations, which is a direct violation of ACS HI.XVIII.E.K1. This could also constitute operation outside the aircraft's limitations under 14 CFR 91.9. Before committing to the approach, the applicant should have conducted a proper reconnaissance of the landing area, assessed the slope angle, and compared it against the manufacturer's published maximum slope limitation in the RFM. If the slope exceeds the published limit, the applicant must select a different landing site or abort the approach.

questions.question: Why might a helicopter manufacturer publish different maximum slope angles for upslope-skid-first versus downslope-skid-first landing techniques, and how does the parallel slope approach relate to this consideration?
questions.answer: Manufacturers may differentiate slope angles by technique because the dynamic rollover risk differs depending on which skid contacts the slope first. Landing downslope-skid-first on a steep slope creates a greater moment arm and higher rollover risk due to the lateral center of gravity shift. Upslope-skid-first is generally considered safer and may permit a steeper slope angle. The parallel slope technique specifically involves contacting the uphill skid first, which is why manufacturers may publish it as the preferred or required method for steeper terrain. The pilot must know which technique the RFM authorizes and at what maximum slope angle for each technique.

questions.question: A pilot operating an aircraft with no published slope limitations in the RFM argues that since there are no manufacturer restrictions, he can land on any slope he judges to be safe. As an examiner, how do you address this position, and what regulatory and aeronautical principles would you apply?
questions.answer: While the ACS states manufacturer limitations apply 'if published,' the absence of a published limitation does not grant unlimited authority. Under 14 CFR 91.13, the pilot still cannot operate the aircraft in a careless or reckless manner. Structurally, every helicopter has a physical limit to what lateral skid load and fuselage stress it can handle. Dynamic rollover remains a risk on any slope regardless of published limits. The pilot must apply sound aeronautical decision-making, understand the helicopter's design limitations found in the RFM general section, and recognize that the 'no published limit' condition means the manufacturer has not tested or certificated operation beyond certain structural or operational bounds. Best practice is to remain conservative and treat the absence of a published limit as a reason for extra caution, not as blanket permission.
questions.follow_up: If a pilot lands on a slope significantly steeper than any helicopter was designed for and causes structural damage, what regulatory violation might the FAA cite even in the absence of a specific slope limitation in the RFM?
questions.follow_up_answer: The FAA could cite 14 CFR 91.13(a) — careless or reckless operation — and potentially 14 CFR 91.7(a) for operating the aircraft in a condition not within its approved limitations if evidence shows the slope exceeded structural design loads. Additionally, if the aircraft was damaged and the pilot continued to fly it, 14 CFR 91.7(b) requires a pilot in command to discontinue flight when a mechanical, electrical, or structural malfunction occurs.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.7; 14 CFR 91.9; 14 CFR 91.13; ACS HI.XVIII.E.K1; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10

questions.question: During a helicopter instrument instructor checkride, the applicant is asked about slope operations and correctly states the manufacturer's published limit for their aircraft. The examiner then asks: what is the relationship between the manufacturer's slope limitation and the dynamic rollover critical angle, and are they necessarily the same number?
questions.answer: They are not necessarily the same number, and the distinction is important. The dynamic rollover critical angle is the point at which the helicopter's center of gravity passes beyond the pivot point of the grounded skid, making rollover unrecoverable — this is a physical/aerodynamic threshold specific to the rotor system and CG envelope. The manufacturer's published slope limitation is a conservatively derived operational limit that is typically set well below the true dynamic rollover critical angle to provide a safety margin. The published limit also accounts for variables like load configuration, uneven terrain, pilot reaction time, and rotor flap clearance to the ground. A pilot who reaches the published slope limit has not yet reached dynamic rollover, but the margin is intentionally thin. Operating beyond the published limit erodes that margin and brings the pilot closer to the unrecoverable dynamic rollover threshold.
questions.follow_up: If you are on a slope within the manufacturer's published limit but you notice the rotor disc is tilting toward the upslope terrain, what immediate action must you take and why?
questions.follow_up_answer: You must immediately take off — fly the helicopter off the slope before the rotor disc contacts the terrain. Rotor disc clearance from upslope ground is a critical concern on any slope landing, especially with articulated or semi-rigid rotor systems. Even within the published slope limit, terrain irregularities, load shifts, or control inputs can reduce disc-to-ground clearance. The manufacturer's slope limit often incorporates minimum rotor clearance calculations, but visual monitoring of disc clearance is always the pilot's responsibility. Waiting too long risks catastrophic rotor strike, which is not survivable.

questions.question: If the helicopter you are flying has no published slope limitation in the flight manual, what is the generally accepted range of slope angles for demonstrating slope operations?
questions.answer: When no slope limitation is published in the Rotorcraft Flight Manual (RFM), parallel slope operations of approximately 5 to 10 degrees may be demonstrated. This range serves as a practical guideline in the absence of manufacturer-specific data.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 10; ACS HI.XVIII.E.K2

questions.question: Where is the first place you should look to find the maximum allowable slope angle for your helicopter before attempting slope operations?
questions.answer: The pilot must first consult the Rotorcraft Flight Manual (RFM) for the specific helicopter being flown. Manufacturers may publish slope limitations in the Limitations section of the RFM. Only when no slope limitation is published does the general guideline of 5–10 degrees apply.

questions.question: Why do slope limitations vary between different helicopter models when no universal standard applies?
questions.answer: Slope limitations vary because each helicopter design has different rotor system geometry, landing gear width, skid or wheel configuration, and main rotor clearance from the ground. These factors determine the maximum tilt the helicopter can sustain before the rotor system contacts the terrain or the helicopter becomes laterally unstable. The manufacturer determines these limits through testing, and when none are published, the 5–10 degree guideline provides a conservative operational reference.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 10; ACS HI.XVIII.E.K2

questions.question: You are flying a light training helicopter and the RFM is silent on slope operations. A pilot in command asks you whether it is acceptable to land on a 12-degree slope. How do you respond, and what is your reasoning?
questions.answer: A 12-degree slope would exceed the general guideline of 5–10 degrees that applies when no RFM limitation is published. I would advise against it. Without manufacturer data validating safe operations beyond 10 degrees, attempting a 12-degree slope introduces significant risk of dynamic rollover, rotor-to-terrain contact, or an uncontrollable lateral slide. The conservative action is to treat the 5–10 degree range as the operational ceiling in the absence of published limits, and either select a shallower landing area or contact the manufacturer for specific guidance.

questions.question: During a mountain rescue pre-mission briefing, you identify a potential landing zone on a slope estimated at 8 degrees. No slope limitations are published for your helicopter. Describe the key physical hazards you must assess before committing to this landing, specifically related to the slope angle.
questions.answer: At 8 degrees — within the acceptable 5–10 degree range for helicopters with no published limit — the key hazards include: (1) rotor blade clearance from the uphill terrain, which decreases as the rotor disk tilts with the helicopter; (2) dynamic rollover risk if the uphill skid or wheel catches or if cyclic is not properly managed; (3) the tendency of the helicopter to slide downhill if surface friction is inadequate; (4) cyclic travel limits — on steep slopes, full uphill cyclic may be required just to maintain level rotor disk, leaving no margin for wind corrections; and (5) the potential for the tail rotor to strike the slope on tail-low helicopter configurations. Even within acceptable slope range, a thorough reconnaissance is required.

questions.question: You are flying two different helicopters — one has a published slope limitation of 6 degrees, and the other has no published limitation. On which aircraft are you more operationally restricted, and why does the ACS guideline of 5–10 degrees not simply override the published 6-degree limit?
questions.answer: The aircraft with the 6-degree published limitation is more operationally restricted, and that published figure must be respected absolutely. The 5–10 degree ACS guideline is a fallback reference only applicable in the absence of manufacturer data — it does not supersede or modify any limitation the manufacturer has established through certification testing. A published RFM limitation is a legally binding operating limit under 14 CFR 91.9. Exceeding a published limitation, even if within the general 5–10 degree range, would place the pilot in violation of federal regulations and outside the certified envelope of the aircraft.

questions.question: A student pilot argues that the 5–10 degree slope guideline means any slope in that range is automatically safe for any helicopter with no published limitation. Explain the flaw in that reasoning, and describe what additional factors could make an 8-degree slope unsafe even when it falls within the published guideline.
questions.answer: The flaw is treating a general operational guideline as an unconditional safety guarantee. The 5–10 degree range is a conservative starting reference, not a certification boundary. An 8-degree slope can still be operationally unsafe depending on several factors: (1) surface conditions — ice, loose gravel, or wet grass dramatically reduce friction and increase the likelihood of a downhill slide; (2) rotor blade ground clearance — on a helicopter with low blade-to-ground clearance, 8 degrees may bring the uphill blade dangerously close to the terrain even within guideline range; (3) wind direction and velocity — a crosswind from the downhill side on a slope compounds lateral instability and may demand cyclic inputs that exhaust available travel limits; (4) cargo or passenger loading — asymmetric weight distribution can shift the effective tilt threshold significantly; and (5) pilot skill and currency — slope operations require specific training and currency; an inexperienced pilot faces greater risk even at acceptable angles. The guideline identifies a zone where demonstrations may be conducted, but pilot judgment, aircraft-specific characteristics, and environmental conditions always govern the final go/no-go decision.
questions.follow_up: If the helicopter begins to slide downhill on a slope before full skid contact is made, what is the immediate correct technique, and why is hesitation dangerous?
questions.follow_up_answer: If the helicopter begins sliding downhill during a slope landing before full skid contact, the pilot must immediately apply upward collective and fly away from the slope — aborting the landing. Hesitation is dangerous because once lateral momentum builds, dynamic rollover becomes increasingly likely. Dynamic rollover occurs when the pivot point (the downhill skid or wheel) becomes fixed or dragged while the helicopter's center of gravity continues to move laterally, creating a rolling moment that can exceed the corrective authority of the cyclic. At that point, even full opposite cyclic may be insufficient to arrest the roll. Early recognition and immediate go-around is the only reliable recovery option.

questions.question: During a checkride, an applicant successfully demonstrates a slope landing at approximately 7 degrees with no published RFM limitation. The examiner then asks: what is the lateral cyclic limitation concern unique to slope operations, and at what point would that concern alone require you to abort regardless of whether the slope angle appears acceptable?
questions.answer: The lateral cyclic limitation concern is that on a slope, the pilot must apply uphill (into-slope) cyclic to maintain a level rotor disk and prevent the rotor tip-path plane from tilting with the fuselage. As slope angle increases, progressively more uphill cyclic is consumed just to maintain disk attitude — not to maneuver. If the slope requires so much lateral cyclic that the pilot has little or no remaining cyclic authority in the uphill direction, any gust, weight shift, or control input demand from the downhill side cannot be corrected. The point at which the pilot should abort is when cyclic authority is approaching its mechanical or practical limit before all skids are firmly on the ground, or when any additional environmental input — such as a wind shift — would consume the remaining cyclic reserve. Operating at the edge of cyclic travel means the pilot has lost the ability to respond to dynamic rollover, and aborting at that moment is mandatory regardless of slope angle.
questions.follow_up: How does a low-inertia rotor system change the urgency of that cyclic limit concern compared to a high-inertia system during a slope abort?
questions.follow_up_answer: A low-inertia rotor system, typical of lighter training helicopters, has less stored rotational energy and is more sensitive to sudden collective changes and power interruptions. If a slope abort is initiated and collective is rapidly increased to fly away, a low-inertia rotor can experience rapid RPM decay if the power demand exceeds what the engine can deliver instantly. This means the pilot must be especially smooth and deliberate on collective during the abort to avoid compounding the emergency with low rotor RPM. A high-inertia system has more stored energy and tolerates abrupt collective changes better. Therefore, on a low-inertia helicopter, slope abort technique demands even greater precision — the pilot must recognize the need to abort earlier, while there is still sufficient RPM margin and collective range available to execute a clean go-around.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10 and Chapter 11; ACS HI.XVIII.E.K2

questions.question: During a helicopter checkride, which specific slope landing orientations are explicitly excluded from testing by the ACS?
questions.answer: Landings with the helicopter's longitudinal axis aligned uphill or downhill are explicitly excluded from testing during certification (per ACS HI.XVIII.E.K3). The tested maneuver requires the helicopter to be positioned with its longitudinal axis across the slope contour, on a slope typically between 5 and 10 degrees.

questions.question: Why do you think the ACS specifically prohibits testing of uphill and downhill-facing slope landings during certification? What hazard makes these orientations more dangerous than sideward slope approaches?
questions.answer: Uphill and downhill-facing slope landings present a significantly elevated dynamic rollover risk. When the helicopter's longitudinal axis is aligned with the slope, the skid or wheel that touches first acts as a pivot point along the helicopter's roll axis. In this configuration, the pilot has very limited cyclic authority to counteract the rolling tendency before the main rotor blade can strike the terrain. Sideward slope operations, while still demanding, allow the pilot to apply cyclic into the slope and are considered a more manageable training scenario for certification purposes.

questions.question: Just because uphill and downhill slope landings are not tested on a checkride, does that mean a certificated pilot is prohibited from performing them in the real world?
questions.answer: No. The ACS exclusion applies only to what will be tested during the certification checkride — it is not a regulatory prohibition on performing those maneuvers after certification. Certificated pilots may conduct uphill or downhill-facing slope landings operationally, provided they are properly trained, the aircraft performance allows it, and the operation is conducted safely within the aircraft's limitations. Pilots operating in mountainous or confined terrain environments often receive additional training specifically for these orientations.

questions.question: You're flying a utility helicopter job in mountainous terrain and your landing zone requires you to set down with the nose pointed uphill. Your checkride never covered this. How do you approach this operation safely, given you were never tested on it?
questions.answer: The fact that uphill and downhill landings are excluded from checkride testing does not mean they are impossible or always prohibited — it means the applicant was not evaluated on them during certification. Prior to attempting this operation, you should seek specific training from a qualified instructor in the maneuver, thoroughly review your RFM/POH for slope limitations (typically expressed as a maximum allowable slope angle, often 8–12 degrees depending on aircraft), perform a thorough aerial reconnaissance of the LZ, confirm your power margin exceeds OGE hover requirements, brief an abort point, and account for the elevated dynamic rollover risk inherent in nose-uphill orientations. Never attempt an untrained maneuver in an operational environment without prior dual instruction.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10; ACS HI.XVIII.E.K3; RFM/POH slope limitations

questions.question: An examiner asks you to perform a slope landing during your checkride and positions the aircraft so it would require you to land facing downhill. What is the correct response?
questions.answer: The applicant should respectfully inform the examiner that according to ACS HI.XVIII.E.K3, landings with the helicopter facing downhill are explicitly not tested during certification. The applicant should offer to perform a sideward slope landing, which is the appropriate tested maneuver. This is not a refusal — it demonstrates knowledge of the ACS standards and professionalism. An examiner who sets up this scenario may be specifically testing whether the applicant knows this ACS exclusion.

questions.question: During slope operations training with a CFI — not a checkride — your instructor wants you to practice a downhill-facing slope landing on a gentle 5-degree slope. What factors should both you and your instructor evaluate before attempting this maneuver?
questions.answer: Before attempting a downhill-facing slope landing in training, both the CFI and student should evaluate: (1) aircraft slope limitation per the RFM/POH — most helicopters limit slope operations to 8–12 degrees on one side; (2) available power margin — OGE hover capability may be needed; (3) tail rotor clearance from terrain, since in a downhill orientation the tail may be closer to the upslope ground; (4) main rotor blade terrain clearance on the uphill (high) side; (5) dynamic rollover risk — the downhill skid will touch first, creating a pivot axis along the roll direction; (6) wind direction relative to slope — tailwinds downslope increase risk; (7) surface conditions such as loose soil or vegetation that could shift the aircraft; and (8) a clearly defined abort criteria before touchdown. The CFI must confirm the student is prepared and the environment is suitable for this advanced training scenario.

questions.question: The ACS excludes uphill and downhill slope landings from testing. From a standardization and safety standpoint, why might the FAA have drawn the line specifically at these two orientations rather than simply limiting all slope operations to low angles, and what does this tell you about how the FAA approaches risk categorization in certification standards?
questions.answer: The FAA excluded uphill and downhill orientations not because they are always dangerous at any slope angle, but because the risk profile changes qualitatively — not just quantitatively — in those orientations. In a sideward slope landing, the pilot's primary corrective input (cyclic into the slope) directly counters the rollover tendency, and the rotor disk geometry provides meaningful margin before a blade strike. In uphill and downhill orientations, the rollover axis aligns with the helicopter's least favorable cyclic authority plane, and terrain proximity to the main rotor and tail rotor becomes much more difficult to manage simultaneously. The FAA's approach reflects a philosophy of excluding maneuvers where a student error under examiner observation could produce a non-recoverable outcome — dynamic rollover is one of the most catastrophic and rapid failure modes in helicopter operations. This tells us that ACS exclusions are not simply about difficulty; they reflect scenarios where the training environment cannot adequately mitigate the risk to an acceptable level for standardized testing. Operationally, this risk is managed through specific additional training, not prohibition.
questions.follow_up: If dynamic rollover is the core concern, what is the critical angle concept related to dynamic rollover, and how does helicopter design affect it?
questions.follow_up_answer: Dynamic rollover occurs when the helicopter reaches a critical rollover angle — typically around 5 to 8 degrees — at which point the rolling moment exceeds what the pilot can correct with full opposite cyclic. Beyond this angle, rollover is unavoidable. The exact critical angle varies by helicopter design: rotor height above skids, lateral distance between skid contact point and CG, rotor thrust vector geometry, and lateral cyclic authority all influence it. Helicopters with taller mast-to-skid ratios and narrower skid tracks have lower critical rollover angles and are more susceptible. This is why the RFM specifies a maximum allowable slope angle — it provides a margin below the critical rollover angle for that specific airframe.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10 and Chapter 11 (Dynamic Rollover); ACS HI.XVIII.E.K3

questions.question: A newly certificated commercial helicopter pilot tells you: 'Since downhill and uphill slope landings aren't on the checkride, I'll just avoid them forever — I'll never need to know them.' As a CFI, how do you respond, and what practical scenarios might legally require this pilot to understand and potentially perform these maneuvers?
questions.answer: This is a dangerous and operationally unrealistic attitude. The ACS exclusion is a testing limitation — not an operational prohibition or a skills exemption. Numerous real-world operations demand competency in uphill and downhill slope landings: (1) EMS operations where the LZ orientation is dictated by the patient's location or terrain, not pilot preference; (2) utility and external load operations in mountainous terrain where the only available LZ faces upslope or downslope; (3) firefighting and aerial application operations; (4) offshore or backcountry operations. A pilot who has never trained in these orientations and encounters one operationally is actually at greater risk than a pilot who has received formal instruction. The correct professional response is to seek out mountain flying or advanced slope operations training with a qualified CFI, understand the RFM slope limitations for every aircraft flown, and build a realistic mental model of when these maneuvers are and are not safe to attempt. Certification is a minimum standard — not the ceiling of required competency.
questions.follow_up: What FAR obligation, if any, requires a pilot to be trained in a maneuver before attempting it operationally, even if that maneuver was not on the checkride?
questions.follow_up_answer: 14 CFR 61.57 covers recent flight experience requirements, but the most relevant regulatory hook is 14 CFR 91.103, which requires that a pilot become familiar with all available information concerning that flight before beginning — this includes performance limitations and terrain hazards. More directly, 14 CFR 61.31 requires type-specific training for certain operations, and 91.9 prohibits operating beyond aircraft limitations. If a pilot attempts a downhill slope landing without training and exceeds the aircraft's slope limitation or causes an accident, the pilot may face enforcement action under 91.13 (careless or reckless operation). For commercial operations, 14 CFR 135 operators must have operations specifications and training programs that address the specific operations their pilots conduct — which would include advanced slope work if that is part of the operation.
questions.regulatory_ref: ACS HI.XVIII.E.K3; 14 CFR 61.31; 14 CFR 91.9; 14 CFR 91.13; 14 CFR 91.103; 14 CFR Part 135

questions.question: Before conducting slope operations, what is the primary purpose of thoroughly reviewing the intended area?
questions.answer: The primary purpose is to ensure clearance from hazards. The pilot must identify obstacles, terrain features, surface conditions, and any other factors that could interfere with safe landing, maneuvering on the slope, or departure. This reconnaissance is performed before committing to the approach so that abort options are identified and the safest touchdown point is selected.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10, Advanced Flight Maneuvers — Slope Operations

questions.question: Name at least four specific types of hazards a pilot should look for when reviewing a slope operations area.
questions.answer: Hazards to identify include: (1) obstacles such as trees, rocks, stumps, or fencing near the intended landing spot; (2) surface conditions such as loose soil, gravel, snow, ice, or uneven terrain that could cause a skid to slide or sink; (3) slope angle — whether it exceeds the helicopter's lateral or longitudinal cyclic limit; (4) tall grass or brush that can hide rocks or holes and mask rotor clearance; (5) wire hazards or other linear obstacles on or near the slope; and (6) drainage features or erosion channels that could destabilize footing. The goal is to identify anything that could contact rotor blades, destabilize the airframe, or prevent a safe escape.

questions.question: How does a pilot typically conduct a pre-landing reconnaissance of a slope operations area, and at what altitude is it normally performed?
questions.answer: The pilot performs a low-level high reconnaissance (typically at a safe altitude allowing a good view of the entire area, often 300–500 feet AGL) followed by a low reconnaissance (hover or slow flight closer to the surface) to examine surface conditions, slope angle, obstacle proximity, and rotor clearance. The high recon gives the overall picture including escape routes, while the low recon confirms surface details. The pilot should circle the area and observe it from multiple angles, including upslope and downslope perspectives, before committing to the approach.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10, Reconnaissance Procedures and Slope Operations

questions.question: You are asked to land on a grassy hillside to drop off a passenger. During your area review, you notice the grass is about knee-high and the slope appears gentle. What specific hazards might you be unable to fully assess from the air, and how should that affect your decision-making?
questions.answer: Tall or dense grass can conceal rocks, stumps, holes, drainage ditches, fencing wire, or soft saturated ground beneath the surface — none of which are visible from altitude. Additionally, rotor downwash may flatten the grass during hover, making it impossible to judge surface texture or slope angle accurately until you are very close. The pilot should account for these unknowns by planning a hover-taxi over the area if possible to assess the surface with rotor wash before committing full weight to the skids, and by maintaining an abort plan. If hazards cannot be confirmed clear, the safest option is to select an alternate landing site. The rule is: when in doubt, don't land.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10, Slope Operations and Confined Area Operations

questions.question: During your slope area reconnaissance, you identify a suitable touchdown point but notice scattered trees 20 feet upslope from the landing spot. Why is upslope obstacle clearance particularly critical during slope operations, and what rotor component is most at risk?
questions.answer: During slope landings, the uphill side of the helicopter is lower relative to the rotor disk because the skids are on an incline. As a result, the rotor disk tilts toward the upslope terrain. The uphill rotor blade has reduced clearance from obstacles and the slope itself compared to level-ground operations. This makes upslope trees, rocks, or terrain especially dangerous because a blade strike can occur even when ground contact appears safe. The main rotor blade tips are the component most at risk. The pilot must ensure there is sufficient clearance between the upslope rotor arc and any obstacle, accounting for blade flex under load and any rotor flap that may occur during the transition from hover to ground contact.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10, Slope Operations — Rotor Clearance

questions.question: You complete your reconnaissance and determine the slope angle looks acceptable, but you have no slope angle indicator or inclinometer onboard. What in-flight technique can you use to estimate whether the slope is within your helicopter's limits before touching down?
questions.answer: The pilot can use a low hover over the intended landing spot and observe how much lateral or longitudinal cyclic input is required to hold a position directly over the slope while in a wings-level hover attitude. If the cyclic is displaced significantly toward the uphill side just to maintain position over flat ground, it indicates the slope may be steep. Additionally, the pilot can visually reference the rotor mast or skid attitude during a slow hover-taxi along the slope to assess angle. Most importantly, before landing, the pilot should consult the RFM/POH for the specific aircraft's maximum allowable slope angle (typically 8–10 degrees for most helicopters) and compare it to their best visual estimate. If there is any doubt that the slope exceeds limits, a different site should be selected.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10, Slope Operations; Aircraft RFM/POH slope limitations

questions.question: A pilot conducts a thorough reconnaissance of a slope site and identifies no obvious hazards. They land successfully, shut down, and return the next morning to depart. Why might the hazard review need to be repeated before the departure, even though the same site was used the night before?
questions.answer: Conditions at a slope site can change significantly overnight or over any period of time. Overnight precipitation can saturate the soil, making it soft or creating mud that allows skids to sink or slide. Frost or dew can make the surface slippery. Wildlife (deer, bears, livestock) may have moved through the area, leaving the ground disturbed or introducing new obstacles. Wind can deposit debris. Shadows, different sun angles, or reduced visibility at dawn may reveal or conceal hazards not visible the day before. Additionally, the helicopter's own weight may have caused the skids to settle, changing the departure attitude. The pilot must treat each departure from a slope as a new operation requiring a fresh hazard assessment — the fact that a site was safe yesterday does not guarantee it is safe today.
questions.follow_up: If during your pre-departure check you discover one skid has sunk two inches into saturated soil overnight, how does that change your departure procedure and what specific hazard does it introduce?
questions.follow_up_answer: A sunken skid means the helicopter is no longer resting on a predictable surface and the airframe may be tilted at an unexpected angle. The primary hazard is dynamic rollover — as collective is applied to lift off, the sunken skid may act as a pivot point. If the helicopter begins to roll toward the sunken side before becoming fully airborne, and the pilot applies corrective cyclic too aggressively or too late, the rotor can contact the ground on the low side. The correct procedure is to apply collective very slowly and smoothly, monitoring for any lateral roll tendency. At the first sign of uncommanded roll toward the sunken skid, the pilot must immediately reduce collective rather than applying opposite cyclic, because once dynamic rollover exceeds 8–12 degrees, cyclic alone cannot stop it. The pilot may also need to re-evaluate whether a vertical lift straight up is required rather than a running or sliding departure.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10, Slope Operations; Chapter 11, Dynamic Rollover

questions.question: During your slope area reconnaissance, everything looks good — slope angle is acceptable, surface appears firm, and rotor clearance is adequate. However, the wind is calm and you notice the slope faces directly into the afternoon sun, creating a uniform appearance with no distinct shadows. What visual illusion hazard is present, and how does it threaten your hazard clearance assessment?
questions.answer: Flat, uniform lighting from a low sun angle shining directly onto a slope can create a phenomenon where surface texture, rocks, depressions, and elevation changes are washed out — all features appear as a smooth, featureless surface. This effect is similar to the depth-cue loss in whiteout conditions but occurs in any uniformly lit terrain and is more accurately called 'flat light' or 'loss of shadow contrast.' Shadows are what give the human eye the depth cues needed to distinguish terrain features. Without shadows, a rock, a stump, or a depression can be completely invisible from the air. The pilot may incorrectly assess the surface as clear when significant obstacles are present. The mitigation strategy is to delay the approach until sun angle changes to produce shadow relief, approach from a different direction that creates better contrast, or conduct a thorough low hover with rotor wash to disturb the surface and reveal hidden objects before committing full weight. If none of these options are feasible, an alternate landing site must be selected.
questions.follow_up: You decide to use rotor wash to reveal the surface before landing. As you hover low over the intended touchdown spot to blow away debris and assess what's underneath, what operational hazard do you need to manage during that process?
questions.follow_up_answer: When hovering low over a slope to use rotor wash for surface assessment, the pilot must actively manage brownout or debris ingestion.
