questions.answer: The three critical immediate control inputs at autorotation entry from cruise airspeed are: (1) lower collective to reduce pitch angle on the rotor blades, decreasing drag and allowing upward airflow through the rotor disk; (2) apply aft cyclic to slow the aircraft and increase airflow up through the rotor disk, which helps maintain or recover rotor RPM; and (3) apply appropriate pedal input to maintain trim. Together these inputs allow the rotor to enter autorotative flight with RPM in the normal operating range. Low-inertia rotor systems decay rapidly, so these inputs must be immediate.

questions.question: You are at 600 feet AGL in a training area when your engine fails unexpectedly. The wind is reported at 25 knots gusting to 35 knots. Even though you are above the 500-foot AGL minimum, what additional risk management considerations apply given the strong wind condition, and how does this affect your decision-making?
questions.answer: With winds at 25 gusting 35 knots, 600 feet AGL may not provide adequate margin above the effectively higher minimum required for strong wind conditions. Key considerations include: (1) Turbulence near the surface could cause rotor RPM fluctuations and control difficulty; (2) Wind gradient (wind decreasing near the surface) may affect the flare timing and effectiveness; (3) Groundspeed on final approach will be very low in a headwind or dangerously high in a tailwind, changing the energy management picture significantly; (4) Landing zone selection is limited at 600 feet with a turbulent environment. The pilot should immediately establish best autorotative airspeed, select the most favorable landing area aligned into the wind, and recognize that margins are thin — precise technique is critical and a power recovery may be the safer outcome if altitude permits.

questions.question: A student wants to practice straight-in autorotations at your home airport. The runway is into the wind, the wind is calm, and the traffic pattern altitude is 700 feet AGL. The student suggests entering from traffic pattern altitude directly to the runway. What risk management discussion would you have about entry altitude and setup before allowing this practice?
questions.answer: While 700 feet AGL exceeds the 500-foot minimum in calm winds, the instructor should discuss: (1) Pattern altitude entry gives limited time to stabilize rotor RPM and establish the proper glide before the flare zone — many instructors prefer 800–1000 feet AGL for training to allow more coaching time; (2) The entry point must be far enough out that the approach angle is manageable — too close at 700 feet creates a very steep approach; (3) Rotor RPM must be verified in the normal operating range promptly at entry — with low-inertia rotors, delay is not tolerable; (4) A power recovery plan should be briefed and both pilot and instructor must agree on the go/no-go decision altitude; (5) Obstacle clearance on the approach path must be confirmed. The 500-foot minimum is the floor, not the recommended training altitude.

questions.question: During a checkride, you are flying at 800 feet AGL and the examiner calls for a simulated engine failure. You notice the wind is strong from the left and you are currently flying parallel to a ridge that creates mechanical turbulence. How does this environmental picture change your assessment of whether 800 feet AGL is truly sufficient for a safe straight-in autorotation entry?
questions.answer: Although 800 feet AGL exceeds the 500-foot minimum, the combined hazards of strong wind and mechanical turbulence from the ridge substantially increase risk. Mechanical turbulence can cause sudden rotor RPM fluctuations, unpredictable aircraft yaw, and loss of visual reference to the landing area. The wind component parallel to the ridge suggests possible rotor wash or standing waves that complicate the descent profile. The ACS standard explicitly states higher minimums apply in strong wind conditions, and turbulence is a direct product of those conditions here. The appropriate risk management action is to communicate the concern to the examiner, maneuver away from the ridge before executing the autorotation, and increase entry altitude to provide additional decision-making time. Proceeding at 800 feet in these conditions may not meet the spirit of the ACS requirement.

questions.question: The 500-foot AGL minimum is described as a floor, not a standard. Walk me through how rotor system inertia — specifically the difference between a low-inertia and high-inertia rotor — affects the practical minimum safe entry altitude for a straight-in autorotation, and how should this influence your pre-flight risk assessment?
questions.answer: Rotor inertia is determined by the mass and distribution of the rotor blades. High-inertia rotor systems (heavier blades, mass farther from the hub) store more kinetic energy and decay more slowly when collective is lowered at entry — this gives the pilot more time to establish autorotative flight before RPM drops to a dangerous level. Low-inertia rotor systems (lighter composite blades, mass closer to the hub) decay very rapidly after engine failure, sometimes in only 1–2 seconds if collective is not immediately lowered. For a low-inertia helicopter, the 500-foot minimum may provide only marginal safety margin because the pilot must react immediately, and any delay — even 1 second — can result in rotor RPM entering the caution or danger range before a stabilized autorotation is established. Pre-flight risk assessment should include review of the specific aircraft's POH for rotor RPM decay characteristics, minimum entry altitudes recommended by the manufacturer, and honest self-assessment of reaction time. In strong winds or high density altitude, low-inertia helicopters demand even greater entry altitude buffers.
questions.follow_up: If you are flying a low-inertia helicopter at high density altitude and your rotor RPM decays below the minimum before you can recover in autorotation, what happens and is there any recovery?
questions.follow_up_answer: If rotor RPM decays below the minimum autorotative RPM range at low altitude in a low-inertia system, the rotor blades will stall. Unlike fixed-wing aircraft where a stall can be recovered with nose-down pitch and acceleration, a rotor stall in a helicopter is catastrophic and non-recoverable. The FAA Helicopter Flying Handbook states explicitly that 'rotor stalls in helicopters are not recoverable; early recognition of low RPM condition is imperative.' With insufficient altitude and insufficient rotor energy remaining, the helicopter will lose all lift and control authority. This is why the 500-foot minimum is a floor for ideal conditions only, and why immediate collective reduction at engine failure is the most critical single action in helicopter emergency procedures.

questions.question: You are the pilot-in-command conducting a Part 91 training flight. Your student is about to practice straight-in autorotations. The ATIS reports winds 18 knots gusting 28 knots. You both agree to use 700 feet AGL as the entry altitude. After three uneventful runs, the student asks: 'We've been doing fine at 700 feet — can we drop to 500 since the winds haven't caused any problems?' How do you respond, and what does this scenario reveal about the risk management principle of normalizing deviation?
questions.answer: The request must be denied, and the reasoning is important: just because three runs were completed without incident does not mean 700 feet is barely adequate — it means the margin has been working. Reducing to 500 feet in 18G28-knot conditions directly contradicts the ACS standard, which requires a higher minimum than 500 feet in strong wind conditions. The greater concern this scenario reveals is normalization of deviation — a human factors trap where repeated exposure to a risky condition without negative consequences creates a false sense that the risk no longer exists. The Helicopter Flying Handbook and ADM principles teach that the error chain is often built from exactly this kind of accumulated complacency. The pilot's job is to recognize that 'nothing bad happened' is not the same as 'the risk was acceptable.' The appropriate response is to explain that the 500-foot minimum applies in calm or light wind conditions, that the current wind exceeds those conditions, and that the standard requires higher entry altitude — not lower — in today's environment. As PIC under 14 CFR 91.3, you are responsible for the safe conduct of the flight and this decision is not negotiable.
questions.follow_up: What specific FAA ADM concept describes the mental trap the student has fallen into, and what tool or technique can a pilot use in-flight to counter it before it leads to an accident?
questions.follow_up_answer: The student has fallen into the 'invulnerability' hazardous attitude combined with the human factors concept of normalization of deviation — also described in ADM literature as 'it hasn't hurt me yet so it won't.' The FAA's ADM framework identifies five hazardous attitudes: anti-authority, impulsivity, invulnerability, macho, and resignation. Invulnerability is the belief that accidents happen to others, not to you. The antidote is: 'It can happen to me.' The broader concept of error chain management teaches that breaking even one link changes the outcome — in this case, declining to reduce the entry altitude breaks the chain before it progresses. The Trescott Tip from the FAA Helicopter Flying Handbook is also directly applicable: if an action will only 'probably' work out, choose an option known to work. Staying at or above the wind-adjusted minimum entry altitude is the option known to work.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11 and Chapter 13; 14 CFR 91.3; ACS HI.XVIII.F.R1

questions.question: During a straight-in autorotation on a checkride, what does the ACS standard mean when it says 'do not sacrifice safety of flight to force a landing'?
questions.answer: It means that if the autorotation is not proceeding safely — whether due to poor glide angle, improper RPM, bad landing surface, or any other factor — the pilot must execute a power recovery rather than press on to touchdown. Completing the maneuver is never worth accepting an unsafe outcome. A go-around or power recovery is always the correct decision when safety is in question.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; Helicopter Instrument ACS HI.XVIII.F.R2

questions.question: At what point during a straight-in autorotation is it still acceptable to initiate a power recovery instead of completing the landing?
questions.answer: A power recovery can be initiated at any point in the autorotation prior to a point where recovery is no longer possible — generally any time the engine is available, rotor RPM is within limits, and sufficient altitude remains to safely arrest descent. There is no point in the maneuver where completing the landing takes priority over safety. The pilot should not delay recovery hoping conditions will improve.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; Helicopter Instrument ACS HI.XVIII.F.R2

questions.question: Name at least three conditions during a straight-in autorotation that should prompt a pilot to execute a power recovery rather than continuing to touchdown.
questions.answer: Conditions warranting a power recovery include: (1) rotor RPM outside normal operating range; (2) excessive sink rate that cannot be arrested before touchdown; (3) landing area obstructed, too short, or has changed since commitment; (4) airspeed too high or too low for a safe flare; (5) loss of situational awareness in IMC; (6) improper glide path that puts the aircraft short of the landing zone. Any single unsafe condition is sufficient justification.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; Helicopter Instrument ACS HI.XVIII.F.R2

questions.question: You're on final during a straight-in autorotation checkride task. You notice your rotor RPM is at the low end of the green arc and the landing zone is closer than expected. You think you can probably make it work. How should the ACS standard for this task influence your next action?
questions.answer: The ACS standard — do not sacrifice safety of flight to force a landing — directly addresses this situation. The word 'probably' is a red flag in aeronautical decision-making. If there is any doubt that RPM is sufficient for a safe flare and touchdown, a power recovery must be initiated immediately. Pressing on when conditions are marginal to avoid a go-around on a checkride is exactly the type of judgment error this risk management standard is designed to prevent. Declare the power recovery and explain your reasoning to the examiner.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11 and Chapter 13; Helicopter Instrument ACS HI.XVIII.F.R2

questions.question: How does checkride-induced pressure — the desire not to fail a task — represent a specific human factors threat during a straight-in autorotation, and what strategy mitigates it?
questions.answer: Checkride pressure creates a 'press-on' bias where a pilot may accept increasing risk to complete a maneuver rather than admit the approach has gone unsatisfactorily. This reflects the hazardous attitude of invulnerability or machismo. Per 14 CFR 91.3, the pilot-in-command retains final authority and responsibility for safe flight regardless of external pressure. The mitigation strategy is to pre-brief personal abort criteria before the maneuver begins, treat the examiner as a crew member, and recognize that a demonstrated power recovery with sound aeronautical decision-making and reasoning shows superior judgment to a forced, unsafe touchdown.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13; Helicopter Instrument ACS HI.XVIII.F.R2

questions.question: You are conducting a straight-in autorotation in IMC conditions as part of an instrument helicopter checkride. At 200 feet AGL, you break out of the ceiling and see the touchdown zone is covered in standing water of unknown depth. Walk me through your risk management decision-making at that moment.
questions.answer: At 200 feet AGL with engine available, a power recovery is still executable. The risk factors are: unknown surface hazard (standing water could mean soft ground, debris, or dynamic rollover risk), combined with the surprise of a late visual acquisition. Per HI.XVIII.F.R2, safety of flight is never sacrificed to complete the task. The correct action is immediate power recovery — announce the decision, apply collective to arrest descent, restore climb attitude, and advise the examiner. The degraded landing area is sufficient justification. This also demonstrates positive SRM and sound judgment, which the examiner is evaluating.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11 and Chapter 13; Helicopter Instrument ACS HI.XVIII.F.R2

questions.question: A pilot executes a straight-in autorotation on a checkride, recognizes at 150 feet that the approach is unstabilized, but decides to continue because the examiner said nothing and the pilot assumes silence means approval. How does this scenario represent a systemic risk management failure, and what does the ACS standard require instead?
questions.answer: This scenario illustrates multiple compounding failures: (1) authority gradient — deferring safety judgment to the examiner rather than acting as pilot-in-command; (2) misuse of expectation bias — interpreting examiner silence as tacit approval; (3) violation of HI.XVIII.F.R2, which places responsibility for safety of flight entirely on the pilot, not the examiner. The ACS standard requires the pilot to make independent, proactive safety decisions. The examiner's silence is not an authorization to continue an unsafe approach. The pilot must self-declare the abort criteria, execute the power recovery, and verbalize the reasoning. Passing a checkride task never supersedes PIC authority and responsibility under 14 CFR 91.3.
questions.follow_up: If the examiner had verbally encouraged the pilot to 'just go ahead and land' during an obviously unsafe autorotation, and the pilot complied, who is responsible for the outcome — and what should the pilot have done instead?
questions.follow_up_answer: Under 14 CFR 91.3, the pilot-in-command is directly responsible for and is the final authority as to the operation of the aircraft. Examiner encouragement does not transfer PIC responsibility. The pilot should have rejected the examiner's suggestion, executed the power recovery, and verbalized: 'I'm initiating a power recovery — this approach is not safe to complete.' Compliance with an unsafe instruction — even from an FAA examiner — does not relieve the pilot of responsibility. This is a foundational tenet of SRM and crew resource management: the most junior person in the aircraft has both the authority and the obligation to reject an unsafe action.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.3; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13; Helicopter Instrument ACS HI.XVIII.F.R2

questions.question: Low-inertia rotor systems decay RPM rapidly during autorotation entry. How does rotor system type specifically affect the risk window referenced by HI.XVIII.F.R2 — 'do not sacrifice safety to force a landing' — and at what point does a low-inertia system narrow the pilot's decision margin to the point where a power recovery may no longer be feasible?
questions.answer: Low-inertia rotor systems (common in lighter, piston-powered helicopters) store less kinetic energy in the rotor disk. During an autorotation, if RPM decays into or below the lower limit of the green arc, the pilot has a critically short time window to apply collective and arrest descent before blade stall becomes unrecoverable. The Helicopter Flying Handbook states rotor stalls in helicopters are not recoverable — making early recognition imperative. In practical terms, for a low-inertia system, the 'safe' abort window may close well above 200 feet AGL if RPM has been allowed to decay. A pilot who delays the power recovery decision — perhaps due to checkride pressure — may find that by the time they act, insufficient RPM remains to cushion the landing. The risk management implication is that abort criteria must be applied earlier and more aggressively for low-inertia systems than for high-inertia systems.
questions.follow_up: If a pilot flying a low-inertia rotor helicopter reaches the flare altitude during a straight-in autorotation with RPM at the bottom of the green arc, is a power recovery still the right call, or has the decision point passed?
questions.follow_up_answer: At flare altitude with RPM at the bottom of the green arc, the pilot is at the margin of a survivable autorotation. A power recovery attempt at this point may actually be more dangerous than committing to the autorotation because applying throttle rapidly or incorrectly could cause a transient RPM fluctuation or tail rotor yaw anomaly at low altitude. The correct technique depends on aircraft-specific emergency procedures in the RFM/POH. However, the broader lesson is that this situation should never occur — RPM excursions that threaten recovery should have triggered an abort decision much earlier in the approach. HI.XVIII.F.R2 is most meaningfully applied at mid-approach where the decision window is still wide open, not at flare altitude where options are severely constrained.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; Helicopter Instrument ACS HI.XVIII.F.R2; Aircraft RFM/POH (aircraft-specific)

questions.question: What is the minimum altitude AGL at which you must initiate a straight-in autorotation during a checkride?
questions.answer: The ACS requires autorotation to be initiated at no less than 500 feet AGL. However, this minimum may need to be higher depending on wind conditions — stronger or gusty winds may require initiating at a greater altitude to ensure adequate time and distance to complete the maneuver safely.

questions.question: When simulating an engine failure entry into autorotation from cruise flight, what are the three primary immediate control inputs and in what order should they be applied?
questions.answer: The three primary control inputs are: (1) Lower the collective immediately to reduce pitch and allow upward airflow through the rotor disk to maintain rotor RPM, (2) Apply aft cyclic to increase pitch attitude and slow airspeed, which increases descent rate and sustains upward airflow through the disk, and (3) Apply pedal input to maintain directional trim and control—the specific direction (left or right) depends entirely on the aircraft's rotor rotation direction and design and must be determined from the aircraft POH/RFM. These inputs must be nearly simultaneous, with collective being the most time-critical.

questions.question: During a straight-in autorotation, what maintains heading control and antitorque while the engine is not producing power?
questions.answer: During autorotation, the tail rotor continues to be driven by the main rotor transmission, which is still spinning via the freewheeling unit. Because the tail rotor remains powered, the pilot maintains heading control using the antitorque pedals in the same manner as normal flight. The amount of pedal input required will change as rotor RPM and collective position change throughout the autorotation.

questions.question: You are flying at 600 feet AGL and 80 knots into a 25-knot headwind when the engine fails. Walk me through your decision-making process for initiating and configuring the straight-in autorotation, and explain how the headwind specifically affects your approach.
questions.answer: At 600 feet AGL — just above the 500-foot minimum — with a 25-knot headwind, I would immediately lower collective, apply aft cyclic, and trim with pedals to enter autorotation. The headwind is actually favorable: it increases the effective translational lift, reduces groundspeed (improving the glide angle relative to the ground), and lowers the approach angle, giving more time and a longer ground track to reach the landing zone. I would maintain best glide airspeed per the RFM (commonly around 60–70 KIAS depending on the aircraft), set up a stabilized approach angle aiming for a clear landing area, and monitor rotor RPM throughout. The strong headwind may allow a steeper power-off approach profile if needed. Despite the favorable wind, 600 feet AGL is close to the minimum so I must prioritize a timely, committed entry with no hesitation.

questions.question: You are on final approach in autorotation at 200 feet AGL and notice your rotor RPM is bleeding toward the low end of the green arc. What specific control action corrects this and why does it work aerodynamically?
questions.answer: To recover low rotor RPM in autorotation, reduce collective pitch if any has been added, and if cyclic has been brought aft enough to slow the airspeed excessively, apply a slight forward cyclic input to increase airspeed — this increases the relative airflow up through the rotor disk, which in turn increases the driving region of the blade and accelerates rotor RPM. Additionally, a slightly steeper descent angle increases inflow velocity through the disk. At 200 feet AGL this is time-critical; rotor stall in helicopters is not recoverable, so early recognition and prompt correction is imperative. The FAA explicitly states that rotor stalls are unrecoverable, making any delay dangerous.

questions.question: During your straight-in autorotation practice, you initiate the maneuver at exactly 500 feet AGL but then realize there is a 30-knot direct tailwind. What are the handling consequences, and how does the ACS standard address this situation?
questions.answer: A 30-knot tailwind significantly degrades the autorotation profile: groundspeed is much higher, the glide angle is shallower relative to the ground (covers more ground distance), and the relative wind through the rotor is reduced at a given airspeed, slightly reducing rotor efficiency. Flare effectiveness is also reduced because groundspeed is higher. Most critically, the ACS standard states that autorotation must be initiated at 500 feet AGL OR HIGHER as required by wind conditions — meaning a 30-knot tailwind likely requires initiating the maneuver at a greater altitude than 500 feet to allow adequate distance and time to manage the approach. Initiating at exactly 500 feet with a strong tailwind may not provide sufficient margin for a safe touchdown, and this would be a judgment deficiency on the checkride.

questions.question: A low-inertia rotor system helicopter loses engine power at 550 feet AGL during cruise at 90 knots. How does rotor inertia fundamentally change the urgency and technique of your entry inputs compared to a high-inertia system, and what happens if you are even one second slow on the collective?
questions.answer: Low-inertia rotor systems — typically found on lighter, smaller helicopters — have significantly less stored kinetic energy in the spinning rotor blades. When the engine fails, rotor RPM decays much faster than in a high-inertia system. A one-second delay in lowering the collective can result in the rotor RPM dropping below the recoverable range, potentially leading to an unrecoverable low-RPM or rotor stall condition. The FAA Helicopter Flying Handbook specifically identifies this as a critical distinction: low-inertia rotors decay rapidly, making the immediate collective reduction the most time-critical action in the entire autorotation sequence. In contrast, a high-inertia system (such as those found on medium or heavy helicopters) provides a slightly longer window — perhaps 2–3 seconds — before RPM becomes critically low. Technique does not fundamentally differ, but timing tolerance is drastically reduced in low-inertia systems. At 550 feet AGL, this margin is already thin regardless of rotor type.
questions.follow_up: If the rotor RPM has already decayed below the power-off minimum during the delay, is there any recovery action available, and what does the FAA say about rotor stall?
questions.follow_up_answer: No — the FAA Helicopter Flying Handbook explicitly states that rotor stalls in helicopters are not recoverable. Unlike a fixed-wing aircraft where a stall recovery is standardized and achievable, a fully stalled helicopter rotor system cannot be re-energized through control inputs alone once RPM has decayed below the minimum. The rotor blades lose the ability to generate lift, and the helicopter will descend uncontrollably. This is why the handbook emphasizes early recognition of low RPM as imperative, and why any delay in collective reduction during autorotation entry in a low-inertia helicopter is potentially fatal.

questions.question: During a straight-in autorotation, at what point in the maneuver is it no longer possible to execute a go-around?
questions.answer: Once the collective is raised to cushion the landing and rotor RPM begins to decay below a recoverable level, a go-around is no longer possible. The practical point of no return is typically when the aircraft is very low (below 10-20 feet AGL at low airspeed) and engine power cannot be restored quickly enough to arrest the descent before ground contact. In a powered go-around, the pilot must have sufficient altitude, airspeed, and rotor RPM to transition back to powered flight before committing to the landing.

questions.question: What are the primary flight control inputs required to execute a go-around from a straight-in autorotation at 200 feet AGL with adequate airspeed?
questions.answer: To execute a go-around from an autorotation, the pilot simultaneously applies throttle to restore engine power to the operating range, smoothly increases collective pitch to arrest the descent while managing rotor RPM, applies appropriate right pedal to counteract the increased torque, and adjusts cyclic to establish a climb attitude. The collective must be raised smoothly — too abrupt an increase will overpitch the blades and cause a rapid RPM decay. Once engine power is confirmed and a positive rate of climb is established, the pilot transitions to normal climb configuration.

questions.question: Name three examples of landing area safety concerns that could require a go-around during a straight-in autorotation.
questions.answer: Examples of landing area safety concerns requiring a go-around include: (1) a vehicle, animal, or person entering the landing zone that was not present during the initial setup; (2) a surface hazard becoming visible at low altitude such as a ditch, wire, or debris that was not identifiable from higher altitude; (3) another aircraft entering or crossing the intended landing path; (4) wind shift or sudden gust creating an unsafe crosswind or tailwind condition; and (5) an obstruction such as a wire or fence becoming apparent that was not visible during the approach setup. These are hazards beyond the applicant's or evaluator's control.

questions.question: You are on a straight-in autorotation to a grass field at 150 feet AGL and 60 knots when a deer runs onto the centerline of the landing area. You have full engine power available. Walk me through your go-around decision and execution.
questions.answer: At 150 feet AGL with 60 knots and full engine power available, a go-around is absolutely warranted and feasible. Execution: Immediately announce 'go-around' (if with an evaluator). Simultaneously advance the throttle to restore full operating RPM, smoothly raise collective to arrest the descent rate while monitoring rotor RPM to avoid an overpitch condition, apply right pedal proportional to the torque increase, and transition cyclic to a climb attitude. With 60 knots of airspeed the rotor should be at or near operating RPM, providing the energy needed for a clean power recovery. Climb out at best rate of climb airspeed, clear any obstacles, and advise ATC or evaluate alternate landing areas. The key is acting early — hesitation at 150 feet is manageable, but the same hesitation at 30 feet may not be.

questions.question: During a straight-in autorotation checkride, the evaluator announces a go-around at 75 feet AGL because a vehicle has entered the landing zone. As you initiate the go-around, you notice your rotor RPM is at the low end of the green arc. How does this affect your go-around technique?
questions.answer: Low rotor RPM at go-around initiation is a critical complicating factor. With RPM at the low end of the green arc, you have a reduced RPM margin before entering a stall condition. The technique must be modified: apply throttle to restore engine power, but raise collective more slowly and deliberately than you would at normal RPM — an aggressive collective pull at low RPM will further load the rotor and cause rapid RPM decay, potentially entering a rotor stall condition which is unrecoverable. The priority sequence is: restore engine power first, allow RPM to build toward the upper green arc, then gradually increase collective to control descent. Aft cyclic may be used momentarily to increase airflow through the disk and help recover RPM. Do not sacrifice RPM recovery for immediate climb — a controlled descent at recovering RPM is preferable to an uncontrolled descent with stalled blades.

questions.question: How does the type of rotor system on your helicopter — articulated versus semirigid — affect the handling characteristics during a go-around from a low-inertia autorotation?
questions.answer: Rotor system type significantly affects go-around characteristics. Semirigid (teetering) rotor systems allow feathering and flapping but no lead-lag movement. They typically have higher rotor inertia due to the rigid mast connection, meaning rotor RPM is more stable during autorotation but the system has less blade-flapping freedom during gusts or aggressive control input. Articulated rotor systems have separate flapping and lead-lag hinges, allowing individual blade motion and more complex inertia characteristics depending on design. Both system types require smooth collective inputs to avoid overshooting rotor RPM limits in the high direction or decaying into the stall range during power restoration. The specific RPM range limitations are found in the applicable Pilot's Operating Handbook (POH) or Aircraft Flight Manual (AFM) and must be managed precisely during any go-around.

questions.question: An applicant on a checkride is performing a straight-in autorotation and encounters an obstruction at 40 feet AGL. They initiate a go-around, but their technique results in a rotor RPM overspeed into the yellow arc. As the evaluator, how do you evaluate this performance, and what would constitute a disqualifying versus acceptable response to this situation?
questions.answer: This is a nuanced evaluation. A brief excursion into the yellow arc during an aggressive but necessary go-around from a late-recognition obstruction scenario represents a stress-induced control error, but the evaluator must weigh it against the totality of the situation. Disqualifying factors would include: sustained operation in the yellow arc without corrective action, entering the red arc, losing positive aircraft control, or demonstrating no awareness of the RPM exceedance. Acceptable (though imperfect) performance would include: a brief yellow arc exceedance with prompt corrective action (reducing collective slightly to allow RPM to stabilize within green), maintaining directional control throughout, establishing a positive climb, and demonstrating awareness by callout or subsequent verbal explanation of the overspeed. The ACS evaluates whether the applicant maintains positive aircraft control and manages the go-around safely — a momentary RPM exceedance with immediate recognition and correction in a genuinely hazardous situation may reflect appropriate instinctive action rather than deficient skill. The evaluator's own callout of the go-around at 40 feet AGL is also a factor in assessing what was a reasonable pilot response.
questions.follow_up: If the applicant's go-around results in the RPM decaying into the low red arc rather than overspeeding, and ground contact appears imminent, what is the evaluator's obligation at that point?
questions.follow_up_answer: The evaluator has a safety-of-flight obligation that supersedes the evaluation. If the applicant's inputs are leading to an unrecoverable condition — RPM into the low red arc with ground contact imminent and insufficient altitude or speed for recovery — the evaluator must take the controls and announce 'I have the aircraft' to prevent an accident. This is not a graded event; FAA policy requires evaluators to intervene when continued flight under applicant control poses an immediate risk to safety. The evaluation is automatically discontinued and the applicant does not receive a passing grade for that task. However, the evaluator should document exactly what occurred, what inputs the applicant made, and at what point intervention was required, as this affects whether a retest is appropriate and what remedial training should be recommended.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; FAA Order 8900.2; ACS HI.XVIII.F.S2

questions.question: During a straight-in autorotation at night to an unfamiliar landing zone, you identify at 100 feet AGL that the surface lighting you were using was actually vehicle headlights that have now moved, leaving you with no reliable surface reference. You are at 45 knots. Explain your go-around decision-making process using sound ADM principles and what specific hazards accompany this scenario.
questions.answer: This scenario requires immediate go-around decision-making. Using ADM: the 'error chain' began with inadequate pre-approach reconnaissance — using vehicle headlights as a landing reference at night is a risk that should have been identified earlier. At 100 feet AGL and 45 knots with engine power available, a go-around is not only warranted but is the only acceptable choice given loss of reliable surface reference. Execute: power on, smooth collective, right pedal, climb attitude, and transition to instruments if no visual horizon is available. Specific hazards in this scenario include: (1) spatial disorientation — losing the visual reference at low altitude at night can produce immediate vestibular illusions; (2) CFIT — without surface reference the pilot cannot confirm obstacle clearance during the go-around climb; (3) inadvertent IMC transition if the surrounding area is dark; (4) target fixation leading to continued approach despite lost reference. The Trescott principle applies directly here — if the landing will only 'probably' be okay without surface reference, choose the option known to work: the go-around. After climbing to a safe altitude, establish radio contact, request lighting assistance if available, or divert to a lighted landing area.
questions.follow_up: If this pilot had continued the autorotation and landed safely despite losing the surface reference, would that outcome validate the decision to continue?
questions.follow_up_answer: No. Outcome bias is a documented cognitive trap in ADM. A safe outcome does not validate a poor decision. Flying a night autorotation to an unlit, unknown surface without reliable visual reference exposes the crew to CFIT, wire strikes, terrain obstructions, and spatial disorientation — regardless of whether the outcome was fortunate. The FAA Helicopter Flying Handbook explicitly states that approximately 80% of aviation accidents are caused by human factors, and the error chain typically involves multiple poor decisions. A pilot who continues in this scenario and lands safely has not demonstrated sound judgment — they have demonstrated luck. An evaluator observing a decision to continue the approach in these conditions would have grounds for discontinuing the test based on a demonstrated lack of aeronautical decision-making, even in the absence of an actual accident.

tasks.title: Operational Requirements – X. Performance Maneuvers, Task C: Autorotation with Turns in a Single-Engine Helicopter

questions.question: What is the minimum entry altitude for performing an autorotation with turns in a single-engine helicopter?
questions.answer: The minimum entry altitude is above 700 feet AGL. This threshold ensures the pilot has sufficient altitude to complete the maneuver, establish a stable autorotative descent, and execute a safe recovery or landing.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 11; ACS HI.XVIII.G.K1

questions.question: Why does the ACS standard for autorotation with turns specify a higher minimum entry altitude in strong wind conditions compared to calm wind conditions?
questions.answer: Strong winds can significantly affect the helicopter's groundspeed, glide path, and rate of descent during autorotation. Wind gusts can disrupt rotor RPM stability and alter the flight path unpredictably. A higher entry altitude provides additional time and margin for the pilot to maintain rotor RPM control, manage the turning maneuver, and establish a safe landing profile despite the degraded environmental conditions.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 11; ACS HI.XVIII.G.K1

questions.question: Is 700 feet AGL a hard floor or an absolute minimum for autorotation with turns? What does the ACS standard actually say?
questions.answer: The ACS states the minimum entry altitude must be *above* 700 feet AGL — meaning 700 feet AGL itself is not acceptable. The standard requires an altitude greater than 700 feet AGL under normal conditions, and a 'suitable higher entry altitude' when strong winds are present. The word 'above' is intentional and means the pilot must initiate the maneuver at an altitude exceeding 700 feet AGL.

questions.question: You are about to demonstrate an autorotation with turns for a student on a day with sustained winds of 25 knots and gusts to 35 knots. How does this affect your planned entry altitude, and what factors would you consider when selecting a 'suitable higher entry altitude'?
questions.answer: Under strong wind conditions, I would increase the entry altitude above the 700-foot AGL minimum to provide additional margin. Factors to consider include: (1) gust intensity — stronger gusts require more recovery time and altitude; (2) rotor inertia characteristics of the specific helicopter — low-inertia rotors decay faster and demand faster pilot response; (3) the degree of turn planned — larger turns require more altitude; (4) landing zone selection — a suitable area may require maneuvering that consumes additional altitude; and (5) turbulence — gusty conditions can cause rotor RPM fluctuations that require corrective collective inputs, potentially affecting descent rate. A prudent entry altitude might be 1,000 feet AGL or higher depending on these variables.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 11; ACS HI.XVIII.G.K1

questions.question: During an autorotation with turns practice maneuver, your student initiates the turn at exactly 710 feet AGL in calm wind conditions and the rotor RPM decays into the low-warning range during the turn. What does this scenario tell you about the relationship between entry altitude, rotor RPM management, and turn coordination in autorotation?
questions.answer: This scenario illustrates why the minimum altitude standard exists and why the emphasis is on *above* 700 feet AGL. At 710 feet AGL, the available altitude margin is razor-thin. When rotor RPM decays during the turn, the pilot must apply corrective inputs—typically lowering collective or reducing bank—which takes both time and altitude to resolve. The Helicopter Flying Handbook notes that aft cyclic during autorotation entry increases descent rate and inflow velocity, helping to rebuild RPM, but in a turn this input is compromised. Low-inertia rotors decay rapidly, and a complete rotor stall is extremely difficult to recover from at low altitude. The proper response is to shallow the bank or reduce turn rate, allow RPM to recover via lowered collective, and terminate the maneuver safely. This event reinforces that 700 feet AGL is a minimum, not a target, and that recognition of incipient RPM decay in the caution range—and immediate corrective action—is essential to prevent progression to an unrecoverable condition.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 11; ACS HI.XVIII.G.K1

questions.question: You are planning a training flight that includes autorotations with turns. The published traffic pattern altitude at your training area is 800 feet AGL. Can you use the traffic pattern altitude as your entry altitude for this maneuver? Why or why not?
questions.answer: 800 feet AGL exceeds the 700-foot AGL minimum under the ACS standard, so it is technically above the floor. However, 800 feet AGL provides only about 100 feet of margin above the minimum, which may be insufficient depending on helicopter type, pilot experience, degree of turn planned, and wind conditions. Additionally, initiating an autorotation at pattern altitude introduces conflict with other aircraft in the traffic pattern. Best practice is to conduct autorotation-with-turns training well above pattern altitude — typically 1,500 feet AGL or higher — to provide adequate margin, ensure traffic separation, and allow the full maneuver to be completed safely. Compliance with the minimum is a floor, not a target altitude for practical training.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 11; ACS HI.XVIII.G.K1; 14 CFR 91.119

questions.question: The ACS specifies 'a suitable higher entry altitude in strong wind conditions' but does not define a specific number. As an examiner, how would you evaluate whether an applicant selected an appropriate entry altitude on a day with 20-knot crosswinds and intermittent turbulence, and what would cause you to disapprove the maneuver based on altitude selection alone?
questions.answer: I would evaluate the applicant's pre-maneuver decision-making process — specifically whether they verbalized or demonstrated awareness that wind and turbulence require a higher entry altitude than the 700-foot minimum, and whether they selected an altitude that provided adequate margin given those conditions. On a day with 20-knot crosswinds and turbulence, I would expect an applicant to choose at least 1,000–1,200 feet AGL or higher, depending on the helicopter's rotor inertia characteristics and the degree of turn planned. I would disapprove the maneuver on altitude selection alone if: (1) the applicant initiated at or below 700 feet AGL; (2) the applicant initiated at a marginal altitude (e.g., 720 feet) with no acknowledgment of the wind/turbulence factor; or (3) the applicant could not articulate why a higher altitude was appropriate for the conditions. The inability to adjust a standard to real-world conditions reflects a failure of aeronautical decision-making, not just a knowledge deficiency.
questions.follow_up: If the applicant selected 1,500 feet AGL but the helicopter's rotor RPM decayed significantly during the turn and they failed to take corrective action, would the altitude selection still be considered adequate?
questions.follow_up_answer: No. Adequate altitude selection is a necessary but not sufficient condition for a satisfactory autorotation with turns. Even if the entry altitude was appropriate for conditions, failure to maintain rotor RPM within the normal operating range during the turn represents a separate skills deficiency. The Helicopter Flying Handbook is explicit that rotor stall is not recoverable, and early recognition of low RPM is imperative. An applicant who selects a safe altitude but then allows RPM to decay without correction has failed the skills component of the task regardless of their knowledge of the altitude standard.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 11; ACS HI.XVIII.G.K1

questions.question: How does the rotor system type — articulated versus semirigid versus rigid — affect your determination of a 'suitable higher entry altitude' for autorotation with turns in strong wind conditions, and which system type demands the greatest altitude margin?
questions.answer: Rotor system type directly influences rotor inertia, which determines how quickly RPM decays when lift/drag is disrupted. Articulated rotors allow blade pitch change, flapping, and lead/lag movement; the Coriolis effect on lead/lag in turbulent conditions can cause rotor RPM variations that require corrective inputs. Semirigid rotors allow feathering and flapping but not lead/lag, meaning less mechanical damping of RPM fluctuations from turbulence. Rigid rotors allow only feathering and have the least blade movement to absorb disturbances, but they typically have higher structural loads in turbulence. However, the most critical factor for altitude margin is rotor inertia — a helicopter with a low-inertia rotor system (common in lightweight turbine and piston machines, regardless of system type) will experience faster RPM decay in turbulence and during turns, requiring greater altitude margin to allow time for corrective action. The pilot must know their specific aircraft's rotor inertia characteristics, RPM decay rate, and manufacturer guidance on autorotation entries in turbulence. There is no single universal answer — the determination is aircraft-specific, and the FAA expects applicants to apply that knowledge to their actual training helicopter.
questions.follow_up: If a helicopter's Rotorcraft Flight Manual does not specify a minimum autorotation entry altitude for training maneuvers, what sources would you use to establish an appropriate altitude for this maneuver?
questions.follow_up_answer: In the absence of RFM-specific guidance, the pilot should use: (1) the ACS standard of above 700 feet AGL as the regulatory floor; (2) the FAA Helicopter Flying Handbook Chapter 11 guidance on autorotation procedures and rotor RPM management; (3) manufacturer training supplements or type-specific operating procedures if available; (4) the advice of a qualified CFI-H familiar with the specific aircraft's performance characteristics; and (5) conservative personal minimums that account for wind, turbulence, terrain, and the pilot's own proficiency. The absence of RFM guidance does not eliminate the pilot's responsibility to exercise good aeronautical decision-making — it increases it.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 11 (Glossary: Articulated, Semirigid, Rigid rotors; Coriolis Effect); ACS HI.XVIII.G.K1

questions.question: During an autorotation with turns checkride task, what is the minimum turning requirement you must demonstrate — in terms of number of turns and direction?
questions.answer: You must perform at least two 90-degree turns in the same direction, or one continuous 180-degree turn. Both options satisfy the ACS standard. The key constraint is that partial turns in opposite directions do not meet the requirement — the turns must be coordinated in the same direction if done as two separate 90-degree turns.

questions.question: If you choose to satisfy the autorotation-with-turns requirement using two 90-degree turns, can you make the first turn to the left and the second turn to the right?
questions.answer: No. The ACS standard specifically requires that both 90-degree turns be performed in the same direction. Two turns in opposite directions — for example, 90 degrees left followed by 90 degrees right — do not satisfy the standard. You must turn 90 degrees left then 90 degrees left again, or 90 degrees right then 90 degrees right again.

questions.question: What total heading change is achieved whether you perform two 90-degree turns in the same direction or one continuous 180-degree turn during an autorotation with turns?
questions.answer: Both options result in a total heading change of 180 degrees. Two 90-degree turns in the same direction equal 180 degrees combined, and a single continuous 180-degree turn is exactly 180 degrees. The ACS provides two mechanically equivalent options for completing the same total heading change.

questions.question: You are established in autorotation at best glide airspeed and your examiner asks you to perform the autorotation with turns using the two 90-degree turn option. How does initiating each bank affect your rotor RPM and what must you monitor closely between turns?
questions.answer: When you bank the helicopter, the horizontal component of lift increases drag on the rotor system and the vertical component of lift decreases, requiring a slight collective adjustment or accepting a minor RPM change. During the turn, rotor RPM may decay slightly if collective is held too high or flare is insufficient. Between the two 90-degree turns, you must monitor rotor RPM closely — if it has decayed outside limits, you may need to briefly unload or adjust collective before initiating the second turn. Airspeed management is equally important; turns increase the load factor and effective sink rate, so the pilot must ensure adequate airspeed and RPM are available before rolling into the second 90-degree segment.

questions.question: A student asks whether it matters which option they choose — two 90-degree turns or one continuous 180-degree turn — when demonstrating autorotation with turns. As their instructor, how would you explain the practical difference between the two options in terms of altitude and timing management?
questions.answer: Both options satisfy the ACS standard, but they have distinct practical trade-offs. Two 90-degree turns with a brief straight segment between them give the pilot a natural pause to re-assess altitude, airspeed, and rotor RPM before committing to the second turn — this can be advantageous for students still building scan habits. A continuous 180-degree turn demands uninterrupted bank control and rotor RPM management through the entire arc, with no recovery pause; it requires a more disciplined and fluid control technique. The continuous 180-degree turn is typically more efficient in terms of glide path and altitude management because it avoids any transition between turns. The student should choose based on proficiency and remaining altitude at turn initiation.

questions.question: During an autorotation with turns, after completing the required 180 degrees of turn, you find yourself not aligned with your intended landing area. You are still at sufficient altitude. Can you make additional turns to realign, and how does this interact with the ACS turning requirement?
questions.answer: Yes, you may make additional corrections after satisfying the minimum turning requirement. The ACS standard establishes a floor — at least two 90-degree turns in the same direction or one continuous 180-degree turn — but does not prohibit additional corrective turns if altitude and rotor energy permit. Practical autorotation technique demands landing area alignment as a priority, so a pilot demonstrating good judgment who makes a small corrective turn after the required 180 degrees is showing sound aeronautical decision-making, not violating the standard. The examiner is evaluating overall control, RPM management, and landing area judgment throughout the maneuver.

questions.question: During the checkride, a candidate completes two 90-degree turns in the same direction during autorotation, but the examiner observes that the candidate rolled out of the first 90-degree turn, momentarily transitioned to a slight opposite bank before correcting, and then completed the second 90-degree turn in the original direction. Has the ACS turning requirement been met, and what is your evaluation rationale?
questions.answer: This is a judgment call, but technically the requirement has not been cleanly met. The ACS requires two 90-degree turns in the same direction — the intent is a disciplined, intentional 90-degree turn, pause or transition, and a second intentional 90-degree turn in the same direction. A momentary bank reversal between the two turns introduces an interruption of directional intent and may indicate insufficient rotor RPM awareness, spatial disorientation tendency, or poor bank control. As an examiner, I would evaluate whether the reversal was minor and corrective in nature versus a significant deviation. If the reversal exceeded a few degrees and lasted more than momentarily, I would likely note it as a discrepancy in turning execution and assess whether it reflects a pattern of poor control rather than an isolated blip. The spirit of the standard is continuous, intentional directional control through the turn sequence.
questions.follow_up: If the candidate's first 90-degree turn was actually only 75 degrees before they rolled out, would you require them to redo the maneuver, or could they compensate by making the second turn 105 degrees?
questions.follow_up_answer: The ACS standard specifies at least two 90-degree turns — meaning each turn should achieve approximately 90 degrees of heading change. A 75-degree turn does not satisfy the individual turn requirement even if the total cumulative heading change reaches 180 degrees, because the standard defines the minimum per-turn criteria, not just a total aggregate. However, as an examiner, I would consider whether the shortfall was significant and whether it reflects a skill deficiency or a minor judgment error. A 75-degree turn is close enough that I might allow the candidate to demonstrate the correct technique again before making a final determination, depending on the overall quality of the maneuver. Compensating with a 105-degree second turn would achieve 180 degrees total but does not retroactively satisfy the first turn's requirement of 90 degrees.

questions.question: A candidate is flying a low-inertia rotor helicopter and initiates autorotation with turns. Halfway through a continuous 180-degree turn, rotor RPM approaches the lower limit of the green arc. What should the pilot do, and how does this scenario highlight a unique risk of the continuous 180-degree turn option compared to the two 90-degree turn option?
questions.answer: The pilot should immediately respond to low rotor RPM by reducing collective if any residual collective pitch remains, shallowing the bank angle to reduce disk loading and induced drag on the rotor system, and slightly increasing forward cyclic to convert potential glide energy into rotor RPM. The priority is rotor RPM recovery — turn completion is secondary to maintaining the rotor within limits. This scenario illustrates a key risk of the continuous 180-degree turn: once committed, the pilot has no natural break point to assess rotor energy. Low-inertia rotors, as noted in the FAA Helicopter Flying Handbook, decay rapidly with increased load or reduced energy input. The two 90-degree turn option provides a brief straight segment between turns where the pilot can assess RPM, airspeed, and altitude before committing to the second turn — giving a natural decision point to abort or delay the second turn if rotor energy is marginal. Instructors should emphasize that the continuous 180-degree turn demands proactive RPM monitoring throughout the entire arc, not reactive correction.
questions.follow_up: If rotor RPM reaches the red line lower limit during the turn and the pilot cannot recover it within the turn, is it acceptable to abandon the turning maneuver entirely and transition to a straight-ahead autorotation?
questions.follow_up_answer: Absolutely — rotor RPM control is the highest priority in any autorotation. The FAA Helicopter Flying Handbook explicitly states that rotor stalls in helicopters are not recoverable, making early recognition and response to low RPM imperative. Abandoning the turning maneuver to preserve rotor RPM is the correct aeronautical decision and demonstrates sound risk management. No ACS maneuver completion requirement overrides the fundamental imperative to keep the rotor within operating limits. On a checkride, a candidate who correctly prioritizes rotor RPM over maneuver completion is demonstrating superior judgment. The examiner would evaluate whether the candidate communicated the decision, transitioned smoothly, and managed the subsequent straight autorotation correctly.

questions.question: When we talk about a 180-degree turn in an autorotation, what exactly does '180 degrees' refer to — your heading on the compass or something else?
questions.answer: The 180-degree turn in autorotation refers to a 180-degree change in ground track, not an exact reciprocal compass heading. Your goal is to reverse the direction you are traveling over the ground, which may require more or less than a precise 180-degree heading change depending on wind conditions.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 11; ACS HI.XVIII.G.K3

questions.question: Define 'ground track' as it applies to the 180-degree autorotation turn.
questions.answer: Ground track is the actual path the helicopter travels over the surface of the earth, as opposed to the direction the nose is pointed. In a 180-degree autorotation turn, the pilot reverses this over-ground path so that the helicopter is now traveling in the opposite direction from where it started, regardless of the compass heading required to achieve that result.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 11; ACS HI.XVIII.G.K3

questions.question: Why does the distinction between heading and ground track matter specifically during an autorotation turn?
questions.answer: During an autorotation the helicopter is descending unpowered, so the pilot must select a suitable landing area and arrive there with controlled airspeed and rotor RPM. Wind causes the helicopter's ground track to differ from its heading. If the pilot focuses only on rolling out at a reciprocal compass heading rather than reversing the actual over-ground path, wind drift can carry the helicopter away from the intended landing point, reducing accuracy and safety.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 11; ACS HI.XVIII.G.K3

questions.question: You are flying a 090-degree heading into a 15-knot direct crosswind from the north when your engine fails. To execute a 180-degree autorotation turn back toward your departure point, do you roll out on 270 degrees? Explain your reasoning.
questions.answer: Not necessarily. Because you had a crosswind from the north pushing you southward, your ground track before the failure was not exactly 090 degrees — it was somewhere south of 090. To reverse that ground track and travel back toward your departure point, you will need to roll out on a heading slightly north of 270 degrees to compensate for the continued northerly crosswind during the descent. The exact rollout heading depends on wind correction angle, but the objective is to reverse the ground track, not achieve a precise reciprocal heading of 270 degrees.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 11; ACS HI.XVIII.G.K3

questions.question: During an autorotation turn practice, your student consistently rolls out on a precise reciprocal heading every time, regardless of wind conditions, and misses the intended landing area. What fundamental misunderstanding are they demonstrating, and how would you correct it?
questions.answer: The student is confusing heading with ground track. They are applying a fixed 180-degree heading change when they should be focused on reversing their over-ground path of travel. To correct this, I would explain that the 180-degree turn refers to a 180-degree change in ground track, then have them verbalize their actual ground track direction before the simulated failure and identify what ground track reversal looks like visually over the ground. I would also introduce wind awareness exercises so they learn to apply wind correction during the turn and roll out on whatever heading is needed to track back over their original ground path.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 11; ACS HI.XVIII.G.K3

questions.question: You are departing runway 18 (southbound) with a 20-knot direct tailwind. You suffer an engine failure shortly after takeoff. If you execute a 180-degree autorotation turn using ground track as your reference, roughly what heading will you roll out on, and why?
questions.answer: With a 20-knot tailwind pushing you southbound, your ground track is southbound. To reverse that southbound ground track and track back northward toward the departure runway, you will roll out on approximately 360 degrees (north). The key distinction is that you are navigating by ground track (your actual path over the ground), not by magnetic heading alone. During the turn, wind continues to drift your position, so you observe your ground track and adjust your rollout heading as necessary to ensure you are tracking back toward your departure point. This is why a simple 180-degree turn from your outbound magnetic heading may not be sufficient—you must reference your actual movement over the ground.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 11; ACS HI.XVIII.G.K3

questions.question: In strong crosswind conditions during a 180-degree autorotation turn, a pilot who focuses only on reversing the compass heading may actually end up with a ground track that does not return them to their departure point at all. Walk me through exactly how this error develops geometrically during the turn.
questions.answer: Here is how the error develops: Before the engine failure, the pilot is, for example, tracking eastbound over the ground but the wind from the north requires a heading slightly north of east to maintain that ground track. At engine failure the ground track is east. If the pilot simply plans to roll out on a heading exactly 180 degrees opposite — slightly north of west — they are thinking about heading rather than ground track. During the actual 180-degree turn, the crosswind continuously drifts the helicopter southward throughout the arc of the turn. By the time the pilot rolls out on that reciprocal heading, the helicopter's accumulated drift through the turn has pushed its ground track significantly south of west. The pilot is now heading in a compass direction that is reciprocal to their pre-failure heading, but their actual over-ground position and travel direction are skewed well south of the intended return path. The correct approach is to visualize the ground track reversal and roll out on whatever heading — which will be north of the reciprocal — keeps the ground track aligned back toward the departure point, accounting for both the drift during the turn and the continued crosswind correction needed during the straight glide.
questions.follow_up: If altitude is critically low and there is no time to complete a full 180-degree ground track reversal, what is the correct decision-making priority?
questions.follow_up_answer: When altitude is insufficient for a safe 180-degree turn, the priority shifts immediately to selecting the best available forced landing area within the survivable glide range straight ahead or with only a slight turn. Attempting to force the 180-degree turn at critically low altitude risks exceeding the safe bank angle limit for that rotor system and altitude combination, which can lead to blade stall, loss of RPM, or terrain impact during the turn. The 180-degree autorotation turn is only appropriate when sufficient altitude exists — typically a minimum of 500 feet AGL in most training environments, though actual minimums depend on helicopter performance, rotor inertia, and airspeed at the time of failure. Below that threshold, land ahead.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 11; ACS HI.XVIII.G.K3

questions.question: A candidate tells you that because wind causes the helicopter to drift during the 180-degree autorotation turn, the pilot should simply add or subtract the wind correction angle from the reciprocal heading to get the correct rollout heading. Is this reasoning correct? What nuance are they missing?
questions.answer: The reasoning is partially correct as a rough approximation but is missing an important nuance. Applying a static wind correction angle to the reciprocal heading would work if the turn were instantaneous, but the turn takes time — typically 10 to 20 seconds depending on bank angle and rotor system. Throughout the arc of the turn the wind is continuously displacing the helicopter laterally. The amount of displacement depends on wind speed, the radius of the turn, the bank angle used, and the airspeed. A faster, steeper turn results in less accumulated drift than a slow, shallow one. Additionally, the wind correction angle needed during the subsequent straight glide may differ from the correction angle that perfectly reverses the ground track at rollout, because the helicopter's position relative to the landing point has shifted during the turn. The correct mental model is not a fixed formula but a continuous visual reference to the intended ground track reversal — pilots should reference a ground point that represents where they came from and maneuver to track back to it, adjusting rollout heading empirically based on observed drift rather than applying a predetermined formula.
questions.follow_up: How does rotor system type — specifically high-inertia versus low-inertia rotors — affect the pilot's bank angle choice during the 180-degree autorotation turn, and how does that bank angle choice then affect the ground track drift problem you just described?
questions.follow_up_answer: Low-inertia rotor systems, such as those found on many light turbine helicopters, bleed RPM much more rapidly during the entry phase of an autorotation. To conserve RPM, the pilot of a low-inertia helicopter must avoid excessive bank angles during the 180-degree turn, because high bank angles increase the load factor, which increases induced drag on the rotor disk and accelerates RPM decay. This means the low-inertia pilot is typically restricted to shallower bank angles — perhaps 30 degrees or less — to maintain adequate rotor RPM. A shallower bank produces a larger radius turn, which takes longer to complete, which means the helicopter is exposed to the crosswind displacement for a longer time, resulting in more accumulated drift. This makes precise ground track reversal harder to achieve in a low-inertia helicopter in crosswind conditions. High-inertia systems tolerate steeper banks better, allowing a tighter, faster turn with less accumulated drift. The pilot must therefore understand both rotor system characteristics and the wind when planning and executing the 180-degree autorotation turn.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 11; ACS HI.XVIII.G.K3

questions.question: What must the evaluator direct an applicant to do if the applicant fails to roll out of an autorotation turn by 300 feet AGL, and what is the consequence for the task?
questions.answer: The evaluator must direct the applicant to execute a power recovery (restore engine power to arrest the descent), which transitions into a go-around maneuver. These are sequential actions in the recovery sequence. The task is marked unsatisfactory because the applicant failed to complete the autorotation turn within the required altitude parameter (rolling out no lower than 300 feet AGL).

questions.question: A student asks why 300 feet AGL is the rollout standard for autorotation turns rather than a lower altitude like 100 feet. How would you explain the aerodynamic and safety reasoning behind that specific altitude threshold?
questions.answer: At 300 feet AGL, a pilot still has enough altitude to transition from a banked attitude to wings-level, establish a proper descent profile, and complete either a normal touchdown or a power recovery go-around safely. Below 300 feet AGL in a bank, the helicopter's effective glide path is disrupted by the turn, rotor RPM management becomes more critical, and there is insufficient altitude to recover from any developing low-RPM or improper flare condition. The 300-foot threshold provides a safety buffer to prevent a banked autorotation from deteriorating into an unrecoverable situation close to the ground.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA Instrument Rating ACS, HI.XVIII.G.K4; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11

questions.question: During a checkride, an applicant rolls out of a 180-degree autorotation turn at exactly 300 feet AGL but then immediately notices their rotor RPM is near the low end of the green arc. As the evaluator, how do you assess this situation in relation to the 300-foot rollout standard?
questions.answer: The applicant has technically satisfied the rollout requirement by completing the turn at exactly 300 feet AGL, so the task is not automatically unsatisfactory on the rollout criterion alone. However, the low rotor RPM condition is a separate and serious concern. The evaluator must assess whether the RPM is within limits and whether the applicant correctly identifies and manages it. If the RPM drops below the green arc and the applicant does not correct it, that constitutes a separate safety-of-flight issue that could result in a task failure on different grounds. The 300-foot rule addresses rollout timing; RPM management is evaluated independently.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA Instrument Rating ACS, HI.XVIII.G.K4; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11

questions.question: An applicant performing an autorotation with a 90-degree turn enters the turn too late and realizes at 400 feet AGL that they will not complete the rollout before reaching 300 feet AGL. What is the correct action the applicant should take at that point, and what is the outcome?
questions.answer: The applicant should proactively initiate a power recovery and go-around before reaching 300 feet AGL. This demonstrates sound aeronautical decision-making by declining to press into an increasingly unsafe situation. However, the task remains unsatisfactory/failed because the applicant did not complete the autorotation turn to landing within the ACS altitude standard, regardless of when the recovery was initiated. Early self-recovery shows better judgment than waiting for evaluator intervention, but it does not retroactively satisfy the task standard.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA Instrument Rating ACS, HI.XVIII.G.K4; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11

questions.question: The ACS states that failure to roll out by 300 feet AGL makes the task unsatisfactory. Can an evaluator use discretion to pass an applicant who rolls out at 280 feet AGL if the overall autorotation was otherwise flawless, and how does the concept of evaluator authority interact with an explicit ACS standard?
questions.answer: No. The 300-foot AGL rollout requirement is an explicit, non-discretionary standard written into the ACS. When a standard uses mandatory language — 'the evaluator must direct' and 'the task is considered unsatisfactory' — the evaluator has no discretion to waive it based on overall performance quality. The ACS defines the minimum acceptable performance, and an evaluator who passes an applicant who failed a mandatory standard is not applying the ACS correctly and could face FAA oversight concerns. The evaluator's role is to apply the standard as written, not to substitute personal judgment for a codified requirement.
questions.follow_up: If the applicant disagrees with the unsatisfactory finding and believes 280 feet AGL is close enough to 300 feet to be within instrument error or practical test tolerances, what recourse do they have?
questions.follow_up_answer: The applicant's only formal recourse is to file an appeal or complaint through FAA channels — for example, contacting the FSDO or filing a complaint against the examiner if they believe the evaluation was conducted improperly. However, the 300-foot AGL standard has no stated tolerance band in the ACS; it is an absolute threshold, not a range like altitude or airspeed tolerances. The argument that 280 feet is 'close enough' is not supported by the ACS language. The applicant's best path forward is to schedule a retest and demonstrate proper rollout timing on the next attempt.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA Instrument Rating ACS, HI.XVIII.G.K4; FAA Order 8900.2 (General Aviation Airman Designee Policy)

questions.question: During an autorotation with turns, the evaluator fails to direct a power recovery when the applicant is clearly not going to roll out by 300 feet AGL, and the helicopter continues into a banked autorotation touchdown that results in a hard landing. Who bears responsibility under the FAA's legal and operational framework, and what does this scenario illustrate about the evaluator's duties?
questions.answer: The evaluator bears significant responsibility in this scenario. The ACS explicitly states the evaluator 'must' direct a power recovery — this is not optional guidance but a mandatory safety intervention duty. By failing to act, the evaluator did not fulfill their designated examiner obligations and may have contributed to an unsafe outcome. The applicant, as pilot-in-command, retains legal responsibility for the safe operation of the aircraft under 14 CFR 91.3, but an evaluator's failure to intervene as required by the ACS may expose them to FAA enforcement action, suspension or revocation of their designee authority, and potential civil liability. This scenario illustrates that evaluators are not passive observers — they have active, codified safety duties that are legally and operationally binding.
questions.follow_up: After a banked autorotation hard landing caused partly by evaluator inaction, the applicant files an incident report with NASA's Aviation Safety Reporting System (ASRS). What protections does that report provide the applicant, and are there any limitations?
questions.follow_up_answer: Filing an ASRS report within 10 days of the incident provides the applicant with immunity from FAA certificate action for violations that are inadvertent and not deliberate or criminal in nature. However, the ASRS waiver does not protect against: (1) accidents involving criminal activity, (2) violations that are not disclosed in the report, or (3) situations where the FAA has already begun enforcement action before the report is filed. The ASRS report also does not prevent the FAA from using the information to identify system safety issues, though identifying information is stripped before the report is shared. The protection is specifically for FAA certificate action, not for civil liability or other legal proceedings.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.3; FAA Instrument Rating ACS, HI.XVIII.G.K4; FAA Order 8900.2; NASA ASRS Advisory Circular AC 00-46F

questions.question: Why must the minimum entry altitude for autorotation with turns be raised above 700 feet AGL in strong wind conditions (typically 15+ knots)?
questions.answer: Strong winds introduce additional variables that complicate autorotation execution, including increased groundspeed on downwind legs, turbulence that disrupts rotor RPM stability, and wind gradient effects near the surface that affect the flare and touchdown. These factors reduce the margin for error. As a practical guide, when wind speed exceeds 15 knots, increase the minimum entry altitude to 800–900 feet AGL or higher to maintain adequate time to assess and correct developing problems during the maneuver. The exact increment depends on wind magnitude and local training standards.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 11; ACS HI.XVIII.G.R1

questions.question: How does performing a turn during autorotation affect the helicopter's rate of altitude loss compared to a straight autorotation?
questions.answer: Turns during autorotation increase the rate of altitude loss. Applying cyclic to bank the helicopter shifts lift inward to generate centripetal force, reducing the vertical component of lift. To maintain rotor RPM through the turn, the pilot may need to adjust collective, and the overall descent rate increases. The steeper the bank angle, the greater the altitude loss per unit of time, which is precisely why a higher entry altitude is required.

questions.question: You are set up to practice autorotation with turns over a training area. The altimeter reads 1,400 feet MSL and the field elevation is 750 feet MSL. A 25-knot wind is reported at the surface. Is this altitude acceptable for the maneuver, and what factors should drive your decision?
questions.answer: Your AGL altitude is only 650 feet (1,400 MSL minus 750 feet field elevation), which is below the 700-foot AGL minimum required for autorotation with turns. The maneuver should not be initiated from this altitude. Additionally, the 25-knot surface wind is a strong wind condition that increases complexity and requires raising the minimum entry altitude above the standard 700 feet. Depending on aircraft performance and local training standards, climb to at least 1,000–1,200 feet AGL before entry. Consult your training program or flight manual for the specific altitude requirement in windy conditions.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 11; ACS HI.XVIII.G.R1
